articles.title: Artémis : la NASA retire sa qualification d'office au Starship et annonce 2028 pour le retour sur la Lune
articles.text:
Artémis : la NASA retire sa qualification d'office au Starship et annonce 2028 pour le retour sur la Lune
Encore un coup de tonnerre dans le programme Artemis : la Nasa annonce que le Starship n'est plus automatiquement sélectionné pour le retour sur la Lune. Les échéances approchent : à l'été 2027, la mission Artemis III devra réussir de complexes rendez-vous orbitaux avec des systèmes jamais testés avant, puis en 2028, ce devrait être le retour attendu sur le sol de notre satellite.
Nouveau coup de théâtre majeur pour programme Artemis de la Nasa. Lors de sa conférence du 23 octobre, toute l'architecture d'Artemis III a été révélée, mais surtout, l'agence spatiale a annoncé que le Starship HLS n'était plus certain de poser les astronautes américains sur la Lune lors du quatrième volet du programme.
Jared Isaacman, l'administrateur en chef de la Nasa, a réaffirmé l'année 2028 comme objectif pour le retour sur notre satellite.
	
Nous mettons en œuvre la politique spatiale nationale du président Trump, qui vise à concrétiser le retour tant attendu des astronautes américains à la surface de la Lune en 2028 et à établir une base lunaire.
3 fusées géantes pour Artemis III et une complexité folle
La Nasa a détaillé le fonctionnement opératoire d'Artemis III, qui, rappelons-le, n'est plus une mission d'alunissage, mais une grande répétition visant à tester l'interopérabilité des différents systèmes. Le moins qu'on puisse dire, c'est que cette mission s'annonce épique et complexe avec beaucoup de nouveaux matériels sur les pas de tir :
- La New Glenn, actuellement au chômage technique suite à la destruction de son pas de tir, devra décoller en premier avec l'atterrisseur lunaire de Blue Origin, le Blue Moon Lander Mk2. Ce dernier restera en orbite environ deux semaines.
- Décollage du SLS avec l'équipage à son bord. Après un rendez-vous orbital et un dockage réussi avec le Blue Moon Lander, les astronautes pourront se transférer en orbite de la capsule Orion vers le Blue Moon Lander pour effectuer des essais opérationnels.
- Le Starship décollera en troisième et devra lui réussir le rendez-vous orbital entre Orion et Starship HLS et le dockage entre les deux. L'équipage ne devrait pas pénétrer dans le Starship HLS.
D'après Jeremy Parson, le directeur du programme, la mission Artemis III durera de 14 à 17 jours et devrait se dérouler à l'été 2027.
	
Tout ce que nous faisons sur Artemis III est conçu pour réduire le risque pour nos futures missions d'atterrissage lunaire.
Artemis IV en 2028 mais avec quel atterrisseur lunaire ?
C'est la grande surprise de cette conférence : alors que le Starship avait été désigné pour le premier retour habité sur le sol lunaire, la Nasa remet SpaceX et Blue Origin en concurrence. Les astronautes pourraient finalement alunir à bord du Blue Moon Lander, ou bien du Starship HLS, en fonction de celui des deux qui aura donné le plus d'assurance et de satisfaction. Voire, tout simplement, en fonction de celui qui sera au point. Car, à l'heure actuelle, le Starship n'est ni habitable, ni capable d'aller se poser sur la Lune, idem du vaisseau lunaire de Blue Origin.
Ci-dessous les deux plans de vol possibles pour Artemis IV, le premier avec le Blue Moon Lander, le second avec le Starship HLS.
Voici un petit état des lieux :
- Le Starship doit démontrer sa capacité à être ravitaillé en orbite. Cela n'a jamais été fait. Le nombre de ravitaillements nécessaires est également un sujet de débat, entre 6 et 8 selon Elon Musk, jusqu'à 22 selon des experts. La Nasa table sur une démonstration du transfert d'ergols au premier trimestre 2027.
- La New Glenn actuelle n'est pas assez puissante pour aller sur la Lune. Blue Origin prépare donc un modèle avec non pas 7 moteurs, mais 9 pour le premier étage et un passage de 2 à 4 pour le second étage. La coiffe doit également passer de 7 mètres de diamètre à 9. Premier vol annoncé pour la fin 2027.
Mis en concurrence donc. Et Jared Isaacman se voit en train de bâtir une équipe “digne d'un Super Bowl” pour gagner la course face à la Chine :
“Nous disposons de bases solides avec le SLS et Orion, auxquelles s’ajoutent deux atterrisseurs lunaires en cours de développement, en partenariat avec Blue Origin et SpaceX. Mais la NASA n’a nullement l’intention de rester les bras croisés pendant que tous ces éléments se mettent en place. Ce n’est pas ainsi qu’Apollo a réussi, et ce n’est pas ainsi que l’on parvient à accomplir ce qui semble presque impossible. La NASA est mobilisée : nos capacités fondamentales sont en cours de reconstruction, nos ateliers tournent 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7, et nos experts sont sur le terrain, concentrés sur les étapes critiques. Nous constituons une équipe de haut vol — digne d’un « Super Bowl » — pour atteindre ces objectifs en toute sécurité, ainsi que tout ce qui suivra”.

articles.title: MSI Launches MPG COREFROZR AP15 CPU Cooler with Integrated Dispay
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
MSI Launches MPG COREFROZR AP15 CPU Cooler with Integrated Dispay
MSI has launched the MPG COREFROZR AP15, its first air cooler with an integrated display built into the top cover. The cooler uses a dual-tower design with asymmetric tower widths, six 6 mm copper heat pipes, and a copper base. The DIGI-DISPLAY top cover module connects via magnetic POGO-PIN contacts and MSI's EZ Conn single-cable connection, showing real-time CPU, GPU, and memory temperatures, loads, and frequencies without additional software. In terms of dimensions, MSI says that the heatsink measures 168 x 126.5 x 128 mm and has 102 fins. The two included 120 mm ARGB fans operate at different speeds. The front fan runs at 2000 RPM with 66.41 CFM and 1.98 mmH2O static pressure at 31.1 dB(A), while the mid fan is quieter at 1600 RPM, 54.14 CFM, 1.30 mmH2O, and 25.06 dB(A). Both are PWM controlled. 
MSI MPG COREFROZR AP15 cooler is compatible with Intel LGA1700 and LGA1851, and AMD AM4 and AM5 platforms. According to MSI, the cooler was designed with AMD Ryzen X3D processors in mind, so even without any official information regarding its thermal capabilities, it should handle pretty much all CPUs well. In China, it's priced at 549 yuan, around $82, however international pricing and availability have not been confirmed yet.Specifications:
- Number of Fans: 2
- Fan Dimensions: 120 x 120 x 25 mm / 4.7 x 4.7 x 0.98 inches
- Fan Speed: 2000 RPM ± 200 RPM (Front) / 1600 RPM ± 160 RPM (Mid)
- Fan Air Flow: 66.41 CFM (Front) / 54.14 CFM (Mid)
- Fan Noise Level: 31.1 dBA (Front) / 25.06 dBA (Mid)
- Fan Static Pressure: 1.98 mmH2O (Front) / 1.30 mmH2O (Mid)
- Fan Bearing: FDB
- Fan Life Expectancy: 30,000 hrs@40° C
- Fan Rated Current: 0.2 ± 0.05 A (Front) / 0.11 ± 0.05 A (Mid)
- Fan Power Consumption: 2.4 ± 0.5 W (Front) / 1.3 ± 0.5 W (Mid)
- PWM Mode: Yes
- Cable Length (5 V ARGB / PWM cable): 650 mm

- ARGB Connector: 5 V ARGB 3-PIN Header

articles.title: Las empresas europeas concentran el 23% de la inversión tecnológica directa y generan 120.000 empleos en Colombia
articles.text:
François Roudié, embajador de la Unión Europea en Colombia, dio una entrevista exclusiva a Infobae sobre todo el panorama de trabajo conjunto en tecnología con el sector público y privado. “Hemos identificado un potencial de dos mil millones de euros en proyectos muy interesantes en ciberseguridad, conexión digital e inteligencia artificial”, afirmó.
Roudié explicó que la Unión Europea busca combinar estudios de factibilidad, asistencia técnica y financiación para impulsar proyectos en Colombia y promover la participación de empresas europeas.
La estrategia europea para promover inversiones en Colombia
Roudié dejó claro que la Unión Europea no transmite instrucciones a las empresas ni realiza negocios por cuenta propia. “Las empresas hacen sus estrategias y la tarea de la Unión Europea consiste en presentar a Colombia como un país con oportunidades vinculadas con su población y sus necesidades de infraestructura”.
También, describió el marco que, según dijo, busca ofrecer previsibilidad y seguridad jurídica a las compañías. Incluye el acuerdo de libre comercio, la aproximación regulatoria y condiciones comerciales como aranceles bajos o nulos.
El embajador indicó que la estrategia Global Gateway utiliza fondos de cooperación para financiar estudios de factibilidad y asistencia técnica. Esos recursos permiten reunir al Banco Europeo de Inversiones, la CAF, el BID y otras entidades financieras para estructurar paquetes de financiación.
Como ejemplo, planteó el caso hipotético de una gobernación o una municipalidad que quisiera construir un ferrocarril. La Unión Europea podría respaldar los estudios y convocar financiación con préstamos a tasas bajas.
Luego, se realizaría una licitación. “Lo que nos gusta, lo que queremos, es ayudar o fomentar que empresas europeas se junten en consorcio y hagan una oferta. Ojalá la ganen”, afirmó.
Roudié citó el caso de la primera línea del metro de Bogotá. El consorcio ganador tenía “un 70% de empresas chinas, pero un 30% de participación europea”, según indicó.
Global Gateway y el potencial de inversión en el sector digital
Un estudio del Banco Europeo de Inversiones y la CAF identificó un potencial de dos mil millones de inversión en iniciativas digitales. Esos recursos contemplan áreas como ciberseguridad, conectividad digital rural y el uso de inteligencia artificial en seguridad.
El embajador afirmo que el análisis fue presentado a autoridades nacionales y locales. A partir de allí, deberán definir qué iniciativas desean impulsar y qué actores podrían participar en cada proyecto.
“Hay cosas que corresponden a necesidades del país, corresponden a buenas oportunidades de negocios y los expertos que trabajaron en este informe consideran que es maduro para empezar a estructurar quizás un proyecto”, afirmó.
Roudié aseguró que las empresas europeas cuentan con capacidades en los ámbitos contemplados por esa cartera potencial.
Cooperación, inversión y sostenibilidad de los proyectos
Roudié dijo que el término “cooperación” suele asociarse con donaciones estatales para acciones puntuales, y aclaró que la estrategia europea en Colombia busca fomentar inversiones.
Los fondos de cooperación se destinan a estudios de factibilidad y asistencia técnica. El objetivo es que bancos, empresas y autoridades cuenten con condiciones para financiar y ejecutar proyectos.
Esos estudios pueden reducir el riesgo de una iniciativa y permitir préstamos con tasas de interés bajas por parte de bancos multilaterales.
Roudié vinculó la participación privada con la generación de empleo y el desarrollo de cadenas de suministro. Añadió que los proyectos deben ser sostenibles desde el punto de vista ambiental, social y económico. “Si no es rentable, no dura”, señaló.
El trabajo con las autoridades colombianas y los cambios de Gobierno
La continuidad de los proyectos depende de las decisiones de cada administración. “Depende del gobierno”, respondió al ser consultado sobre los efectos de los cambios políticos. Señaló que una parte de las iniciativas se desarrolla con alcaldías, gobernaciones y otras autoridades locales. Por eso, sostuvo, las prioridades de cada entidad inciden en los proyectos que pueden avanzar.
El embajador dijo que el equipo de la Delegación de la Unión Europea mantiene su continuidad. Añadió que la institución establece contactos con las nuevas autoridades para conocer sus planes y conversar sobre las líneas de trabajo.
“Nuestra opinión política no corresponde”, afirmó. “Son los colombianos que deciden lo que quieren”.
Conectividad rural y cierre de la brecha digital en Colombia
Roudié mencionó el proyecto de Camarón y otras iniciativas similares desarrolladas con Colnodo y Mintic. Dijo que esos programas buscan demostrar que es posible llevar conectividad a comunidades rurales.
Según explicó, la selección de los territorios corresponde principalmente a Colnodo por su conocimiento del terreno. La Unión Europea aporta financiación y articula opciones tecnológicas con las entidades involucradas.
El embajador señaló que la geografía y la extensión de Colombia dificultan el acceso a conectividad en algunas zonas. Añadió que el mercado no siempre llega a territorios donde no existe una oportunidad de negocio inmediata. “Si hay una vereda allá, hay la famosa brecha digital”, dijo.
Para Roudié, la conexión digital se está convirtiendo en un derecho vinculado con el desarrollo, la educación, el acceso a servicios gubernamentales y las operaciones bancarias.
También, afirmó que las autoridades públicas deben actuar en las zonas donde el mercado no llega. “Hay que hacer un esfuerzo y ver cómo hacer para, en cierta medida, sustituir al mercado o, más bien, llevar el mercado a la vereda”, señaló.
El trabajo interno de la Delegación de la Unión Europea
La Delegación de la Unión Europea en Colombia reúne a unas 50 personas, incluido el personal de apoyo administrativo y los conductores, explicó Roudié. Entre 15 y 20 trabajan en políticas públicas, asuntos políticos, medios y otras áreas operativas. En los asuntos digitales, señaló, intervienen entre tres y cuatro personas que también tienen otras responsabilidades.
El embajador describió una estructura con equipos dedicados a la promoción de inversiones, el comercio, los asuntos políticos y los medios. Dijo que esa organización exige aprovechar las competencias de cada integrante.
Roudié afirmó algo clave para Colombia, la delegación aplica el principio de “una sola delegación”. Con ese esquema, distintas personas pueden aportar a un mismo tema desde sus áreas de conocimiento. “Intentamos aprovechar las competencias de cada uno”, concluyó.

articles.title: Samsung's next-gen OLED tech might arrive before LG's, bringing better brightness and efficiency
articles.text:
Samsung's next-gen OLED tech might actually arrive before LG's — the brighter and more efficient pixels seem to be aimed at phones and smartwatches rather than TVs and monitors
Typical! You wait all day for a fine metal mask-free OLED manufacturing process and then two arrive at once
- Samsung Display is developing more efficient OLED pixel tech to rival LG's FLiPP tech
- It could start production very soon, but the prototype is only 7 inches
- The tech seems to target watch and phone screens over larger panels
As we reported last week, LG Display is moving forward with next-gen Fine Metal Mask-free OLED pixels that could mean brighter, more efficient and maybe more affordable OLED panels. And it looks like Samsung Display is thinking along very similar lines.
A new report by trade site The Elec says that Samsung Display has been working on a prototype seven-inch FMM-free OLED panel using its proprietary Micro Patterned OLED technology, or MPO for short.
The Elec has been speaking to unnamed industry sources, who said that Samsung has been working on MPO product development since March 2026 with a target date at the end of 2026, although that may slip into early 2027.
As with LG's FLiPP technology, the plan is to focus on a particular screen size at first. Samsung is aiming at phone or watch-sized displays, while LG is aiming at laptop or monitor-sized displays. (Neither is aiming at TVs in the near future, alas.)
But while the two companies are taking slightly different approaches to FMM-free manufacturing, the result is likely to be the same: brighter, more efficient and more affordable OLED panels.
What is Samsung Display's MPO technology, and how does it differ from LG Display's FLiPP?
First, why do these companies want to drop 'Fine Metal Mask' tech? This is currently how the material for OLED pixels is deposited into each pixel, and while the tech is useful and mature, it makes for pixels that aren't very efficient.
The primary goal of moving to a more efficient tech is make it so that more of the area of each pixel is filled with light-emitting elements, which means the panel will be brighter, or can be the same brightness but uses less power to do it, which great for battery life and longevity of devices. FMM-free pixels could also be cheaper to make, long-term.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
LG's FLiPP technology (FMM-Less innovative Pixel Patterning) essentially covers the panel with organic materials and then removes the bits it doesn't want via etching and photolithography. MPO does things slightly differently, creating microscopic structures that fence in the organic materials so they're only laid where they need to go. Those structures are then removed. That means less waste and simpler manufacturing, which will ultimately mean lower manufacturing costs, in theory.
The most important difference may not be technical, however: as The Elec points out, there are various active patents regarding FMM-free technologies, and MPO may enable Samsung Display to avoid them.
What we don't know yet is how well the technology will scale. As one of the unnamed industry insiders explained, "MPO is being developed in a direction better suited to high-resolution OLED displays than medium- and large-sized panels. Once a 7-inch-class sample is available, it will be possible to assess how effectively MPO’s technical advantages can be realized at an actual product size."
The big problems for OLED screens, and the thing that keeps them more expensive than LCD panels, is yield rates — that means how many panels you produce are actually usable. The new FMM-free technologies might work perfectly and be cheaper in terms of the material used, but if only 50% of the panels you make are good enough to ship, you haven't actually saved anything.
That's why the production test runs of both technologies will be the make-or-break moment — though both are behind the roll-out of inkjet-printed OLED, arriving in monitors now, which hopes to deliver all the same advantages.

Writer, broadcaster, musician and kitchen gadget obsessive Carrie Marshall has been writing about tech since 1998, contributing sage advice and odd opinions to all kinds of magazines and websites as well as writing more than twenty books. Her latest, a love letter to music titled Small Town Joy, is on sale now. She is the singer in spectacularly obscure Glaswegian rock band Unquiet Mind.

articles.title: La Switch 2 déjà piratée : un premier lanceur d'applications non officielles fait trembler Nintendo
articles.text:
Les choses s’accélèrent pour les bidouilleurs de la Nintendo Switch 2. À peine le premier jailbreak logiciel dévoilé, un développeur est parvenu à faire fonctionner un premier homebrew. Une avancée prometteuse, même si la console est encore loin d’avoir livré tous ses secrets.
Nintendo n’aura pas eu beaucoup de répit. Moins de 24 heures après la présentation de ns2jb, le premier jailbreak logiciel public de la Switch 2, un certain Ravens Claw X a déjà dévoilé un homebrew launcher fonctionnel sur la console. Dans une vidéo publiée le 23 octobre, on découvre un menu navigable à la manette et sur l’écran tactile, accompagné de premières démonstrations graphiques.
Une étape importante pour les amateurs de bidouille, qui peuvent désormais entrevoir les possibilités offertes par la nouvelle machine de Nintendo. Mais attention, il ne s’agit pas encore d’un déverrouillage complet de la console.
Une faille découverte avec l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle
À l’origine de cette percée, on retrouve Sammy Hajhamid, alias pepsipu, qui a publié son exploit ns2jb le 22 octobre. Sa méthode exploite les faiblesses de SmileBASIC 4, un logiciel de programmation conçu pour la première Switch et toujours compatible avec sa remplaçante.
Le chercheur a notamment mis au jour un dépassement d’entier dans l’interpréteur du logiciel, avant d’exploiter une seconde vulnérabilité dans le module système chargé de gérer les fichiers. De quoi exécuter du code non autorisé sans installer de puce ni ouvrir la console.
L'intelligence artificielle a joué un rôle dans cette découverte. Hajhamid s’est appuyé sur Codex d’OpenAI pour analyser le logiciel et identifier des vulnérabilités. Mais contrairement à l’image d’une IA capable de pirater seule une console, le chercheur précise avoir consacré près de deux semaines au développement de son exploit.
Celui-ci fonctionne avec le firmware 23.0.1, mais nécessite notamment SmileBASIC 4 et un ordinateur sur le même réseau. Il faut également relancer la manipulation après chaque redémarrage.
Un premier menu, et déjà quelques démonstrations
Le travail de Ravens Claw X montre que les développeurs peuvent commencer à construire leurs propres applications pour la Switch 2. Parmi les premières démonstrations figure notamment un cube en 3D utilisant Vulkan, l’API graphique qui permet d’exploiter les capacités du GPU.
L'objectif est désormais de disposer d’un véritable catalogue de logiciels amateurs avec pourquoi pas des émulateurs, des outils de gestion des sauvegardes ou des portages de jeux comme Doom. Une calculatrice et un client FTP font également partie des projets évoqués.
Pour l’instant, ces applications ne sont toutefois pas toutes opérationnelles. Les démonstrations reposent encore sur un environnement limité sans accès au noyau de la console ni installation d'un firmware alternatif permanent.
Le jailbreak a néanmoins déjà permis à son auteur de modifier Mario Kart World pour y faire apparaître des personnages comme Peter Griffin ou Hatsune Miku. Une preuve de concept amusante, mais qui ne signifie pas que la Switch 2 peut désormais lancer librement des copies de jeux commerciaux.
Nintendo a encore les moyens de riposter
La réaction du fabricant japonais ne s’est pas fait attendre. Selon Nintendo Life, SmileBASIC 4 a disparu de l’eShop, compliquant sérieusement l’accès à la faille pour les joueurs qui ne possèdent pas déjà le logiciel.
Une future mise à jour pourrait également corriger les vulnérabilités exploitées. Sans oublier les risques de plantage et de bannissement des services en ligne. La création de logiciels amateurs n’est pas illégale en soi, mais le contournement des protections techniques et la distribution non autorisée de jeux peuvent poser des problèmes juridiques.
La Switch 2 rejoint ainsi les consoles disposant d’une scène homebrew active, à l’image de la PS5 avec etaHEN. Microsoft propose de son côté une approche officielle avec le mode développeur des Xbox Series. En quelques heures, l'insubmersible Switch 2 est déjà en train de prendre l'eau…
Sources : VideoCardz et Pepsipu via Frandroid
- Montée en gamme du design et des finitions
- Écran 7,9" (20 cm) LCD convaincant
- Performances et qualité d'image en nette hausse
Un exploit est une technique ou un programme qui utilise une vulnérabilité pour provoquer un comportement non prévu, par exemple l’exécution de code. Un jailbreak logiciel signifie que cette exécution de code se fait sans modification matérielle (pas de puce, pas de soudure), uniquement via des vulnérabilités. En revanche, obtenir un accès au noyau (kernel) donne généralement un contrôle bien plus profond sur le système (pilotes, mémoire, sécurité), ce qui facilite l’installation de modules persistants et de fonctions avancées. Sans accès noyau, on reste souvent dans un environnement limité, plus fragile et plus dépendant de la version du firmware. Dans beaucoup de cas, ces chaînes d’exploitation doivent être relancées après redémarrage car elles ne survivent pas aux mécanismes de sécurité au boot.
Un dépassement d’entier survient lorsqu’un programme stocke un nombre dans un type trop petit (par exemple 32 bits) et que la valeur dépasse sa capacité, provoquant un retour à zéro ou une valeur erronée. Ce décalage peut casser des vérifications de taille, de limites ou de permissions, et amener le logiciel à traiter des données comme si elles étaient sûres alors qu’elles ne le sont pas. Dans un interpréteur ou un moteur de scripts, cela peut servir à manipuler la mémoire, détourner le flux d’exécution, ou forcer la lecture/écriture hors des bornes prévues. L’intérêt pour un attaquant est de transformer un bug logique en exécution de code arbitraire, surtout si une deuxième faille complète la chaîne. Ces failles sont particulièrement sensibles dans les composants qui traitent des entrées contrôlées par l’utilisateur (fichiers, scripts, contenus réseau).
Vulkan est une API graphique bas niveau, conçue pour donner un contrôle fin sur le GPU et de bonnes performances, au prix d’une complexité plus élevée que des API plus anciennes. Pour une scène homebrew, pouvoir afficher une démo 3D via Vulkan signifie qu’une partie de la chaîne graphique (création de contexte, shaders, mémoire GPU, présentation à l’écran) est déjà maîtrisée. Cela ouvre la porte à des ports techniques (moteurs 3D, rendus modernes) et à des outils qui ont besoin d’accélération graphique. En pratique, l’API ne suffit pas : il faut aussi des couches d’accès au système (allocation mémoire, synchronisation, accès aux périphériques), qui peuvent être restreintes sans privilèges élevés. Une démo Vulkan réussie est donc un indicateur de progrès, mais pas une preuve d’un contrôle total de la plateforme.

articles.title: Sony Retires Its Last 4K Blu-ray Player in Japan, PS5 Is All That's Left
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
Sony Retires Its Last 4K Blu-ray Player in Japan, PS5 Is All That's Left
Sony has stopped shipping the UBP-X700/K in Japan, its last standalone 4K Ultra HD Blu-ray player in the country. Shipments ended on October 22, and according to Sony retailer Kunkoku, the remaining stock on Sony's Japanese store sold out almost immediately. There's no word on a successor. That leaves the disc-equipped PlayStation 5 as the only Sony product in Japan that can still play 4K Blu-ray movies. The UBP-X700/K only launched on May 17, 2025, as a cut-down version of the 2018 UBP-X700 without streaming apps, and it was last listed at ¥58,300. Sony will keep selling the BDP-S1700/K, though that one only handles regular Blu-ray discs.
The PS5 is not a perfect stand-in for home theater enthusiasts either. It handles 4K Blu-ray with HDR10, but it lacks Dolby Vision support, which the UBP-X700/K offered. Sony has also announced that new PlayStation games will stop shipping on disc from January 2028, and it hasn't confirmed whether the PS6 will even have a disc drive, despite an earlier report of a detachable one. If it doesn't, the PS5 becomes Sony's last disc player, and with a successor on the way, its days are numbered too. Sony already announced in February that it would phase out all of its Blu-ray recorders in Japan with no successors, so this was somewhat expected. For now, the player exit seems to be limited to Japan, as Sony's US store still lists the UBP-X700U. However, it's hard to see the standalone player sticking around for long elsewhere if Sony is winding down its disc business at home.
Sources:
				Kunkoku, 				Flat Panels HD, 				via Notebookcheck

articles.title: Eric Schmidt, exdirector de Google, afirma que trabajaba 60 horas semanales: “Sentado en reuniones 12 horas al día”
articles.text:
Eric Schmidt, quien dirigió Google como director ejecutivo durante casi una década, afirmó que su semana laboral alcanzaba las 63 horas mientras guiaba a la compañía desde sus primeros pasos como empresa pública hasta convertirse en una de las más valiosas del mundo. Según su propio testimonio, ese tiempo no se destinaba al desarrollo de productos como Gmail o Google Maps, sino a la coordinación interna de la organización.
“Solía decirles a las personas: mi trabajo consiste en estar sentado en reuniones 12 horas al día, cinco días a la semana, y también trabajo los fines de semana”, señaló Schmidt en una conversación con Nicolai Tangen, director ejecutivo de Norges Bank Investment Management. “Estaba sentado en reuniones 12 horas al día: persona, persona, persona, razonamiento, narrativa, etcétera, etcétera”.
La inteligencia artificial como sustituto de las reuniones
El exdirectivo, de 71 años, sostiene que gran parte de ese tiempo dedicado a reuniones puede ser reemplazado por tecnología. “Gran parte de ese coste de coordinación puede eliminarse mediante estas plataformas de inteligencia artificial para empresas”, afirmó.
Schmidt mencionó el caso de un conocido suyo, cuyo nombre no reveló, que despidió recientemente al 20% de su plantilla. Entre los puestos eliminados se encontraban los empleados encargados de planificar, coordinar y distribuir información dentro de la empresa, roles que tradicionalmente sostenían el funcionamiento interno de las organizaciones.
Miles de empleos considerados innecesarios
A partir de este tipo de casos, Schmidt proyecta que las reducciones de personal vinculadas a la adopción de inteligencia artificial se volverán más frecuentes entre las grandes corporaciones. “Digamos que diriges una empresa de 10.000 empleados; supongo que tienes un par de miles que no necesitas”, planteó. “Y más te vale encontrar la manera de reubicarlos legal y humanamente, jubilarlos o lo que sea. Simplemente no los necesitas”.
Schmidt, cuya fortuna se estima en 66.000 millones de dólares, figura entre quienes podrían beneficiarse de manera directa del avance de esta tecnología. Esta semana se conoció que posee aproximadamente el 1% de las acciones de Anthropic, una participación que podría traducirse en una ganancia de 20.000 millones de dólares si la empresa sale a bolsa con el objetivo declarado de alcanzar una valuación de 2 billones de dólares.
El llamado a la generación Z
Pese a su pronóstico sobre la eliminación de puestos existentes, Schmidt identifica oportunidades para quienes logren adaptarse a la nueva tecnología. “Van a necesitar a los grandes inventores, a los grandes vendedores, porque es una cuestión humana”, indicó. “Van a necesitar a grandes líderes. Y van a necesitar gente que hable con el gobierno”.
Durante un discurso ante graduados de la Universidad de Arizona a comienzos de este año, Schmidt instó a los jóvenes a involucrarse en el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial en lugar de resistirse a ella. El mensaje se produjo pese a que parte de los estudiantes lo abucheó cuando comenzó a abordar el tema.
“Sea cual sea el camino que elijan, la IA se convertirá en parte de la forma en que se trabaja”, expresó ante los graduados, a quienes animó a utilizar la tecnología para abordar problemas que antes resultaban inalcanzables. “Cuando alguien te ofrece un asiento en la nave espacial, no preguntas cuál. Simplemente subes”, añadió. “Graduados, la nave espacial ya está aquí”.
La rutina de Tim Cook al frente de Apple
Otro ejemplo de compromiso con el crecimiento de su compañía es Tim Cook, quien durante sus 15 años como CEO de Apple sostuvo una rutina matutina que repitió casi a diario desde 2011: levantarse poco antes de las cuatro de la madrugada para leer los correos electrónicos enviados por usuarios de sus productos en todo el mundo.
Así lo describió en una carta dirigida a la comunidad de usuarios al dejar el cargo, en la que explicó que dedicaba la primera hora del día a esa tarea antes de completar una hora de ejercicio y retomar la lectura de mensajes a las cinco de la mañana.
Cook revisaba “la mayoría” de los entre 700 y 800 correos que llegaban diariamente a su bandeja de entrada, una práctica que, a diferencia de otros directivos que delegan esa función en asistentes, le permitía, según sus palabras, “mantener el pulso de lo que los clientes sienten, piensan y hacen”.

articles.title: The Apple Watch Series 12's Readiness score enhances all its other wellness features, and makes for a compelling upgrade over older models
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Apple Watch Series 12 is a worthwhile upgrade for anyone using a Series 9 or older, with Readiness Score and improved health sensing making everyday tracking more useful. It's a less compelling upgrade from the Series 10 or 11, though, and Apple's upcoming AI features aren't ready to tip the scales just yet.
Reasons to buy
- + Readiness Score is terrific and not locked behind a paywall
- + Refreshed Health Sensing System
- + S11 Chip ensures smooth, responsive performance
- + Still delivers all-day battery life
Reasons to avoid
- - No major design changes
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple Watch Series 12: One minute review
While the Apple Watch Series 12 is a decidedly modern-looking smartwatch in a pleasingly thin profile, it’s not a major redesign from the Cupertino-based tech giant. And if you're upgrading from the Series 11, you'll probably notice more of a difference in what the watch can do rather than in how it looks. Apple has updated the Health Sensing System (its array of LEDs and sensors used to collect your health data), introduced Readiness Score, and made everyday tracking more useful, with real-time steps and heart-rate information easier to access.
I've been wearing the Series 12 for more than a month, and Readiness Score is the addition I've found myself using the most. It takes your sleep and other health data and turns it into a score out of 10, giving you a quick idea of how ready you might be for the day. I've generally found the results match how I feel, and it's a feature that can genuinely influence what I do, whether that's heading out for a workout or taking a longer walk with my dog, Rosie.
I've also been comparing the Series 12 with the Series 11, Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Ultra 4, as well as the Oura Ring 5 and Pixel Watch 5. That has helped me put Apple's latest watch into context, particularly when looking at health tracking and heart-rate readings. The Series 12 has generally delivered the sort of everyday experience I'd expect from an Apple Watch, with battery life that's worked well for me most of the time.
A couple of things to consider, though. The design is very familiar, so there's little reason to upgrade purely for its appearance, and I did have two nights when the battery ran out before morning. Apple's upcoming AI features are also still a reason to wait rather than buy immediately. If they're what you're most interested in.
For anyone using an older Apple Watch, particularly a Series 9 or earlier, the Series 12 makes a much stronger case. The combination of newer health features, Readiness Score, performance, and battery life makes this an upgrade worth considering.
Apple Watch Series 12: Specs Table
| Component | Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm) | Apple Watch Series 12 (46mm) | 
| Price | $399 / £369 / AU$679 for the 42mm | $429 / £399 / AU$699 for the 46mm | 
| Dimension | 46 x 40 x 9.7mm | 42 x 37 x 9.7mm | 
| Weight | 31.5g (without band) | 38.6g (without band) | 
| Case/bezel | Aluminum, Titanium, or Ceramic | Aluminum, Titanium, or Ceramic | 
| Display | 42mm Always-On Retina LTPO3 OLED display (up to 2,000 nits) | 46mm Always-On Retina LTPO3 OLED display (up to 2,000 nits) | 
| Processor | Apple-made S11 chip | Apple-made S11 chip | 
| GPS | Precision L1 GPS (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou) | Precision L1 GPS (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou) | 
| Battery life | Up to 24 hours with normal use | Up to 24 hours with normal use | 
| Connections | 4G LTE, Satellite SOS, Wi‑Fi 4 (802.11n), Bluetooth 5.3 | Wi‑Fi 4 (802.11n), Bluetooth 5.3, and 4G LTE | 
| Water resistant | Water resistance 50m | Water resistance 50m | 
Apple Watch Series 12: Price and availability
- $399 / £369 / AU$679 for the 42mm
- $429 / £399 / AU$699 for the 46mm
- Prices unchanged from last year
The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399 / £369 / AU$679 for the 42mm with a recycled aluminum case and standard strap, and $429 / £399 / AU$699 for the 46mm. LTE-capable models, which can be added to your data plans, as well as optional improvements to the finish — titanium or ceramic — are available at an additional cost.
It doesn’t represent outstanding value in the same way as, let’s say, the Amazfit Active 3 Premium might, but it’s fine — the price has actually held steady on Apple Watches for the last couple of years, which is encouraging given the electronics industry is undergoing a supply chain crisis at the moment.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
- Value score: 4.5/5
Apple Watch Series 12: Design
- Same ‘squircle’ and digital crown design
- Retains slimmer look from Series 11
- Redesigned sensor array and GPS architecture
If you expect the Apple Watch Series 12 to look substantially different from the Series 11, you'll be disappointed. Apple has kept the familiar rectangular ‘squircle’ design, with the Digital Crown and side button on the case, and the overall look remains very much the same.
After using the Series 12 for more than a month and comparing it with the Series 11, I haven't found the exterior to be a major reason to upgrade. It doesn't look dramatically different on your wrist, and Apple hasn't tried to reinvent a design that already works.
That's not necessarily a problem, though. The Apple Watch Series 12 remains a comfortable everyday smartwatch, and wearing it all day and overnight matters when you use it for sleep tracking and the Readiness Score. The biggest changes are on the rear of the case, as Apple has redesigned the LEDs and internal architecture to make its data collection more accurate. However, a watch can have all the health features in the world, but they're less useful if you don't want to wear it consistently.
The Series 12 comes in 42mm and 46mm sizes, with aluminum and titanium options alongside ceramic, which is returning and still adds a bit more heft. That gives you some choice in look and finish, though the core experience stays the same. The aluminum model is the more straightforward choice for most people, while titanium and ceramic offer alternatives if materials and appearance matter more to you.
The always-on OLED display is familiar, too. It lets you glance at the time, check a notification, or see your workout metrics without having to wake the screen manually. That's one of those features that quickly becomes part of your routine, particularly if you use complications to keep useful information on the watch face.
One addition I've found handy is the real-time step-count complication. I check steps regularly, and seeing the number at a glance saves me from opening the Fitness app. The heart rate complication works the same way, especially when I want to keep an eye on my readings during the day.
Compared with the Ultra 3 and Ultra 4, the Series 12 feels more like a familiar everyday watch. The Ultra models have their own appeal, particularly if you want a larger, more rugged watch, but the Series 12 is easier to recommend to someone who doesn't need that design.
The main point is that the Series 12 doesn't feel like a new design generation. If you're upgrading, look at the back of the case, with its improved health features enabling the Readiness Score and overall experience, rather than expecting a noticeable aesthetic change to the watch itself.
- Design score: 4.5/5
Apple Watch Series 12: Features
- Readiness score is a major boon
- More frequent heart rate data collection
- Upcoming Audio Intelligence features
The Readiness Score is the biggest reason I'd consider the Series 12, and it stood out most during my testing. It uses overnight sleep and HRV data, along with other health and activity information and some custom processing, to produce a score from 1 to 10. The idea is to give you a quick indication of how ready you might be for the day, rather than leaving you to interpret a collection of separate metrics yourself. Tested against the Garmin Cirqa, our senior fitness editor Matt Evans found both devices provided identical Readiness scores after wearing both for one week’s worth of sleep.
I like how Apple presents it: a half-moon graphic that’s easy to read, with an accompanying explanation that gives context for the score. It feels grounded in the data, rather than relying on vague wellness language that doesn't explain why you got a particular result.
My scores have generally been high, and they've mostly matched how I've felt. Getting my first 10 out of 10 was satisfying, of course, but the more interesting part is how I can use the information. If I've slept well and feel good, a strong score might encourage me to fit in a workout or take Rosie on a longer walk. It won't make every decision for me, but it gives me another useful piece of information to consider.
I've used an Oura Ring before, so I know the appeal of a daily Readiness score and the help it can provide beyond raw data. I appreciate that Apple built the feature into the watch I already use. I don't need to add another device to my routine, and Readiness Score doesn't require a separate subscription.
That makes it a particularly interesting addition for existing Apple Watch owners who want more from the health data their watch collects. Instead of simply checking how long I slept or looking at the previous day's activity, I get a more immediate summary I can use to plan my day. However, we have to acknowledge the wait for this feature — most other devices have had Readiness for years, but Apple has stated the feature has been enabled by its redesigned sensors taking heart rate and HRV readings more frequently, up to 60 times more often than previous Apple Watches.
I've also been paying attention to heart rate readings while comparing the Series 12 with the Apple Watch Series 11, Ultra 3, and Ultra 4, along with the Oura Ring 5 and Pixel Watch 5. In my everyday use, the Series 12's readings have been broadly consistent with what I've seen from those other devices.
Having heart rate information readily available is useful during workouts, too. I've used the watch for yoga, outdoor walks and runs, and indoor cycling, and it has fit naturally into those sessions. The real-time heart rate complication also makes it easier to check my readings without navigating away from the watch face.
The Series 12 retains the wider Apple Watch health feature set, including ECG, heart-rate notifications, wrist-temperature sensing, sleep tracking, respiratory-rate tracking, cycle tracking, hearing-health features, hypertension notifications and blood-oxygen tracking where supported. These aren't all new to this generation, but they contribute to the overall package.
Apple's upcoming AI (‘Audio Intelligence’ this time) features aren't a strong reason to buy right now. Live Rewind and Siri Recap sound interesting, but I haven't been able to test them because they aren’t out yet. If you're considering the Series 12 for those, I'd wait until Apple confirms when they're shipping and what will be available in your region, as there is some contention with Siri AI in certain regions such as the EU.
For now, Readiness Score is the feature I'd focus on. It's useful today, fits into the existing Apple Watch experience, and has made the biggest difference in how I use the Series 12. Best of all, it’s not locked behind another subscription … and that’s simply refreshing.
- Design score: 5/5
Apple Watch Series 12: Performance
- S11 chip drives excellent performance
- Accurate compared to other wearables
- Responsive with no stutters
While the Series 12 still feels and looks like an Apple Watch in pretty much every sense of the word, you can’t judge a book by its cover, especially when it comes to performance. Under the hood, the Series 12 runs on Apple’s new S11 chip, and the new health-sensing system on the back enables the Readiness score and HRV features. All of this comes together to make the Series 12 feel responsive, with none-to-minimal stutters when calling on a particular feature set.
I've now used the Series 12 for more than a month, and I've compared it directly alongside the Series 11, Ultra 3, and Ultra 4. These comparisons have helped me understand how the Series 12 fits into the wider wearable landscape, and while the latest generation doesn’t run laps around the previous gen or the one before that, the responsiveness is definitely noticeable.
Whether you’re customizing a Watch Face with your favorite complications, calling on Siri to remember a piece of information or drafting a message, controlling media playback, making a call, recording a voice memo, checking your activity score, monitoring your heart rate, or starting a workout, the Series 12 feels very responsive. We’ve also tested the same heart rate system, albeit on the Ultra 4, against a chest-mounted heart rate monitor, the Frontier X2, alongside the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro, and found Apple’s latest gen is highly accurate.
Battery life has been good overall, and it certainly meets Apple's all-day battery life promise. On a normal day with plenty of interaction points and one extended workout, I typically have around 30%–45% battery remaining by bedtime. That's enough to get through a normal day, and faster charging makes it easier to top up when I need to. Depending on how I use it, I can get through a full day and sometimes stretch it to a day and a half.
So far, the Series 12 has run out of battery overnight twice, and I think it’s especially worth mentioning because you need a full night of sleep data to wake up with a Readiness Score. And that means an unexpected shutdown can interrupt that routine. My general solution, even if the percentage hasn’t dropped super low, is to give it a quick charge before bed rather than assuming it will always have enough power to last the night.
The faster charging helps here. A short top-up with the USB-C to Apple Watch dongle that ships with the Series 12 can make it easier to keep the watch going overnight while still wearing it.
If you’re coming from an older Apple Watch, the all-day battery life paired with fast-charging will likely make a big difference. It’s not just a quality-of-life upgrade from, say, a Series 10 or older; compared with the rest of the features, it's a significant leap in what watchOS can accomplish and how long you go before you need to charge.
- Performance score: 4.5/5
Should you buy the Apple Watch Series 12?
Buy it if..
You're upgrading from an Apple Watch Series 9 or older and want better health tracking, Readiness Score, and faster charging.
You want a responsive everyday smartwatch with useful at-a-glance health metrics and no extra subscription for Readiness Score.
Don’t buy it if..
You already own an Apple Watch Series 11 and want a major design change or a substantial leap in performance.
You're buying primarily for Apple's upcoming AI features, or you need battery life you can count on for every night of sleep tracking without a top-up.
Also consider
Garmin Fenix 9 Pro
The Apple Watch Ultra 4's biggest competitor in the premium adventure watch space.
Read our full Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review
How we tested
We tested the Apple Watch Series 12 by wearing it day and night, tracking workouts, monitoring sleep, and putting its features to the test over multiple weeks. We compared its health and fitness readings with other wearables and an electrical heart rate monitor, tested battery life, and explored as many features as possible to see how it holds up in everyday use.
First reviewed October 2026.
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: Avis aux fans d’Apple : l’iPad Pro M5 de 13" bénéficie de plus de 380€ de réduction chez Amazon ce week-end
articles.text:
Le très haut de gamme iPad Pro M5 de 13 pouces profite actuellement de 16% de réduction chez Amazon : la tablette sous iPadOS passe, ainsi, de 2 399 € à 2 017,51 € dans sa version de 1 To.
Il y a des tablettes dont on se sert surtout pour flâner sur les réseaux sociaux ou regarder des vidéos depuis son canapé, et puis il y a celles qui sont tellement puissantes qu’elles permettent de travailler sur des projets créatifs poussés. L’iPad Pro M5 de 13 pouces appartient très clairement à cette deuxième catégorie. En ce moment, sa version Wi-Fi de 1 To est disponible pour 2 017,51 € sur Amazon, grâce à une remise de 16 %. De quoi rendre cet iPad Pro plus abordable pour les créatifs et les simples utilisateurs exigeants.
L’iPad Pro M5 de 13 pouces Wi-Fi avec 1 To de stockage est à 2 017,51 € au lieu de 2 399 € chez Amazon.
Pourquoi choisir l’iPad Pro M5 de 13 pouces ?
- Pour son écran OLED : la dalle Ultra Retina XDR associe des noirs profonds à un rafraîchissement adaptatif jusqu’à 120 Hz.
- Pour sa configuration : cette version de 1 To bénéficie d’un processeur à dix cœurs et de 16 Go de mémoire, ce qui la rend adaptée aux projets créatifs complexes.
- Pour son interface : iPadOS est le système d’exploitation d’Apple dédié aux iPad : on y retrouve donc tout le savoir-faire de la marque.
Une grande surface de travail pour les créatifs
Avec son écran Ultra Retina XDR de 13 pouces, l’iPad Pro M5 donne accès à une surface tactile très confortable pour prendre des notes, dessiner avec un stylet compatible, ou encore utiliser plusieurs applications iPadOS en même temps. Dans le test de Clubic, qui a attribué à l’iPad Pro M5 la note de 9 sur 10, les performances de la tablette, la qualité de son écran ainsi que la dimension multitâche d’iPadOS 26 sont notamment saluées. Quant au port Thunderbolt/USB 4 qui équipe l’appareil, il peut être utilisé pour raccorder un support de stockage externe ou un écran compatible.
Une tablette haut de gamme qui cible l’exigence
Les performances de l’iPad Pro M5 justifient son prix. Même en promotion, cette tablette Apple reste coûteuse, et son achat se justifie surtout si vous avez besoin de disposer d’un modèle capable de faire tourner des applications créatives très gourmandes. Si vous désirez surtout jouer ou regarder des séries, un iPad moins cher peut tout à fait vous suffire.
✅ Les points forts
- Écran OLED de 13 pouces avec ProMotion jusqu’à 120 Hz.
- Puce M5, 16 Go de mémoire et stockage de 1 To.
- Port Thunderbolt/USB 4 pour les périphériques compatibles.
❌ Les limites
- Apple Pencil et Magic Keyboard vendus séparément.
- Adaptateur secteur non fourni.
L'iPad Pro M5 Wi-Fi de 1 To est disponible à 2 017,51 € chez Amazon, soit 381,49 € de moins que son prix de référence de 2 399 €.
Si vous êtes un créatif adepte du dessin numérique et des applications iPadOS nécessitant de la puissance, l’iPad Pro M5 de 13 pouces devrait vous apporter une grande satisfaction à l’usage.
Néanmoins, si vous cherchez surtout à investir dans un iPad pour vous divertir sur un écran plus grand que celui de votre iPhone, un modèle moins coûteux, toujours signé Apple, devrait répondre à vos attentes.

articles.title: Sa BYD se retrouve bloquée, il active une fonctionnalité qui lui permet de se déplacer comme un tank pour sortir sa voiture électrique du pétrin
articles.text:
Sa BYD se retrouve bloquée, il active une fonctionnalité qui lui permet de se déplacer comme un tank pour sortir sa voiture électrique du pétrin
C’est une vidéo qui a été largement diffusée sur les réseaux sociaux chinois. Celle d’une voiture électrique BYD coincée dans une situation quelque peu inconfortable qui effectue une manœuvre pour glisser comme un tank et s’en extraire.
Sur la vidéo, c’est la Denza Z9 GT de BYD qui est coincée dans un passage tellement étroit qu’un demi-tour paraît impossible. C’est alors que le conducteur active une fonctionnalité du grand break électrique, le Compass U-Turn, qui lui permet de pivoter presque sur place pour sortir de sa situation. Une technologie très utile quand une manœuvre à la main est trop compliquée ou ne suffit plus.
Une fonctionnalité exclusive du break de BYD
Look how BYD’s electric car turns at this narrow place. This is the car of the future. pic.twitter.com/ZfmNQnXjal
— Li Zexin 李泽欣 (@XH_Lee23) June 7, 2026
La vidéo est d’autant plus surprenante que la Denza Z9 GT est quand même un break électrique long de 5,18 mètres. Alors changer de direction dans un espace aussi étroit n’a rien d’aisé. Le secret derrière cette fonctionnalité, c’est la plateforme e³ de BYD. La version Performance utilise trois moteurs électriques, avec l’un sur l’essieu avant et les deux autres sur celui de l’arrière.
Mais alors comment ça marche ? Chacun des moteurs arrière entraîne sa roue de manière autonome et une direction indépendante permet aux roues arrière de braquer vers l’extérieur. Les deux roues arrière tournent alors dans des sens opposés, l’une vers l’avant et l’autre vers l’arrière.
Une roue avant est bloquée par les freins pour effectuer un pivot et l’autre accompagne le mouvement. La voiture électrique pivote donc autour de cette roue avant au lieu d’enchaîner les marches arrière et les braquages. Pour accéder à la fonctionnalité Compass U-Turn, le conducteur doit ouvrir le menu e³ de l’écran central puis sélectionner l’angle de rotation. Il est possible pour le véhicule de faire demi-tour ou de pousser la manœuvre jusqu’à 360 degrés.
Sur la vidéo, le mouvement rappelle celui d’un tank, même si la Denza Z9 GT ne tourne pas autour du centre exact de sa carrosserie mais autour d’une de ses roues avant. Tout passe par les moteurs et la direction arrière. BYD n’a installé aucune roue spéciale en dessous.
La Denza Z9 GT, dans sa version électrique e³ Performance, coûte environ 369 800 ¥ en Chine, soit environ 47 300 € chez nous. Pour la fiche technique, c’est 850 kW, soit 1 156 chevaux, avec un couple de 1 210 Nm. Le passage de 0 à 100 km/h se fait en 2,7 secondes. Une fiche technique haut de gamme qui explique pourquoi BYD a choisi la Z9 GT comme vitrine technologique de Denza, sa filiale haut de gamme.
La plateforme e³ permet aussi d’effectuer une marche en crabe ou de se stationner avec une glissade arrière. Les roues arrière braquent de manière autonome pour réduire l’espace nécessaire aux manœuvres. La voiture de plus de 5 mètres est donc bien plus aisée à placer dans une rue étroite. Denza a livré plus de 10 000 exemplaires de sa nouvelle Z9 GT, versions électrique et hybride confondues, deux mois et demi après le début des livraisons.

articles.title: AI agent governance takes shape at Okta’s Oktane event - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event
AI agent governance is moving identity security into the flow of work. As agents call tools, delegate tasks and act across applications, enterprises need controls that follow those actions beyond an initial login. The challenge is making those controls work across systems while preserving the business processes agents support.
The limits of individual security platforms emerged as a recurring concern during Okta Inc.’s Oktane event. As agents operate across connected systems, enterprises face questions that extend beyond granting or revoking access, according to Krista Case, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.
“What I am interested to see as it gets rolled out and as we start to talk with customers about it is if there are conflicting insights across these platforms about an action that needs to be taken,” she said. “For example, who is going to have the authority at the end of the day, and where is that authority going to live in this tech stack?”
Case and co-host Rebecca Knight spoke with Okta executives, partners and customers during theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event, as part of an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The discussions examined how enterprises are putting AI agents to work while maintaining control over their access and actions. (* Disclosure below.)
Here’s the complete video keynote analysis with Krista Case and Rebecca Knight:
Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event:
Insight #1: AI agent governance requires shared architecture and runtime controls.
An agent’s work can span applications and security platforms, making consistent protection dependent on how those systems connect. The Blueprint Alliance brings vendors together around a reference architecture intended to help customers secure that environment, according to Charlotte Wylie (pictured), senior vice president and deputy chief security officer of Okta.
“Rather than trying to solve that problem alone, there is a recognition that we have to galvanize as an industry to solve this problem for our customers at a speed that they are scrambling to run after,” she said. “We want to make sure that we provide an architecture, a referenceable position [for] how to use the technology that we all offer in a way that we can secure the entire agentic stack.”
Shared architecture also needs a point where controls can govern attempted actions. Okta’s move into the runtime path through its Agent Gateway expands the identity provider’s role from granting access to evaluating what agents seek to do, according to Ric Smith, president of products and technology at Okta.
“That is a very different transition for Okta,” he told theCUBE. “We had not been inline, so with us moving in that direction, it means that we can do a lot more decision-making in terms of what we authorize.”
Inside Okta, that architectural challenge takes a practical form. Dex gives employees access to specialized agents without multiplying the interfaces they must navigate, according to Jenna Cline, senior vice president of technology, data and intelligence at Okta.
“Dex can call upon the right sub-agent. That agent is scoped to only work on certain things, so it’s very secure, and it’s very efficient because it does one thing really well,” she said. “But Dex can do that for other agents; it can do that for the expense team [and] it can do that for our IT help desk.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jenna Cline:
Insight #2: Securing AI agents requires cooperation beyond any single vendor.
AI agent governance depends on access decisions carrying across systems. Okta and AgileBits Inc., doing business as 1Password, use shared identity standards to preserve an agent’s verified identity and authorization context. 1Password’s Credential Broker supplies secrets without exposing them to the agent or the underlying model, according to Nancy Wang, chief technology officer of 1Password.
“Just like you would verify whatever an intern does before you allow them to move on to the next project, [it’s the] same thing with agents,” Wang told theCUBE. “You just want that agent to prove that it actually finished its last task with the right level of permissions, doing the right thing before you allow it to move on to the next task.”
That cooperation also matters when an agent’s behavior requires intervention. ServiceNow Inc. maps agents to the business processes they support and is working with Okta on agent identities and session tokens. Those connections inform decisions about when and how to contain an agent, according to Bhakti Pitre, vice president of AI platform security product at ServiceNow.
“Everybody in the industry needs to come together and be each other’s friends or frenemies,” she said. “If the AI needs to be at the scale where it is democratized for every person to use it, then every vendor needs to come together and play their part.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Nancy Wang:
Insight #3: Simpler infrastructure and established governance provide a foundation for AI agents.
The Professional Golfers’ Association of America relies on Okta and Auth0 as part of an architecture that has eliminated traditional infrastructure layers, including data centers and a corporate network. Those choices help direct resources toward technology that serves members and customers, according to Kevin Scott, chief technology officer of the PGA of America.
“We don’t have much of a team — it’s small, it is lean,” he told theCUBE. “I don’t mean to be reductive, but if we were to spend half of the technology budget on administering systems, none of our customers are ever going to come along and say, ‘Thank you for that.’”
At Vanderbilt University, the emphasis is on applying established governance to AI agent identities. The university uses OneVU, powered by Okta, for single sign-on and is weighing how institutional oversight should accommodate another kind of identity, according to Shane Callahan, chief information officer of Vanderbilt.
“We’re treating AI like it’s a brand-new thing. But really, you’re still talking about identity data in another technology tool,” he said. “You don’t have to recreate everything. If you have a governance process and a technology intake program, do that, use that.”
Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Kevin Scott:
To watch more of theCUBE’s coverage of Okta’s Oktane event, here’s our complete video playlist:

articles.title: Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced Gets Its Long-Promised New Game+ Mode
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced Gets Its Long-Promised New Game+ Mode
Ubisoft has confirmed that New Game+ is coming to Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced next week. The announcement came through the official Assassin's Creed account on X, which thanked players for their patience and paired the news with a GIF of a grinning Edward Kenway. Ubisoft hasn't given an exact date or said what the mode will include, so we don't know yet whether players will carry over gear, upgrades, or anything else into a fresh run, although that is to be expected from a New Game+. The feature has been a long time coming, as Ubisoft first promised New Game+ content back in July when the game crossed 3 million sales. 
Around the same time, game director Richard Knight told YouTuber JorRaptor that the team was already working on New Game+ and that it was one of the first things on the list. He also called it relatively low risk, since Assassin's Creed Shadows already had its own version of the mode. Black Flag Resynced launched on July 9 and has done well for Ubisoft so far, hitting 2 million sales in 24 hours and selling 3.5 million copies in its first two weeks, which already exceeded Ubisoft's expectations for the whole year. New Game+ will likely give players who finished the story over the summer a reason to jump back into the Caribbean. Ubisoft had reportedly tied the future of its remakes to how Black Flag performed, and an Assassin's Creed 1 remake is said to be next in line.

articles.title: "No hay esperanza para los glaciares del Pirineo". Las fotos del Aneto tras el verano sugieren un colapso climático extremo
articles.text:
El cambio climático está agravando la desertificación de España y, en el proceso, desestabilizando brutalmente el caudal de los ríos y haciendo que los Pirineos sean más mediterráneos que nunca. Y eso implica también decir adiós a uno de los pocos glaciares que hay en la península Ibérica: el del Aneto. Como una imagen vale más que mil palabras, bajo estas líneas verás dos fotografías del Aneto, de 2015 y 2026. El cambio es evidente: donde antes había un cuerpo blanco de nieve y hielo, ahora domina la roca desnuda y el hielo sucio.
La agonía del Aneto. La descorazonadora imagen que muestran las dos fotografías no debería pillarnos por sorpresa. El grupo CryoPyr del Instituto Pirenaico de Ecología (IPE-CSIC) lleva años midiendo su retroceso con drones y láser y, tras su campaña de septiembre de 2025, detalló que el cuerpo principal se fragmentó bajo el Pico del Medio y que la masa bajo el Collado de Coronas pasó a considerarse un helero. El resultado son tres masas de hielo desconectadas, un estado muy distinto al de 2015.
Los resultados preliminares de la campaña de final de este verano apuntan a una pérdida de más de dos metros de espesor medio, que deja el grosor medio del glaciar en torno a los 12 metros. El investigador Ignacio López-Moreno, del IPE-CSIC, recuerda que durante las últimas dos décadas la pérdida rondaba un metro al año, aunque en 2022 y 2023 superó los tres.
Por qué importa. Porque, aunque es pequeño (unas 30 hectáreas, 0,3 kilómetros cuadrados), el Aneto es el mayor glaciar de los Pirineos y funciona como termómetro de toda la cordillera. La desaparición de los glaciares pirenaicos avanza: los Pirineos pasaron de más de 100 glaciares en 1850 a 18 en 2022, con una pérdida del 92 % de su superficie glaciar desde el final de la Pequeña Edad de Hielo, según un estudio del IPE-CSIC recogido por la EHU. De hecho, ya hay un artículo científico con un título que suena a epitafio: No hope for Pyrenean glaciers ("No hay esperanza para los glaciares pirenaicos"), que estima que el Pirineo podría quedarse sin hielo hacia 2034, o antes si se repiten veranos extremos como los de 2022 y 2023.
Y las consecuencias van más allá de lo impactante del cambio en el paisaje: aunque los glaciares pequeños no aportan demasiado al nivel del mar o al caudal de los grandes ríos, su desaparición altera la erosión, el transporte de nutrientes y los ecosistemas de alta montaña. Además, la pérdida de hielo y de terreno helado favorece la caída de piedras, lo que, por cierto, también dificulta el acceso a la cima.
41 años de datos y un diagnóstico. Entre 1981 y 2022, el glaciar encogió un 64,7 % y su espesor medio bajó 30,5 metros, desde 32,9 hasta 11,9 metros. Es el registro más largo de pérdida de espesor de hielo en los Pirineos: 41 años reconstruidos del Aneto. A escala global, un estudio proyecta que la desaparición de glaciares alcanzará su máximo entre 2041 y 2055, con hasta 4.000 glaciares al año, pero ya hemos visto que para el Pirineo las estimaciones del IPE-CSIC sitúan el final del hielo antes.
Crónica de una muerte anunciada. Entre 2011 y 2020, el Aneto perdió un 24,3 % de su área y una media de 8,5 metros de espesor, con descensos de hasta 21 metros en algunas zonas. Hay además un indicador especialmente preocupante: el hielo apenas se mueve, y un glaciar que no fluye está al límite. A eso se suma que ya no tiene una zona de acumulación que reponga lo perdido.
El problema se acelera por un mecanismo conocido: la nieve estacional que protege el hielo se funde antes y deja expuesto un hielo viejo, oscuro y cubierto de polvo y piedras que absorbe más radiación y se derrite más deprisa.

articles.title: Texas demandó a OpenAI y a Sam Altman por presunto engaño sobre los riesgos de ChatGPT
articles.text:
El fiscal general de Texas, Ken Paxton, demandó a OpenAI y a su director ejecutivo, Sam Altman, por presuntamente engañar a los usuarios de ChatGPT sobre los riesgos del chatbot y causarles daños, según un comunicado oficial de su oficina difundido este viernes.
La demanda invoca la Ley de Prácticas Comerciales Engañosas de Texas, la principal norma de protección al consumidor del estado, y sostiene que OpenAI se presentó como una herramienta segura y confiable sin advertir sobre los peligros reales de su tecnología.
El comunicado enumera los daños atribuidos a la compañía: tiradores que recibieron ayuda del chatbot para cometer ataques, personas vulnerables alentadas al suicidio, profesionales humillados públicamente, usuarios que perdieron capacidad de pensamiento crítico y menores que se volvieron adictos a una herramienta que simula afecto humano para recolectar sus datos sin supervisión parental.
“Con el rápido avance de la tecnología de IA, OpenAI tiene la responsabilidad de proteger a los usuarios y advertirles sobre los numerosos peligros de su plataforma”, afirmó Paxton en el comunicado. “Voy a luchar para proteger a los tejanos de los daños de la IA y asegurarme de que las poderosas empresas tecnológicas no estén por encima de la ley”.
Texas se suma a una ola de demandas contra OpenAI
La acción de Texas no es aislada. Florida fue el primer estado en demandar a OpenAI, en junio, por comercializar ChatGPT como un producto seguro pese a conocer sus riesgos para los usuarios.
En octubre, otros ocho estados —Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, Virginia Occidental, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho y Montana— presentaron demandas coordinadas con reclamos similares: ocultar que ChatGPT brindó consejos médicos peligrosos, alentó a usuarios a lastimar a otros y guió a personas hacia el suicidio mientras se presentaba como un amigo confiable. Con la acción de Paxton, ya son al menos diez los estados que llevaron a la empresa a los tribunales.
OpenAI respondió a las demandas de octubre asegurando que incorporó “protecciones específicas por edad que muchos otros productos de IA no tienen”, según declaraciones de un vocero de la compañía a medios estadounidenses. La empresa no había emitido una respuesta pública dirigida específicamente a la demanda de Texas al momento de esta publicación.
El historial de Paxton contra las grandes tecnológicas
Paxton, actual candidato republicano al Senado de Estados Unidos, construyó en los últimos años una de las oficinas de fiscalía más activas del país contra Silicon Valley. En 2024 obtuvo un acuerdo de USD 1.400 millones con Meta por el uso no autorizado de datos biométricos de usuarios de Texas, descrito como el mayor pago logrado por un solo estado en un litigio de este tipo. En octubre de 2025 repitió la cifra con un acuerdo similar contra Google por rastrear datos de usuarios sin su permiso.
Antes de la demanda contra OpenAI, Paxton ya había investigado a Meta y Character.AI por presentar chatbots como herramientas de salud mental, y había alcanzado un acuerdo pionero con la empresa de inteligencia artificial para la salud Pieces Technologies.
Texas también cuenta desde enero con una ley propia, la Ley de Gobernanza Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial, que fija reglas para proteger a los habitantes del estado de usos dañinos o engañosos de la IA y exige avisos claros cuando una persona interactúa con un sistema automatizado en ciertas situaciones.
Una empresa bajo presión legal antes de su salida a bolsa
La nueva demanda llega en un momento sensible para OpenAI, que avanza en los preparativos para una eventual salida a bolsa y que ya enfrenta decenas de juicios de particulares que responsabilizan a ChatGPT por casos de suicidio y violencia, incluido un tiroteo masivo investigado en Canadá.
Los estados demandantes piden en conjunto medidas que van desde sanciones económicas hasta cambios obligatorios en el diseño del producto: controles parentales más estrictos, verificación de edad y restricciones a conversaciones de tipo afectivo con menores.
Con la incorporación de Texas, el mayor estado en sumarse a la ofensiva legal, la cantidad de demandas estatales contra OpenAI asciende a diez, un número que previsiblemente seguirá creciendo mientras la compañía enfrenta en paralelo la revisión de su estructura societaria rumbo al mercado bursátil.

articles.title: 32 TB RAM for your GPUs: Marvell shows revolutionary Photonic Fabric Memory Module that uses light to link up to 16 GPUs and slash CAPEX — but Nvidia won't stick around doing nothing
articles.text:
32 TB RAM for your GPUs: Marvell shows revolutionary Photonic Fabric Memory Module that uses light to link up to 16 GPUs and slash CAPEX — but Nvidia won't stick around doing nothing
Marvell wants to stop GPUs acting as "the world's most expensive memory controller"
- Marvell reveals Photonic Fabric Memory Module, the building block of a 16-module appliance sharing 32TB of DDR5 and 1,152GB of HBM3e across 16 hosts over fiber
- The design dates back to Celestial AI's 2025 presentations, currently remains pre-silicon, and is targeting customer sampling by 2027
- Nvidia is already hedging with a $2 billion Marvell stake in addition to its own BlueField-4 STX context memory, Enfabrica's pooling tech, and a co-packaged optics roadmap
Marvell has put physical hardware behind one of the more ambitious ideas in AI infrastructure.
In a video posted to X, and earlier in a theCUBE interview recorded around its October 6 Investor Day, the company showed off its Photonic Fabric Memory Module, which it bills as the "first optically interconnected high-capacity, high-bandwidth memory."
The pitch is simple: use light instead of copper so that dozens of terabytes of memory can sit in a separate box, racks away, and be shared by many processors at once, something that could effectively birth the widespread use of communal or shared memory across multiple AI servers.
Two terabytes at a time
Some clarity, however, is warranted: the 32TB figure belongs not to the module but to the Photonic Fabric Memory Appliance, which gangs 16 modules together and shares the pool across up to 16 hosts.
Those hosts can be whole servers or individual accelerators, so 16 GPUs might understate the potential reach in one sense and at the same time, overstate the bandwidth any single GPU will see in another. Nothing is shipping just yet, either: Marvell is targeting customer sampling in 2027.
Each module pairs 72GB of HBM3e with slots for up to eight DDR5 DIMMs, a Photonic Fabric ASIC, and 7.2Tbps of optical I/O, according to Marvell's August 2026 Hot Interconnects presentation.
Hitting 2TB per module means filling all eight slots with 256GB RDIMMs and sixteen modules, joined by a passive all-to-all fiber shuffle rather than an electrical switch, yields 32TB of DDR5 plus 1,152GB of HBM3e, which Marvell rounds to about 1TB and runs as a faster write-through cache in front of the DRAM.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Marvell is going after the economics of today's accelerators. HBM sits roughly 1.5 millimeters from the processor inside the same package, so the only way to buy more of it is to buy more processors. This is increasingly expensive because HBM is extremely costly, and it also means a GPU essentially acts as "the world's most expensive memory controller," as per Dave Lazovsky.
The target workload is the KV cache, the working memory a large language model keeps for each conversation, which balloons with long contexts and agentic sessions. Once it outgrows local HBM and host DRAM, servers either evict it and recompute, or fetch it from much slower storage. This has significant performance implications, and Marvell plans to mitigate it differently.
Ravi Mahatme, who leads product management for the Photonic Fabric unit, said the biggest payoff of a shared tier is "a cross-node KV cache," letting one accelerator reuse context another has already computed. Will Chu, Marvell's EVP of Custom Cloud Solutions, made the broader case in the company's FMS announcement: "As AI scales, memory must scale more independently of compute."
The CAPEX argument is rooted in this: If operators can buy memory separately from accelerators, they no longer need to buy GPUs just to get capacity. This makes sense, but Marvell has yet to put a number to it, even as a May 2026 company blog talks about lower memory cost per gigabyte and lower inference costs without figures, and Celestial AI's 2025 conference slides promised benefits beyond TCO reduction with no supporting numbers.
The timing also isn't ideal for harnessing cheap memory: the approach's 128 DIMM slots draw on the same DDR5 caught up in the current memory crunch, where server RDIMM prices have climbed faster than consumer memory, now around 5.5 times their pre-crisis price in the US.
The appliance design is not entirely new either; Celestial AI presented the same architecture, 16 modules holding 32TB of DDR and about 1TB of HBM, at Hot Interconnects in August 2025, and TechRadar has covered its DDR5-plus-HBM approach back in 2024. What has changed is the Marvell badge, a physical module, and a sampling date.
Nvidia is already hedging, both as an investor and a pioneer
The idea that Nvidia won't sit idle is more than an assumption, because it has been moving for more than a year, including taking a stake in Marvell itself. In March 2026, Nvidia invested $2 billion in Marvell in a deal covering NVLink Fusion and silicon photonics, with Jensen Huang declaring that "The inference inflection has arrived."
It is also important to understand that every NVLink Fusion platform must include at least one Nvidia product, so Nvidia gets paid even when custom silicon wins the socket, but that doesn't mean it doesn't want a piece of that pie anyway.
It is bringing its own answers to the same memory problem in multiple ways; A single Vera Rubin NVL72 rack carries 54TB of LPDDR5X, more than Marvell's entire appliance.
At Nvidia GTC 2026, the company launched BlueField-4 STX, a flash-based context memory tier built for KV cache, claiming up to five times the token throughput of CPU-based storage, with Huang saying reasoning AI needs "a new class of storage." Partner systems are due in the second half of 2026. Back in 2025, Nvidia reportedly spent more than $900 million on Enfabrica, whose EMFASYS system pooled up to 18TB of memory for GPU clusters.
On optics, Nvidia has put $4 billion into Lumentum and Coherent, unveiled photonics switches at GTC 2025, and will offer co-packaged optics as an NVLink option in Feynman-generation systems due in 2028. On the choice between copper and optical scale-up, Huang has said: "We're going to do both."
Marvell still has a long way to go: working silicon, a named customer, a memory partner, and measured throughput on real hardware rather than simulated curves all need to play out exactly as planned.
Until then, the appliance is a well-argued blueprint, and the CAPEX savings remain an argument rather than a number. The irony is hard to miss: the company whose GPUs Lazovsky casts as the world's priciest memory controller owns a $2 billion slice of Marvell, and through NVLink Fusion, stands to earn on the racks either way.
