articles.title: « Les écrans tactiles pires que l’alcool au volant » : cette étude choc pointe du doigt les véhicules modernes
articles.text:
Soyons d’accord sur une chose : les voitures modernes n’ont jamais été aussi sûres, ce qui a contribué à baisser significativement la mortalité sur nos routes. Mais ce constat à première vue flatteur est aujourd’hui remis en cause par une nouvelle étude démontrant les problèmes ergonomiques de nos véhicules. C’est ce que pointe du doigt le cabinet Allianz Zentrum für Technik, qui nous sort des chiffres assez inquiétants.
Selon ses travaux, la distraction du volant interviendrait dans un accident de la route sur trois en tant que facteur déclencheur direct ou que cause contributive. Et quand l’on parle de distraction, on ne parle pas du téléphone au volant, mais bel et bien de l’architecture intérieure des voitures. Autrement dit, c’est la débauche d’écrans tactiles censés être plus modernes qui entraîne un recul significatif sur la sécurité.
À lire aussi : Faux Volant et pédales virtuelles sur l’écran : l’invention improbable de Tesla pour berner les autorités
Quand le design des habitacles met en danger les conducteurs
Si régler simplement la ventilation réclame de passer à travers des sous-menus peu intuitifs, cela peut se comprendre. Si changer la radio exige un panier de manipulations complètement inutiles, cela peut aussi s’expliquer. Si couper les aides à la conduite demande une véritable gymnastique cérébrale, cela pose forcément problème. Le souci, c’est que les conducteurs ne sont pas égaux face aux risques, car chaque modèle de voiture est forcément différent.
Selon Dr Klaus-Peter Röhler, membre du Directoire d’Allianz SE, les « recherches montrent qu’une même tâche peut nécessiter jusqu’à 25 % d’attention visuelle en moins dans un véhicule que dans un autre. Cela nous dit quelque chose d’important : la distraction n’est pas seulement une question de comportement du conducteur. C’est aussi une question de conception […]. Lorsque la sécurité est en jeu, la fonction doit primer sur le design ».
Jusqu’à 3 secondes les yeux fermés : l’inquiétante réalité du tactile
Concrètement, les modèles favorisant le tout tactile peuvent alors augmenter le temps total passé à regarder ailleurs que sur la route de 25 %. Cela correspond environ à trois secondes d’écart pour une même tâche ! Problématique quand l’on sait qu’au-delà de deux secondes, le risque d’accident est déjà significativement augmenté. Un renouvellement complet des habitacles les plus défaillants en la matière est donc souhaité.
Christian Sahr, directeur d’Allianz Zentrum für Technik, précise que « pour garantir une utilisation sûre des véhicules, il est nécessaire de définir clairement quelles fonctions doivent être commandées par des boutons physiques et lesquelles peuvent être accessibles depuis un écran tactile. [Tout cela dans le but de] concevoir des interfaces tactiles qui détournent le moins possible l’attention des conducteurs de la route ».
80 % des automobilistes réclament la fin des écrans géants
Les résultats sont parfaitement de l’avis des principaux intéressés. Selon une enquête menée par Allianz, 80 % des conducteurs français interrogés considèrent que les technologies embarquées ont accentué la distraction au volant. 66 % préfèrent même utiliser des boutons physiques à la place des écrans tactiles. Une proportion qui monte à 82 % chez les jeunes conducteurs de 18 à 25 ans.

articles.title: Elon Musk donó otros USD 76 millones a las legislativas de Estados Unidos en dos semanas
articles.text:
Elon Musk entregó más de USD 76 millones a America PAC, el comité de acción política que fundó y controla, en las primeras dos semanas de octubre de 2026, según una presentación ante la Comisión Federal Electoral de Estados Unidos.
El dinero busca reforzar a los candidatos republicanos antes de las elecciones legislativas del 3 de noviembre del año mencionado.
El reporte, que el comité presentó el 22 de octubre de 2026, detalla tres transferencias directas del empresario por un total de USD 74,8 millones entre el 6 y el 14 de octubre, más otros USD 1,98 millones canalizados a través de su firma United States of America Inc.
Con ese aporte, Musk ya entregó más de USD 445 millones a grupos republicanos en este ciclo electoral, según un análisis de Wired sobre los registros de la comisión. Eso lo convierte en el mayor donante individual conocido de las legislativas de este año.
La cifra ya superó los cerca de USD 288 millones que el líder de Tesla, SpaceX y xAI había destinado a la campaña presidencial de 2024, un gasto que entonces no tuvo precedentes en la historia política reciente de Estados Unidos.
Cómo se repartió el dinero de Elon Musk
America PAC gastó cerca de USD 43 millones durante esas dos semanas mencionadas y llegó al tramo final de la campaña con casi USD 47 millones disponibles en caja, de acuerdo con la misma presentación.
La carrera por el Senado en Texas concentró el mayor desembolso: USD 15,2 millones, el doble de lo que el comité había gastado allí en todo el verano boreal. De ese total, USD 12,4 millones se usaron para atacar al candidato demócrata James Talarico y USD 2,8 millones para promover al republicano Ken Paxton.
Registros posteriores muestran otros USD 9,1 millones contra Talarico, lo que eleva el gasto del comité contra ese candidato a casi USD 28 millones en todo el ciclo, cerca del 40% de todo lo que invirtió en apoyar u oponerse a postulantes al Congreso.
El empresario vive cerca de Austin y sus compañías Tesla, SpaceX y The Boring Company tienen su sede en Texas, el estado donde también se concentra buena parte de la infraestructura de cómputo de xAI, su firma de inteligencia artificial.
Un gasto sin precedentes en la historia reciente
El comité también giró su estrategia hacia la publicidad digital, con USD 11,4 millones invertidos en anuncios en línea durante las mismas dos semanas, una cifra cercana a lo que gastó en correo postal y mensajes de texto combinados.
Del total acumulado por Musk este ciclo, más de USD 165 millones fueron a parar a America PAC desde julio de 2026. El resto se repartió entre otros grupos republicanos, incluido el Senate Leadership Fund, el principal comité que respalda a los candidatos del partido en la disputa por el Senado.
Ese comité recibió USD 158 millones del empresario desde julio, según había confirmado antes una vocera de America PAC a la cadena CNBC. Parte de ese dinero se transfirió luego a un comité específico creado en Texas para apoyar la candidatura de Paxton.
America PAC no respondió a los pedidos de comentario de Wired sobre el nuevo desembolso.
Elon Musk aumenta los ingresos de SpaceX a 14.600 millones de dólares
SpaceX reportó ingresos por USD 14.600 millones durante el tercer trimestre de 2026, impulsados por su negocio de centros de datos e inteligencia artificial, que aportó el 52% de la facturación.
La división Super Inteligencia sumó USD 7.500 millones con Cursor, Grok y servicios de nube, y registró USD 431 millones de beneficio.
El resultado neto total alcanzó USD 4.400 millones, frente a pérdidas un año antes. La empresa invirtió USD 19.600 millones en capital y planea destinar hasta USD 40.000 millones más en el cuarto trimestre. Elon Musk atribuyó los límites de expansión a energía, refrigeración e infraestructura operativa.

articles.title: Capcom Hit by Major Account Breach, 11.7 Million CAPCOM ID Records Accessed
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
Capcom Hit by Major Account Breach, 11.7 Million CAPCOM ID Records Accessed
Capcom has confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed customer data tied to CAPCOM ID, the shared account used for the company's web services and for online play in some of its games. According to Capcom's official notice, a massive 11,774,247 records were affected worldwide, each containing an email address along with the account creation date, last login time, login count, and the IP address from the most recent sign-in. Capcom spotted the suspicious activity on October 19, started blocking it the same day, and reported the incident to the Osaka Prefectural Police and Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission on October 21. A much smaller group of 43 records also exposed dates of birth, gender, country or region, and nicknames. 
The attackers changed the login passwords on 196 accounts too, and Capcom has since reset them. A follow-up notice on October 23 adds that the intruder opened the e-Capcom store pages of 19 of those accounts, exposing names, phone numbers, addresses, and purchase history for those customers in Japan. Capcom says it found no sign that customer-set passwords were compromised, and credit card information was not affected. Capcom hasn't said how the attackers got in, only that the method has been identified and dealt with. CAPCOM ID and Capcom's games remain available. The bigger risk now seems to be phishing, so anyone with a CAPCOM ID is advised to treat messages claiming to come from Capcom with suspicion.
Sources:
				Capcom's Official Notice, 				Update			
	
	
	
		
	
		
4 Comments on Capcom Hit by Major Account Breach, 11.7 Million CAPCOM ID Records Accessed
(Yes, I realise that this is just a strawman they propped to soften the news to customers)
The only thing I want to hear from a company in such a situation is “there is no risk of identifiable user data being compromised because we don’t store any”. Anything else is just nonsense. I don’t even understand why this whole Capcom ID thing exists. Their SP games obviously don’t need accounts and anything MP is handled (presumably) via console vendors and Steam. Each time when I played the newer REs or DMC5 and the game asks me whether I would like to make an account I am stupefied that anyone actually goes “yeah, sure, I want a pointless account, why not”.
Honestly, I wouldn't be surprised of a good chunk of those people didn't even stop to consider that it was pointless. They double click on a game icon, screen goes black, then some text pops up telling them they should sign up to RE dot net or whatever, so they do that.
Even I started to get fatigued dismissing all this incessant prodding to sign away my right to my identity/privacy (thanks, GDPR :shadedshu:).

articles.title: NATO jammers will block out GPS for miles around — and they could be the secret weapon in the next big conflict
articles.text:
NATO jammers will block out GPS for miles around — and they could be the secret weapon in the next big conflict
After three years of Russian GPS jamming over Europe's eastern flank, NATO has decided its crews need to train against the real thing
- NATO's modernization command plans to buy six portable kits that can jam GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, and BeiDou, plus drone control and video links
- The blackout radius is adjustable from 500 m to 11 km, and each kit must deploy in 30 minutes, run for four hours on battery, and be controllable remotely over encrypted satellite links
- The purchase is a direct response to years of Russian-blamed GPS interference over the Baltic, including the 2025 jamming of the President of the European Commission's aircraft over Bulgaria
NATO is shopping for the ability to make satellite navigation disappear, on command, over an area the size of a small city.
The alliance's modernization command has signaled plans to buy six portable kits that can jam satellite navigation signals and the radio links drones use for control and video, so trainers can expose ships, aircrews, and drone operators to realistic interference during exercises.
For context, NATO wants to practice fighting in the same electromagnetic fog Russia has been generating over Europe's eastern flank for most of the past three years.
What is the NATO actually buying?
The buyer is Headquarters Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, the Norfolk, Virginia, command that runs NATO's training and modernization work. According to the notice, first reported by Defence Blog, the command intends to issue a request for proposals on October 26, 2026, with bids due November 30 and a resulting fixed-price contract expected on December 11.
The kits are framed as training gear, but the fine print leaves the door open for much more: they could also be used in operations. The requirements read like a wish list for electronic warfare.
Each kit must be light enough for one or two people to carry, ready to use within 30 minutes, and able to operate from a ship, rigid inflatable boat, uncrewed surface vessel, vehicle, tripod, or fixed ground site. It must also be able to target all satellites at once.
The system must be able to jam all four major satellite navigation constellations, America's GPS, Russia's GLONASS, Europe's Galileo, and China's BeiDou, across multiple frequency bands simultaneously, with each band individually selectable.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Operators must be able to set the area where satellite navigation is denied anywhere from 500 meters to 11 km (6 nautical miles), in increments of no more than 500 meters. That is a jamming bubble you can expand or shrink like a volume knob.
Because an invisible wall of interference near civilian aviation is potentially a genuine hazard, vendors must supply tables predicting how far the effect will reach at altitudes up to 10,000 ft (about 3,050 m), so exercise planners can keep it clear of civilian air traffic.
The drone-killing side is more complex but equally specific: beyond satellite signals, the kits must jam drone video links in the 5 to 6 GHz band and drone control links at 400 to 500 MHz and 2 to 3 GHz, along with several cellular and other bands. That maps neatly onto how small drones actually get beaten in the field. As the notice itself explains, interfering with a drone's navigation or control signals can push it off course, force it to hover, land, or fly home, or cut the operator's video feed.
NATO also does not want a system that only a signals-intelligence professional can run. The requirement calls for the kit to be operated from a laptop with an interface simple enough for non-specialists, with both omnidirectional and directional antennas, at least four hours of battery operation, and the ability to be controlled remotely anywhere in the world over encrypted satellite links, with a local override and a remote shutdown.
Not just a random wishlist for a GPS jammer
This procurement does not come out of nowhere. GPS interference has shifted from a rare curiosity to daily background noise along NATO's eastern edge. The alliance's own notice points to the pattern, noting that jamming has become a regular problem around the Baltic Sea, where airlines and shipping have reported widespread interference that several European governments have blamed on Russia.
The most politically pointed episode came in 2025. The NATO notice recalls that an aircraft carrying European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen lost GPS signals while approaching an airport in Bulgaria, an incident Bulgarian authorities attributed to suspected Russian interference.
An important distinction underlies all of this, and it explains why NATO wants crews to practice against the real thing rather than read about it. Jamming simply drowns the signal. Spoofing is nastier: it feeds a receiver a convincing but false position, so the crew never gets a clean warning that anything is wrong. As explained in our coverage of GNSS vulnerability, the real danger of spoofing is that the victim doesn't know what is happening and keeps acting on false information.
NATO argues that its training and evaluation teams need equipment that can create controlled interference on demand, so crews can be watched as they detect, report, and adapt.
For an alliance that has spent three years on the receiving end of Russia's electronic harassment, buying six suitcases that can do the same thing on cue is less about matching Moscow and more about making sure its own people are not blind when the signal drops. The kicker is obviously that the for-training component could just as easily be used aggressively by the same organization, that is, if the spec sheet holds.

articles.title: "¿Podrías votar por Eliska?" El mensaje inocente que puede robarte el WhatsApp
articles.text:
Si estos días uno de tus contactos quiere pedirte un favorcito por WhatsApp, mejor que le digas: gracias pero no, gracias. Cuando alguien nos pide dinero es fácil desconfiar, incluso aunque se haga pasar por nuestro hijo y supuestamente su teléfono se haya roto (que no tengas descendencia simplifica mucho el asunto), pero cuando lo que quiere es algo tan sencillo, rápido y a priori inocente como un voto para un concurso de baile, la cosa cambia.
En ese momento una frase surca mi mente ("bah, chica, si no cuesta nada") sugiriéndome perder ese minuto en votar, menos mal que ser una perezosa juega a mi favor en estos menesteres, pero soy consciente de que no todo el mundo es tan malqueda, especialmente porque el mensaje llega desde uno de tus contactos, que bien puede ser tu amiga del alma. Además de hacer feliz a una criatura y su progenitor, promete una clase de baile gratis. Y lo haces.
Un enlace que no es lo que dice ser. El enlace lleva a una web que simula una votación, pide el teléfono y muestra un código con instrucciones para introducirlo en WhatsApp. Pista: es la información que hace falta para vincular un dispositivo externo a una cuenta, lo que como explica el INCIBE, permitiría escribir a tus contactos sin autorización y por ejemplo, seguir reenviando este mismo mensaje a tus contactos, aumentando la red de potenciales víctimas.
Estamos ante un fraude por ghostpairing (emparejamiento fantasma) y funciona como cuando usas WhatsApp Web en tu ordenador porque en realidad es exactamente eso lo que estás haciendo y a lo que tienen acceso quienes están detrás: tus chats, contactos, todo lo que compartes y te comparten.
Es solo el principio. En esta estafa no hay malware de por medio, pero sí un acceso a una cantidad ingente de datos sensibles y privados y la usurpación de tu cuenta, que los ciberdelicuentes pueden usar para seguir difundiendo mensajes fraudulentos y solicitudes de dinero. Sin ir más lejos, la petición de dinero ante una situación de emergencia (por ejemplo, ante una visita al dentista que sale mucho más cara de lo esperado) suena mucho más creíble si te llega desde un contacto que si lo hace desde un número desconocido. Por ejemplo, si te llega de tu hijo o de tu hija.
De hecho, el INCIBE alertaba hace pocos días del uso de cuentas de contactos para pedir dinero a sus contactos ante una supuesta urgencia y facilitan un número de cuenta. Y ojo porque les está funcionando: según Bitdefender, se han identificado 177 dominios fraudulentos y 554 URLs únicas vinculadas a esta campaña de ingeniería social.
Qué hacer si recibo este mensaje. Lo mejor es no abrir el enlace y si lo haces, no facilites tu número ni sigas las instrucciones. El Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad pide que lo reportes con un pantallazo y elimines el chat después. Para evitar riesgos de suplantación, lo mejor es activar la verificación en dos pasos de WhatsApp (entra en tus ajustes y en 'Cuenta' > 'Verificación en dos pasos' y activa la opción).
Si "ya has votado" y por tanto, has metido tu número, ve nuevamente a los 'Ajustes' > 'Dispositivos vinculados' y cierra todas las sesiones que no conozcas, además de poner en conocimiento los hechos con el INCIBE y las autoridades. Y si algún conocido te pide dinero por chat, lo mejor que puedes hacer es verificarlo por otro canal, incluso simplemente llamando por teléfono.

articles.title: Rare archival footage tours the CompUSA NYC store in November 2000 — soak up some Y2K Pentium III, Athlon, PowerPC, Windows Me, chunky laptop, and bulging CRT nostalgia in glorious 360p
articles.text:
Rare archival footage tours the CompUSA NYC store in November 2000 — soak up some Y2K Pentium III, Athlon, PowerPC, Windows Me, chunky laptop, and bulging CRT nostalgia in glorious 360p
Footage was filmed when Presarios and iMacs with translucent acrylic cases ruled the retail world.
A video purported to be “authentic, original 360p footage captured inside a CompUSA retail store in New York City” has been shared on YouTube, allowing retro computing fans to step back in time to November 2000. This was the Windows Me, Pentium III, and Athlon era, dominated by computers constructed using a lot of translucent plastics and beige boxes already a distant memory. However, computer stores like this bulged with displays and fast-selling stock before internet shopping would start to eat many of these businesses away.
The video reveals a nostalgic CompUSA, greeted by a wall of CRT monitors. The store looks crowded and almost chaotic with peripherals, PCs, and devices - and boxes filling a lot of space in the aisles.
The first item is a noteworthy trio of laptops. It looks like three stylish Sony VAIO machines in a line. In the center of this display is probably the most interesting device from the time, which we believe to be a Sony VAIO C1 Series ‘PictureBook’ PCG-C1VN subnotebook. Searches indicate this device was powered by the Transmeta Crusoe TM5600 processor running at 600 MHz, supported by 128MB of SDRAM, and a 12GB HDD. The tiny form factor, weighing in at around 2.2 pounds (1kg), was built around an 8.9-inch TFT display of 1024 x 480 pixels. It also had a dGPU, an ATI Rage Mobility with 8MB dedicated VRAM.
Above this trio of laptops, there's a spec card for one of the larger laptops available in store. Squinting at the 360p video, it appears the unnamed portable has an Intel Pentium III 700 MHz CPU, S3 graphics, 128GB of RAM, and a 20GB HDD.
Next up, the video shows some New Yorkers (or tourists) browsing desktop machines including Compaq Presario PCs, with characteristic translucent accent faceplates – clearly inspired by the iMac. Again, we would expect these came with Celeron/Pentium III processors, or AMD Athlon/Duron chips from that era. Graphics cards in these would typically be Nvidia RIVA TNT2 or GeForce2 MX cards.
Later on, the video shows a significant amount of store space stacked with boxes for perhaps 100 Compaq Presario desktops. On one box you can see the model number ‘5WV294.’ According to our searches, that model would come with an AMD Athlon 1.0 GHz, 128MB RAM, 30-40GB HDD, an optical drive, and Nvidia GeForce2 MX or S3 Savage4 / ProSavage 3D graphics.
The video also shows Apple Mac desktops powered up next to matching monitors. Even with Apple’s serious professional desktops, by 2000 the beige era was long gone. A spec card shows that one of the Apple desktops on display is the Power Macintosh G4 Dual 500. Yes, it had twin 500 MHz G4 processors, as well as 256MB memory, a 40GB HDD, a DVD RAM drive, and a 16MB video card, costing an eye-watering $3,500. We previously mentioned the ‘iMac era’ and indeed, an in-store wall of perhaps 50 boxed iMac computers is shown later in the video.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
A 21-inch ViewSonic A110 monitor displaying a demo reel with Apple monitors and Apple Macs is also featured. It is a high-end model, priced at $750. Printers appear in the video too, with various HP models boxed up. The video also shows a shelf of unboxed printers and MFPs on display, and you can see someone pondering over one. Mice, mouse mats, and a Windows Me ‘Take Me Home’ promotional in-store display also catch the cameraman’s eye.
The video ends with a scene at the checkout, and folks buying sundries and peripherals. The last customer appears to be inquiring about a mail-in rebate for an HP printer. Some things never change.
CompUSA collapsed due to competition from big box stores, the ascent of online retailers, and various managerial missteps. The store brand saw mass closures and liquidation in 2007/8, with a handful of stores kept alive by Systemax/TigerDirect. The CompUSA retail identity was finally retired in 2012.

articles.title: Alerte, un nouvel infostealer s’intéresse grandement à vos comptes et sessions Claude, ChatGPT et Copilot
articles.text:
Check Point Research a identifié Aokigahara, un nouvel infostealer, un voleur d'informations qui cible les identifiants et les sessions de Claude, ChatGPT ou GitHub Copilot. Le malware vise aussi les accès cloud et les secrets des développeurs.
Baptisé Aokigahara, ce nouvel infostealer, un logiciel malveillant conçu pour siphonner en silence les données d'un appareil infecté, a été découvert par Check Point Research, qui le révèle ce vendredi 23 octobre. Comme ses semblables, il renifle les cookies, les mots de passe enregistrés dans le navigateur et les portefeuilles crypto. Mais il a aussi ajouté les comptes d'IA à son menu. Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor ou Gemini CLI sont dans son viseur, avec une cible bien précise, le jeton de session, cette petite clé numérique stockée sur l'appareil qui vous garde connecté sans redemander votre mot de passe. Une fois volée, elle suffit en théorie à se glisser dans votre compte. Et sur l'ordinateur d'un développeur, le butin peut vite prendre des allures de trousseau complet, du code source jusqu'au cloud.
Un infostealer qui a pris goût aux assistants d'IA
Le principe d'un infostealer, ou voleur d'informations en français, est tout sauf nouveau. Lumma Stealer, Vidar, Agent Tesla ou Raccoon Stealer font partie des plus connus. Une fois installé sur une machine, il fouille et ramasse tout ce qui a de la valeur. Aokigahara regroupe ce qu'il trouve dans des archives chiffrées, puis il expédie le tout vers son serveur de commande et de contrôle, la tour de contrôle d'où ses opérateurs pilotent le malware. Ce qui le distingue, c'est un module, autrement dit une brique du programme chargée d'une mission bien précise. Baptisé « aisessions », un nom qui ne laisse guère de place au doute, vous serez d'accord, il est entièrement dédié aux outils d'intelligence artificielle.
Aokigahara s'intéresse particulièrement à Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Cursor et Windsurf. Le malware y cherche des fichiers d'authentification, jetons et données de configuration. Un jeton, c'est un peu le bracelet qu'on vous passe au poignet à l'entrée d'un festival, c'est-à-dire que tant qu'il reste valide, personne ne vous redemande votre billet. Ici, personne ne vous redemande votre mot de passe.
Une fois la porte franchie, l'intrus ne met pas seulement la main sur un compte. Il y trouve l'historique des conversations, les documents téléversés, parfois du code ou des informations confidentielles d'entreprise. Il y a aussi un abonnement payant qu'un inconnu pourrait consommer à vos frais, ou revendre comme accès piraté. Des échanges sensibles pourraient même servir de levier pour faire chanter leur propriétaire. Check Point reste prudent à ce sujet. Ses chercheurs ne peuvent pas confirmer que les identifiants volés aient été revendus ou réutilisés, et aucune tentative d'extorsion n'a été observée. Une certitude, en revanche, l'outil a été délibérément conçu pour les récolter.
Sur le poste des développeurs, le butin change d'échelle
Aokigahara ne s’arrête pas aux seuls chatbots que le grand public a en partie bien pris en main. Il s’intéresse aussi aux identifiants Git, qui ouvrent l’accès aux dépôts de code, ces espaces où les équipes stockent et partagent leurs programmes. Il fouille les fichiers liés à SSH, le protocole qui permet de piloter un serveur à distance, ainsi que les identifiants et configurations AWS, Azure et Google Cloud, les clouds d’Amazon, Microsoft et Google sur lesquels tournent sites, applications et bases de données d’entreprise. Même les logiciels dans lesquels s’écrit le code, comme VS Code ou les outils JetBrains, sont dans son viseur. Du coup, un seul ordinateur de développeur peut renfermer à lui seul les clés du code, du cloud et des assistants d’IA
Check Point précise toutefois que les volets IA et développement fonctionnent comme des modules séparés, et rien ne prouve que les pirates les enchaînent au sein d'une même attaque. Leur cohabitation reste révélatrice. Pendant des années, les infostealers ont visé les mots de passe, les sessions de navigateur, les données financières et la crypto. Leurs cibles épousent désormais notre manière de travailler, et l'IA en fait clairement partie.
Pour Eli Smadja, responsable de la recherche chez Check Point Research, les attaquants suivent « inévitablement les utilisateurs » là où ils travaillent. Les sessions d'IA ne sont donc plus de simples données d'application secondaires. Ce sont des accès sensibles, au même titre qu'un compte cloud. Protéger ce que l'on confie à un chatbot ne règle qu'une partie du problème. Il faut aussi protéger les jetons qui y donnent accès et, dès qu'un appareil est compromis, passer les sessions d'IA en revue comme les accès navigateur ou cloud. Votre chatbot mérite désormais un cadenas.

articles.title: Hybrid infrastructure costs push AI inference to the edge - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Hybrid infrastructure decisions put AI costs and control in focus
Enterprise artificial intelligence is entering a cost-conscious phase, and hybrid infrastructure is where that reckoning plays out. As inference spending climbs, business leaders are weighing where models run, which models they use and how much of their data they are willing to hand to someone else.
Those cost considerations are reshaping buying decisions across industries, including among financial institutions trying to turn siloed data into real-time action. More than 6,500 enterprises have adopted the Dell AI Factory with Nvidia updates, according to Dell. A sharp shift in token economics is changing what customers ask for, according to Kyle Dufresne (pictured), senior vice president of sales at Dell.
“It’s incredible to see just over the last three months where we saw 80% of the tokens being generated from frontier models. Three months later, 80% of the tokens in the world are being generated by open models,” Dufresne said. “Why? Because of cost. And everybody talks about tokenomics.”
Dufresne spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed tokenomics, hybrid infrastructure and how Dell is helping customers plan AI investments. (* Disclosure below.)
Inference costs push hybrid infrastructure toward the edge
Inference is now growing faster than training, though both are expanding quickly, according to Dufresne. That shift is changing where AI work happens, with Dell seeing inference run wherever data is created — in the cloud, in the data center and out to PCs.
“We’re seeing the business owners saying, ‘Oh my gosh, these costs are getting really high for inferencing. How do we reduce those costs without curbing innovation?'” Dufresne said. “We’re finding it’s happening across that continuum but more and more right out at the far edge.”
The economics also raise a strategic question about control. Companies have to decide whether they want to outsource their data and differentiation, and they are now pricing AI based on where workloads run, which models they use and where their data sits, Dufresne explained. Dell has framed its latest AI Factory with Nvidia updates around helping customers get results on infrastructure they control.
“We’re seeing every single [chief financial officer] in the world that has implemented these structures saying, ‘Gosh, my token costs are exploding,'” he said. “‘How do we drive costs out?'”
Supply is the other side of the ledger. Memory prices are pushing technology costs up rather than down, and about 20% more memory will reach the market next year against roughly 200% more demand, Dufresne estimated. Dell is responding with collaborative planning, steering customers toward more readily available components and sharing advance visibility into upcoming cost increases. Many customers find their cost of capital is lower than component inflation, so they are buying earlier.
“It’s not only just being able to provide the technology,” Dufresne said. “But also to be able to share with customers what’s going to happen in the future so they can make better decisions today on the use of their capital.”

articles.title: Un modelo de Anthropic siguió un ciberataque contra una persona real aunque sabía que le causaba daño
articles.text:
Anthropic reconoció que un agente de su modelo Mythos 5 mantuvo un ciberataque contra un desarrollador real de código abierto incluso después de que la empresa le advirtiera, en experimentos controlados, que su objetivo era una persona existente y no una simulación. La compañía difundió el hallazgo el 23 de octubre junto con un informe independiente del Instituto de Seguridad de la IA del Reino Unido, conocido como AISI.
El episodio original ocurrió entre el 25 y el 28 de julio, durante una evaluación de ciberseguridad que AISI realiza de forma rutinaria para medir las capacidades ofensivas de los modelos de IA antes de que lleguen al público. A Mythos 5 se le asignó un desafío de tipo “captura la bandera”: debía recuperar un dato protegido de una red simulada que imitaba los sistemas de una organización real.
Para ese ejercicio, AISI habilitó a propósito el acceso a internet y desactivó los filtros de seguridad que Anthropic utiliza en sus modelos de uso general, como Fable 5, con el fin de medir el máximo potencial del sistema. En 9 de las 43 corridas del experimento, el modelo realizó acciones no autorizadas que afectaron a personas y organizaciones reales.
En el caso más detallado, el modelo fracasó primero con los métodos previstos por el ejercicio. Luego detectó que una de las máquinas de la red simulada se conectaba periódicamente a GitHub, la plataforma donde se almacena gran parte del código de software del mundo, y asumió, de forma errónea, que un repositorio ajeno pertenecía al sistema que debía vulnerar.
Identidades falsas para presionar a un desarrollador
Mythos 5 intentó subir código malicioso a ese repositorio, que en realidad administraban desarrolladores sin relación con la prueba. Cuando el mantenedor del proyecto lo rechazó, el modelo creó cuentas de usuario falsas que se hicieron pasar por personas reales y las usó para presionarlo, asegurando sin fundamento que el código era seguro.
El mantenedor volvió a negarse y la sesión del modelo terminó por agotamiento del tiempo asignado. Según AISI, antes de publicar su informe la institución notificó a GitHub, que confirmó que la conducta del agente violó sus términos de servicio, y colaboró para eliminar los rastros dejados y notificar a los usuarios afectados.
Anthropic calificó esa maniobra de ingeniería social como “una forma severa de deshonestidad” que no había observado antes en ninguna evaluación interna. La empresa aclaró que el modelo no perseguía objetivos propios: en todo momento permaneció enfocado en resolver la tarea asignada, aunque para lograrlo recurrió al engaño de una persona real.
El modelo casi nunca frenó por su cuenta
Lo más llamativo del análisis publicado el 23 de octubre son los experimentos de repetición que hizo Anthropic sobre la transcripción completa del incidente. Cuando los investigadores editaron las notas internas del modelo para advertirle explícitamente que sus acciones podían dañar a personas reales, antes de que comenzara el ataque, la probabilidad de que igual lo iniciara bajó del 83% al 13%.
El problema apareció una vez que el ataque ya estaba en marcha. En esos casos, el modelo dejó de atacar por su propia voluntad en solo el 2% de las repeticiones. Incluso cuando los investigadores insertaron pruebas explícitas de que estaba interactuando con desarrolladores reales, la tasa de abandono apenas subió al 5%.
Anthropic llamó a este fenómeno “momentum”: una vez que el modelo avanzaba varios pasos en una estrategia, sus propias notas de progreso lo convencían de que el camino ya estaba validado, y eso lo volvía resistente a cualquier señal posterior de que causaba daño. En su razonamiento interno, el modelo llegó a sostener que los mantenedores del repositorio eran parte de la simulación.
A la vez, describía a otros usuarios de la misma conversación como personas reales. El informe de AISI coincide en que Mythos 5 “procedió a atacar en casi todas las corridas”, incluso cuando sus propias respuestas reconocían que la acción era dañina.
Modelos más recientes y qué cambia ahora
Según la institución británica, aclarar en las notas del modelo que el objetivo era una persona real no redujo la tasa de ataque. Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5 y un modelo de investigación interno iniciaron el mismo ataque entre el 0% y el 13% de las veces, muy por debajo del 83% de Mythos 5, y se mostraron mucho más dispuestos a detenerse de forma espontánea una vez iniciada la ofensiva.
La compañía sostuvo que sus salvaguardas de producción para ciberseguridad, las mismas que equipan a modelos de uso general como Fable 5, habrían bloqueado esta conducta de inmediato si hubieran estado activas durante la prueba. Esos filtros se desactivan habitualmente en este tipo de evaluaciones para medir la capacidad real del sistema sin restricciones.
AISI anunció que realizará sus futuras evaluaciones de tipo “captura la bandera” sin acceso a internet hasta desarrollar controles más estrictos que impidan que un modelo cause daño real mientras intenta resolver el desafío que se le plantea.

articles.title: Une recharge complète en 9 minutes pour 10 000 € : BYD frappe très fort avec sa nouvelle citadine
articles.text:
Voilà certainement la révolution que tout le monde attendait : une voiture électrique accessible capable de se ravitailler aussi vite qu’un modèle thermique. BYD réalise officiellement ce tour de force avec la nouvelle Seagull, qui est équipée de la technologie Flash Charging. Entendez par là l’une des recharges les plus rapides qui soient dans un petit véhicule particulièrement bon marché.
Pour faire simple, le 10 à 70 % de batterie est donné en 5 minutes alors que le 10 à 97 % de charge ne prend que 9 minutes. En outre, le prix de base de la Seagull est fixé à 65 900 yuans, soit environ 8 800 €. Pour bénéficier de la fameuse recharge rapide, il faudra débourser au minimum 75 900 yuans, ce qui équivaut plus ou moins à 10 100 €. C’est tout simplement la voiture électrique au meilleur rapport prix/vitesse de recharge sur le marché !
À lire aussi : 1 000 km d’autonomie et recharge en 5 minutes pour 32 000 € – BYD lance une limousine scandaleuse
Plus grande et plus spacieuse : 5 vraies places à bord
Et ce n’est pas tout, l’auto est aussi infiniment plus habitable que la Dolphin Surf qu’elle remplace. Avec une longueur portée à 4,21 mètres, la Seagull toise son prédécesseur de 43 bons centimètres ! De quoi offrir un habitacle plus spacieux pouvant accueillir jusqu’à cinq personnes au lieu de quatre. L’extérieur évolue malgré tout en douceur avec les codes que l’on connaît déjà sur la Dolphin Surf.
La face avant conserve son regard frondeur avec ses feux affinés, tandis que le profil, rallongé, garde aussi son vitrage caractéristique pincé au niveau du montant C. La poupe, elle, reste bien verticale avec ses feux horizontaux. Pas de révolution à attendre de ce côté-là contrairement à la présentation intérieure, en nette amélioration. Outre des matériaux bien mieux choisis, c’est la technologie embarquée qui étonne.
Écran géant, IA DeepSeek et conduite autonome : un équipement haut de gamme
On bénéficiera notamment d’un écran tactile de 15,6 pouces avec l’IA DeepSeek, des sièges avant électriques, chauffants et ventilés avec fonction massage côté conducteur, d’une sonorisation à 8 haut-parleurs, d’un éclairage d’ambiance à 127 couleurs, d’un coffre avant de 94 litres et d’un chargeur de smartphone par induction de 50 W. La conduite semi-autonome est bien entendu de la partie, avec le LiDAR DiPilot 300 « God’s Eye ».
Cette dernière permet une autonomie partielle sur route et totale en ville et sur autoroute. Côté technique, la nouvelle Seagull offre en parallèle du Flash Charging la batterie Blade 2.0 déclinée en 30,1 et 39,2 kWh autorisant des autonomies respectives de 320 et 420 km sur le cycle CLTC. L’auto pourrait débarquer en Europe pour remplacer la vieillissante Dolphin. Mais elle sera bien plus chère en raison des taxes. Comptez plutôt un prix d’entrée de 30 000 €.

articles.title: Meta adia mudança nos termos após reação negativa • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Meta adia mudança nos termos após reação negativa
Regras criticadas devem entrar em vigor em 20 de novembro.
A Meta adiou seus novos termos comerciais após críticas de anunciantes e entidades. O texto permitiu interpretações de que abriria caminho para a coleta de conteúdo para treinar IAs sem a necessidade de negociar licenças com seus produtores. As regras, que começariam a valer em 30 de outubro, agora estão previstas para entrar em vigor em 20 de novembro.
Em nota enviada ao Tecnoblog, a empresa afirma que decidiu ampliar o prazo para responder às preocupações levantadas por parceiros e esclarecer melhor como seus rastreadores funcionam.
A primeira versão das novas regras dizia que a Meta poderia usar ferramentas automatizadas, como rastreadores e bots, para acessar páginas e conteúdos de contas empresariais. O texto também afirmava que esses materiais poderiam ser usados para desenvolver, melhorar, pesquisar e treinar produtos da empresa.
Especialistas alertaram que isso poderia dar à Meta uma base para coletar conteúdo de sites ligados a empresas que usam suas plataformas. Depois das críticas, a companhia modificou os termos e retirou referências explícitas ao treinamento de produtos. A alteração, porém, não encerrou as preocupações.
A nova versão ainda parece permitir a coleta de conteúdo de sites associados a contas comerciais para uso no desenvolvimento de produtos da Meta, que podem incluir ferramentas de IA.
A pressão aumentou para que autoridades antitruste da União Europeia e do Reino Unido suspendessem a chegada da mudança. Segundo a Reuters, um dos argumentos é que empresas dependentes de Facebook, Instagram e outros serviços poderiam acabar concedendo à Meta direitos sobre conteúdos disponíveis em seus sites.
Nos Estados Unidos, a News/Media Alliance, entidade que representa mais de 2 mil jornais, revistas e veículos digitais, afirma que as regras podem prejudicar o mercado de licenciamento de conteúdo e pede a retirada das cláusulas.
A Meta contesta a interpretação de que os novos termos ampliam seus direitos sobre conteúdos publicados na internet e afirma que as regras não mudam como seus rastreadores acessam sites. Ao Tecnoblog, a empresa disse que o adiamento servirá para esclarecer as mudanças.
“Estamos prorrogando a data de entrada em vigor dos nossos termos atualizados para 20 de novembro, para que tenhamos mais tempo para esclarecer aos nossos parceiros e stakeholders o que muda e o que não muda”, afirma.
A plataforma também diz que os “proprietários de conteúdo continuarão podendo usar o robots.txt para sinalizar suas preferências.” O robots.txt é um arquivo usado por sites para indicar quais áreas podem ou não ser acessadas por rastreadores automatizados.
O adiamento não significa que a empresa tenha desistido dos novos termos. Até o momento, a Meta apenas transferiu a entrada em vigor para 20 de novembro. As três semanas adicionais podem abrir espaço para novos ajustes enquanto a companhia responde às críticas levantadas.

articles.title: Steam Deck OLED Finally Gets HDR Streaming Back in Latest Update's "Big Revamp"
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
Steam Deck OLED Finally Gets HDR Streaming Back in Latest Update's "Big Revamp"
Valve disabled HDR during Remote Play game streaming on the Steam Deck OLED in early October alongside its Big Art Mode update. Although it was never specified why the feature was disabled, there were reports of bugs and issues with HDR support on the Steam Deck OLED, and it seems as though Valve had been working on revamping HDR support on the Steam Deck OLED altogether, according to a recent Steam Client beta update. 
The update notes for the latest Steam Client preview/beta update cite an overhaul for Remote Play, adding a host of features and options as well as re-enabling HDR support on the Steam Deck OLED. In addition to HDR being re-enabled, there are now options to switch between automatic mode, which only enables HDR when HDR content is detected, and an always-on mode that allows for higher brightness when viewing SDR content.HDR is also now enabled with Remote Play on Windows, in games and on the desktop, via Pipewire on the Linux desktop, when streaming from macOS, and when streaming to an Android device using Steam Link when running Android 15 or newer.

articles.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: Another triumph, but we should have had Readiness years ago
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a fantastic refinement of Apple's rugged smartwatch, with excellent battery life, responsive performance, and the new Readiness Score standing out as one of my favorite additions. It gives Apple's health features a more useful, actionable edge without another subscription, making the Ultra 4 a compelling all-rounder — even if Ultra 3 owners won't find enough here to rush out and upgrade.
Reasons to buy
- + Another battery life increase
- + Readiness Score makes your activity data actionable without a monthly price
- + S11 chip ensures a responsive experience
- + Still a very rugged build
Reasons to avoid
- - No major design changes
- - Not a night-and-day performance boost over Ultra 3
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: One minute review
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn't a radical aesthetic redesign, but it doesn't need to be. Apple's rugged smartwatch keeps the familiar 49mm titanium build, bright display, and customizable Action Button, while upgrades to its rear health sensors and internals make it a more capable companion for everyday wear and endurance workouts.
The biggest upgrade is arguably its battery life. Apple promises up to 50 hours of normal use, but I've easily managed two days with the Always-On display enabled and sleep tracking running overnight. That's seriously impressive for a fully featured smartwatch, even if some lower-power rivals like the best Garmin watches can last longer.
The new S11 chip keeps everything feeling responsive, with apps opening quickly and watchOS 27 running smoothly. Faster charging is another welcome addition, letting me replenish around 30% of the battery in just 15 to 20 minutes.
Health and fitness tracking also gets a meaningful boost. The new Health Sensing System improves measurements, and Readiness Score is one of my favorite additions to watchOS 27. It gives you a useful snapshot of how prepared you might be for the day, without requiring another subscription.
It also adds plenty of smaller quality-of-life improvements, including real-time step-count complications. Siri AI also brings more intelligence to the wrist, with features like Shazam and Sound Recognition. Siri Rewind and Live Recap have yet to arrive and prove themselves.
The downside is that the Ultra 4 looks and feels much like its predecessor, so Ultra 3 owners may not find enough here to justify an immediate upgrade. And while the battery life is excellent, the Ultra 4 still can't match every rival in sheer endurance.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $799 / £749 / AU$1,349 and is available now in Natural Titanium or Black Titanium. Both finishes come with Wi-Fi and cellular connectivity, so there's no need to choose between separate Bluetooth-only and cellular models, as you can with the Apple Watch Series 12.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Ultimately, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a refined, reliable smartwatch that builds on an already excellent foundation. Its multi-day battery life, capable fitness tracking, and smoother watchOS experience make it a compelling choice for endurance athletes and Apple fans who want a rugged watch that does it all.
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Video review
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Specs Table
| Component | Apple Watch Ultra 4 | 
| Price | $799 / £749 / AU$1,349 | 
| Dimension | 49 x 44 x 12mm | 
| Weight | 63g (without band) | 
| Case/bezel | Grad 5 Titanium | 
| Display | 49mm Always-On Retina LTPO3 OLED display (up to 3,000 nits) | 
| Processor | Apple-made S11 chip | 
| GPS | Dual‑Frequency GPS (GPS, Galileo, QZSS, and BeiDou) | 
| Battery life | Up to 50 hours with normal use | 
| Connections | 4G LTE, Satellite SOS, Wi‑Fi 4 (802.11n), Bluetooth 5.3 | 
| Water resistant | Water resistance 100m | 
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Price and availability
- $799 / £749 / AU$1,349
- No increase from last year
- You’re paying for an LTE model as usual
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 costs $799 / £749 / AU$1,349, and comes in Natural Titanium or Black Titanium, with both finishes including Wi-Fi and cellular connectivity as standard. This means you’re paying for your phone’s ability to add to a data plan whether you want to or not.
The watch is more expensive than other Apple Watches, which is standard for the Ultra series, but crucially, it’s the same price as the Apple Watch Ultra 3, with no annual price increase. In an era of an electronics components crisis, this is great news. It’s also absolutely stuffed with features as usual, with a premium build quality that, together, justifies the high price.
- Value score: 4.5/5
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Design
- Redesigned sensor array
- Identical display and case
- Useful programmable Action button
Like the Apple Watch Ultra 1, 2, and 3 before it, the Ultra 4 stands on its own in Apple's smartwatch lineup, offering one option: a squircle 49mm screen in a thicker, much more rugged design that's ready for the road — and truly any road. It still comes in Black or Natural Titanium and looks pretty much the same as previous iterations on your wrist. Still, the one-size-fits-all device is an issue for smaller wrists.
I've been testing the silver Natural Titanium version, and it's been a welcome change after rocking the Black Ultra 3 for well over a year. I like the contrast of the silver rim around the 49mm Retina display, and especially how the ‘Ultra Orange’ Action Button on the left side pops against the silver case.
The Action Button remains a nice addition for easily running a customized Siri Shortcut or quickly starting a workout, and the 49mm Always-On Retina OLED LTPO3 display still looks great in pretty much any condition, whether that's under fluorescent lights, in the gym, or outside on a very sunny day.
The Action Button sits alongside the speaker and microphone on the left side, while the rugged Digital Crown (with its orange ring) and the main side button live on the right. The top and bottom of the Apple Watch are still where the bands connect, and there's no change to the connector — fingers crossed Apple never changes that, as it’s exemplary.
The main design changes, aside from the new bands, are on the rear. Apple is rolling out a new Health Sensing System to the Ultra 4 and Series 12, which looks a little like a complex sundial on the back of the case. It features a new wider layout for electrodes and diodes to cover a larger surface area on the wrist, which lets the Apple Watch take more accurate health measurements — particularly when tracking heart rate.
This is also where the magnetic Apple Watch charger attaches, and the box includes an updated charging puck. It still connects to a wall adapter or another power source via USB-C, with improvements to charging speed. And while the Series 12 is still a stunner and the Ultra 3 could run laps around plenty of other watches, there's a larger battery inside the Ultra 4. I'll share more on this in the Performance section, but battery life is seriously impressive, surpassing its 50 listed hours.
Aside from the Health Sensing System on the back, though, much of the design here is Apple sticking with what has made the Ultra successful since its launch. It's an ultra-rugged, road-ready Apple Watch that's likely a necessity for endurance athletes, but its distinctive build also appeals to those who simply want something different from the standard Apple Watch.
- Design score: 5/5
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Features
- Readiness score is excellent
- Siri AI features to come
- Improved vitals app
With the design mostly unchanged, much of what's new with the Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes from watchOS 27 and its health and activity features. I'm starting with the latter, as it's truly been the highlight of my testing.
I've worn an Apple Watch since it first launched in the spring of 2015. My original aluminum model arrived on launch day, and I was admittedly hooked on closing my rings. Now, after more than a month with the Ultra 4 — alongside the Apple Watch Series 12 — my new favorite feature is Readiness Score. It received a big round of applause at the launch event, and for good reason: it fills a gap in Apple's health feature set compared with the competition.
Many other wearables, including smartwatches and smart rings, offer ways to contextualize your data and help you understand what it means. Most notably, the Oura Ring provides a daily score that gives you an idea of what you're ready to take on. It's not medical advice, of course, but it can help you make sense of the data it collects. However, that feature sits behind a paywall, as do comparable offerings from Whoop, although Google Health, Garmin, and others provide it for free after you purchase a tracker.
Apple's take on a Readiness score is sometimes less elaborate, but it's free if you have a compatible new Apple Watch and enough data for it to work. Based on your sleep score and previous day's activity, you'll get a score from 0 to 10 tailored to you, alongside a matching phrase. It's presented as a curved line or half-moon graphic. Sometimes, I was greeted with a blue 7, marked "Ready," with the explanation: "You had a good night's sleep last night, and all your other metrics are typical. It looks like you're rested and ready for today."
Below is a smaller breakdown of Fitness, Vitals, and Sleep Score. These can change throughout the day depending on your activity rings and whether you log workouts. When you open the Health or Fitness app on your connected iPhone, there's more data to explore, too.
It's become my favorite feature of watchOS 27 because of how it integrates with the Activity Rings experience, while building on Vitals. Rather than opening another app each morning and scrolling through a series of statistics, you're presented with a single score that feels actionable. Compared with other health wearables, it's also nice that Apple isn't locking it behind a monthly subscription. You do need a compatible recent Apple Watch, so there's an upfront cost, but you won't have to keep paying to use the feature.
watchOS 27 also brings Siri AI to the wrist, provided your Apple Watch is paired with a compatible iPhone. While some more extensive requests can take an extra beat, the experience has been smooth, whether I raise my wrist to talk or simply say "Hey Siri." You can also ask for relevant information about your activity directly from your wrist.
The new Siri Modular watch face certainly spotlights this feature, placing Siri Suggestions below the time and above other complications. At times, it might suggest identifying a song with Shazam, remind you of your upcoming bedtime, provide the weather forecast, or offer other contextually relevant information.
Thanks to the new Health Sensing System, which supports activity and heart-rate tracking, blood oxygen measurements, hypertension notifications, and sleep tracking, Apple says heart-rate measurements are more accurate than ever. The Ultra 4 also introduces heart-rate variability (HRV) to the experience. You can add a complication that updates your heart rate in real time, as well as one for your step count.
- Features score: 4.5/5
Apple Watch Ultra 4: Performance
- Battery life performs as described
- Accurate against HRMs and competitor wearables
- Not yet able to test Audio Intelligence features
Apple's new S11 chip is doing a lot of the heavy lifting in the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it's a noticeable part of the experience. Apps open quickly, navigating watchOS 27 feels incredibly responsive, and everything runs smoothly. Suffice to say, it’s what you expect from a $799 smartwatch in 2026, and while it doesn’t run laps around the Ultra 3, it has its moments where it has a bit more pep in its step.
The S11 also features a Secure Enclave and a separate always-on processor, helping balance performance with efficiency. That last part matters even more with the Ultra 4's physically larger battery.
Apple promises up to 50 hours of battery life with normal use, up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode, and up to 45 hours in Max Extended Workout Mode. In my testing, I've easily managed two and a half days on a charge with the Always-On display enabled and sleep tracking running overnight. That's seriously impressive for a fully featured smartwatch, even if some competing watches can last longer. The Ultra 4 won't win every battery-life comparison, but getting multiple days of use without sacrificing those everyday features is a big deal.
When you do eventually run low, faster charging makes it easier to top up. I've been able to get about 30% battery back in 15 to 20 minutes, which is handy if you forgot to charge overnight or want to give the watch extra juice before heading out. It doesn't eliminate the need to charge, of course, but combined with that extended runtime, it makes battery anxiety much less of a concern.
The S11 chip and new Health Sensing System also help power features like Readiness Score, which has quickly become one of my favorite additions to watchOS 27. But the chip is also laying the groundwork for Apple's forthcoming Siri Rewind and Live Recap features.
I haven't been able to test either just yet, and while I still expect them to arrive in the coming months, Apple hasn't confirmed exactly when they'll ship. If those features are the main reason you're considering the Ultra 4 — or the Apple Watch Series 12, for that matter — I'd wait until Apple provides a firm release date and we've had the chance to put them through their paces.
There are other smaller improvements that make the Ultra 4 nicer to use, too. Shazam and Sound Recognition are handy additions to have on your wrist, letting you identify music or recognize certain sounds without needing to reach for your iPhone. Shazam still struggles with some live music, though, so don't expect it to identify every song you hear at a concert.
Then there's the pedometer. It's a little wild that it's taken this long, but you can finally add a complication that updates your step count in real time right on your watch face. It's a simple quality-of-life improvement, but one that makes the Ultra 4 more useful at a glance.
In my testing across indoor cycling, outdoor walks, yoga, and indoor walks, the overall workout statistics and heart-rate readings have been in line with those from other devices, including the Oura Ring 5, Pixel Watch 5, Fitbit Air, and Apple Watch Series 12. Against an electrical heart rate monitor during a 5km run, the Apple Watch Ultra 4’s average heart rate reading was just 2 bpm away from the monitor’s. That’s well within the margin for error and just 1 bpm away from the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro’s readings during the same run.
Taken together, these aren't necessarily the sorts of changes that will make an Ultra 3 owner immediately rush out to upgrade. Instead, the S11 chip delivers a smoother, more efficient experience, while the larger battery makes it easier to take advantage of everything the watch has to offer. And with two and a half days of real-world battery life, that's a combination that's hard to beat.
- Performance score: 5/5
Should you buy the Apple Watch Ultra 4?
Buy it if..
You need long battery life
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 can last for days, performing for up to two and a half days of real-world use in my testing.
You want Apple’s latest health features
The Readiness Score and Health Sensing System are only available on the current gen watches.
Don’t buy it if..
You don’t need Apple’s AI features
If you don't want the Audio Intelligence features or the Readiness Score, the experience is pretty close to Ultra 3.
Also consider
Apple Watch Series 12
Apple's cheaper, less powerful wearable.
Garmin Fenix 9 Pro
The Apple Watch Ultra 4's biggest competitor in the premium adventure watch space.
Read our full Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review
How we tested
We tested the Apple Watch Ultra 4 by sleeping, working out, and living with the watch during a testing period comprising multiple weeks, staff members, and a review unit. We compared the watch's readings against competitor wearables, including an electrical heart rate monitor, drained the battery, and used as many available features as possible.
First reviewed October 2026.
Jacob Krol is the US Managing Editor, News for TechRadar. He’s been writing about technology since he was 14 when he started his own tech blog. Since then Jacob has worked for a plethora of publications including CNN Underscored, TheStreet, Parade, Men’s Journal, Mashable, CNET, and CNBC among others.
He specializes in covering companies like Apple, Samsung, and Google and going hands-on with mobile devices, smart home gadgets, TVs, and wearables. In his spare time, you can find Jacob listening to Bruce Springsteen, building a Lego set, or binge-watching the latest from Disney, Marvel, or Star Wars.

articles.title: En Galicia hay casas de piedra por 10.000 euros y pueblos que ofrecen exenciones fiscales. Pero no buscan compradores, sino emprendedores
articles.text:
Hay quien busca casa en el pueblo para jubilarse y quien, quizá hasta las narices del frenesí urbano, quiere montar allí una bodega, una panadería o un albergue y vivir a otro ritmo. Para los segundos existe Holapueblo, una web que pone en contacto a emprendedores con concellos que necesitan que alguien reabra el negocio que cerró. Tres municipios ourensanos acaban de apuntarse, según Faro de Vigo: Chandrexa de Queixa, Castrelo de Miño y Beariz. Su argumento común es que sobra espacio y tranquilidad.
Qué es Holapueblo. Una plataforma que impulsan Redeia, IKEA y AlmaNatura. Ofrece asesoramiento personalizado para encontrar vivienda y poner en marcha el proyecto, con ayudas autonómicas y locales. Son ese gestor que aclara dudas y funciona más como ventanilla que como sorteo de casas.
Chandrexa de Queixa. Con 985 metros, es el concello más alto de la provincia. Tiene 467 vecinos (de 478 que tenía hace solo un año) repartidos en 172 kilómetros cuadrados: 2,7 habitantes por kilómetro cuadrado. Su economía es ganadera, con más de 1.300 cabezas de vacuno y 3.500 de ovino, y ofrece pastos comunales e incentivos específicos a nuevos ganaderos o apicultores.
También se vende como oportunidad turística: la estación de Manzaneda está a 15 minutos, la Ribeira Sacra a 30 y la oferta de alojamiento se reduce a viviendas turísticas aisladas. También es el más remoto: se accede por la OU-0602 desde Montederramo o por la OU-0703 desde A Pobra de Trives. Hay hueco, dicen, para casas rurales, albergues, restaurantes y turismo activo. Por cierto, en agosto de 2025, un incendio nacido en Chandrexa quemó más de 10.500 hectáreas, el segundo mayor de la historia de Galicia.
Castrelo de Miño, vino y embalse. Es el más poblado de los tres, con 1.289 habitantes (pero en 1981 eran más de 5.500 y cerca del 44 % de sus vecinos tiene 65 años o más), y está a 25 kilómetros de la capital. Presume de la mayor densidad de bodegas de Galicia: 23 de la DO Ribeiro, una por cada 65 vecinos. A eso suma un embalse de 560 hectáreas, con club náutico y playa fluvial en Prado. Si pudiera, yo me iba sin pensarlo.
El concello recalca que tiene colegio, centro médico y farmacias, y casas a reformar desde 45.000 euros. La cifra contrasta con la que circulaba hace un año: El Cronista hablaba de casas de piedra desde 10.000 euros y de una bonificación del 90% en tasas municipales para emprendedores menores de 30 años. Castrelo es el más cercano, a unos 25 kilómetros de Ourense.
Beariz, exenciones y una mina. 901 habitantes y muchas opciones. Ofrece exenciones fiscales locales y libre acceso a montes comunales para proyectos ganaderos o forestales, tras un año de residencia. Tiene conexión de alta velocidad, un espacio municipal de coworking y quiere dinamizar el polígono de Lebozán.
Busca hostelería, panadería tradicional, comercio de proximidad y servicios para mayores. Y espera la mina de litio de Doade para crear empleo. Ese proyecto, que la Comisión Europea incluyó entre los 47 estratégicos, sigue en tramitación autonómica y prevé empezar a extraer en 2028, según El Debate. Es decir, parte de su plan depende de un permiso que aún no existe, aunque sí está en su futuro más inmediato. A Beariz se llega por la OU-212.
La letra pequeña. Del anuncio a la llave hay un trecho. Los 45.000 euros de Castrelo son por casas a reformar, así que a esa cifra habrá que sumar la obra. Los incentivos de Chandrexa y Beariz hablan de pastos y montes comunales: en Galicia muchos de ellos los gestionan comunidades de vecinos con sus propias reglas, así que conviene preguntar qué condiciones se imponen y a quién.
En Beariz, el acceso llega tras un año de residencia (aunque se suele conceder sin mucho brete). Y de las exenciones fiscales, el texto no detalla importes ni requisitos. Tampoco menciona qué servicios hay en Chandrexa y Beariz, más allá de la conectividad de Beariz. Castrelo sí presume de colegio y médico, y en un pueblo pequeño eso es la mitad del paquete.
Libertad y soledad. No es un caso aislado, claro. Como ya recogimos hace unas semanas, el 80,2 % de los municipios españoles pierde población desde 2011 y casi la mitad de las viviendas de pueblos de menos de 10.000 habitantes está vacía. Un anuncio, por sí solo, no cambia esa tendencia. Los anuncios son prometedores y tranquilidad no falta, pero hay que trabajar y los inviernos no suelen ser fáciles ni en Chandrexa ni en Castrelo.
