articles.title: Las cartas de Pokémon han conseguido un hito inesperado equiparándose a Nvidia como el activo con mejor rendimiento del mundo
articles.text:
El oro, las obras de arte de artistas consagrados e incluso los bolsos más exclusivos son las alternativas de inversión a los valores de los índices bursátiles como el S&P500 más conocidas. Sin embargo, uno de los activos más rentables en la actualidad no cotiza en bolsa ni se expone en galerías de arte, sino que lleva décadas esperando pacientemente en el fondo de alguno de tus cajones: las cartas coleccionables de Pokémon.
Estas cartas nacieron para cambiarlas en el patio del colegio. Nadie las miraba como algo que pudiera dar dinero de verdad. Hoy hay quien las compara con las acciones de la empresa más valiosa del planeta. Y hay gráficos que, de momento, le dan la razón.
Dos curvas casi gemelas. Un gráfico generado por la plataforma de datos Blockworks, pone frente a frente varios activos de inversión en un histórico desde 2019. El índice Pokémon de Card Ladder, que evalúa el precio promedio de una cesta de cartas coleccionables de Pokémon, se ha multiplicado por unas 40 veces en los últimos siete años.
Por si parte, durante este mismo periodo Nvidia se ha convertido en la primera empresa en superar los cinco billones de dólares en bolsa, gracias al auge de la IA y a la enorme demanda de sus procesadores. Ese ascenso meteórico de su capitalización ha hecho que los inversores de la compañía fundada por Jensen Huang y sus amigos hayan multiplicado por 41 su inversión inicial. Es decir, un simple juego de cartas ha sido casi tan rentable como la empresa con mayor capitalización del mundo.
Un valor refugio. Aunque pueda parecer algo tan ilógico como la burbuja de los tulipanes, el valor de las cartas responde a las leyes del mercado: valen tanto como lo que está dispuesto a pagar el más osado de sus compradores. Entre los jóvenes millonarios ya se ven como un refugio lejos de los vaivenes de la bolsa.
En tres meses, el índice CL50 (que agrupa las 50 cartas Pokémon más icónicas) ha subido más de un 16%. Según datos de MarketScreener, en el mismo periodo, el S&P 500 apenas ha alcanzado un incremento del 3,3%, mientras que el Nasdaq 100 lo hacía en un 2,29% y el MSCI World lo hacía en un 2,42%.
Un Pikachu de 16,5 millones. En febrero, Logan Paul, un reconocido coleccionista e inversor en este activo, vendió su Pikachu Illustrator con nota PSA 10 en una subasta de Goldin. El precio final de la operación fue de 16,49 millones de dólares. Por una sola carta Pokémon. Guinness World Records lo certificó como la carta más cara jamás vendida en subasta.
Sin embargo, lo más llamativo de la operación es que Paul ya había conseguido ese mismo reconocimiento cuando la compró en 2021 por 5,275 millones. Entonces dijo: "Esta carta me costó más que mi rancho. Mi rancho de 84 acres". En cinco años, el precio de esta carta se ha triplicado.
Un 10 sobre 10 lo cambia todo. La clasificación de PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator) puntúa cada carta del 1 al 10 según su estado, exclusividad o demanda. Un punto de diferencia en esta escala mueve miles de dólares. Un Gengar Holo de Expedition de 2002 con un PSA 9 costaba en agosto unos 4.680 dólares en julio de 2026. El 18 de octubre se anotó una venta de 24.900 dólares, según los registros de Card Ladder.
La escasez pesa tanto como la nota de valoración de PSA, por eso la carta vendida por Logan Paul alcanzó el esa cifra récord en su subasta: es rara y se encuentra en un estado impecable. Según publicaba Fortune, se han impreso más de 75.000 millones de cartas Pokémon, y la propia Pokémon Company asegura que imprime "a máxima capacidad". Sin embargo, solo se pagan fortunas por aquellas que pertenecen a ediciones especiales y son muy raras. Es decir, aquellas clasificadas como PSA 10.
Lo que el gráfico no cuenta. Al igual que cualquier otro activo, las cartas de Pokémon también pueden sufrir sus altibajos debido a desequilibrios entre la oferta y la demanda. Tal y como contaba The Daily Economy, durante la pandemia hubo una fiebre por las cartas de Pokémon que disparó su precio e hizo que muchos coleccionistas se animaran a poner a la venta sus piezas. Ese incremento en la oferta hizo que su precio se desplomara. Una carta de Pikachu de McDonald's pasó de unos 51 dólares en febrero de 2021 a poco más de 6 dólares en julio de 2024.
Con los relojes de lujo pasó algo parecido. La burbuja que inflaron nuevos millonarios terminó explotando y causando el desplome de los precios de los relojes exclusivos de segunda mano.

articles.title: Micron’s memory boom: Is the industry's cyclicality really ending? - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Micron’s memory boom: Is the industry’s cyclicality really ending?
In Breaking Analysis 322, we shared with you that our forecast of a $1 trillion silicon business arrived two years earlier than we had forecast.
The reason for our 24-month miss was the bottleneck had moved from graphics processing units to memory. Micron Inc. gave us a new datapoint in its third-quarter earnings print. It said DRAM prices rose by more than 60% sequentially in the quarter, while the number of bits shipped barely grew. Today we address what that means. Here’s the key question we ask today:
Is this undersupply temporary or is there a structural change in the economics of memory?
We believe both forces are at work. This week we participated in a webcast with Micron President and Chief Technology and Products Officer Scott DeBoer. The roadmap he showed us underscores the importance of memory with respect to artificial intelligence performance. New customer take-or-pay agreements Micron has introduced a change how risk is shared.
At the same time, customers are being forced to adapt to higher costs. Qualitate’s proprietary research gives us a window into those customer decisions. Our investigation tries to determine whether these changes can make memory less cyclical, and what evidence would tell us that the familiar cycle is returning.
In this Breaking Analysis, we share how AI is changing the economics of memory. We reason through the implications of the massive divergence between memory average selling prices and bit growth, we discuss the strategic role of high-bandwidth memory and the changing memory storage hierarchy in the context of Micron’s roadmap. We’ll then bring in data from Qualitate and go deep within the supply chain. Specifically, we’ll dig into how fabless designers, IDMs, hyperscaler custom-silicon teams and design-verification engineers are dealing with HBM and Chips-on-Wafer-on-Substrate or CoWoS supply constraints. We’ll also share how memory price increases are affecting the buying patterns of end customers.
Finally we’ll close with some keys to watch as to whether memory cyclicality will return or if there’s a permanent change in the cycle dynamics because of AI.
Access the full slide deck here with bonus data in the appendix.
How AI is changing memory economics
The working premise we’re testing is that a structural change and a strong memory cycle can coexist.
Memory increasingly determines whether an AI system can keep its expensive processors utilized and productive. Delivering that memory consumes more manufacturing resources and requires closer engineering collaboration with design partners. Those changes mean that Micron, SK Hynix Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. are becoming significantly more strategic suppliers.
But today’s price increases are a function of scarcity. High prices bring more investment but also give customers a stronger reason to defer spending, redesign architectures or consume infrastructure differently. The key is trying to understand the difference between ongoing strategic importance and the magnitude of the current scarcity price premium. We believe Micron can become more differentiated but over time it will still be exposed to cycles. The unanswered question is how much pricing power and profitability endure as supply loosens and and customers adapt.
The divergence in ASPs and bit volumes breaks the normal memory pattern
As Dr. Robert Castellano describes in his newsletter, the divergence between memory ASPs and bit volume growth is a new and defining characteristic of today’s semiconductor market. Historically, these two metrics moved in the same direction and a collapse or surge in pricing typically reflected a proportional shift in overall unit demand.
Today, a significant gap between high ASPs and flattish bit shipments exposes structural, supply-side tightening and an aggressive shift toward specialized AI hardware rather than an organic, broad-based demand explosion.
This was our starting observation which showed up in Micron’s own earnings deck. In fiscal Q3, DRAM average selling prices increased sequentially in the low-60s percentage range, while bit shipments increased only in the low single digits. As a result, DRAM revenue rose 67%.
Micron’s most recent Q4 print gives us new data. Specifically, price growth moderated to the high teens, but prices continued to rise, and bit growth remained in the mid-single digits. This speaks to a continued strong price environment, not equivalent growth in the physical amount of memory shipped. Remember, too, that the ASP reflects a blended rate. So product mix is a key determinant of revenue and margin.
Low shipment growth does not mean weak demand when supply is constrained like it is today. The obvious conclusion is that supply constraints are producing a large near-term revenue boost. The question is how much of that benefit continues when production expands and customers adapt to the changing economics of AI. That is what the roadmap, contracts and customer data help us assess.
It’s not just about HBM
There’s a tendency to put everything into an HBM story. In Q4, Micron’s Cloud Memory business reported a lofty 83% gross margin, flat with the prior quarter. Management said higher pricing helped, but a higher mix of HBM offset that benefit. Micron doesn’t disclose HBM standalone margins, but the shift in manufacturing capacity toward HBM underscores the dynamic we discussed earlier between ASPs and bit growth.
Specifically, Micron tells us that HBM3E requires roughly three times the wafer supply to produce the same number of bits as DDR5 at the same technology node, with more complex packaging. As well, the HBM prices in Q4 were negotiated in 2025, whereas DRAM pricing was more exposed to spot pricing dynamics. So these factors put pressure on what are elevated margins.
Micron expects higher HBM pricing in calendar 2027 to narrow its margin gap with conventional DRAM. But the long-term test is whether Micron earns attractive returns through product transitions and weaker pricing conditions, rather than whether one product has the highest margin during a shortage.
Memory capacity and bandwidth serve different needs
Scott DeBoer laid out his view of the expanding data center memory hierarchy with standard, custom and vertical HBM at the top (near memory), followed by high capacity and lower power DRAM (main memory), then SSDs and AI-class NAND (context memory) and high capacity SSDs for databases and data lakes.
A key point is that AI performance depends on where information lives and how quickly it can reach the processor. Capacity is the amount of data that fits in the package. Bandwidth is the amount of data that moves each second. HBM is key because it gives the GPU a fast local working space.
Server memory provides additional capacity, while flash storage holds data and selected cached context at lower cost. During inference, the system saves intermediate calculations in the key-value cache so it can reuse work as it generates an answer. Longer conversations and more concurrent users can expand that working data set and can flush the KV cache; so storage suppliers such as Vast Data Inc., Dell Technologies Inc. and others create a virtual space with lower-cost solid-state drives so that the KV cache doesn’t have to endure a refresh.
Ultimately, the buyer’s objective is a balanced system that meets a specific workload’s latency, throughput and reliability needs. Buying more memory can help when memory is the constraint. It does not always improve every workload. The right viewpoint is cost per useful task at the required service level, including the effect on GPU utilization, energy and the number of systems needed.
How HBM sucks up more manufacturing capacity and what that means
There are always opportunity costs when producing particular types of memory. At the KeyBanc investor conference, Micron’s Sumit Sadana described a three-to-one ratio between HBM3E and conventional DDR.
In other words, capacity that could produce roughly three units of DDR bits instead produces one unit of HBM bits. He said that moves closer to four-to-one by HBM4E. The reason for this is that very high bandwidth requires more connections, more silicon resources and more complex packaging.
We believe this is the clearest example of the tradeoffs facing memory makers between the technical roadmap and conventional memory pricing. Specifically, more AI memory can absorb resources that would otherwise support other DRAM products, so investment does not translate directly into proportional growth in saleable bits.
But the dynamic works in both directions. If HBM demand weakens, reallocating capacity could release more conventional DRAM supply over time. Of course it’s not that simple. There’s qualification, equipment and learning curve constraints that require time.
How Micron prioritizes investments in its roadmap
The company is pulling two levers at once. It is making memory more specialized and closely integrated with the customer’s processor, while at the same time increasing the number of bits manufactured in a given area. HBM4 is already in high-volume manufacturing.
HBM4E and later memory placed directly on the processor are roadmap items, with target dates. On the manufacturing side, Micron is looking to get a mid-20s percentage improvement in DRAM bit density with its next generation, called one-delta, ramping in the second half of 2027. Its G11 flash roadmap targets approximately twice the density of G9. That is for NAND development; it does not affect HBM capacity.
We believe these gains are an essential element in the context of scarcity. Meaning better density and yields will improve Micron’s economics. Their ultimate impact depends on learning curve and other dynamics – for example, ramp speed, the product mix, Micron’s capital investments and of course end customer demand. The roadmap we heard from DeBoer emphasizes the continuing importance of memory but no one can guarantee that peak pricing is a permanent condition.
Qualitate data shows how chip designers are dealing with supply challenges
Qualitate’s silicon design and sourcing panel gives us a fresh view of the supply problem. Eight of 22 respondents in the survey said memory or HBM was their largest current constraint. Seven said the main constraint was advanced packaging.
Remember, these are small-N, deep-dive interviews and the responses support the view that constraints extend beyond a single chip or an announced wafer capacity data point. The implication for our premise is that new fabrication capacity alone may not resolve every constraint. Qualification, packaging and system integration still determine how quickly useful hardware reaches customers.
Qualitate data tells us that chip designers across hyperscalers, integrated device manufacturers or IDMs, and fabless firms are responding to acute HBM and advanced packaging shortages by fundamentally replacing the traditional “design-then-source” workflow with a supply-aware co-design methodology. Because physical availability has become the key constraint on shipping finished silicon, engineering teams are employing specific architectural, packaging and procurement strategies to mitigate these bottlenecks.
These include:
- Architectural adaptations and design compromises such as trading peak performance for supply;
- Downsizing HBM configurations;
- Leaning more heavily on larger SRAM designs;
- Moving away from silicon interposer constraints to reduce reliance on TSMC CoWos packaging;
- Standardizing on open chiplet interfaces like UCIe;
- Building specialized ASICs;
- Dozens of other innovative strategies to reduce their supply constraints.
In a moment, we’ll turn to a separate Qualitate data set that describes what enterprise practitioners are doing about higher infrastructure costs. But first let’s look how memory is affecting the infrastructure bill of materials.
Memory is becoming a much larger portion of the AI infra BoM
To do this we need a way to discuss the customer’s bill. Below we take a hypothetical scenario to model how memory is affecting overall infrastructure costs.
The percentage of memory costs for AI infrastructure will vary by customer and the nuances of the rack configuration. But we can use rules-of-thumb and a sensitivity analysis to understand how price increases affect the portion of the BoM that is memory.
Assume for a moment an unchanged system configuration, unchanged non-memory costs and a 60% increase in the purchase price of its memory:
- If memory began at 20% of the bill of materials, total cost rises 12%;
- At 35%, total cost rises 21%;
- At 50%, total cost rises 30%.
The higher the starting memory content, the greater the exposure. The actual customer response can include less memory, a different system or greater utilization. Our point is that memory can materially change the business case even when the rest of the system stays the same.
How enterprise customers are addressing the memory price challenge
Let’s come back to a different Qualitate data set from the enterprise customer perspective to better understand how practitioners are dealing with the challenge of higher memory prices.
According to the Qualitate data, memory and central processing unit cost inflation is being felt across the entire infrastructure estate. Enterprises are responding through a consistent set of coping strategies, none of which involve simply absorbing the cost.
One healthcare practitioner sums up the changing price and tech inflation dynamic saying: To get the same number of GPUs this year as opposed to two years ago, to get the same GPU capacity is what, three to four times the cost? That’s pretty insane when you’re used to following Moore’s Law.
One practitioner describes trying to push purchases out, saying, It is not a no, but it is a not-now push. A security-focused organization says higher hardware costs shift the equation toward cloud consumption.
The following table shows how end customers are dealing with these pricing challenges:
Source: Qualitate, 2026
We will watch whether these responses reduce deployment, improve utilization or simply move the demand elsewhere.
Customers are getting smarter about model routing and capacity utilization
One practitioner says the organization has reduced usage of some large frontier models where smaller or open-weight alternatives passed its benchmarks. Another questions keeping premium dedicated GPUs available around the clock for variable demand. Quantization, batching and smaller models are among the strategies the customers point to. Their effectiveness depends on the application, and we don’t know exactly how memory was affected, but these operational moves are direct responses to memory price increases.
Our interpretation is that expensive memory raises the value of doing less unnecessary work and keeping expensive resources productive. That can lower memory or compute needed per task. At the same time, lower task costs can often catalyze more usage. The best indicator to watch is useful-task cost at a service-level agreement, together with utilization and aggregate deployed capacity. Scarcity pricing increases the demand for efficiency and techniques or products that emphasize efficiency are increasingly attractive in the current environment.
Customers are changing suppliers when they can get capacity
Let’s look at a third set of responses to test platform and supplier choices.
One practitioner chose Advanced Micro Devices Inc. because it provided the ability to fit more of the model on one card. That is directly relevant to our thesis in that a customer can value more memory per accelerator because it may reduce the number of accelerators or the communication needed for a workload.
Separately, a practitioner describes choosing a supplier that could deliver comparable equipment. That is evidence of availability affecting a selection. Today, any credible supply will get scooped up. The point is, taken together, these examples show how memory fit and delivery availability influence supplier choices.
The practical indicators practitioners should consider are delivered performance, software effort, interconnect requirements, time to production and total cost per useful task. These are the measures that will validate or challenge Micron and other AI vendors’ pricing power over time.
The outcome and its cost determine customer value
Putting the customer angle at the center of our conclusion is important. Suppliers are reporting strong demand while individual practitioners describe strategies around deferral and redesign. Those two dynamics can coexist because customers, workloads and budgets differ. Dell’s quarterly filing reports substantial inflation in memory components and its pricing response. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. management, when asked about passing through higher memory prices, had no hesitation in referring to its customer discussions about higher prices.
These are the themes we’re hearing from vendors. Qualitate gives us examples of buyers making selective tradeoffs. We believe the best measure is cost per useful task or outcome at the required quality and latency. More memory can increase the hardware bill but lower task cost if it avoids extra GPUs or keeps them productive. Conversely, an expensive system with low utilization can undermine the business case. The indicator is whether customer ROI supports continued deployment after the price premium hits the final bill.
How Micron is using strategic supplier agreements
Let’s look at how Micron is capitalizing on the current demand picture. The most obvious business-model change is the strategic customer agreement.
By the Q4 report, Micron had signed 26 SCAs, which are committed volume and/or take-or-pay contracts. Micron estimates these agreements cover more than 35% of its revenue through 2030. These are multiyear supply arrangements, generally with binding purchase volumes. Three-quarters of the expected revenue under these agreements has a defined pricing framework, and a majority of that portion uses price bands. Customers receive supply assurance and, in many cases, a ceiling on prices. Micron receives volume commitments, often a floor on prices, and more confidence to plan capacity.
We believe this is substantive evidence that the industry’s economics are evolving. It does not remove risk. Micron’s own filing warns about enforcement disputes, customer inventory and oversupply when final demand falls short. Our test will be what these agreements actually protect through the next weaker market.
Does this end the cyclicality in memory?
Let’s poke at the cyclical argument that everyone’s concerned about. In other words, will AI smooth out the brutal cycles that investors in Micron have endured for years?
The strongest argument is very high prices fund new capacity, better manufacturing yields and more efficient use of each bit. Micron’s own roadmap contains evidence of this response. Its fab program adds multiyear capacity. But customers can reduce specifications, delay purchases or move workloads. And if HBM demand weakens, suitable capacity can eventually return to conventional DRAM, increasing supply there and potentially creating conditions for returned cyclicality.
Micron explicitly warns about this mechanism in its risk factors from its latest 10K filing. Take-or-pay contracts can ease the pain, but they do not make final demand disappear as a key variable. A buyer that committed to more than it needs can accumulate inventory. We therefore have no choice but to leave the end of cyclicality as a somewhat open question. The meaningful milestone will be saleable supply at useful yields meeting productive demand over time.
The likelihood that at some point in the future, demand and supply will come into balance is reasonably high.
What to watch in the months and quarters ahead
First, watch ASPs together with bits. The bull case is attractive economics as physical volume and productive use expand. A price decline alone doesn’t signal a bust if it unlocks deployment. Second, watch margins after the current price surge. Product mix, new-fab costs and utilization will be important. Third, watch the supply ramps. A cleanroom or first wafer milestone does not tell us how much qualified memory customers can actually procure.
The question is whether salable output from the fabs comes into a robust market or if it hits after demand has slowed. We believe these tests are more useful than just extrapolating the current margin or putting a precise date on a future glut. The evidence today is clear. Supply is scarce and the industry is ramping up to meet demand.
The other tests are closer to the customer. Do strategic agreements stay in place when the market weakens? It’s unlikely. Watch volumes, pricing protections and any disputes, renegotiations or force majeure situations like we saw with Oracle and Blue Owl. Do customers earn enough useful output to justify their memory bill? The Qualitate examples show how the configuration, model choice and ownership decision can change.
Finally, do orders turn into productive installations, or do commitments outrun consumption? Tight supply encourages customers to overstate forecasts or reserve more than they ultimately need, which Micron itself identifies as a risk. The bull case becomes stronger if contract performance, customer returns and actual deployment remain healthy as supply expands.
That is how we will distinguish a more durable business from an unusually strong phase of the cycle.
There’s no question that today the cycle has changed. The question is what will happen if and when the demand picture reverts.
The cycle has changed, for now…
Our conclusion is that memory’s economics are changing and AI has positively smoothed the cyclicality for the mid-term. But the data does not convince us that cyclicality has ended. The bull case/structural argument is that memory is central to useful AI performance, high-bandwidth products consume more manufacturing capacity, and Micron is building a more differentiated relationship with customers.
The bear case/cyclical argument is just as credible in our opinion. Specifically, an extraordinary price environment invites supply, optimization and delayed purchases. Qualitate data shows the customer response already taking several forms. For suppliers such as Micron, the test is the return they earn after scarcity eases. For customers, the test is productive work delivered at the required service level.
We believe the best way to follow this story is to keep both sides on your radar. If volume, customer returns and contract performance improve as capacity arrives, the business may become less volatile. If inventories rise and demand fails to absorb supply, the familiar cycle will assert itself and the classical memory cycles will return.
What’s your call? Is the memory boom permanent and is the risk of oversupply under control by the memory makers? Or will the cycle re-emerge before the end of the decade?
Let us know what you think.

articles.title: Demandan a Suno y Anthropic por usar 1.900 canciones de Joni Mitchell y Madonna sin permiso
articles.text:
La editora musical Reservoir demandó a Suno y a Anthropic ante un tribunal federal de California por usar, sin autorización, más de 1.900 canciones de su catálogo para entrenar sus sistemas de inteligencia artificial, entre ellas temas de Madonna, Johnny Cash y Joni Mitchell.
Las dos demandas se presentaron el miércoles 21 de octubre ante el Tribunal de Distrito de Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de California. Reservoir reclama en conjunto más de USD 337 millones entre ambos casos, según el cálculo de los propios escritos judiciales.
Contra Suno, la compañía de música generada por IA, Reservoir identifica 1.050 composiciones cuyos derechos de autor en Estados Unidos dice poseer o controlar en exclusiva. El reclamo pide hasta USD 150.000 por cada obra infringida de forma deliberada, lo que eleva el pedido a USD 157,5 millones solo por ese cargo.
La demanda agrega dos cargos adicionales por la ley de derechos de autor digital de Estados Unidos (DMCA), que sanciona eludir controles de acceso y borrar la información que identifica al autor de una obra. Esos dos cargos suman otros USD 28,875 millones, con lo que el total pedido contra Suno llega a USD 186,4 millones.
Contra Anthropic, la empresa detrás del chatbot Claude, Reservoir enumera 853 composiciones cuyas letras habría usado para entrenar sus modelos. El pedido por ese cargo asciende a USD 127,95 millones, y los dos cargos del DMCA suman otros USD 23,5 millones, para un total de USD 151,4 millones.
Suno, acusada de raspar música de plataformas pagas
La demanda contra Suno sostiene que la empresa, con sede en Massachusetts, admitió haber copiado “esencialmente todos los archivos de música de calidad razonable accesibles en internet” para entrenar su generador de canciones, un conjunto de decenas de millones de grabaciones.
El escrito afirma que Suno obtuvo ese material eludiendo controles técnicos de acceso en servicios como Spotify, YouTube, SoundCloud y Tidal, además de plataformas abiertas como Jamendo y MusicBrainz. También cita los acuerdos de licencia que Suno firmó este año con Warner Music Group, BMG y Believe como prueba de que existe un mercado para licenciar música de entrenamiento, algo que, según la demanda, Suno eligió no pagarle a Reservoir.
Suno cerró en junio una ronda de inversión de más de USD 400 millones que la valuó en USD 5.400 millones, y la demanda sostiene que la compañía proyecta ingresos anuales de USD 1.000 millones para 2028. Una vocera de Suno no respondió a una solicitud de comentarios de Billboard sobre la demanda.
Claude, acusado de reproducir letras casi intactas
En el caso de Anthropic, la demanda cita una respuesta reciente de Claude en la que el propio chatbot habría admitido que sus versiones de ciertas canciones “quedan muy cerca de los originales, con la misma estructura, los mismos estribillos reutilizados con cambios leves de palabras”, lo que según el escrito excede el límite de inspirarse en una obra para pasar a reproducirla.
El escrito sostiene que Anthropic entrenó a Claude con letras tomadas de bases de datos como Common Crawl y The Pile, y que ese material habría llegado sin licencia desde sitios de letras y plataformas de streaming. Según la demanda, Anthropic reconoció en pleitos anteriores haber copiado materiales protegidos a gran escala para entrenar sus modelos.
Una vocera de Anthropic dijo a Billboard que la compañía está en desacuerdo con las acusaciones y tiene intención de defender el caso con fuerza. La demanda también señala que, a la fecha de su presentación, había al menos otras cinco causas por composiciones musicales contra Anthropic en el mismo distrito judicial.
Una de ellas, iniciada en 2023 por Concord Music Group, Universal Music y ABKCO, llegó a una audiencia por mociones de resumen el mismo 21 de octubre ante la jueza Eumi Lee, quien escuchó los argumentos de ambas partes sobre si entrenar a Claude con letras de canciones constituye un uso justo bajo la ley de derechos de autor, sin emitir todavía un fallo.
Reservoir pide en ambos casos una orden judicial que obligue a destruir o inutilizar las copias no autorizadas de sus obras, incluidas las que, según alega, permanecen en los conjuntos de entrenamiento, los repositorios internos y los parámetros mismos de los modelos de inteligencia artificial. El próximo paso en el litigio será la respuesta formal de Suno y Anthropic ante el tribunal de California.

articles.title: 8BitDo Ushers in the Next-Generation of Ultimate, Launching the 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Controller for XBOX
articles.text:
Friday, October 23rd 2026
8BitDo Ushers in the Next-Generation of Ultimate, Launching the 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Controller for XBOX
Game Outlet Europe, an independent distributor of video games and gaming accessories, announced today that leading gaming hardware brand 8BitDo has begun shipping their most advanced XBOX controller yet, with the Ultimate 3E Controller for XBOX available across the UK and Europe starting today.
Designed for professional gamers but accessible to all, the new Ultimate 3E Controller harnesses 8BitDo's years of development and engineering know-how, delivering the next generation of Ultimate for XBOX gamers.The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Controller for XBOX is officially licensed for use with XBOX, ensuring full compatibility with XBOX Series X|S as well as XBOX One. Offering gamers a choice of a rock solid 2.4Ghz wireless, or a standard wired connection for tournament use, the Ultimate 3E is also compatible with Windows, and thanks to integrated Bluetooth technology, the controller is ideal for use with Apple and Android devices for mobile gaming on the go.
Key to the power of the Ultimate 3E lies in the unrivalled level of customisation available to the gamer, allowing them to shape the controller to match their competitive playstyle. Loaded with modular, swappable parts (included), players can fine tune their feel, swapping ABXY modules, Thumbsticks and D-pads.
Will it be smooth or perhaps you prefer tactile - gamers can choose between the silicone or micro-switch ABXY module for two distinct button feels in one controller. Gamers no longer need to settle for a standard or a circular D-pad, why not have both?! Classic precision or smooth directional rolls can be chosen via the two premium D-pad options available. With the Ultimate 3E, two standard Thumbsticks come equipped, with additional options including two Tall Thumbsticks, one Thick-Neck Thumbstick and one Dome Thumbstick, providing hot-swappable options for every gamer and every gameplay scenario.
The Ultimate 3E features an all-new design for 8BitDo, offering a wider grip angle to improve comfort and silicone side-grips for better stability during intense gameplay sessions.Those playing competitively on PC can be assured of lighting fast reaction times, featuring a polling rate of up to 1000 Hz. With Ultimate 3E, the dual Thumbsticks are powered via TMR technology, paired with a 12-bit ADC sampling chip that provides enhanced precision and stability. Interactive RGB Fire Rings surrounding the Thumbsticks provide real-time visual feedback during gameplay. 
Hall-effect Impulse Triggers allow gamers to choose between two trigger stops, perfect for fast paced shooters. Furthering the pro-level specification, extra fast Bumpers (L4 and R4) deliver even faster reaction times when under pressure, and two pro-level Back Buttons allow gamers to remap action button functions to the rear of the controller, meaning there's no need to take your thumbs off the sticks during complex manoeuvres.
The Ultimate 3E features customisable 6-Axis motion control, allowing players to enjoy enhanced motion-based aiming and gameplay with 6-axis motion control when using 2.4Ghz mode on PC. Gamers can use the powerful free 8BitDo Ultimate Software X to tweak sensitivity further. The same software provides users with a massive selection of customisable options, including button mapping, Thumbstick sensitivity, Trigger range, Vibration feedback intensity and so much more, creating a controller as unique as the gamer using it.
When game time is over, players can store and charge their gamepad via the included Charging Dock, powering the internal rechargeable battery to provide up to 18 hours of continuous gaming when fully charged.
With an additional Accessory Pack included and complete with robust Travel Case, the Ultimate 3E provides a peerless experience for XBOX, PC and Mobile gamers.
The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Controller for XBOX is shipping across the UK and Europe from today and is available across major European retailers and online storefronts for an MSRP of: £124.99 / €139.99

articles.title: Stranger Than Heaven director says RGG 'took a lot of inspiration from what we researched' for its multi-era game but 'historical accuracy wasn't the goal from the very beginning'
articles.text:
'Historical accuracy wasn't the goal from the very beginning' — Stranger Than Heaven director says while research for its era-spanning game was 'really difficult,' the cities will still have 'a lot of fiction'
"No one knows what it was like back in 1915 Kokura, or 1929 Kure"
- Stranger Than Heaven director Mikinobu Abe says RGG Studios did a lot of "difficult" research to depict the game's many cities across different time periods
- However, Abe says "historical accuracy wasn't the goal from the very beginning," and the team took creative liberties
- He says there is a lot of "fiction" woven through the cities for the player experience
RGG Studio did plenty of research for its multi-era action role-playing game, Stranger Than Heaven, but director Mikinobu Abe has said historical accuracy wasn't the end goal.
In a discussion with TechRadar Gaming about the early stages of development, Abe confirmed that a story spanning 50 years and five cities in Japan required a lot of research, which "itself was really difficult," and that RGG visited all the cities depicted in the game and libraries for material.
"No one knows what it was like back in 1915 Kokura, or 1929 Kure," Abe said. "So, we had to dig into a lot of our pictures, and we visited a lot of museums. We even bought a lot of books that were published back then, or magazines that were published back then, and read every single one of them. There was one time that bugs were coming out of them, which was not good to have in the office! We did a lot of research like that."
However, as much as research was vital to get a sense of the time periods RGG wanted to depict, the director said "historical accuracy wasn't the goal from the very beginning," and the team took creative liberties.
"We took a lot of inspiration from what we researched, but we wanted to depict the city in a way that we feel really represents the video game experience that we want the player to have," Abe explained. "There's a lot of fiction within the cities, but we wanted to capture the tone of what it could have been like or how it could have felt to be in that place."
It wasn't just historical research; Abe said he and the art director, Daishi Kanaya, researched paintings, vintage lenses, and film that were created during these decades, and that they "took a lot of inspiration from the equipment side of things," like what brush artists used when drawing at the time.
"We took a lot of inspiration from those and re-imagined how we, as creators in 2026, would use that equipment and create this new vibe or atmosphere for the game," he said. "That's just how this older colour, and the look, and the tone, and the atmosphere of the city came to life.

"I don't think 1915 Kokura was that populated or was that big of a city, but you know, we really wanted to capture the essence and humanise it in a way that we feel like it's really entertaining for people to play."
Stranger Than Heaven releases on January 15, 2027, for PS5, Xbox Series X and Series S, and PC.

It has a very fast 240Hz refresh rate for seamless gaming, and thanks to the OLED tech, the gray-to-gray response time is a staggeringly low 0.03ms, giving your games very smooth motion and avoiding ghosting compared to slower monitors. This monitor also fully supports AMD's FreeSync Premium tech, so you can match the refresh rate of the monitor to the frame rate of your games to eliminate screen tearing completely, for a much better gaming experience.

You can connect your gaming PC and even a couple of game consoles thanks to the inclusion of two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 1.4 port. Plenty of connections for the ultimate gaming battlestation.

articles.title: Managed services support keeps neocloud GPU capacity healthy - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Managed services support keeps neocloud GPU capacity healthy
Neoclouds are multiplying as AI labs and enterprises hunt for dedicated graphics processing unit capacity, but standing up a cluster is only the start. For smaller providers, managed services support from hardware partners increasingly decides whether that capacity stays healthy and profitable after go-live.
Specialized AI clouds are carving out a role alongside the hyperscalers, particularly where sovereign cloud requirements dictate where data lives and who controls it. A young provider cannot staff every layer of a complex GPU deployment on its own, according to Tom Richer (pictured), executive vice president of Alpha Compute Corp.
“You can cobble together a lot of different providers, but then when stuff goes wrong, the finger-pointing starts,” he said. “You just want that integrated solution provider who can ensure success, help you with all of the build-out, then all of the … managed services to keep it going healthy and to keep everything performing in line with [service-level agreements].”
Richer spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed managed service support, sovereign AI infrastructure and neocloud financing. (* Disclosure below.)
Managed services support anchors a sovereign neocloud
Alpha Compute moved into AI infrastructure less than a year ago after starting out in digital assets, and it now leads with sovereign and confidential computing powered by Dell Technologies Inc. and Intel Corp. hardware. Its approach, which the company calls sovereign by design, starts at the silicon and keeps data in-country for customers subject to rules such as the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation, Richer explained.
“We start with the hardware. Think of a stack. All the way down to the chip level, we are creating enclaves,” Richer said. “We’re a Dell partner, so we use Dell technology as well as Intel technology.”
That stack is already running in production. The company’s 72-node St. Louis cluster pairs Nvidia Blackwell systems from Dell with InfiniBand networking and direct liquid cooling inside a retrofitted brownfield data center, and Alpha Compute has outlined plans for additional Blackwell clusters. Alpha Compute announced a binding term sheet for a $31.9 million nonrecourse loan facility secured by Nvidia B300 hardware.
“There’s kind of a trinity there, though. You need the off-taker, a good off-taker,” Richer said. “But also you need that kind of land, power [and] shell.”
Once a cluster is live, Alpha Compute owns the client relationship. Tickets, remediation and hardware returns run through a joint team with Dell, which has made AI factories central to its enterprise strategy. Alpha Compute’s clients to date are AI labs that want the provider managing everything below the operating system. Enterprises are likely to ask for more, according to Richer.
“With Dell as our managed services partner, we can go above the [operating system] on day two,” Richer said. “The powerful thing with Dell and their integrated approach is we can go to any level.”
That depth of managed services support also shapes how Richer sees neoclouds competing. Rather than replacing public cloud, purpose-built providers with no “noisy neighbors” or multitenant sharing will take on the most demanding and sensitive GPU workloads, he explained.
“I really see neoclouds now accompanying and fusing with public cloud for enterprise choices in that hybrid manner,” Richer said. “For those superintelligence workloads that are really demanding, enterprises can send those sensitive, intense high-performance computing workloads over to the neocloud, so they can work in concert.”

articles.title: « Un échec » cuisant pour la cybersécurité : pourquoi les failles PHP ont plongé une partie d'Internet dans le noir
articles.text:
Quand une faille de sécurité est découverte, le monde de la cybersécurité suit un protocole bien précis : la « divulgation coordonnée ». Une fois la vulnérabilité débusquée, le correctif est préparé dans le plus grand secret par les développeurs. Pour éviter que des pirates exploitent la faille dans le cadre de cyberattaques, seul un petit cercle d’éditeurs et d’hébergeurs est prévenu à l’avance de l’arrivée d’une mise à jour. L’information est gardée la plus secrète possible, surtout si la défaillance est critique.
À une date déterminée en amont, tout est rendu public d’un seul coup. Tout le monde doit alors se dépêcher d’installer la mise à jour pour prendre les pirates de court. Pour les failles PHP2Shell qui ont secoué tout Internet, la divulgation publique était prévue le 22 octobre… mais rien ne s’est passé comme prévu.
Une faille trop complexe… sauf pour l’IA
L’histoire de la découverte des failles PHP2Shell commence deux ans plus tôt, en 2024. Cette année-là, un développeur de PHP repère les premiers signes d’une défaillance lors d’un audit. À ce moment-là, les risques sont jugés théoriques. Les tentatives de correctif s’enlisent, faute de moyens du côté de la PHP Foundation. Il faudra attendre l’été 2026 pour que des chercheurs prouvent qu’on peut réellement s’en servir pour prendre le contrôle d’un serveur.
Selon les chercheurs de Wiz, qui ont débusqué les failles à l’aide de l’IA, les vulnérabilités n’étaient pas particulièrement faciles à exploiter. En fait, l’exploitation nécessitait « une chaîne d’étapes complexe, à la limite de ce que des chercheurs humains pouvaient réaliser ». Il aura fallu que l’intelligence artificielle entre en scène pour que les choses changent, et que la faille soit prise un peu plus au sérieux. La fondation PHP admet que ce retard fut « un échec structurel, dû au processus de décision de l’équipe de sécurité et à son manque de ressources ».
À lire aussi : Failles PHP – pourquoi c’est un vrai casse-tête pour l’Internet mondial
Exploitation et fuite
Une fois que Wiz s’est penché sur la faille, un correctif a été rapidement mis sur pied. Comme évoqué plus haut, celui-ci devait être annoncé dans la journée du 22 octobre. Quatre jours avant la date prévue, le 18 octobre, Amazon repère une première tentative d’exploitation de la brèche de PHP. En théorie, aucun pirate n’était pourtant au courant de la vulnérabilité. Pour le moment, « on ne sait toujours pas comment l’acteur a obtenu les informations avant la divulgation », indique CJ Moses, responsable sécurité d’Amazon.
Deux jours plus tard, un utilisateur du forum Hacker News publie les identifiants officiels des deux vulnérabilités (CVE-2026-109618 et -109619), qui étaient censés rester secrets encore pendant 48 heures. Le message, rapidement supprimé par son auteur, précise même que les vulnérabilités n’ont pas encore été divulguées. Face aux fuites, l’équipe de sécurité de PHP sort du silence dans la journée du 21 octobre. La fondation confirme travailler sur les correctifs, corrige les fausses informations qui circulent, et se réserve le droit de publier les mises à jour plus tôt que prévu. Les autorités lancent des alertes d’urgence. Le correctif est finalement publié, un jour avant la date initiale prévue.
Un correctif diffusé 6 heures trop tot
Ce n’est pas tout. L’entreprise Chainguard, qui avait reçu le correctif en avance pour préparer ses clients, a commis une bourde. La société a en effet mis en ligne des versions corrigées de PHP avant la date prévue. Ces correctifs ont permis aux cybercriminels de repérer où se trouvent les failles, ouvrant la voie à des cyberattaques.
« N’importe quel attaquant pouvait désormais étudier le correctif sous forme binaire pendant que tous les autres utilisateurs de PHP attendaient encore la publication », déplore la PHP Foundation, soulignant que des semaines de coordination ont été réduites à néant.
Le 22 octobre, « plus de six heures avant la publication coordonnée, Chainguard a rompu l’embargo de manière unilatérale ». Moins d’une heure plus tard, les chercheurs d’ELLIO ont enregistré les premiers signaux d’attaques. Le PDG de Chainguard, Dan Lorenc, explique avoir « pris la décision de les sortir plus tôt quand des tactiques d’exploitation sont apparus dans la nature ».
À l’ère de l’IA, le moindre grain de poussière dans les rouages d’une divulgation coordonnée peut avoir des conséquences catastrophiques. Comme l’explique CJ Moses, « le délai entre un correctif et un exploit fonctionnel se réduit », car « l’analyse assistée par IA rend bien moins coûteux de transformer un correctif en exploit fonctionnel ». De nos jours, « un nombre croissant d’acteurs peuvent désormais agir en quelques heures, voire quelques minutes ». C’est pourquoi les diverses fuites qui ont émaillé le processus de divulgation des failles se sont rapidement soldées par une vague de cyberattaques… Cloudflare a recensé des dizaines de milliers de tentatives dans les 45 minutes après la divulgation, des centaines de milliers au bout de deux heures, puis des millions dès le lendemain.

articles.title: Galaxy A36 e mais celulares Samsung recebem a One UI 9 • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy A36 e mais celulares Samsung recebem a One UI 9
Atualização também chegou ao Galaxy A27 e Z Fold 5. Galaxy A56 começou a receber nova versão nesta semana.
A Samsung ampliou nesta semana a presença da One UI 9 nos celulares da marca no Brasil. O Galaxy A36, o Galaxy A27 e os dobráveis de quinta geração começaram a receber a atualização na terça-feira (20/10), segundo os changelogs publicados pela fabricante.
O Galaxy A56 também começou a receber o novo sistema aparentemente nesta quinta-feira (22/10), embora a Samsung ainda não o tenha registrado oficialmente. A One UI 9 é baseada no Android 17 e vem sendo distribuída gradualmente no país desde setembro.
Com a nova rodada, a linha Galaxy Z elegível fica completa no Brasil. Os Galaxy Z Fold 5 e Z Flip 5 recebem, com a One UI 9, sua última grande atualização de sistema, como previsto pela Samsung. Entre os modelos que já foram atualizados estão as famílias Galaxy S26, S26 e S24, parte da linha S23, os dobráveis da sexta e sétima geração e o Galaxy A57.
A One UI 9 também já vem instalada de fábrica nos Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra, Z Flip 8, Galaxy S26 FE e Galaxy Tab S12.
Na linha S, ainda falta receber o Galaxy S23 FE, enquanto o Galaxy A37 é o modelo por fora entre os aparelhos intermediários.
Lembrando que, para verificar se o seu dispositivo já recebeu o pacote manualmente, basta acessar a opção “Atualização de software” nas Configurações do celular.
A Samsung apresentou a One UI 9 em julho, junto com os Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra e Z Flip 8, iniciando a distribuição para aparelhos mais antigos em setembro. O principal foco da atualização é a expansão da Galaxy AI:

articles.title: Infosys AI revenue jumps 29%; Apple’s foldable iPhone fully pre-booked in week 1
articles.text:
Infosys AI revenue jumps 29%; Apple’s foldable iPhone fully pre-booked in week 1
Infosys reported steady revenue growth in Q2 FY27, driven by strong AI demand and large deal wins.
Dear Reader,
Cybercriminals wasted little time turning a software disclosure into an opportunity. Cloudflare detected millions of attempts to exploit vulnerabilities in PHP soon after they were made public, underscoring how quickly attackers can move to target exposed systems. The surge in attacks has renewed concerns about the security of widely used systems and the urgency of patching vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.
Meanwhile, Apple appears to have struck a chord with India’s premium smartphone buyers. The company’s first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Duo, has reportedly seen its first week’s inventory fully booked through pre-orders. The response signals continued appetite for high-end devices as Apple enters the foldable phone market.
But not every digital trend brings good news. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has cautioned investors against fraudulent WhatsApp groups promising stock tips and profits. Such groups may use fabricated testimonials and misleading claims to gain trust before pushing unauthorised trading advice or suspicious apps. Investors have been advised to verify intermediaries before acting on recommendations.
On the jobs front, India’s healthcare global capability centres (GCCs) are expected to create 67,000 job openings in 2026, according to a Quess Corp report. Demand for specialised talent across technology and healthcare operations is expected to support this growth, reinforcing the sector’s shift towards more technology-driven work.
In today’s newsletter:
- Infosys sees 6.2% rise in Q2 net profit, AI revenue jumps 29% QoQ
- How AI is democratising creativity: Canva India’s Chandrika Deb
Here’s your trivia for today: Which is the world’s oldest known surviving epic poem? (Scroll down for the answer)
Corporate
Infosys sees 6.2% rise in Q2 net profit, AI revenue jumps 29% QoQ
Infosys reported steady growth in Q2 FY27, with AI emerging as a key revenue driver amid continued macroeconomic uncertainty. However, soft demand in North America and sector-specific challenges weighed on its outlook. The IT major lowered its full-year revenue growth guidance to 1-2% from 1.5-3% despite strong large deal wins.
Key takeaways:
- AI revenue grew strongly, accounting for a larger share of Infosys’ overall revenue, even as automation puts pressure on revenues.
- Infosys lowered its FY27 revenue growth guidance amid demand softness and macroeconomic headwinds, particularly in North America.
- The company’s large deal wins are expected to provide a cushion for growth, while Infosys continues to hire fresh graduates.
TechSparks
How AI is democratising creativity: Canva India’s Chandrika Deb
AI is making creativity more accessible by helping people overcome barriers of skill, resources and confidence. At TechSparks 2026, Canva India’s Chandrika Deb discussed how AI is reshaping creative workflows and workplace collaboration. She emphasised that human judgement and intent remain critical to creating relevant content.
Key takeaways:
- AI tools help people turn ideas into creative outputs faster, without requiring specialised skills or large teams.
- While AI can generate content, human intent, cultural understanding and audience awareness determine its relevance and quality.
- AI enables teams across marketing, sales, product and leadership to participate in creative work, while specialists continue to ensure quality and brand consistency.
News & updates
- Social Media: Greece’s parliament has passed a law banning children under 15 from using social media, citing concerns over minors’ health and safety. The ban will take effect on January 1, 2027, requiring platforms to introduce age-verification systems that protect users’ privacy. The move is part of wider efforts across Europe to curb excessive screen time and protect children from online harm.
- AI Diagnosis: Microsoft has developed an AI tool that diagnoses patients through a step-by-step process, achieving more than twice the accuracy of physicians in complex medical cases. Published in Science, the research will be followed by real-world testing at Boston’s Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to assess its use in emergency departments.

Answer: The Epic of Gilgamesh, originating in ancient Mesopotamia.

articles.title: [Weekly funding roundup Oct 17-23] VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals
articles.text:
[Weekly funding roundup Oct 17-23] VC funding falls below $100M amid lack of big deals
Venture capital funding in the third week of October recorded a sharp fall due to lower number of deals and absence of large value transactions.
Venture capital funding for Indian startups saw a steep decline in the third week of October, primarily due to a lower number of deals and the absence of any large-value transactions.
Venture capital funding during the week stood at just $96 million across 15 deals. In contrast, startups raised a total of $180 million in the previous week.
This sharp drop in venture capital funding highlights the challenges the Indian startup ecosystem continues to face in raising a steady flow of capital. This is also the eighth time so far this year that weekly venture capital funding has fallen below the $100 million mark.
The only large deal during the week was Even Healthcare’s $50 million raise. The other deals were worth $11 million or less. While transactions during the week saw investors place their bets across segments such as healthcare, consumer and AI, there were no other significant deals.
The biggest challenge for the Indian startup ecosystem so far this year has been the low number of large-value deals. In fact, there have been just 16 deals worth $100 million or more. This does not bode well for the ecosystem as 2026 draws to a close.
However, there is hope for a revival in 2027.
Key transactions
Even Healthcare raised $50 million from Khosla Ventures and Alpha Wave.
The Pant Project, a premium menswear label, raised Rs 109 crore ($11.4 million approx.) from Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Sorin Investments, Alteria Capital, and family offices.
Rural healthcare platform CureBay raised Rs 100 crore ($10.4 million approx.) from IvyCap Ventures, Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital and VentureSoul Partners.
Chapter Home, a home and kitchen consumer brand, raised Rs 63 crore ($6.6 million approx.) from Bessemer Venture Partners, Stride Ventures, influencer Tanmay Bhat, and select family offices.
Traveltech startup TravClan raised $5 million from Flipkart, August One, and Trifecta Capital.
AI startup Hunar AI raised Rs 40 crore ($4.2 million) from Blume Ventures, Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures and startup founders.

articles.title: « La situation va empirer » : après le chaos PHP, Anthropic prédit d'autres turbulences sur l’Internet mondial
articles.text:
Ce mardi 20 octobre 2026, deux failles critiques ont été découvertes dans le langage informatique PHP qui est utilisé par environ 70 % des sites à travers le monde. La situation s’est révélée être un véritable casse-tête pour l’Internet mondial, tant le langage PHP est omniprésent, mais aussi souvent invisible. Certains sites ont d’ailleurs pris la décision de se mettre tout simplement hors ligne, à l’image d’Orange, qui a suspendu temporairement l’accès à certains de ses sites et applications par mesure de précaution. L’Internet mondial a donc connu une période de crise, et cela ne devrait pas s’arranger si l’on en croit les propos de Jason Clinton, responsable adjoint de la sécurité des systèmes d’information chez Anthropic.
L’IA pourrait provoquer 18 mois de turbulences sur Internet
Jason Clinton, cadre chargé de la cybersécurité chez Anthropic, l’annonce sans détour : l’intelligence artificielle va déceler dans les mois à venir de nouvelles failles critiques sur l’Internet mondial, et celles-ci risquent d’engendrer de réelles perturbations. Sur le réseau social X, il explique : « Même si la situation s’est déjà considérablement dégradée ces quatre derniers jours, elle va encore fortement empirer avant de s’améliorer ».
Jason Clinton ouvre tout de même une fenêtre d’espoir en annonçant que la situation s’améliorera. Mieux encore, il donne un laps de temps durant lequel la situation s’annonce compliquée : « Nous devons tenir environ 18 mois ». Pourquoi ce laps de temps de 18 mois ? Pour l’instant, il existe un déséquilibre marqué entre les capacités de l’IA à détecter les failles et celles des entreprises concernées à y faire face. À terme, ces dernières devraient parvenir à mieux repérer les vulnérabilités avant qu’elles ne soient exploitées par des acteurs malveillants et à les corriger plus rapidement, notamment grâce à l’IA. Par ailleurs, les développeurs devraient de plus en plus se servir de l’IA pour détecter des failles dès la conception d’un logiciel.
L’IA fait entrer la cybersécurité dans une nouvelle ère
Les deux failles critiques présentes dans le langage informatique PHP ont été découvertes par une intelligence artificielle. OpenAI, l’entreprise derrière ChatGPT, a qualifié cette découverte comme « l’une des vulnérabilités les plus lourdes de conséquences de ces dernières années », tout en estimant que cela marque « le début d’une nouvelle phase, dans laquelle l’IA est capable de détecter des failles de sécurité susceptibles d’avoir un impact à l’échelle d’Internet ».
Autant dire qu’il est difficile de donner tort à OpenAI. En avril dernier, nous vous expliquions qu’Anthropic avait décidé de ne pas rendre Claude Mythos accessible au grand public, car ce modèle est capable de repérer des failles critiques et de les exploiter. Cette décision est aujourd’hui particulièrement illustrée par la découverte des deux failles critiques dans PHP. Et la situation pourrait donc encore s’aggraver dans les mois à venir.

Points forts
- Écran bien calibré et très lumineux.
- Présence du Snapdragon 8 Elite.
- Volet photo complet.
- Excellente autonomie.
- Expérience One UI 7.
Points faibles
- Design déjà vu.
- Téléobjectif assez décevant.
- Charge limitée à 25 W en 2025 !?
Alors oui, ce Galaxy S25 a tout d’un S24 amélioré, mais le résultat est là : le millésime 2025 surpasse le précédent. Son format compact, son écran réussi et sa puce surpuissante et économe en énergie en font un modèle aussi fluide qu’endurant. L’expérience photo gagne en précision, même si tout n’est pas parfait, notamment du côté du téléobjectif. On peut aussi regretter une puissance de charge encore limitée par rapport à la concurrence. Cependant, l’expérience offerte par One UI 7 et les nombreuses fonctions d’IA apportent un vent de modernité. À moins de posséder le modèle de 2024, cette itération est donc hautement recommandable. Samsung prouve ici que dans la tech comme en amour, il ne faut pas se fier aux apparences, et que l’important, c’est ce qu’il y a à l’intérieur.

articles.title: « On va me haïr » : cette romancière a écrit 371 livres grâce à ChatGPT, Claude et Grok, et elle assume
articles.text:
Thélyson Orélien a finalement admis « qu’une partie du processus d’écriture [du roman C’était ça ou mourir] a reposé sur l’IA ». Coral Hart, elle, assume pleinement avoir recours à l’IA pour écrire ses romans, comme elle l’explique à l’AFP. En fait, cette quadragénaire sud-africaine en a fait un véritable business. Elle propose même de générer des romans à votre place : 260 $ pour un livre unique et 705 $ pour une trilogie.
Près de 400 romans écrits à l’aide de l’IA en moins de 2 ans
En l’espace de 20 mois, Coral Hart a écrit, ou plutôt généré, 371 romans à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle. Un chiffre qui donnerait certainement le tournis à George R. R. Martin, l’auteur de Game of Thrones. Le processus de travail de Coral Hart est relativement simple. Tout d’abord, elle établit les grandes lignes de l’histoire, les personnages ou encore la structure globale du livre. Ensuite, elle fournit ces indications à une IA qui délivre un texte. Cependant, Coral Hart explique que la première version est systématiquement « mauvaise ». C’est pourquoi elle demande à une autre IA d’harmoniser l’ensemble notamment la continuité du récit et la cohérence globale. Enfin, un relecteur humain s’assure que l’IA n’a pas laissé d’erreur ou d’incohérence. Il peut même réécrire certains passages s’il le faut.
La romancière explique par ailleurs jongler avec différentes IA. ChatGPT serait ainsi « très bon sur les dialogues », Claude « incroyable pour la prose » et Grok « totalement désinhibé », et donc particulièrement utile pour générer des scènes osées.
260 dollars pour obtenir un livre généré par l’IA
Coral Hart explique sur son site Internet : « J’ai écrit 96 nouvelles à la dure [sans l’IA], phrase après phrase, et personne n’en a voulu. Puis, j’ai trouvé une méthode plus rapide [l’IA] et j’ai trouvé la solution ». Elle assure aujourd’hui avoir dépassé le million de livres vendus et généré un million de dollars de chiffre d’affaires en 2026.
Mais la romancière sud-africaine ne se limite pas à écrire des livres à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle puisqu’elle propose également d’en générer à votre place. Ainsi, elle peut vous fournir un livre pour 260 $, une trilogie pour 705 $ et une saga de 6 tomes pour 1 335 $. La seule chose à faire est de fournir une série d’informations sur le roman que l’on désire obtenir : les différents personnages, le scénario, les grandes lignes de l’histoire, etc. Soit, une bible de l’univers.
Ses méthodes de travail ne sont quant à elles pas vraiment bien vues. Il suffit de faire un tour dans la section commentaires des posts qui parlent d’elle. Coral Hart explique d’ailleurs à l’AFP qu’elle a reçu « des dizaines de milliers » de messages haineux et plusieurs menaces de mort. La place du processus créatif, qui passe en grande partie par l’écriture, mérite tout de même d’être posée au regard de ses méthodes de travail, la phase de rédaction ne se limitant pas à agencer des idées.
« Aujourd’hui, si je le dis, on va me haïr, ajouter mon nom à une liste et me menacer », explique l’auteure, soulignant que « les lecteurs ne lisent pas les mauvais livres, ils les renvoient ».

Source : France 24 avec l'AFP

articles.title: Ahórrate el IVA en Carrefour: cinco teles para aprovechar la nueva campaña de ofertas con modelo LG, Samsung y más
articles.text:
Carrefour está celebrando una vez más su campaña Ahórrate el IVA. Con la compra de una gran selección de productos, el importe correspondiente al IVA se traslada a un cupón que podemos canjear en futuras compras, algo interesante si solemos comprar en sus supermercados con cierta frecuencia. Hay bastantes televisores que entran dentro de esta promoción, por lo que vamos a repasar los cinco mejores chollos que hemos encontrado.
Eso sí, la campaña finalizará el próximo 26 de octubre y únicamente está disponible en la tienda online, aunque en algunos casos se puede comprar en web y pedir que la envíen a un establecimiento físico. Además, Carrefour no menciona la cifra exacta que luego se transferirá al cupón para próximas compras, ya que este cupón lo envía tras realizar la compra.
- Samsung TQ65QN73HAU por 669 euros, un televisor Neo QLED de 65 pulgadas.
- Xiaomi TV A Pro (2026) por 349 euros, una tele con Google TV y Dolby Audio.
- TCL 55C6K por 549 euros, con tasa de refresco de hasta 144 Hz y altavoces firmados por Onkyo.
- Samsung TQ55S93HAEXXC por 1.099 euros, un televisor OLED con tratamiento antirreflejos.
- LG OLED65B6ELC por 1.199 euros, un buen televisor con pantalla de 65 pulgadas.
Samsung TQ65QN73HAU
Si lo que queremos es un televisor con una buena relación calidad-precio dentro de la marca Samsung, el modelo Samsung TQ65QN73HAU tiene un precio de 669 euros. Se trata de una tele Neo QLED lanzada este año que cuenta con Alexa, viene con una pantalla de 65 pulgadas y dispone de función Multi-View para reproducir dos contenidos diferentes a la vez.
Samsung TQ65QN73HAU
Xiaomi TV A Pro (2026)
Si queremos un televisor un poco más pequeño, Carrefour tiene el Xiaomi TV A Pro (2026) por un precio de 349 euros. Se trata de un televisor de 55 pulgadas que viene con panel QLED y sistema operativo Google TV. Ofrece ángulos de visión de 178º (horizontales y verticales) y alcanza una tasa de refresco de 120 Hz a través de software.
TCL 55C6K
El televisor con mejor relación calidad-precio de este listado es el TCL 55C6K, que ahora mismo cuesta 549 euros. Incorpora un panel QD-Mini LED con diagonal de 55 pulgadas, es compatible con Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ y Dolby Atmos, su tasa de refresco es de hasta 144 Hz y sus altavoces están firmados por Onkyo.
Samsung TQ55S93HAEXXC
En cambio, si lo que queremos es un televisor de gama alta, Carrefour tiene el modelo Samsung TQ55S93HAEXXC por 1.099 euros. Se trata de un televisor con panel OLED que destaca sobre todo por su tratamiento antirreflejos. Su diagonal es de 55 pulgadas, ofrece una tasa de refresco de hasta 165 Hz por software (100 Hz nativos) y es compatible con HDR10+y Dolby Atmos.
Samsung TQ55S93HAEXXC
LG OLED65B6ELC
Carrefour también tiene el modelo LG OLED65B6ELC por 1.199 euros, que es ideal si queremos un televisor OLED con pantalla de 65 pulgadas. Ofrece una tasa de refresco de 120 Hz, es compatible con Dolby Vision y con Dolby Atmos y también es compatible con la tecnología gaming Nvidia G-Sync.

articles.title: Pour la première fois, des avions de chasse britanniques ont participé à un raid nucléaire simulé de la France
articles.text:
Des chasseurs Typhoon de la Royal Air Force ont pris part à un exercice nucléaire français aux côtés des Rafale, pour la toute première fois. Baptisée « Rummy », l'opération scelle un rapprochement inédit entre les deux puissances nucléaires européennes.
Les 20 et 21 octobre, des Rafale français ont simulé une frappe nucléaire au-dessus de la Méditerranée, avec des Typhoon britanniques pour escorte, nous apprend le ministère des Armées ce vendredi. Aucune arme nucléaire n'était à bord, mais le symbole est évident, d'autant plus que jamais l'Angleterre n'avait pris part aux répétitions de la dissuasion aéroportée française. Paris et Londres prennent pourtant soin de préciser que chacun garde seul la main sur son arsenal.
Typhoon et Rafale, un duo inédit au service de la dissuasion
Pour cette première, l'aventure a débuté à Saint-Dizier, en Haute-Marne. Cette base aérienne accueille les Forces aériennes stratégiques (FAS), le commandement de l’armée de l’Air et de l’Espace chargé de la mission nucléaire. La dissuasion française repose à la fois sur des sous-marins capables de tirer des missiles depuis les océans, et des Rafale qui peuvent emporter le missile nucléaire ASMPA-R, tiré depuis les airs.
Ce sont ces Rafale qui ont mené le raid fictif, encadrés par des Typhoon de la RAF dans le rôle d’escorte, c’est-à-dire chargés de les protéger d’éventuels chasseurs ennemis. Le tout sous des règles de sécurité strictes, avec un objectif clair, celui d'apprendre aux équipages des deux pays à se coordonner et à parler le même langage.
Rafale et Typhoon se connaissent bien, puisque les deux chasseurs s'entraînent régulièrement ensemble, qu'il s'agisse d'intercepter un appareil suspect ou de surveiller l'espace aérien. Ce qui change cette fois, c'est la nature de la mission. Le Royaume-Uni ne possède en effet plus d'arme nucléaire larguée depuis un avion depuis la fin des années 1990. Sa dissuasion repose tout entière sur ses sous-marins, armés de missiles Trident. Pour retrouver un rôle dans les airs, Londres mise sur des F-35A américains, capables d'emporter des bombes nucléaires américaines dans le cadre de l'OTAN. Voir des Typhoon prendre part à un exercice nucléaire français est donc une vraie première, salue Catherine Vautrin, pour qui la coopération entre les deux pays « ne cesse de s'approfondir ».
France et Royaume-Uni, deux arsenaux nucléaires qui volent en formation
Ce rapprochement découle de la Déclaration de Northwood, signée le 10 juillet 2025 par Emmanuel Macron et Keir Starmer, alors Premier ministre britannique, lors de la visite d'État du président français au Royaume-Uni. Paris et Londres avaient affirmé, pour la première fois également, que leurs dissuasions, tout en restant indépendantes, pouvaient être coordonnées. Les deux pays se dotaient ainsi d'une instance commune pour piloter cette coopération. L'exercice mené ces derniers jours, baptisé « Rummy », le nom anglais du rami, est considéré par Wes Streeting, le secrétaire britannique à la Défense, comme « un nouveau chapitre » dans un monde « de plus en plus dangereux ». Il invoque une « responsabilité commune » des deux pays envers la sécurité euro-atlantique, et prévient que leurs adversaires « ne doivent avoir aucun doute » sur leur unité.
Coordonner ne veut pour autant pas dire fusionner. Chaque pays conserve des forces souveraines, la décision d'employer l'arme ne se partage pas, et ce recours ne serait envisagé que dans des circonstances extrêmes de légitime défense. « Avoir des forces nucléaires indépendantes n'exclut pas la coordination », résume la ministre française, qui y voit un atout pour la sécurité de l'Alliance atlantique. Après le tir à blanc du dernier missile balistique français début octobre, le M51.3, Paris affirme un peu plus ses nouvelles ambitions militaires.

articles.title: In AI, it's a tale of two diverging investor classes - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
In AI, it’s a tale of two diverging investor classes
Depending on where you sit as an investor, artificial intelligence still looks like a massive opportunity, or it’s now looking way too risky given growing infrastructure investments and the public’s souring on AI and all the data centers needed to power it.
Really, it’s both. This week saw continued big venture capital investments in AI companies such as OpenAI, DeepSeek, Legora, Otter.ai, Flapping Airplanes (really) and more. But on Thursday, continued worry about potentially excessive data center spending — such as at Meta, which plans to issue new shares to pay for even more expansion — knocked AI stocks such as SpaceX and CoreWeave way down Thursday.
That volatility isn’t likely to change anytime soon, as more big earnings reports are coming next week, including the major cloud and AI providers Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft as well as Intel. Then there’s the prospect of Anthropic’s initial public offering of stock, which looks to vacuum up so much public investor money that some wonder if that will blunt their appetite for other AI stocks.
Still, the excitement of the people using AI, and the companies offering technologies to make it easier for them, seems to be undiminished, judging from several conferences this week, such as Nvidia’s GTC in Berlin and the PyTorch Conference and AGNTCon+MCPCon in San Jose. Among the highlights were Nvidia introducing new reference architectures. At PyTorch, Google and Amazon Web Services offered new tools leveraging the open-source deep learning framework used to build and train AI models, aiming to wrest some control of AI factories using Nvidia technologies.
And out of AGNTCon this week came open AI agent protocols from the Linux Foundation’s relatively new Agentic AI Foundation. They’re intended to keep big tech companies from dominating the key agent protocols and rails — the perennial battle that emerges with every significant new technology. More on that below.
AI managed to find long-hidden vulnerabilities in PHP, the open-source scripting language for the web, and suddenly some 70% of websites had to scramble to apply patches — but that takes awhile, so many remain in danger and thus, so do we. The rising capabilities of AI in finding vulnerabilities also means the defensive edge AI provided defenders so far is fading or gone already — as Mythos itself apparently proved when it tried to send malicious code to an open-source project.
This just in: Dave Vellante’s latest Breaking Analysis looks at how AI is changing the economics of the semiconductor and whether the industry’s cyclicality is over.
Many people who don’t live inside enterprise technology have at best a fuzzy idea of what ServiceNow is all about — workflow automation among other things — but now it’s looking to move into a pole position in AI. With its new AI Control Tower, it’s aiming to discover and govern any agent, work across models and clouds, track cost and value, and shut down behavior that violates policy. In his latest Breaking Analysis, Dave looks at the reality and the prospects.
A couple of important events arrive next week, including Oracle AI World in Las Vegas, and theCUBE’s and theCUBE Research’s own timely virtual event, the AI Cybersecurity & Resiliency Summit.
Here’s all of this week’s enterprise and emerging tech news, analysis and commentary from SiliconANGLE and beyond:
Analysis, opinion and food for thought

Left alone with nothing to do, AI agents started playing (per TechCrunch)

New models and services
Coverage from the AGNTCon+MCPCon conference:

And a few thoughts from attending the event, which came just weeks after another installment in Amsterdam:
At AGNTCon+MCPCon, the Linux Foundation extended its play to provide protocols for the emerging agentic AI stack, pointedly eyeing the big tech and AI companies all hoping to carve out pieces they can essentially own.
The goal is to prompt those companies to do something like what Google did with the software container orchestrator Kubernetes: Help establish it as the standard and then hand it off to a vendor-neutral organization, in that case the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, to extend it.
“If you’re not careful, one company ends up owning the plumbing and you pay rent,” Manik Surtani, formerly Block’s head of open source and now co-founder and chief technology officer of the Agentic AI Foundation, noted during a keynote at the event. “The agentic era is still being built… and we should ensure it’s built in the open. The plumbing of the agentic era shouldn’t belong to one entity. It should belong to all of us.”
The Agentic AI Foundation, Executive Director Mazin Gilbert said, aims to be that “neutral home where the agentic AI stack is being built.” And there’s demand for vendor-neutral protocols and platforms: It has been adding new members like crazy, now counting 305 since starting 10 months ago.
Paul Nashawaty, an analyst with theCUBE Research, SiliconANGLE’s sister market research firm, and with Efficiently Connected Inc., said standardization is crucial because “the durable competitive advantage in agentic AI will belong to whoever controls identity attestation, tool-calling protocols, payment rails, and audit trails. Those are exactly the layers the AAIF is trying to standardize in the open.” He added that “the addition of projects from OpenAI, Alibaba, and Hugging Face, three organizations with deeply competing commercial interests, to a single neutral governance structure is a meaningful signal.”
