articles.title: Apple esconde un iPod virtual en su web por los 25 años del reproductor: así se puede encontrar
articles.text:
Apple celebra los 25 años del iPod con una sorpresa interactiva escondida en su página web de Apple Music. Se trata de una versión virtual del reproductor que permite utilizar su característica rueda de navegación desde la pantalla táctil de un iPhone y explorar menús con música de 2001, el año en que se presentó el dispositivo.
El reproductor original fue anunciado por Steve Jobs el 23 de octubre de 2001 y marcó un cambio en la manera de almacenar y escuchar canciones. Su promesa de llevar mil canciones en el bolsillo se convirtió en uno de los símbolos de la compañía y contribuyó a transformar la industria musical.
Para encontrar esta versión digital, es necesario acceder a una dirección específica desde Safari, el navegador de Apple. El iPod virtual aparece en una página de error de Apple Music, por lo que no basta con navegar por las secciones habituales del servicio.
Cómo encontrar el iPod virtual en la web de Apple
El homenaje está escondido en una página que normalmente mostraría un error 404, el código que aparece cuando se intenta acceder a una dirección que no existe. Sin embargo, Apple preparó ese espacio para incluir el reproductor interactivo.
Para acceder desde un iPhone, hay que seguir estos pasos:
- Copiar la dirección https://music.apple.com/es/new/ipod.
- Abrir Safari y pegar la dirección directamente en la barra de navegación.
- Ingresar a la página para visualizar el iPod virtual.
- Deslizar el dedo sobre la rueda para recorrer los menús y tocar el botón central para seleccionar opciones.
Un detalle importante es que conviene copiar y pegar la dirección en Safari en lugar de pulsar directamente sobre un enlace. Si el iPhone abre la aplicación Apple Music, el reproductor virtual podría no aparecer como se espera.
La experiencia reproduce parte de la interacción del dispositivo original: la rueda permite desplazarse por las opciones y el botón central sirve para seleccionar elementos. Además, incluye música vinculada con el año 2001, con categorías como rock, country y alternativa.
De esta forma, Apple recupera uno de sus productos más reconocibles mediante una experiencia que combina nostalgia y tecnología. La compañía no ha precisado cuánto tiempo permanecerá disponible este contenido.
El iPod cambió la forma de llevar música en el bolsillo
Cuando Apple presentó el iPod en 2001, los reproductores portátiles de música tenían limitaciones de almacenamiento y, en muchos casos, dependían de discos compactos o memorias de capacidad reducida.
El dispositivo de Apple destacó por su disco duro de cinco gigabytes, que permitía almacenar aproximadamente mil canciones, según la presentación original de la compañía. Su diseño compacto y la rueda de navegación facilitaron la búsqueda de música sin necesidad de utilizar numerosos botones físicos.
El desarrollo del reproductor también estuvo vinculado con iTunes, el programa que permitía organizar canciones en una computadora y transferirlas al dispositivo. La combinación entre software y hardware ayudó a establecer un modelo de consumo musical que posteriormente evolucionó con las tiendas digitales y los servicios de suscripción.
La rueda de navegación se convirtió en uno de los elementos más distintivos del producto. Su diseño permitía recorrer grandes bibliotecas musicales con movimientos del dedo, mientras que el acabado blanco y los auriculares a juego reforzaron su identidad visual.
Con el paso de los años, Apple lanzó distintas generaciones del iPod, entre ellas los modelos mini, nano, shuffle y touch. Sin embargo, la expansión del iPhone y de los servicios de música por internet redujo progresivamente la necesidad de contar con un reproductor independiente.
Del iPod al iPhone: 25 años de evolución
El aniversario coincide con una etapa en la que Apple apuesta por nuevos formatos de dispositivos y servicios digitales. El iPod fue uno de los productos que ayudaron a consolidar la estrategia de integrar equipos, programas y contenidos dentro de un mismo ecosistema.
Hoy, Apple Music ofrece acceso a millones de canciones mediante internet, mientras que el iPhone reúne en un solo dispositivo funciones que antes requerían equipos separados, como escuchar música, tomar fotografías y comunicarse.
El homenaje virtual recupera precisamente esa transición: un reproductor que nació para guardar canciones y que ahora puede explorarse desde la pantalla de un celular. La rueda que caracterizó al iPod vuelve así como una pieza interactiva de la historia tecnológica de Apple.

articles.title: "Señora, que si quiere bolsa": no, lo que quiero es pagar la compra con Bizum y Mercadona está a punto de dejarme
articles.text:
Hace tanto que pago con el móvil que ya no llevo la tarjeta en la cartera porque mi realidad es que mi teléfono lo mismo me sirve para liquidar esas compras que para ajustar cuentas con mis amigas cuando tomamos algo. Bendito Bizum. Pues bien, la posibilidad de pagar con el móvil pero sin tarjeta se está fraguando en la cadena de supermercados de Juan Roig porque Mercadona está probando el pago con Bizum Pay en las cajas de varios de sus establecimientos.
A punto. Según El Confidencial, el nuevo sistema de pago está en fase de pruebas en varias tiendas seleccionadas de Mercadona, como las de Soria. El objetivo de la compañía es medir la rapidez y la fluidez en la línea de caja para su expansión. Expansión apunta a un estado más avanzado: tras meses de pruebas, la cadena valenciana empezará con el despliegue total este mes.
Por qué importa. Mercadona es la cadena de supermercados que más dinero ingresa en España, así que su decisión pesa mucho. Bizum es un sistema de pagos ya muy extendido que nació para saldar cuentas entre particulares, pero que cada vez sirve más para pagar compras. Que llegue a las grandes cadenas de supermercados para el día a día lo refuerza como alternativa a las tarjetas, un negocio donde las norteamericanas Visa y Mastercard se comen buena parte del pastel.
Los supermercados dicen sí a Bizum. Mercadona ya aceptaba Bizum en su tienda online, así que este es el salto a la tienda física para una compatibilidad total con el servicio. Vaya por delante algo: Mercadona no es ni la única en dar el paso a estas alturas, ya que también se han sumado estos días Eroski o Burger King, ni la primera: Lidl ya aceptaba Bizum en su tienda online en 2023 y desde hace semanas se puede pagar en sus tiendas físicas.
De acuerdo con el diario económico Expansión, la banca española está implantando Bizum Pay en las grandes cadenas de supermercados y empresas de distribución, entre ellas Inditex, Ikea, Carrefour, El Corte Inglés, Eroski, Alcampo, Caprabo, Burger King o Lidl, si bien su despliegue es progresivo y el ritmo es desigual.
Cómo usarlo. Con este protocolo, quien compra paga directamente desde su cuenta bancaria, sin tarjeta de crédito ni de débito: basta con acercar el móvil al datáfono o escanear un código QR. Hace falta comprar en un comercio que ofrezca la opción y tener el servicio activado. Según El Confidencial, además, el banco debe estar integrado en el protocolo presencial. Entre las entidades que lo ofrecen están CaixaBank, Sabadell, Bankinter, Unicaja y Abanca. Si es el caso, basta con disponer de la app.

articles.title: Hegseth warns prediction market bets warp military judgment, endanger troops
articles.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a memo warning military personnel against using nonpublic information to make bets on prediction markets, saying the wagers could give important clues to enemy countries.
“Do Not Compromise Military Operations for Personal Financial Gain,” said the subject line of an October 20 memo published yesterday by CBS News. Hegseth’s memo was sent to senior Pentagon leadership, Combatant Command leaders, and Defense Department field activity directors.
Hegseth wrote:
Our enemies watch movements in these markets. When an American Service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal. That signal can be aggregated, correlated, and exploited by hostile foreign intelligence services to anticipate our movements, targets, and timing. The lives of our Service members often depend on the enemy not knowing what is coming. The men and women who carry our flag into harm’s way deserve a Force that protects them—not one that exposes them to the enemy for personal gain.
In April, a US Army soldier was arrested and charged with using confidential information to make $410,000 in Polymarket bets on the timing of the military’s capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. An August report by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective said the group found 152 suspicious wallets that placed longshot bets on military and defense markets and won a combined $8 million.
Betting can warp judgment, Hegseth says
Hegseth’s memo said the prohibition applies to “all financial platforms,” including traditional betting services and prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi. Defense Department personnel may not make any financial transaction informed by nonpublic information, regardless of whether that information is classified or unclassified, Hegseth wrote.

articles.title: Bambu Lab teases its mysterious H3C tool changer 3D printer — features nine tools and a drop-down rack, slated for November 3 launch
articles.text:
Bambu Lab teases its mysterious H3C tool changer 3D printer — features nine tools and a drop-down rack, slated for November 3 launch
Here’s what we can say about the mystery machine.
Bambu Lab’s long-anticipated tool changer will launch on November 3rd. Dubbed the H3C, the 3D printer has 9 tools held by a Vortex-like rack mounted on the front of the chamber. Tool changers are the wave of the future, as they can switch colors faster and with less waste than Bambu Lab’s current AMS system.
Unfortunately, most of the information about the new 3D printer is shrouded in secrecy, but there are plenty of details that are already public knowledge. Bambu Lab is quite proud of this latest engineering feat, which you can see in the video below, and I’ll admit, I’m pretty impressed, too.
Here’s what we can confirm about the H3C: It is a member of the H-line of flagship printers, which includes the H2S, H2D, and H2C. As you can imagine, it is most similar to its namesake, the H2C, which is a 7-tool induction-heated “nozzle swapper” with a motorized Vortex rack to hold tools not in use. The H2C is one of the larger Bambu Lab machines, with a 330 x 320 x 325mm build volume.
The 11-second-long teaser video shows the tool rack dropping down, along with a satisfying metallic snick. As you might imagine, tool heads that are stored above the build plate are not going to get in your way when you’re watching that first layer go down. This is an annoying problem with the Bondtech INDX system, which we reviewed paired up with a Prusa CORE One, which forces you to peer through the tool rack to see what's going on inside the printer. Visibility on the Bambu H3C is probably better.
If you type “H3C leak” on YouTube, you can find several YouTubers who do not have machines under review dissecting the clues sprinkled around the internet. One “AI-enhanced” image showed 10 spools, which I can now finally confirm is completely wrong. Today’s video clearly shows only nine colorful Bowden tools arching over the top of the printer. We’re not at liberty to say what’s holding the spools, but I think it’s safe to acknowledge that it's a very Bambu sort of system.
The H2 line has been touted as a home manufacturing hub, so you might wonder if the H3C is the same? Perhaps it is. I had an opportunity to talk to Dr. Tao at Formnext last year when the H2C was fresh, and he was very interested in creating multitasking machines that could do more than just 3D print.
Sadly, not everyone was impressed with adding a laser to the H2D, but since the Bambu Lab A2L has an optional blade cutting and embossing tool, we can safely assume that the notion of multitasking is alive and well. I once programmed an Ender 3 to pick up Sharpie markers, so just think about the things a much more sophisticated machine with a team of sharp engineers could program.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
I can’t wait to tell you more about the H3C. There are definitely a couple of surprising things about this printer that are going to come out of left field. We’ll let it all out on November 3rd.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

articles.title: Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: I want to love these wireless headphones, but poor sound dulls their shine
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y know exactly what their own “why” is: to give you the best, most self-expressive out-and-about listening experience a relatively small budget can buy. And they meet the terms of that “why” quite impressively, with a cut-through sonic profile, solid ANC and a bonkers battery life to boot. But that sonic profile crumbles under scrutiny, revealing lacklustre bass and barely-there dynamics when there’s nothing else to compensate for. The Aventho Y don’t quite cut the mustard for at-home or hi-res listening; a real shame for a promising pair of affordable headphones.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent active noise cancellation
- + 90-hour battery life
- + Cool, comfortable design
Reasons to avoid
- - Poor out of the box sonic performance
- - No hi-res Bluetooth codec support
- - Pay more for add-on improvements
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y: Two-minute review
The tagline for Beyerdynamic’s latest consumer-grade, ANC-equipped wireless headphones is “What is your why?” — and, unfortunately, “Why?” was the first question on my lips when I first listened to them. A lacklustre sonic profile is accompanied by a lack of convincing dynamics, at least when listening actively in a quiet room.
My “why?” was answered in part by the Aventho Y’s own “why”: they are clearly designed to be used outdoors, to compete with a constant thrum of traffic and people and cut through accordingly. And this they do, quite commendably. The ANC is impactful, which is more than you can say for most headphones in this price range; there’s also a Transparency mode which is similarly effective outside. The long battery life is a genuine boon, as is the fact you can replace that battery with ease whenever it does eventually lose its edge.
A shoo-in for our best noise-cancelling headphones guide then? Not so fast. Better as the Aventho Y's performance is when on the move, it’s not saved wholly from its shortcomings. It’s necessary to visit the Beyerdynamic app to reintroduce some low end, and there’s still a sense that you’re not hearing songs as they ought to be heard.
Well-designed and well-priced though these headphones are — and excellent as that ANC is for its price — I can’t love the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y as much as I’d like to, purely for how poorly the sound is handled. Curmudgeonly as this review may at some points seem, I am no stranger to whimsy; I did really enjoy my time with these headphones. They shine in loud environments. Anywhere else, though, that shine is predestined to dull.
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Price & release date
- Released on September 3, 2026
- Priced $149.99 / £129 / AU$280
Beyerdynamic is one of the pre-eminent names when it comes to matters of professional audio. The German brand’s reputation precedes itself, thanks to a near-faultless gallery of clean, clear and natural-sounding monitor headphones beloved by audio engineers and pro producers innumerable — and to say nothing of its microphones, too.
Beyerdynamic’s reputation in the wider consumer-audio world is less well-tested, though still hugely positive. The brand’s had its hands in MP3 player-era in-ears, gaming headphones and wireless earbuds over the last two decades, in the middle of which the word ‘Aventho’ first appeared. Most of these consumer-friendly audio interventions trucked in the same professional elegance as the brand’s pro-level interventions, with sharp lines or important-looking negative spaces; a stern-ness of design which makes this latest intervention all the more interesting.
The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y are a pair of wireless, ANC-toting over-ear headphones, and a clear signal of fairly naked ambition by the brand to appeal to a new generation of listeners. Some semblances of the Beyerdynamic signature remain, but they’re overtaken by a quartet of somewhat-bold color options and a somewhat-bolder, somewhat-existential marketing push to accompany them: “What is your why?”
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In terms of succession, the Aventho Y is a young, hip relative of the Beyerdynamic Aventho 300 — which, specs- and price-wise, still appears to be the adult in the room. The Y, then, is a much more expressive and accessible piece of consumer listening gear, taking the long battery and solid audio philosophies of its late-Millennial Dad, cramming them into a pastel-colored knapsack and promptly running for the Reels.
At $149.99 / £129 / AU$280, the Aventho Y hurls itself right into the middle of an already-stacked field of affordable wireless headphones. So, is the Aventho Y’s “why” compelling enough to beat them?
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Specs
| Drivers | 45mm dynamic drivers | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 90+ hours (60+ hours with ANC) | 
| Weight | 316g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0, USB-C, 3.5mm mic input | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz - 20kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP53 | 
| Other features | 1m USB-C to USB-C cable, soft drawstring carry pouch | 
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Features
- Active Noise Cancelling and Transparency modes
- 90-hour battery life (60 with ANC engaged)
- Bluetooth 6.0 with Multipoint
The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y are an affordable set of wireless over-ear headphones, with active noise cancelling and a prodigious battery life to fuel it. More specifically, the Aventho Y boast 90 hours of non-stop listening, or 60 with ANC engaged — that’s easily a month of morning-commute listening, at least. And in the unlikely event that you burn through your Aventho Y’s juice prematurely, you’ll still have the rest of the day’s listening back in no time at all; a five-minute quick charge yields six hours of listening life.
Humongous reservoir of power aside, the Aventho Y sport a pair of 45mm dynamic drivers, serviced by a Bluetooth 6.0 receiver capable of Multipoint connectivity, and of decoding SBC and AAC codecs. On the face of things, it’s a real shame not to see some lossless aptX or LDAC support here, but practically speaking, AAC is fidelity aplenty for day-to-day listening.
That Bluetooth is, of course, two-way too; there’s a microphone on board for wireless phone calls, and some well-sized control buttons for playing, pausing and skipping songs without pulling your phone out. It’s also the means by which the Aventho Y connects to Beyerdynamic’s smartphone app, which allows control of ANC and user-preset EQ modes, amongst other things. As for physical I/O, there’s a USB-C port that supports both charging and wired listening, and a 3.5mm output for an add-on boom microphone (more details of which are yet to surface).
A big win for me on the features front — which you’ll hear more about later on — is the easily-removable, magnetically-attached ear-pads; behind them, you’ll find a replaceable battery and a tellingly-shaped hole for a USB-C dongle. The dongle is also yet to surface, but will reportedly enable low-latency Bluetooth connectivity to other devices, in tandem with better-quality audio from the aforementioned and as-yet-unreleased boom mic.
- Features score: 4.5 / 5
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Sound quality
- Lacklustre, telephonic bass profile
- Performs better when competing with outside noise
- Smartphone-app EQ-ing essential
To be completely honest, my first impression of the Aventho Y’s performance was not a positive one. On connecting to my laptop and streaming some music from Qobuz, the out-of-the-box sound profile threw me for a loop; being accustomed to Beyerdynamic’s flat-response monitor headphones, I wasn’t expecting a near-telephonic treatment of high mids and voices from this consumer-focused entry.
Queens Of The Stone Age’s Everybody Knows That You’re Insane, taken from expansive 2005 slow-cooker Lullabies To Paralyse should be an urgent, propulsive assault of information from bright guitars to thudding bass and kicks, but the Aventho Y presents it as a peaky mess of honky leads and vocals. Why? Or should I say, “Y”? (Sorry.)
Some artists get a little bit of a better break than others. Interpol’s Turn On The Bright Lights demonstrated a clarity with respect to monophonic lead guitars, but at the expense of clarity in other areas. The snare in Untitled sounded boxed-up, restrained — as did the bass, which should swell and envelope but instead seemed stuck behind everything else, revving up in hopes of getting past. It’s a peculiar sensation, really. It feels like these headphones can’t fully handle the music they’re receiving, whether it’s through a lack of headroom, or a lack of vacancy for low end to thrive.
It occurred to me, then, that I wasn’t testing the Aventho Y in the environment they were designed for. Marketing copy, express-yourself colorways and aesthetic ads of headphone-clad models dancing in public all point to the Aventho Y being expressly created for soundtracking your life outside. So that’s where I went.
And the experience was much, much different. Everything I’ve said about the default sound profile stands, but matters much less in public. Contending with the everyday noises of urban traffic means that honky high-mids turn, somewhat, into tactile presence. LA Priest’s latest LP Into The Sky is a gratuitously texture-rich compendium of electronic love songs, and had exactly the bite I was looking for while I waited for the bus.
Against the noise of the outside world, It’s less apparent that your music is straining against the limits of the headphones; it’s designed to compensating for a living, breathing world around you. The bass is still a let-down, but, luckily, there’s an app for that.
The Beyerdynamic app gives you control over a few features, including a customisable graphic EQ. Even just some slight adjustments between 60Hz and 200Hz brought back some essential thump and hum; I just don’t understand “Y” (sorry) the Aventho Y shipped with the sound as is.
I will also say, to the Aventho Y’s credit, that its ANC is frightfully effective — much more so than more expensive headphones I’ve tried before, and to an almost discomforting degree. It does introduce a hissy noise floor, so you aren’t getting a pristine listening environment with it engaged; still, it’s better than cranking the volume over the roar of a bus (or, indeed, the interminable TV-borne whinings of Tempting Fortune’s contemptible contestants while you’re trying desperately to finish a review about some wireless headphones. I mean, honestly).
The Aventho Y also sport a Transparency mode, which pipes a little more of your surroundings into your cans. It’s less effective than the ANC is indoors, but incredibly effective outdoors — albeit with that same underlying hiss.
Sound-wise, the Aventho Y are hard to score. They sound, frankly, quite bad out of the box and in a quiet listening space; they’re clearly not for active listening, or pairing with pricey hi-fi systems. But out and about, they deliver quite well, and especially so when it comes to more practical interventions like ANC and transparency mode. But they wouldn’t sound anywhere near as good as they could without app-based EQ intervention. It’s a mess of “buts”, and all a bit of a shame, really.
- Sound quality score: 3 / 5
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Design
- Cool visual design
- Comfortable for long durations
- Easy to repair and replace elements
The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y are demonstrably nice to look at, courtesy of the smart-and-simple ear cup design and those four tasteful color options. My set are this peachy pastel orange, with tinted cream ear and head cushions — an easy-going Zillennial two-tone, offset by metal-effect silver plastic brackets. That they are plastic is, of course and always, a bit of a shame, but it’s no surprise in a consumer-forward set of wireless over-ears (and even less of one for a pair that ask only for $149 / £129).
A big win for me is the repairability of the Aventho Y, typified by the magnetically-secured ear pads that pull off with a firm-but-fair tug. Beyerdynamic offer velour-clad pad upgrades, too, for an even comfier experience.
Removing the left ear pad unearths the enclosure for the Aventho Y’s battery, allowing easy replacement should your battery eventually die on you. This level of replaceability has been historically rare for consumer-grade products in the same camp as the Aventho Y, which makes this a real breath of fresh air — but only so much in the way of props can be delivered Beyerdynamic’s way.
With the EU now mandating the self-repairability of consumer electronics from 2027, it’s no surprise that new products increasingly bear such customer-friendly design choices, and it’s a shame that, after years of impenetrable products from more unscrupulous brands elsewhere, it’s such a pleasantness to encounter them. Still, I’m allowed to be impressed for now.
While I’m here, I’m also pretty keen on the physical buttons in the ear cups — particularly the literal switch that turns the Aventho Y on and enables Bluetooth pairing. That kind of tactile responsiveness is similarly rare, and hugely welcome.
Finally, I can’t fault the Aventho Y at all on comfort. I could easily wear them for hours (and actually, I have), thanks to some light, comfy ear pads and a fold-up design that lets them sit around your neck without applying undue pressure. How these are put together, and how they interact with you as owner, are easily some of the best things about these cans.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Value
- Excels on all practical fronts…
- …but the sound is hard to get past
- Well-priced for features
At $149.99 / £129 / AU$280, the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y undercut a lot of its large-battery-having, ANC-toting contemporaries as an affordable piece of outdoor-listening kit. There are cheaper headphones, yes, but rarely do headphones as cheap as this offer up to 90 hours of uninterrupted listening and a noise-cancelling algorithm that actually, tangibly makes a difference to your day-to-day. It’s rare also to see a pair of headphones so smoothly designed. The aesthetics and execution are undeniably great. But…
I just can’t get over that initial disappointment I felt listening to them for the first time, at my desk. Beyerdynamic is capable of so much more than this, so it’s difficult to understand “Y” (sorry) they settled on this sound at this price. Without the steady thrum of urban life to contend with, there’s nowhere for the Aventho Y’s sonic shortcomings to hide — and EQ isn’t quite enough to fix them, either.
Again, it’s clear that the Aventho Y’s own “Y” is facilitating some groovy movement in your day-to-day. And they do succeed in that regard, but still need a bit of a helping hand along the way. If you do just want a set of wireless headphones for drowning out the wider world during your commutes, these are excellent value for money. Elsewhere, it’s much harder to truly see what the “why” is with them.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y?
| Section | Notes | Score | Header Cell - Column 3 | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Features | The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y is a pair of wireless over-ear headphones with 90-hour battery, some brilliant ANC and Bluetooth 6.0 Multipoint connectivity — though it’s lacking hi-res codec support. | 4/5 | Row 0 - Cell 3 | 
| Sound quality | Unfortunately, the Aventho Y’s sound quality just isn’t there out of the box. There’s no decent low end to speak of, and the high mids are peaky to the point of discomfort. This makes sense when they’re competing against public hubbub, but even then, the only way to create any weight is by boosting lows in the proprietary Beyerdynamic app. | 3/5 | Row 1 - Cell 3 | 
| Design | The design is (nearly) the best thing about the Aventho Y, with a choice of four tasteful colorways and some clever replaceable ear pads — not to mention a neat fold-up design and hours of listening comfort. | 4.5/5 | Row 2 - Cell 3 | 
| Value | There’s some undeniable value to the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y. The ANC is great, the build quality is good for the price and the battery life is even better. The sound lets them down, insofar as they aren’t wholly suitable for anything but out-and-about. | 4/5 | Row 3 - Cell 3 | 
Buy them if...
You’re always on the move
The long, long battery life is already reason enough to lean into the Aventho Y as your new pair of leaving-the-house headphones, but consider also the fetching color options, on-board controls and outside-friendly sonic profile.
Active Noise Cancelling is a non-negotiable
I’ve found it hard to get good ANC at all, to be honest, let alone at a functionally budget price point. The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y are frankly excellent for noise cancelling, and well worth it for less chaotic commutes.
Don't buy them if...
You’re after wireless headphones for sit-down listening
Quite simply, the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y are not designed for active listening. Between the marketing, battery life and color scheme, they’re begging to be worn out and about, where a near-telephonic frequency response with a honky preference for upper-mids makes far more sense.
You want stellar sound out of the box
The Aventho Y don’t really become themselves until you’ve spent some time tweaking EQs in Beyerdynamic’s app — which, incidentally, you can only do on a smartphone.
Beyerdynamic Aventho Y review: Also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Beyerdynamic Aventho Y | Sony WH-CH730N | JBL Live 780N | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Drivers | 45mm dynamic | 30mm | 40mm | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | Yes | Yes | 
| Quoted battery life | 90+ hours (60+ hrs with ANC) | 75 hours (50 hrs with ANC) | 80 hours (50 hrs with ANC) | 
| Weight | 316g | 207g | 270g | 
| Connectivity | Bluetooth 6.0, USB-C, 3.5mm mic input | Bluetooth 6.0, 3.5mm | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Frequency range | 20Hz - 20kHz | 20Hz - 20kHz | 10 Hz - 40 kHz | 
| Waterproofing | IP53 | No rating | No rating | 
| Extras | 1m USB-C to USB-C cable, carry pouch | 3.5mm to 3.5mm cable | USB-C to analog cable, carry pouch | 
Sony WH-CH730N
These come in a little cheaper than the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y, but sport many of the same features — and a few of the same shortcomings. There’s good ANC and great battery life, but, unlike the Aventho Y, no USB-C audio passthrough. 
Read our full Sony WH-CH730N review
JBL Live 780NC
For slightly more money, you could get yourself a much more aggressively-hued set of these JBL over-ears, with formidable ANC and some respectable sound performance to match. These are solid performers at a solid price. 
Read our in-depth JBL Live 780NC review
How I tested the Beyerdynamic Aventho Y
- Tested for 4 weeks
- Used both in and out of the home
- Predominantly tested using music streamed from Qobuz, via Bluetooth-connected laptop or smartphone
The Beyerdynamic Aventho Y spent around 4 weeks with me, in a variety of listening situations both active and passive. They were tested partly at home, connected to my HP Pavilion 15 laptop via Bluetooth and receiving music from the streaming service Qobuz, as well as from my digital audio library. I also took the Aventho Y out and about on my various day-to-day gallivantings, connected to my Samsung S23 FE via Bluetooth and, again, listening to music streamed from Qobuz.
Read more about how we test at TechRadar
- First reviewed: October 2026

articles.title: Austrália decide: Apple deve abrir iPhone a apps de outras lojas • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Austrália decide: Apple deve abrir iPhone a apps de outras lojas
Decisão do Tribunal Federal do país obriga Apple a tirar exclusividade da App Store dos dispositivos, assim como já acontece aqui no Brasil.
O Tribunal Federal da Austrália decidiu que a Apple deve abrir seus iPhones e iPads para outras lojas de aplicativos além da App Store. Além dos downloads a partir de outras fontes, usuários também terão a possibilidade de usar meios alternativos de pagamento nos dispositivos da maçã. A decisão ocorreu nesta quarta-feira (21/10).
Ainda em 2025, a Justiça australiana havia apontado que a Apple violou as leis antitruste do país ao restringir o acesso a apps e meios de pagamento alternativos. O processo foi movido pela Epic Games, que trava essa batalha há alguns anos contra a empresa estadunidense, desde que o Fortnite acabou excluído da App Store em diversas regiões.
A sentença passa a valer em 1º de março de 2027, mas a Apple ainda pode recorrer. Segundo o juíz responsável pelo caso, Jonathan Beach, a Apple detém “um nível substancial de poder na distribuição de apps do iOS”, restringindo a concorrência. Além do país da Oceania, a empresa também precisou afrouxar suas regras do iOS no Brasil e no Japão, assim como na União Europeia.
A decisão da corte australiana foi celebrada por Tim Sweeney, CEO da Epic Games. Em uma postagem no X, o executivo disse que se trata de “uma grande vitória para consumidores e desenvolvedores”. A Epic esteve diretamente envolvida no caso, uma vez que foi autora do processo que apontou violação das leis antitruste do país tanto pela Apple quanto pelo Google.
A primeira batalha judicial entre as companhias se deu em 2020, nos Estados Unidos, e ainda em 2021 a justiça do país apontou violação das leis antitruste. Ainda assim, apenas meios de pagamento alternativos são permitidos por lá, e lojas de apps externas seguem indisponíveis para usuários de iPhone e iPad.
A Apple vai recorrer da sentença. Ela disse que “vai buscar uma solução que respeite a propriedade intelectual” de seus produtos.
Aqui no Brasil, a liberação de apps e meios de pagamento alternativos no iPhone se deu por meio de um acordo entre a Apple e o Cade (Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica). A medida partiu de uma denúncia do Mercado Livre, que reclamava de venda casada e bloqueio da concorrência no setor de pagamentos.

articles.title: Grünalgen statt Motoren: Dieser weiche Roboterarm bewegt sich allein durch Licht
articles.text:
Grünalgen statt Motoren: Dieser weiche Roboterarm bewegt sich nur durch Licht
Wissenschaftler:innen der niederländischen Technischen Universität Delft (TU Delft) haben einen weichen Greifarm konstruiert, der sich allein durch den Stoffwechsel lebender Mikroalgen verformt. Wie in einer im Wissenschaftsmagazin Nature Communications veröffentlichten Studie zu lesen ist, wandelt das Bauteil einfallendes Licht ohne elektronische Steuerung oder externe Energiequellen in mechanische Biegungen um.
Basis der Konstruktion ist ein zwei Zentimeter langer, fünf Millimeter breiter und ein Millimeter dicker Streifen aus einem wasserbindenden Kunststoff, einem sogenannten Hydrogel. „Unser Proof-of-Concept-Aktor ist ein grüner, weicher Streifen aus zwei unterschiedlichen Hydrogelschichten, auf dessen Oberfläche Mikroalgen wachsen“, erklärt Studienleiterin Marie-Eve Aubin-Tam in einer Mitteilung der TU Delft mit Blick auf das Antriebselement.
TU Delft koppelt Grünalge Chlamydomonas reinhardtii an zweischichtiges Hydrogel
Für die Besiedlung legten Erstautor Fan Jiang und seine Kolleg:innen den Kunststoffstreifen sieben Tage lang in eine Kultur der einzelligen Süßwasser-Grünalge Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Während dieser Zeit bildeten die Mikroorganismen auf dem Material einen rund 71 Mikrometer dicken Biofilm, also eine geschlossene Zellschicht an der Oberfläche.
Der Trägerstreifen selbst besteht aus zwei fest miteinander verbundenen Kunststoffschichten von jeweils einem halben Millimeter Dicke, die unterschiedlich auf den Säuregrad, den sogenannten pH-Wert, ihrer Umgebung reagieren. Während eine passive Schicht aus reinem Polyacrylamid ihr Volumen bei schwankenden Säurewerten nicht verändert, enthält die aktive Schicht zusätzlich spezielle chemische Bausteine auf Basis von Phenylboronsäure, an denen sich die Algen bevorzugt anlagern.
Photosynthese und Zellatmung steuern den pH-Wert im Soft-Robotik-Aktor
Fällt rotes und blaues Licht auf den Streifen, betreiben die Mikroalgen Photosynthese und nehmen gleichzeitig Nitrat aus der Nährlösung auf, um daraus Aminosäuren für ihre Zellen zu bilden. Beide Stoffwechselprozesse verbrauchen Wasserstoffionen direkt an der Oberfläche des Streifens, wodurch das unmittelbare Umfeld im Hydrogel alkalisch wird und der lokale pH-Wert von etwa 8 auf bis zu 11 ansteigt.
Durch diesen Anstieg laden sich die Boronsäure-Gruppen in der aktiven Kunststoffschicht elektrisch negativ auf, stoßen einander ab und lassen das Material durch Wasseraufnahme auf mehr als das Vierfache seines ursprünglichen Gewichts aufquellen. „Da die beiden Hydrogelschichten unterschiedlich auf pH-Änderungen reagieren, quellen sie unterschiedlich stark auf, was dazu führt, dass sich der Streifen biegt“, sagt Doktorand Fan Jiang.
Sobald das Licht erlischt, stellen die Algen die Photosynthese ein, bauen ihre zuvor gebildeten Zuckerreserven über die Zellatmung ab und stoßen dabei Kohlendioxid aus. Das Gas säuert das Hydrogel wieder an, sodass sich die aktive Schicht zusammenzieht und der Streifen sich in die Gegenrichtung krümmt, ohne dass sich der pH-Wert des umgebenden Wassers im Becken nennenswert verändert.
Greifarme der TU Delft bewegen Lasten im Milligrammbereich nur im Zeitraffer
Um die mechanische Funktion zu demonstrieren, fertigte die Arbeitsgruppe neben einer sich öffnenden künstlichen Blüte auch einen Greifer mit vier Fingern sowie einen einzelnen Haken an. Unter Beleuchtung schlossen sich die vier Finger um eine hohle Metallkugel mit einem Gewicht von 18,4 Milligramm, während der Haken einen 52,5 Milligramm schweren Gummiring umschloss und nach dem Abschalten der Lampe wieder freigab.
Ein Blick auf die Messdaten verdeutlicht allerdings die physikalischen Grenzen des biologischen Antriebs. Zwar setzt eine erste messbare Reaktion bereits zehn bis zwanzig Sekunden nach einem Lichtwechsel ein, für eine vollständige Krümmung um 300 Grad benötigt der Streifen jedoch bis zu 18 Stunden, weshalb die veröffentlichten Videos der Universität im 1800- bis 3600-fachen Zeitraffer ablaufen.
Biohybride Robotik ohne Gentechnik hält zwei Monate im Dauerbetrieb durch
Zudem erreicht das System nach 15 Stunden Beleuchtung lediglich eine maximale Stellkraft von 0,8 Millinewton, was etwa der Gewichtskraft einer Masse von 80 Milligramm entspricht, und das eigentliche Anheben der gegriffenen Gegenstände vom Boden erfolgte im Versuchsaufbau durch eine von außen nach oben bewegte Halterung. Außerdem sind die Bauteile dauerhaft auf eine flüssige Umgebung mit gelösten Nährsalzen angewiesen und würden an der Luft austrocknen.
Im Vergleich zu früheren biohybriden Konzepten – also der Kombination lebender Zellen mit künstlichen Materialien – auf Basis tierischer Muskelzellen oder Bakterien, die oft nach wenigen Tagen absterben, blieb der durch den Europäischen Forschungsrat im belgischen Brüssel geförderte Algen-Aktor über mindestens 60 Tage hinweg funktionsfähig. Da die Forscher:innen auf gentechnisch veränderte Organismen verzichten, sieht Aubin-Tam mögliche Einsatzfelder langfristig dort, wo sehr langsame Bewegungen und geringe Kräfte ausreichen, etwa bei lichtgesteuerten Schattierungselementen, in der Landwirtschaft oder bei der Handhabung empfindlicher Proben unter Wasser.

articles.title: "De loin la technologie la plus dangereuse jamais inventée" : pourquoi Bill Gates réclame une taxe sur l’IA et les robots
articles.text:
Des emplois menacés, de nouveaux risques pour la sécurité et une société qui pourrait avoir bien du mal à suivre. Bill Gates s’inquiète des bouleversements provoqués par l’intelligence artificielle et appelle les gouvernements à prendre leurs responsabilités. Sans renoncer pour autant aux immenses promesses de cette technologie.
Bill Gates n’a pas l’habitude de bouder les révolutions technologiques. Mais celle de l’intelligence artificielle semble sérieusement l’inquiéter. Invité du podcast Decoder, publié le 22 octobre par The Verge, le cofondateur de Microsoft prévient que les vingt prochaines années pourraient être marquées par « des gagnants, des perdants et beaucoup de bouleversements ». Une estimation qu’il reconnaît lui-même approximative, mais qui traduit son inquiétude face à la vitesse des progrès.
Et l’homme d’affaires ne mâche pas ses mots. Il considère désormais l’IA comme « de loin la technologie la plus dangereuse jamais inventée », en raison notamment des usages malveillants qu’elle pourrait faciliter.
Des métiers entiers menacés par l’automatisation
L’intelligence artificielle ne devrait pas se contenter de transformer quelques tâches administratives. Selon Bill Gates, ses progrès pourraient remettre en cause l’organisation même du travail, notamment dans la comptabilité, le droit ou le développement logiciel. Les métiers manuels seraient ensuite concernés, à mesure que les robots gagneront en autonomie.
Dans un essai publié le 26 août, il prévenait déjà que « de nouveaux emplois apparaîtront, mais sans politiques adaptées, ils seront bien moins nombreux qu’aujourd’hui ».
Les risques ne s’arrêteraient d’ailleurs pas à l’emploi. Gates redoute également la multiplication des cyberattaques, le recours à l’IA pour préparer des actes de bioterrorisme et l’influence des compagnons virtuels sur les plus jeunes.
Pour autant, il refuse de se ranger parmi les catastrophistes. « Je ne suis pas un prophète de malheur », insiste-t-il dans Decoder. Son inquiétude porte surtout sur notre capacité à encadrer une technologie dont les usages progressent plus vite que les réponses politiques.
Taxer les robots et réserver certains métiers aux humains
Bill Gates ne se contente en effet pas d’alerter. Il propose notamment de réserver certaines professions aux humains, même lorsque des machines seraient techniquement capables de les exercer. Il cite les métiers de l’accompagnement où la relation humaine lui paraît irremplaçable.
Le milliardaire défend également une réforme fiscale assez radicale. « Je pense que nous devrions taxer les tokens d’IA et les robots », écrivait-il dans son essai d’août. Les recettes pourraient notamment financer les reconversions professionnelles et les dispositifs de protection sociale. Il souhaite toutefois une taxe ciblée, qui ne freine pas les usages bénéfiques de l’IA, notamment pour rendre la médecine et l’éducation plus accessibles.
Sur le plan technique, Gates souhaite imposer des garde-fous aux modèles les plus puissants. Il envisage notamment que ceux-ci ne puissent fonctionner que sur des plateformes capables d’empêcher la suppression de leurs protections, y compris lorsque leurs poids sont accessibles.
Car, de son propre aveu, « nous ne sommes pas encore assez bons pour aligner les modèles », c’est-à-dire garantir qu’ils respectent les objectifs et les limites fixés par leurs concepteurs.
Une inquiétude qui ne l’empêche pas d’investir massivement dans l’IA
Bill Gates continue pourtant de croire au potentiel de l’intelligence artificielle, particulièrement dans la santé et l’éducation. Le 14 septembre, sa fondation a annoncé au moins un milliard de dollars de financements sur deux ans pour favoriser l’accès à cette technologie.
Environ 40% de cette enveloppe seront consacrés à l’éducation et autant à la santé, notamment pour développer le tutorat personnalisé, améliorer les diagnostics et soutenir la recherche médicale.
« Nous pouvons mettre l’IA au service du bien. Mais cela ne se produira pas par hasard », prévient-il. Le message résume assez bien son changement de ton. Après avoir contribué à installer des ordinateurs dans tous les bureaux, l’ancien patron de Microsoft s'inquiète pour ceux qui y travaillent.

articles.title: DeepSeek aurait réussi à contourner les défenses de Chrome en 12 heures
articles.text:
Un chercheur en cybersécurité, surnommé Exocija, affirme être parvenu à contourner le bac à sable (sandbox) de V8, le moteur JavaScript de Chrome. Pour y parvenir, il aurait fait appel au modèle V4.1 Flash 1017 de l’entreprise chinoise DeepSeek. Autant dire que les capacités de certaines IA chinoises ont de quoi inquiéter les États-Unis.
L’IA a testé plusieurs chemins
L’un des systèmes de sécurité les plus robustes de Chrome aurait-il été contourné par une IA chinoise ? C’est en tout cas ce qu’affirme le chercheur en cybersécurité Exocija. Il explique sur X : « J’ai dit à Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017 de créer un exploit qui échappe au Sandbox V8 de Chrome. Après 12 heures, il avait un exploit de corruption mémoire multi-étapes qui permet une lecture et écriture complètes du processus ». En l’espace d’une douzaine d’heures seulement, le modèle aurait donc testé frénétiquement différents chemins de code jusqu’à trouver un moyen de contourner les défenses particulièrement solides de Chrome.
Un point important à noter : le modèle DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 n’est pas le plus performant du marché. En revanche, il présente un avantage de taille : il est peu coûteux à utiliser. Grâce à son moteur DeepInfer, développé par DeepSeek, il serait possible de traiter jusqu’à 155 000 milliards de jetons par jour sur un même ensemble de serveurs. Le modèle se distingue également par sa faible consommation de mémoire : seulement 890 octets par jeton pour une partie de la mémoire utilisée pendant le traitement des requêtes.
Par conséquent, le chercheur en cybersécurité Exocija aurait demandé au modèle chinois de détecter durant des heures une faille dans le moteur JavaScript de Chrome, à moindre coût. En d’autres termes, les cyberattaques menées par l’IA deviennent de plus en plus redoutables, mais aussi moins coûteuses.
Les États-Unis s’inquiètent des capacités de certaines IA chinoises
Cet exploit accompli par Deepseek V4.1 Flash 1017, s’il est confirmé, risque d’augmenter encore les inquiétudes concernant les cyberattaques d’envergure menées depuis la Chine. Cette annonce intervient d’ailleurs quelques jours après qu’un pirate chinois soit parvenu à infiltrer les sites de plus de 100 grandes entreprises, en confiant tout simplement la tâche à une armée d’agents IA.
Autant dire que le gouvernement Trump ne doit pas voir tout cela d’un bon œil, c’est le moins que l’on puisse dire. Rappelons au passage que le gouvernement américain vient de bannir DeepSeek dans les systèmes informatiques des administrations civiles fédérales. Du côté de la Chine, aucun ralentissement du développement de l’IA au programme. Pour Pékin, les appels à ralentir et à réguler le développement de l’IA seraient avant tout destinés à freiner le développement de cette technologie en Chine. La rivalité entre la Chine et les États-Unis autour de l’IA ne fait que commencer.

Source : X - Exocija

articles.title: The iPhone Duo's screen is cracking in the same weird L-shape for multiple owners
articles.text:
Cutting corners: When Apple unveiled the foldable Duo, many wondered how well the hinge and screen would hold up. Within hours of the iPhone Duo's launch, images of cracked screens began circulating on social media, and the damage isn't limited to the fold itself.
The iPhone Duo subreddit alone already has multiple threads from users complaining about, and sharing pictures of, cracked screens. Some report that Apple has been generous with replacements for the $2,000 phone so far, but it remains to be seen how the company's policy will evolve as it works through production challenges.
Most of the photos show a break running along the fold, with a bright line of pixels extending from it toward the right edge of the screen. The result resembles a giant white L-shape stretching from one end of the internal screen to the middle.
iPhone Duo screen cracked within 6 hours of ownership
by u/Midnight_Slump in iPhoneDuo
One user in Australia reported the problem just six hours after buying the iPhone Duo, having opened the device fewer than 20 times. He says he felt something along the hinge beneath the screen before hearing a crack as the display broke. There were no marks on the screen's surface or the exterior hinge to suggest anything had been caught.
Apple's phone support offered an express replacement but required a hold for the phone's full price, and couldn't say when the replacement would arrive. He went to the Apple Store instead, where staff immediately granted a full replacement.
Another user reportedly didn't even finish the initial setup before a similar crack appeared. Photos on Reddit, X and the MacRumors forums show comparable damage from the US, Australia and China, including what appear to be demo units in China, though the circumstances behind most of those images are unclear. One user speculates that the tension springs that hold the iPhone Duo in various positions are to blame. It's too early to say how widespread the problem is, and reviewers who put the phone through thousands of folds reported no cracks.
Didn't even make it through setup before I had the screen crack
by u/leftyhyzer16 in iPhoneDuo
It's fortunate that affected users are getting quick replacements, considering Apple's listed repair costs. Without AppleCare+, repairs and replacements go from $49 to $1,499.
Apple's reported manufacturing problems and low yields could also make replacements harder to come by, as demand has outpaced supply. While some customers have picked up units straight from stores, other orders are already backed up into 2027.
Reviewers have been generally positive on Apple's first foldable phone, praising its hinge as the best they've used on a foldable and, in several cases, its speakers. Complaints largely center on the lack of Face ID and on software and developers who have yet to release updates that take full advantage of the large screen.

articles.title: Una IA llamará a restaurantes para consultar la espera y enviará la respuesta al celular
articles.text:
Yelp incorporará un agente de inteligencia artificial capaz de llamar a restaurantes para consultar cuánto tiempo deben esperar los clientes antes de conseguir una mesa. La función, denominada Check for Me, enviará la respuesta mediante un mensaje de texto y estará disponible durante los próximos meses para un grupo de usuarios de iPhone en Estados Unidos.
La herramienta busca simplificar una consulta habitual antes de salir a comer: conocer la demora estimada para ingresar a un restaurante sin reserva. Para utilizarla, el usuario deberá indicar la cantidad de comensales y proporcionar un número telefónico desde la ficha del establecimiento en la aplicación.
A partir de esos datos, el agente realizará una llamada al restaurante y comunicará la información obtenida a través de un SMS. De esta manera, la persona podrá consultar el tiempo de espera sin tener que llamar directamente al negocio.
Por ahora, Yelp no anunció una fecha para el lanzamiento general de Check for Me ni confirmó si la función llegará a todos los celulares. Su implementación inicial estará limitada a determinados restaurantes de Estados Unidos que reciban clientes sin reserva y formen parte del despliegue.
Cómo funciona el agente de inteligencia artificial de Yelp
Check for Me utiliza inteligencia artificial para automatizar una interacción que, hasta ahora, suele depender de la atención telefónica del restaurante. En lugar de que el cliente realice la llamada, el sistema se encarga de preguntar cuánto tiempo tendría que esperar un grupo para conseguir una mesa.
El procedimiento comienza en la ficha del establecimiento dentro de Yelp. Allí, el usuario indica cuántas personas asistirán y el número de teléfono al que desea recibir la respuesta. Después, el agente inicia la comunicación con el local y transmite el resultado mediante un mensaje de texto.
La utilidad de esta tecnología dependerá de que el restaurante responda la llamada y de que el sistema pueda interpretar correctamente la información proporcionada. Si el establecimiento utiliza una central automática o un asistente de voz, la conversación también deberá superar las posibles dificultades para comprender preguntas y respuestas.
La compañía no presentó Check for Me como un sistema de reservas. Su propósito es ofrecer información sobre la espera estimada para que los usuarios puedan decidir si se dirigen al establecimiento o buscan otra alternativa.
Los asistentes de voz podrían comunicarse entre sí
La nueva función representa otro paso en la incorporación de agentes de inteligencia artificial a las tareas cotidianas. En este caso, el sistema no se limita a responder preguntas dentro de una aplicación: interactúa con un negocio mediante una llamada telefónica para obtener información actualizada.
Yelp ya había introducido agentes telefónicos para restaurantes y empresas de servicios, diseñados para responder consultas y gestionar reservas. Con Check for Me, la compañía amplía ese enfoque y desarrolla una herramienta que actúa en nombre del posible cliente.
Sin embargo, esta modalidad también plantea dificultades. Como señaló el medio especializado TechCrunch, la interacción podría producirse entre dos sistemas automatizados: el agente que llama en representación del usuario y el asistente que atiende el teléfono del restaurante.
Si ambos sistemas interpretan de manera diferente las preguntas, los tiempos de espera o las condiciones de atención, la conversación podría terminar sin una respuesta útil. Por eso, la eficacia de la función dependerá tanto de la capacidad del agente de Yelp como de la forma en que los restaurantes gestionen sus llamadas.
Yelp amplía las funciones de su asistente
Check for Me forma parte de una serie de actualizaciones de Yelp Assistant, el asistente de la plataforma que ayuda a los usuarios a encontrar información y gestionar actividades relacionadas con restaurantes.
Entre las novedades también figuran opciones para reservar mesas mediante OpenTable, incorporarse a listas de espera y recibir respuestas que tienen en cuenta información meteorológica. Estas funciones buscan concentrar en una misma aplicación distintas tareas que suelen requerir llamadas, búsquedas o el uso de otros servicios.
Según la compañía, las integraciones con OpenTable, Yelp Reservations, DoorDash y Grubhub permiten gestionar reservas y pedidos en más de 500.000 restaurantes.
El despliegue de Check for Me será gradual y comenzará en iPhone en Estados Unidos. Su alcance dependerá de la cantidad de establecimientos habilitados y de la capacidad del agente para obtener respuestas fiables.

articles.title: Updated Google privacy policy says your Gmail might be used for advertising
articles.text:
Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

articles.title: Startups don't need to go viral to win customers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Getting initial customers as a startup can be one of the most grueling challenges in business. Even when companies manage to snag some early interest, there’s no guarantee those customers will stick around.
At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, Elia Wallen, founder and CEO of travel startup Engine, Gamma founder and CEO Grant Lee, and Crystal Huang, general partner at Google Ventures, shared tips on how to attract and retain customers.
In the current era — when young AI companies like Cluely and Instinct are building big audiences not just through their products but also through their founders’ colorful online presences — social media can seem like a magic bullet for reaching early customers. But founders who want heighten their business strategy with modern marketing, have to be strategic, according to Lee.
Gamma, which sells AI-powered presentation software, managed to scale its business exponentially with a social media strategy that deployed influencers through its Ambassadors (or “Gambassador”) program. The company adopted the plan before influencer-based marketing was a tried-and-true strategy for smaller companies, eventually reaching a multi-billion dollar valuation.
But simply giving influencers a platform and telling them to promote your brand online doesn’t automatically translate to sales, said Lee. There’s more to it than that.
“If you have a product that can serve many different segments or use cases, then you want to basically have creators that can target each one of those,” Lee said. “If you have folks that are in consulting versus people that do all their marketing and create all the decks for their CMO, there’s all these different segments you might want to go after.”
Lee said sometimes founders seem to treat creator marketing or influencer marketing as a sort of set it and forget it thing.
“I think you’re better served by really spending a lot of time with these creators, because if they’re not able to understand how to articulate the value of your product, it doesn’t matter how much money you spend, it’s just going to fall flat,” Lee added.
The effectiveness of social media depends largely on the type of business. Other ways of reaching customers can be just (if not more) effective.
Wallen would know. His company Engine, which manages lodging and travel bookings for midsize businesses, bootstrapped its way to $150 million in bookings before taking on any outside funding. They also had no visible social media strategy at all. For Wallen, traditional sales tactics can be far more useful than a positive TikTok video.
“We did events and we smiled and dialed,” said Wallen. “We still have a lot of people picking up the phone. A lot of people who didn’t grow up with that or don’t understand it think that it’s outdated or it doesn’t work but it does. It’s a hard thing. There are a lot of companies that just refuse to do it or don’t know how to do it well. But they’re missing out on a very big offline client base.” He added: “The phone still works.”
Wallen also shared an in-person tactic that his company deployed during its scrappy early days: hiring a magician named David to perform tricks for prospective clients at events and encourage them to visit the Engine’s booth. In short, old-fashioned personal engagement can work just as well, if not better, than the latest social media tricks.
Huang, who has managed droves of startups and shepherded them to success, said that once you have a customer, a lot of value can be derived from looking at how they use the product.
“Can you look into usage data and figure out if it’s recurring, if it’s increasing, if they are referring their friends?” Huang said. “It can come across in early usage and retention information as well. And then also, do you see some super fans, right, who even want to work at the company, promote the company, be attached to the brand?” She added: “You need to have ways to create evangelists who are really passionate about the product.”

articles.title: 'The game market is going to collapse thanks to AI bros': Epic AI MegaJam challenges devs to build a game in 4 days with AI, and gamers hate the idea
articles.text:
'Vibe your way to $50K': Epic is challenging devs to build a game in 4 days with AI — and gamers are in full rebellion now
Another day at Epic, another shove for AI towards the gaming limelight
- Epic is kicking off an 'AI MegaJam' next month
- It's a four-day competition for developers to build a game with AI, giving away $50,000 worth of prizes
- Coming on top of Epic's recent push of AI in its preview launcher and elsewhere, this has provoked quite the negative reaction from gamers
Epic has announced an 'AI MegaJam' in which you can 'vibe your way to $50K,' a neat little rhyme there, but gamers are predictably bewildered by the idea of this event which rewards game developers using AI.
The MegaJam is a four-day competition that starts on November 12, whereby teams of up to five people can use unlimited AI agents to create a playable game in either Unreal Engine or Unreal Editor for Fortnite (UEFN).
You can compete and code from anywhere, although there will be teams taking part locally (for two days) in San Francisco at Digital Jungle, where Epic promises "teams from Anthropic, Google, Meshy, OpenAI, SpaceXSI" and other big-name AI brands (expect daily livestreams, too).
Epic tells us: "Bring any AI tools into your workflow, from asset generation to coding agents. Get creative! Prototype the mechanic you never had time for, or try the art style you weren't sure you could pull off."
The prize pool is $50,000, which is split up into a bunch of categories. The main prizes are for the best Unreal Engine and UEFN games, which will net $7,500 respectively, with second and third places winning $5,000 and $2,500 in those categories too.
The best student project for either UE or UEFN will also receive $7,500, with the same runner-up prizes of $5,000 and $2,500.
The best team overall will bag a further $5,000, meaning the maximum prize here will be $12,500 (as presumably they must be one of the main category winners). There are a bunch of other modifier prizes, mind you, as extras on top, including best mobile game or solo developer ($2,500 apiece).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Epic also notes that: "Standout Unreal Engine and UEFN entries can earn development continuation grants of up to $50,000 to keep building after the jam."
Analysis: negative vibes
As you might imagine, there's been an immediate and strong negative reaction from gamers. There are multiple observations that Steam is already full of 'AI slop' games, with gamers asking why on earth Epic is encouraging this.
The irony of Epic proclaiming that the invited vibe-coders should "get creative!" isn't lost, either, given that most gamers view AI as the grim reaper for creativity, wielding its pixelated scythe as it kills and extracts the souls of games.
As one Redditor laments: "We're being bombarded with thousands of AI slop games because 'with AI, anyone can make their dreams a reality and become a game dev!' The game market is going to collapse, as seen in the latest Steam Next Fest, all thanks to AI bros and AI billionaires. Oh, how I hate Tim Sweeney."
In short, there's a lot of venting and vexation out there, so does this feel tone deaf from Epic? Very much so, but you wouldn't expect anything else really given CEO Tim Sweeney's recent (and past) comments on the subject of AI in gaming, and what's been going on at Epic lately.
Witness Sweeney's proclamation earlier this month that a "huge pivot" is happening at Epic where it's "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," with the chief exec arguing that AI can be "empowering for creators" and not the death of gaming. And of course there's also the new Epic launcher in preview, which took a tongue-in-cheek approach with a release announcement that declared: "Programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look."
All of which went down swimmingly well with most PC gamers, of course.
Interestingly, the idea for this AI MegaJam may have originated in this discussion on X, where SYD Games Studio suggests such a developer competition. Sweeney replies that it's an "interesting idea" and appears to have taken that ball and run with it (he also observes that AI represents "truly a new age of gaming and software ahead").
I get that AI can be a useful tool when employed by game developers to save some time doing coding grunt work (with the appropriate careful checks in place), but extending vibe-coding more broadly to embrace the entire game-making process is just asking for trouble and heaping on the bad feelings towards Epic here. At this point, Epic seems to be almost trolling gamers, and coding aside, the general vibes are getting distinctly nasty.

articles.title: Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs found inside state-owned China Telecom's network — Nvidia says chip smuggling is 'a drop in the bucket,' insists it remains a non-factor
articles.text:
Illegal Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs found inside state-owned China Telecom's network — Nvidia says chip smuggling is 'a drop in the bucket,' insists it remains a non-factor
A security firm was able to spot 32 of the high-powered chips within the state-owned telecom company's network, but it can't pinpoint where they are physically located.
Lava, an Israeli security firm, says that it has been able to identify 32 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips within the network of China Telecom, a state-owned company that provides telecommunications services within the country. These same chips have already been barred from export by U.S. export controls, a report by The Information notes, which begs the question of how they have turned up in a Chinese data center. Such chips can only be sold to whitelisted buyers who agree not to export them to sanctioned parties, including those in China.
However, banning companies from buying Nvidia's high-performance GPUs and AI data center chips hasn't always worked. In 2025, it was reported that Chinese companies smuggled $1 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips into the country in three months. At the time, the B200 chips were the most sought-after, but some distributors were already gearing up to sell B300-series chips when they became available.
While the latest finding shows that the proliferation of export-controlled chips into China continues to be an issue, Nvidia has downplayed the report but didn't deny the findings. "Governments, researchers, and media have all found insignificant diversion of controlled US products, less than one half of one percent in recent court cases — a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has," an Nvidia spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. "With tens of millions of GPUs in service in approved countries, this report again demonstrates that smuggling is a nonfactor, blocked by governments on both sides of the globe."
It's unknown how B300 chips found their way into China Telecom's server racks, nor can Lava confirm exactly where within the company's network they are located. But they are there, with Lava identifying them via Nvidia's own DCGM Exporter tool. The software can be installed by data center operators and is used to monitor server health and performance, and while designed for internal use, it can oftentimes be accessed beyond the data center's network. Oddly, it doesn't always require password authentication, either. Nvidia previously confirmed it was working on a tool that would allow its chips to be located, but it is yet to be released.
It's easy to see why Chinese firms are keen to get their hands on the Blackwell Ultra B300. Announced in March of last year, the data center GPU is one of the most powerful on the planet, offering huge performance gains with 50% more memory and FP4 compute than the previous-generation B200. At the time, Nvidia touted that the chip was "built for the age of reasoning," while name-checking more sophisticated AI LLMs like DeepSeek R1. At the time of its announcement, the B300 was expected to ship by the end of 2025, and it didn't take long for it to become hot property. In August 2026, nine people were indicted in Taiwan over the illegal export of B300 GPUs to China. This came just days after Supermicro confirmed that it had fired several employees following an investigation into smuggling. The complicated smuggling process included the use of a Taiwanese server trading firm called Flying Tiget Tech — a firm with whitelisted status for GPU purchases.
Nvidia's chips have proven so vital to AI data centers that demand for even its older silicon has caused skyrocketing prices. The company's A100 servers have tripled in price, despite being five years old, and can cost up to $82.,000. The ongoing crackdown on Nvidia chip smuggling has even seen some resort to retooling gaming GPUs to run AI workloads where possible.
