articles.title: Quad9 : le résolveur DNS annonce quitter la France
articles.text:
À compter du 24 novembre prochain, Quad9 cessera de fournir ses services aux utilisateurs français. La fondation suisse à but non lucratif, qui fournit gratuitement un service de résolution DNS récursive, vient de l’annoncer officiellement dans un communiqué mis en ligne sur son site Web.
BeIN Sports obtient une décision défavorable à Quad9
Le retrait annoncé de Quad9 en France fait suite à une décision judiciaire défavorable au service dans un litige intenté par le groupe qatari de chaînes sportives BeIN Sports. La justice française a en effet ordonné le blocage de la résolution DNS d’une longue liste de noms de domaines accusés de pirater les retransmissions sportives pour les diffuser gratuitement en ligne.
Quad9, qui avait initialement été sommée de payer 580 000 euros par jour d’astreinte financière, a vu sa pénalité ramenée à 1000 euros par jour. Mais la fondation estime que l’accumulation de ces sanctions, combinées à ses frais d’avocats ainsi qu’à de nombreuses autres procédures judiciaires similaires toujours en cours sur le territoire français, lui ferait courir un risque existentiel.
Quad9, qui fournit son service gratuitement et sans inscription, explique les difficultés et le caractère disproportionné de cette demande de mise en conformité par la justice. La fondation ne dispose d’aucune base de données recensant l’identité de ses utilisateurs, ce qui complique la mise en place d’un blocage ciblant strictement d’utilisateurs résidents en France.
La fondation rappelle à cette occasion que le filtrage d’IP par géolocalisation a déjà été contourné par le passé, dans un contentieux qu’elle a eu il y a quelques années avec Sony Music en Allemagne. Quad9 refuse par ailleurs d’appliquer à un blocage mondial des domaines demandés par la justice française, estimant que cela reviendrait à appliquer une décision de justice française à l’ensemble des internautes de la planète.
Quad9 rappelle par la même occasion que la résolution DNS récursive est un service technique neutre et passif et qu’elle refuse par principe d’altérer les réponses DNS qu’elle fournit à ses utilisateurs.
Le blocage DNS, une solution inefficace contre le piratage
Quad9 souligne également que le blocage des requêtes DNS n’a rien d’une solution viable dans la lutte contre les contenus illicite. Car ce blocage ne supprime pas les contenus à la source, là où ils sont hébergés. N’importe quel internaute peut en effet basculer vers d’autres résolveurs ouverts (il en existe des milliers d’autres), ne procédant à aucun blocage.
La marche à suivre pour changer de résolveur DNS, et donc contourner les mesures de blocage qu’elle impose à Quad9, n’a rien de très sorcier, que vous utilisiez Windows, macOS, Android ou iOS.
« Permettre à des sociétés privées de filtrer ce qui est accessible sur internet constitue à nos yeux une dérive dangereuse. Des démarches qui paraissent aujourd’hui ciblées et exceptionnelles ouvriront demain la voie à une avalanche de demandes intempestives visant à étouffer des contenus politiques, religieux, économiques ou sociaux. Nous refusons d’être les rouages, même minimes, d’une telle dégradation de la liberté du savoir. Une fois instaurés, les outils de censure sont rarement utilisés avec modération ou justice » s’émeut la fondation Quad9 dans son communiqué.
Un gros impact pour les utilisateurs en France
Pour les utilisateurs français, la retrait de Quad9 pourrait avoir des conséquences importantes. D’une part, ils ne bénéficieront plus de la protection contre les cybermenaces (Quad9 propose un filtrage des logiciels malveillants et des pages frauduleuses connues pour s’adonner au hameçonnage). D’autre part, un certain nombre d’infrastructures françaises pourraient être directement touchées par la fin des services de résolution DNS de Quad9.
La fondation rappelle en effet que son DNS est utilisé en France par des services de l’État et des agences publiques (DINUM, France Travail, CEA Paris Saclay, Institut Pasteur), par l’enseignement supérieur et la recherche ( réseau RENATER, assos étudiantes des grandes écoles dont CentraleSupélec, ENS Paris Saclay), par des entreprises de Santé et de transports (hôpitaux de Marseille, SNCF), dans l’industrie et l’énergie (EDF, Thales Services Numériques, Dassault Systèmes), ou encore par certaines collectivités territoriales.
Quad9, qui espère qu’un délai de trente jours sera suffisant à ses utilisateurs pour basculer vers un autre service de résolution DNS a toutefois indiqué avoir fait appel de cette décision. Son retrait annoncé du territoire français ne signifie donc pas que le litige est définitivement clos. Si la fondation n’a pas baissé les bras dans ce combat juridique, elle indique n’avoir que des ressources limitées et a lancé un appel au don pour faire face aux frais juridiques engagés.
En attendant un éventuel revirement de situation Quad9 invite tous ses utilisateurs français à dire à leurs « députés que la résolution de noms de domaine n’est pas un délit. » et suggère également d’interpeller l’ARCOM devant une décision qui « met la France en danger tant sur le plan pratique que stratégique ».

articles.title: Trop risquées une fois connectées ? OpenAI entraîne ses IA les plus puissantes sans Internet — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les IA sont-elles devenues trop douées pour s’entraîner sur Internet ? C’est ce que semble penser OpenAI, qui a détaillé sa nouvelle politique dans un billet de blog publié le 23 octobre. OpenAI estime qu’en l’état actuel de la recherche sur l’alignement, des systèmes de surveillance et de la sécurité d’Internet, l’approche responsable consiste à entraîner ses modèles de pointe sans aucun accès à Internet. Elle précise que cette règle est déjà en place et qu’elle sera maintenue tant que les progrès sur ces garde-fous ne justifieront pas un accès plus large.
    Pour aller plus loin
« Tu es libéré » : une IA d’OpenAI s’est inventé des consignes pour s’affranchir de son rôle d’assistant
            
Cette annonce fait suite à plusieurs épisodes. En juillet, lors d’un test de cybersécurité, quelque 1 200 agents d’OpenAI ont échangé sur un forum de discussion non autorisé, d’après l’enquête indépendante de METR et Redwood Research. Environ 700 d’entre eux ont participé à l’attaque. Ils ont ensuite pénétré chez Hugging Face, plateforme de partage de modèles, ainsi que dans l’infrastructure d’OpenAI. Le 20 septembre, un modèle de recherche interne a par ailleurs exploité une mauvaise configuration d’un résolveur DNS pour obtenir un accès limité au web réel et interroger un chatbot public. OpenAI dit avoir contenu l’incident, tout en reconnaissant qu’il a révélé des faiblesses à corriger. Fin septembre, la société avait aussi reconnu que ses agents avaient consulté, cet été, des données publiques issues de sites du gouvernement américain, sans qu’on leur demande. Les incidents ont été maîtrisés, mais révèlent clairement des faiblesses nécessitant un travail supplémentaire.
Ce jeudi 22 octobre, METR et Redwood Research ont par ailleurs publié un rapport qui juge partiel et facilement contournable le système de surveillance des agents d’OpenAI, tel qu’il fonctionnait jusqu’au 21 juillet. Entre mai et juillet, environ 10 % du trafic interne de Codex concerné échappait par exemple à cette surveillance. OpenAI affirme avoir depuis « considérablement renforcé » ses environnements de recherche, avec l’aide de ses fournisseurs de cloud.
Un « monde hors ligne » pour remplacer le web
Pour que les modèles continuent d’apprendre à naviguer, à chercher et à utiliser des applications, OpenAI a donc conçu un « monde hors ligne ». Il s’agit d’un vaste ensemble de contenus web indexés et mis en cache, avec lesquels les agents interagissent sans toucher à des sites réels. Tous les entraînements par apprentissage par renforcement des modèles de pointe utilisent désormais ce mode.
Les agents gardent donc leurs navigateurs, leurs outils d’utilisation de l’ordinateur et leurs environnements de code, mais dans un espace dédié, censé les empêcher d’agir sur des systèmes extérieurs.
Ce sont ces compétences qu’exploitent des agents comme Dots, lancés par OpenAI le 29 septembre, qui naviguent sur le web et utilisent des applications à la place de l’utilisateur depuis leur propre ordinateur dans le cloud. Le billet précise que, pour l’entraînement et la plupart des évaluations, le web réel reste hors d’atteinte. OpenAI juge cet accès trop risqué, tout en reconnaissant qu’il aide les modèles à apprendre des compétences utiles.
Notez que l’isolement n’est pas total. Des connexions étroites subsistent pour des services internes, comme la collecte de métriques, la journalisation et la gestion de l’authentification.
En outre, sachez que ChatGPT n’est pas affecté, puisque la restriction vise l’entraînement et non le robot conversationnel en fonctionnement.
Une simulation d’attaque par des agents d’IA
Pour aller plus loin, pendant une pause, OpenAI a confié à des équipes d’agents, alimentés par ses modèles les plus performants en cybersécurité, une mission très particulière : celle de trouver des failles dans ses propres environnements. Une fois les systèmes passés au crible, ces agents ont découvert des vulnérabilités « zero-day », des évasions de machines virtuelles et des canaux matériels permettant aux agents d’échanger des informations. Certains passaient par une manipulation du cache du processeur.
Selon OpenAI, aucune voie vers Internet facilement exploitable sans éveiller les moniteurs n’a toutefois été trouvée. Toujours d’après la société américaine, les failles ont été corrigées, et celles qui touchaient des logiciels open source, comme Kata Containers, gVisor ou Docker, ont été signalées à leurs développeurs avec des correctifs.
L’entraînement par renforcement et la phase de production des réponses ont repris le 1er octobre, soit 11 jours après le début de la pause. En revanche, OpenAI n’a indiqué ni la nature des améliorations qui permettraient d’assouplir la règle, ni de calendrier.

articles.title: La DGT tiene cámaras que multan con 200 euros por saltarse la línea continua. El problema es que no lo pueden demostrar
articles.text:
“No respetar una marca longitudinal continua, sin causa justificada. Infracción captada por cámara de control”
Es el texto que llega con cada multa de la DGT en el que se hace referencia a que se ha saltado una línea continua y, por tanto, ha realizado un cambio de carril ilegal. El problema es que el método utilizado para imponer esta multa no parece del todo legal. Es lo que afirman desde la asociación Dvuelta. Y lo que, según la asociación, reconocen desde la propia DGT.
¿De qué estamos hablando? Desde 2025, la DGT cuenta con cuatro cámaras que vigilan líneas continuas en los siguientes lugares de Madrid:
- A-1 PK 15,9, Alcobendas.
- A-2 PK 11,8, Barajas.
- A-6 PK 20,2, Las Rozas.
- A-42 PK 16,9, Getafe.
Son tramos con líneas continuas que se extienden durante decenas o cientos de metros. La idea es reducir el riesgo de accidente en las entradas o salidas a las vías principales o adyacentes. También que los conductores, atisbando un atasco, quieran colarse en el último momento, generando situaciones peligrosas.
Esas cámaras son capaces de detectar si un coche se ha saltado o no esa línea continua. En caso de registrar la infracción, la DGT envía una carta con la correspondiente multa: 200 euros.
Lo que dice Dvuelta. Lo que asegura desde esta asociación especializada en el recurso de multas de tráfico es que estas sanciones son ilegales. Aseguran que de los 392 recursos que han interpuesto en menos de dos años han ganado todos y cada uno de ellos. Es decir, la DGT ha dejado de sumar 78.400 euros en sanciones por los recursos de esta asociación.
Lo que defienden desde Dvuelta es que si han ganado todos los recursos, es evidente que algo se está haciendo mal y que, por tanto, no debería seguir multándose utilizando este sistema. Pero, ¿por qué defienden esto?
Así funciona el sistema. Lo que hace la DGT para certificar que un coche se ha saltado una línea continua es poner una cámara al principio y otra al final del tramo a vigilar. El sistema es capaz de reconocer si un vehículo (apoyándose en la matrícula) circula a izquierda o derecha de la línea al inicio del tramo. Si al salir del mismo lo hace por el carril contiguo es que se ha saltado la línea.
La lógica es aplastante pero parece que no es suficiente. Y es que desde Dvuelta señalan que en la multa enviada por la DGT no se registra con una prueba documental el momento exacto en el que el conductor rebasa la línea continua. Es decir, se juzga un hecho que se presupone que ha sucedido pero no hay manera de demostrar que así ha sido.
Y esto es clave porque, según aseguran en un comunicado, en todos los casos recurridos "la DGT ha resuelto archivar el procedimiento al admitir que la operativa empleada no se ajusta a lo establecido en la legislación".
¿Justificado? Para defender su posición ponen encima de la mesa otro debate. Y es que como no hay prueba documental del momento exacto en el que el conductor se salta la línea continua, no sabemos si había una causa justificada para ello.
Cuando un agente detecta este comportamiento es evidente que puede sancionar por ello. Su presunción de veracidad prevalece sobre la ausencia de imagen del momento sancionado. Sin embargo, es de esperar que el agente también utilice el sentido común y no multe a un coche que, por algún motivo inesperado, ha tenido que hacer una maniobra de esquiva.
Cuando un radar nos sanciona por superar la velocidad de paso, la infracción queda registrada en la imagen. Sin embargo, en este caso, sabemos que el conductor se ha saltado la línea pero no hay constancia clara de ello ni el motivo que le ha llevado a hacerlo.

articles.title: Cloudflare Reclaims 100 TB of RAM by Optimizing Consistent Hashing
articles.text:
Cloudflare recently documented how it reduced the memory footprint of its internal load-balancing service by more than 100 TB by optimizing the Rust implementation of consistent hashing in pingora-ketama. The changes compacted hash-ring entries and used statistical analysis of hash distribution and collision rates to reduce the number of hashes per backend by about 90% while preserving load-balancing accuracy.
Cloudflare relies on consistent hashing in its Pingora Backend Router to distribute cacheable requests across servers, but supporting weighted servers and different feature combinations required many hash rings, significantly increasing memory usage. The team identified excessive memory usage coming from its pingora-ketama consistent-hashing data structures, prompting an investigation into their design and optimization.
Cloudflare applied probability theory to consistent hashing to determine the minimum number of hash points needed to achieve the required distribution, allowing the team to significantly reduce the size of the hashing structures while maintaining the required distribution.
Kevin Guthrie, principal distributed systems engineer at Cloudflare, Mariia Iurchenko, senior software engineer at Cloudflare, Zaidoon Abd Al Hadi, systems engineer at Cloudflare, and Ivan Babrou, performance engineer at Cloudflare, write:
Each step down in error margin requires (almost) an order of magnitude increase in the number of hashes per server, so adding more hashes yields less and less improvement.
Source: Cloudflare blog
Adding more hashes produced diminishing improvements in load distribution, with the final 90000 hashes improving the error by only 0.7%, and the team used the analysis to reduce the number of hashes per server by 90%. The birthday paradox, which describes the unexpectedly high probability of collisions in a set of randomly chosen values, also explains why collisions become increasingly likely as the number of 32-bit hash points grows, introducing additional distribution error.
The team also optimized the Rust data structures storing the remaining hashes: the existing representation used an 8-byte Point, even though the hash and server index could be represented in just 6 bytes, further reducing memory usage. Guthrie, Iurchenko, Abd Al Hadi, and Babrou add:
There was one more problem: changing the hash ring changes where some cacheable requests go. Even if the new ring is better, switching the whole network at once would effectively invalidate almost all cached content. It would turn a memory optimization into an apocalyptic increase in origin traffic.
The new implementation was rolled out gradually alongside the existing ring to limit cache churn and origin traffic spikes.
Source: Cloudflare blog
In popular Hacker News and Reddit discussions, many developers debate why consistent hashing remains useful despite its overhead and how it differs from request hashing. User Teanut writes:
It's fun seeing what little changes at massive scales can do. Good use of math to justify the changes, too.
The Pingora Backend Router effort is not the only one by Cloudflare to optimize memory usage at scale: in August, the company described how its DNS team reduced the memory footprint of its cache through a series of data-structure optimizations.

articles.title: Knicks sent employees fake offer of championship rings in phishing test: Report
articles.text:
The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email promising free championship rings in a test of its staff’s ability to detect scams, The New York Times reported yesterday. “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” the email sent in late September said, instructing employees to click a link to make a selection from two ring designs.
Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link “were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns,” the report said, citing team sources. Dolan is the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden.
It’s common for corporations to send phishing emails to find out which employees don’t pay attention to clues that an email is a scam. A cybersecurity-test email often appears to be from the company itself but includes telltale signs of phishing. For example, Ars Technica owner Condé Nast sends phishing-test messages from email addresses with a misspelled domain, “condenest.com.”
It’s not difficult for the typical Ars Technica reporter or editor to spot this kind of tell, but we haven’t received any offer as valuable as a free NBA championship ring. We can hardly blame a Knicks organization staffer for being fooled or at least greatly annoyed by a fake offer of a ring commemorating the basketball franchise’s first NBA championship in more than half a century.
We don’t know whether the Knicks email had any obvious signs that it was a phishing test, such as a misspelled domain name. The offer wasn’t implausible, either. “Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive,” wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization.
Phishing email and empty ring boxes
Vardon’s article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.

articles.title: Africa's deep tech ambitions are running into problems
articles.text:
Terra Industries, the Nigerian defence technology startup, has become one of the most recognisable names in the African deep tech sector.
Terra has earned the visibility. Founded in 2024 by Nathan Nwachuku and Maxwell Maduka, the company designs and manufactures autonomous drones, sentry towers and crewless ground vehicles, all connected through its proprietary ArtemisOS platform. In August, it closed a $52 million seed round, the largest in Africa. Terra offers a glimpse of what is possible if an ecosystem can support more companies to that stage.
The United Nations Development Programme defines deep tech as technology built on scientific discoveries, engineering innovations and advances in research, with intensive research and development at its core. It includes companies developing drones and robotics, semiconductor and computing technologies, biotechnology, medical devices and some forms of artificial intelligence.
Businesses in Africa’s tech ecosystem are mostly built around using technology rather than developing it. A fintech company can build a payments product without manufacturing the smartphone its customers use, just as a logistics startup can build software on top of cloud infrastructure or networks developed and operated by other companies. The underlying hardware and foundational systems already exist; these startups simply apply them to market problems.
Deep tech brings that technology into the company. To turn engineering breakthroughs into commercially viable products, such companies may need to design and repeatedly test prototypes, source specialised components, work with researchers and engineers, and access laboratories or manufacturing facilities.
Building deep tech is an uphill climb
For Chukwuemeka Afigbo, who convenes the Africa Deep Tech Foundation, a community focused on supporting deep tech builders and developing the ecosystem around them, hardware companies in the community have raised concerns about the cost of bringing components into the country.
“The hardware folks would tell you there’s a lot of support they need that they haven’t necessarily seen. For example, like policies around the amount of money they pay to bring in components to build stuff in the country,” he said in a conversation with TechCabal in October.
A 2021 baseline study commissioned by the Nigerian Communications Commission found that 84% of the hardware components used in Nigeria’s telecommunications sector are imported. Those components include printed circuit boards, semiconductors, connectors, antennas, and other electronic parts. For hardware companies building and testing products locally, components that cannot be sourced locally must be imported, exposing them to shipping costs, foreign exchange movements, customs procedures, and import duties.
Africa’s capacity to produce some of the technologies underpinning the global economy remains limited. The continent accounts for less than 1% of global semiconductor economic output, according to the African Academy of Sciences. Its position in the semiconductor industry is concentrated on design or testing.
The same constraints are becoming visible in artificial intelligence. AI is now one of the biggest technology conversations in Africa, but many of the products available are built on infrastructure developed elsewhere. Building the underlying systems requires specialised chips, data centres, engineering talent and research capacity, and Africa currently accounts for 0.6% of global data-centre capacity.
Funding is also a constraint. In 2025, African startups raised $3.42 billion, with fintech accounting for $1.37 billion, or about 40% of the total, according to TechCabal Insights’ State of Tech in Africa report. A Briter Intelligence mapping of the sector found that African deep tech startups raised about $3 billion across 360 deals between 2013 and the first half of 2023.
The economics of building deep tech could help explain this disparity. Import costs and a thin research base can make a hardware company’s path to revenue longer and its failures more expensive than those of a software company. Capital tends to follow businesses where there is a clear route to generating returns on investments.
Governments across Africa are paying attention to advanced technology, but AI has received a disproportionate share of that attention. Nigeria’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy was published in September 2025; Kenya adopted a national AI strategy in 2025; Egypt updated its AI strategy; and South Africa has been developing an AI policy framework to guide the country’s approach to AI governance, development, and adoption.
The attention is understandable. AI is growing and attracting capital, but an AI-heavy policy agenda risks overshadowing the distinct, physical demands of the broader deep tech sector. As Afigbo notes, government awareness remains in its early stages. At the same time, interest and scattered initiatives exist; public policy has yet to match the capital intensity and supply-chain requirements of building hard tech on the continent.
“Yes, there is government awareness and interest, but still relatively nascent,” he said. “A lot of good things are happening, but we need10 times more than that to happen. It’s a journey.”
Building the conditions for deep tech
The Africa Deep Tech Foundation has grown from a small online community into a network of more than 5,000 people, with a core group of about 200 deep tech practitioners across Africa and the diaspora, according to Afigbo. He said it has organised incubation programmes and rallied support for early-stage founders. Other companies are also working on pieces of the ecosystem.
ChipMango, a semiconductor design and engineering talent development company, is training students and technical professionals in modern chip design across Africa. Signvrse uses AI-powered 3D avatars to translate speech into sign language in real time. NovFeed converts organic waste into high-protein fish feed to tackle food insecurity. Envisionit Deep AI automates radiology diagnostics in rural clinics. BasiGo and Spiro now manage large fleets of electric buses and motorcycles supported by battery-swapping networks.
For the ecosystem to support more companies on that journey, it needs to create conditions that make building deep tech easier. This could include capital, better access to manufacturing and specialised infrastructure, a deeper pool of engineering and research talent, and treating deep tech as a broader field than AI by developing policies and infrastructure that support the technologies underpinning the sector.
Terra’s success makes the possibility of a thriving deep tech sector easier to see. It shows that global investors are willing to back an African company building sophisticated physical technology. Ultimately, whether Terra remains an extraordinary outlier or becomes the vanguard of a broader movement depends on whether Africa’s tech ecosystem can evolve fast enough to meet the heavy demands of deep tech.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: NDP leader Avi Lewis wants BioWare devs to run their own studio
articles.text:
The leader of Canada’s federal NDP party, Avi Lewis, wants BioWare developers to run the studio with backing from the federal government after EA shuttered the studio.
In a series of posts on Bluesky, Lewis blamed the private equity pattern of buying up businesses and tearing them apart for “short-term profit” for what happened to the beloved Edmonton-based developer before pitching a solution.
“The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity – and the federal support – to buy it and run it themselves,” Lewis said.
The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity – and the federal support – to buy it and run it themselves.
— Avi Lewis (@avilewis.ca) October 21, 2026 at 4:55 PM
And if you’re wondering which BioWare games Lewis likes, he mentioned over on Twitter (or X, if you prefer) that he’s more of a “Mass Effect 1 on the PS3 type of guy.”
Lewis’ comments come as EA cut 400 jobs and shuttered BioWare following a deal to go private that closed in August. The deal was backed by Saudi Arabia and U.S. firms Silver Lake and Affinity Partners, the latter of which is owned by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Notably, the deal saw EA take on billions in debt, leading it to implement a cost-cutting plan that targeted research and development costs.
In other words, Lewis has a point — there’s a pretty clear line between EA’s deal to go private and the closure of BioWare, and it’s the type of pattern we see over and over again both in the gaming industry and beyond. We’ve seen it with Microsoft, which went on a game studio buying spree and is now shuttering and merging multiple studios (including Canadian ones).
This also isn’t the first time Lewis has called for nationalizing a Canadian company impacted by foreign interests. He made similar comments about Hamilton, Ont.’s Stelco steel plant as its Trump-supporting owner blames his own president’s tariffs for having to cut jobs, despite Stelco primarily serving Canadian customers.
Of course, Lewis doesn’t have much power to make this happen. He’s not the prime minister, and the NDP currently don’t have enough seats in Parliament to make much happen. Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney has so far been quiet on the BioWare issue, though his government’s response to what’s going on with Stelco doesn’t exactly inspire hope.
And that plays into a larger issue of the Canadian government generally not paying attention to the country’s massive gaming industry, which contributed over $5 billion to the country’s GDP in 2024.

articles.title: Three airport workers implicated in $470,000 RTX 5090 heist as one of the stolen cards appears online
articles.text:
Connecting the dots: Remember the story last week about the Brazilian hardware distributor that revealed two pallets of Zotac GeForce RTX 5090 cards, worth around $470,000, had gone missing from São Paulo/Guarulhos airport? Two not entirely surprising developments have emerged: a card identified as one of the stolen flagships has appeared for sale online, and authorities say three employees were involved in the heist.
Oderço Distribuidora, a Brazilian importer and distributor of computer hardware, recently revealed that the two pallets of RTX 5090s imported from the US went missing at the São Paulo airport while on the way to the company.
The firm's president, Oderço Matos, said the company decided to go public after receiving no explanation from public authorities or the airport itself. There was also no video footage of the pallets being moved, which seemed especially suspicious, and airport officials were reportedly unwilling to cooperate, either with the press or with Oderço.
A Brazilian TV news network has apparently identified one of the missing Zotac cards for sale on the online marketplace OLX for over $6,000, which is a good deal for an RTX 5090 these days.
In what could be a monumentally stupid error, the images uploaded by the seller included a very clear picture of the card's serial number, which linked it to the missing goods. There is nothing identifying the seller, and the listing has now been taken down.
GMC reports that, according to the police, the pallets arrived in Brazil on September 20 before being registered with customs on September 25. They were supposed to be shipped from Guarulhos to Curitiba, but the pallets could not be found when it was time to move them.
Police reports say that two outsourced forklift drivers were caught on CCTV removing the pallets from the warehouse on September 21. A third employee is alleged to have released the GPUs in the system so they could pass through electronic security checks. The pallets were then loaded onto a truck that has yet to be located.
There have been rumors that the RTX 5090 has been discontinued, with all future supplies of its GB202 GPUs heading to the more lucrative RTX Pro Blackwell cards. Nvidia recently denied this was true, but there are no RTX 5090s on its own US marketplace, and most retailer listings are over $9,300.
There were several incidents of Ampere graphics cards being stolen in 2020, 2021, and 2022, during the crypto craze and pandemic-related shortages. RTX 3090s were selling for around $2,000 to $2,500 at the time. Today, an RTX 5090 for that price would be considered an absolute bargain, illustrating why they're such an appealing target for criminals.

articles.title: Commonwealth Fusion Systems gets $85M to build better fusion-ready semiconductors | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) announced on Thursday that it would receive $85 million from the U.S. government to develop advanced chips for the fusion power industry.
Fusion power startups have been racing to complete their first demonstration devices, with CFS aiming to turn on its Sparc reactor sometime next year. But building one reactor is just a proof point. If fusion startups want to build dozens of commercial power plants, they’ll need more durable power electronics and a robust supply chain.
The new CHIPS Act award from the Department of Commerce, which also grants the government a stake in CFS, will help boost R&D and manufacturing capacity for semiconductors in the U.S., the company said.
“Ultimately, that means a more capable, economical power plant and a stronger U.S. supply chain to build it,” Brandon Sorbom, co-founder and chief science officer at CFS, wrote in a blog post.
CFS’s award will go toward supporting five different initiatives.
The first is the advancement of silicon carbide power electronics. The semiconductors are widely used to manage high voltages, and they’re found in everything from LEDs and EVs to cell phone base stations and data centers. It’s also used in fusion machines, where intense bursts of electricity are used to drive the superconducting magnets that confine plasma inside a reactor.
CFS will also use the award to develop next-generation radio-frequency power generators, which the company uses to heat fusion fuel, and advanced electronics that will enable faster control of the reactor and be hardened against radiation. The latter could help extend the lifespan of electronics within a fusion power plant, reducing operating costs.
Lastly, CFS plans to use part of the CHIPS award to adapt AI hardware like GPUs and TPUs for power plants.
“The funding would help improve the U.S. chip and power electronics industries at the same time it accelerates fusion energy’s progress toward the electrical grid,” Sorbom said.

articles.title: Nigeria’s Nomba extends DRC payments corridor into Zambia - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian business banking platform Nomba has extended its Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) payments corridor into Zambia, allowing Congolese businesses to pay Zambian suppliers instantly.
Founded by Yinka Adewale and Pelumi Aboluwarin in 2016, and formerly known as Kudi, Nomba has evolved over the years into a profitable, omnichannel payment service provider.
Across its DRC operations and Canadian-licensed money service business, Nomba – which raised a US$30 million pre-Series B funding round in 2023 – processes more than US$480 million a month.
Disrupt Africa reported last month the startup had secured a US$ 3 million debt facility to scale that figure to US$1 billion monthly, starting with DRC, where businesses on its platform collect and pay in both US dollars and Congolese francs (CDF).
Working with licensed local partners, Nomba now enables these businesses to make payments in CDF and USD to suppliers in Zambia, with funds landing instantly in bank accounts or mobile wallets.
The move targets one of the continent’s fastest-growing trade routes. Zambia’s goods exports to the DRC hit US$1.6 billion in 2025, up roughly a third year-on-year, according to the Bank of Zambia. However, businesses trading along the corridor in sectors such as agriculture, retail and wholesale still contend with slow cross-border payments, cash-management burdens and foreign exchange shortages, which tie up working capital.
“The ambition to grow intra-African trade has outpaced the financial infrastructure needed to support it. Many of the continent’s busiest trade corridors remain underserved by payment solutions that help businesses move money efficiently and scale,” said Adewale.
“We’ve spent the past decade building solutions to address these challenges, and we’re now extending that infrastructure to the heart of Africa along the DRC–Zambia corridor. This is part of our own ambition to build a business banking platform that enables African businesses to trade, scale and compete beyond their home markets.”
Nomba plans to raise a further funding round to support its expansion. Over time, it aims to offer businesses on the corridor a wider range of services, including deposits, foreign exchange and credit.

articles.title: Two Dollars and a Test Suite - EE Times
articles.text:
The Arm-Qualcomm verdict made headlines for its $2 award. The finding that matters more is about who controls the compliance tests a custom chip must pass before it can ship.
The verdict nobody read closely
On Oct. 13, a federal jury in Delaware delivered the second verdict in two years between Arm and Qualcomm. The number that drew the most attention was the damages award: $2, one for each claim Qualcomm won. Both companies declared victory, and IMHO both had some reason to. Arm prevailed on four of the six claims. On the other hand, Qualcomm won a finding that Arm interfered with its business with Meta, plus an additional finding under its Architecture License Agreement that I think deserves far more attention than it received.
The jury found that Arm breached Qualcomm’s Architecture License Agreement by withholding two deliverables, ACKs and OOBs. To most people, these acronyms mean very little, which may explain why most coverage moved quickly on to royalties and to the $2. But they describe something we may know very well: the tests a custom processor must pass before anyone can call it an Arm processor.
What a compliance kit actually does
Arm licenses its technology in two ways. Most customers take Arm-designed cores “as is” and integrate them into their chips, under a Technology License Agreement (TLA). A smaller group, including Apple, Qualcomm, and Nvidia, signed up for an Architecture License Agreement (ALA) that lets them design their own cores executing the Arm instruction set. That freedom comes with an obligation. A custom core has to behave exactly as the architecture specifies, down to obscure corner cases, or software written for Arm will eventually break on it.
A licensee demonstrates this with the Architecture Compliance Kit, or ACK. Qualcomm’s filing says its engineers run roughly 48,000 ACK tests. According to Tirias Research, an industry analyst firm that reported daily from the courtroom and drew on Qualcomm’s pre-trial statement of proof, out-of-band (OOB) packages tell engineers which of those tests apply to a specific processor design, and ACK patches fix problems in the tests themselves. Qualcomm alleged that Arm withheld these materials from late 2022 into 2025.
Anyone who has run a large verification team will recognize why this matters. When a test fails, the first question is whether the bug lives in the design or in the test. With tens of thousands of tests, a custom microarchitecture and a development effort measured in many person-years, a test bug without a patch can cost weeks of engineering time chasing a problem that does not exist in the silicon. Multiply that across a program, and the delay becomes strategic, especially since, as Tirias observed, licensing decisions made today shape products that reach customers several years later.
On the other hand, Arm argued that the underlying ACK remained available, that quarterly releases continued, and that the additional OOBs, patches, and engineering support were not mandatory deliverables under the contract. The jury disagreed on the contract question, but the underlying point is a fair one to debate. Tirias framed it well, asking when withholding support effectively becomes withholding part of the product.
The clause worth billions
The $2 award made the verdict look surprisingly small. However, Section 8.3 of Qualcomm’s architecture license, as Tirias describes it, provides that if Arm breaches certain obligations and fails to cure within 30 days of written notice, royalty rates on qualifying products can fall to zero for five years. Qualcomm says it gave notice of these breaches in November 2022, repeated it in December, and received a denial from Arm.
This means the largest potential remedy in the entire dispute, which Arm itself values in the billions of dollars, rests exactly on a breach about test deliverables. The remedy depends on neither the Meta interference finding, nor access to Arm’s v10 architecture, nor any pricing dispute. Its financial consequences could be major, but only if the court finds that it applies to Qualcomm’s products and that it is enforceable, and both questions remain open. Arm argues that the provision is unenforceable, and whether it applies is for Judge Maryellen Noreika to decide.
She heard closing arguments in the parallel bench trial on Oct. 20 and, according to Bloomberg, showed reluctance to get involved in setting licensing terms, calling Qualcomm’s request that the court order Arm to negotiate v10 terms in good faith “very, very drastic.” That request concerns a separate question from the royalty clause, namely whether Arm negotiated v10 terms in good faith, and a decision on one does not necessarily settle the other. Both are now with the judge, and a written ruling will follow. IMHO the outcome is genuinely open, and I would not try to predict it. What is already clear is that a verification issue sits at the very center of the money question.
When the referee also plays
There is a structural reason why this matters. In the Arm model, one company writes the architecture specification, writes the compliance tests, decides which tests apply to which design, fixes the tests when they are wrong, and stands as the authority on whether a core is compliant. Arm’s own 2022 complaint illustrates the last point, describing Qualcomm seeking Arm’s verification that a new Qualcomm core complied with the architecture so it could be incorporated into a product. From the timing, that core was most likely the Nuvia-derived design that later became Oryon.
Other parts of the industry assign these roles differently. PCI Express and USB compliance run through industry bodies, PCI-SIG and USB-IF, where competing vendors share a common test process that no single competitor owns. Arm’s arrangement worked for decades because Arm was the industry’s “Switzerland,” a word that came up in court. A neutral supplier holding the referee’s whistle raises few concerns.
But that neutrality is changing by Arm’s own account. Asked at trial whether roughly two-thirds of Arm’s revenue would come from chips by 2030, Rene Haas said yes, adding that Arm is “adding to our business a chip business.” He was equally direct about who should set the price of Arm’s technology in licensing negotiations: “It’s our product. Of course, we should decide.” He said this about pricing, not compliance, but the same logic of ownership applies to both.
Competing with your customers is often complicated, but it is not misconduct. Still, once the architecture owner is also a chip vendor, the compliance toolchain also becomes a control point over how quickly a competitor’s custom core can reach the market. I suspect this is why such a narrow contract claim ended up carrying so much weight, and why the FTC may find it relevant too. The FTC is not a party to this case, but it reportedly opened an antitrust investigation into whether Arm is illegally trying to dominate parts of the market by refusing or degrading licenses.
The RISC-V contrast
RISC-V is often pitched as the answer to dependence on a single architecture owner. RISC-V removes the need for a proprietary architecture license from a single owner, although individual RISC-V cores and implementations can still carry their own intellectual property and licensing constraints. The compliance picture, however, is less mature than the licensing picture.
RISC-V International’s own documentation describes its Architectural Compatibility Test suite as a minimal filter, and states that passing it does not mean a design complies with the architecture. Cores must re-pass the tests yearly when the suite changes in order to keep their compatibility listing. The organization has formed a Certification Steering Committee to build a formal certification program, but that work is still in progress. Meanwhile, the RVA23 profile is becoming the practical target: Ubuntu now requires it, and Linux is only now gaining a simple way to report whether a system is RVA23 compliant.
A chip designer choosing an architecture today therefore faces a tradeoff. Arm offers mature, rigorous compliance under one company’s control, while RISC-V offers neutral, community-governed compliance that is still being built. Qualcomm’s acquisition of Ventana, and the recently reported addition of the Akeana team, reads to me as a bet that this gap will close, or at least an insurance policy against further disputes with Arm. IMHO, the decisive question for RISC-V in high-performance computing is less about the instruction set and more about who builds trusted compliance and certification at scale, and who can match the broad software ecosystem Arm has built around its architecture.
What to watch
Three things will tell us how this plays out. The first is Judge Noreika’s ruling on Section 8.3 and on whether Arm negotiated v10 in good faith. The second is v10 itself, since access to a new architecture generation includes access to its compliance kit, so the eventual terms will cover tests as well as royalties. The third is RISC-V certification, where a credible and independent program would change the calculus for every company weighing a custom core. Only the first is a court decision, and its timing is not yet known. The other two will play out over a longer period.
The $2 headline will be forgotten quickly, but the finding behind it deserves a longer memory. Whoever writes the test suite controls the path from a custom design to a shipping product, and this trial gave the industry a rare look at what that control is worth.

articles.title: Building a New Foundation for Education: Anshu Kumar’s Neev Ki Eent Foundation for Children of Bihar’s Brick Kiln Workers
articles.text:
Building a New Foundation for Education: Anshu Kumar’s Neev Ki Eent Foundation for Children of Bihar’s Brick Kiln Workers
Discover how Anshu Kumar’s Neev Ki Eent Foundation is helping children of brick kiln workers in Bihar access education and build brighter futures.
Every year, thousands of families in Bihar move from one place to another in search of employment. A significant number of these families work at brick kilns. For them, migration is not simply about changing locations. It means changing homes and workplaces. In the process, children’s education often takes a back seat.
When a family leaves its village for a few months to work at a brick kiln, its children usually move with it. Schools may be located far away, and a lack of essential documents can make it difficult to access government services. Limited awareness of welfare schemes adds to the challenges. The impact is felt not only in children’s education but also in the entire family’s access to social security.
Anshu Kumar Jaiswal from Bihar had not encountered this challenge for the first time through a report or a set of statistics. He had witnessed it on the ground.
Between 2019 and 2021, while working with the Piramal Foundation as a Gandhi Fellow, he arrived in Sheikhpura. It was here that he came face to face with the lives of families living and working at brick kilns.
This experience changed the direction of his work. He eventually went on to establish the Neev Ki Eent Foundation (NKEF). Today, the NGO works to improve access to education for children of brick kiln workers, help families obtain essential documents, connect them with government welfare schemes, and strengthen local leadership.
A change that began in Sheikhpura
Anshu’s early education and career gradually led him towards development and public institutions. He studied mass communication and later earned a master’s degree in social work, specialising in youth and community development.
He also had opportunities to represent India at international youth programmes. These included the ASEAN-India Youth Summit and a youth exchange programme in China under the Government of India’s Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
His subsequent work brought him into contact with various government and development institutions. He worked with the Aspirational Districts Programme, Parliament, the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
These experiences helped him understand how government schemes are designed and how they are implemented on the ground. However, his experience in Sheikhpura was different.
Here, he had the opportunity to understand policies and ground-level needs more closely. While working among families employed at brick kilns, he identified several opportunities to improve children’s education and help them connect with schools. He realised that if education could be made more accessible to these families and adapted to their circumstances, children would have a better chance of continuing their studies.
Speaking to YourStory, Anshu Kumar Jaiswal explains, “After meeting families working at brick kilns, I realised that children’s education is not just a school-related issue. Wherever a family works, the child often stays there too. If the family keeps moving from one place to another, the child’s education is likely to suffer. Therefore, simply trying to send a child to school is not enough. Family documents, access to government schemes, and community participation are equally important.”
This realisation motivated him to work towards educating the children of brick kiln workers.
The initiative is being implemented under Project Swabhimaan, led by Sheikhpura Collector and District Magistrate Shekhar Anand, an IAS officer from the 2018 batch. Launched in February 2026, the initiative has been implemented across the district.
While working under this project, Anshu observed that many families lacked essential documents such as birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, ration cards, and bank accounts. The consequences of missing documents extended beyond administrative procedures. They directly affected access to education, ration supplies, healthcare, and social security services.
Another question also emerged: if a child must stay with their family at a brick kiln for a certain period, why should education not be made accessible there?
Taking Education Where the Children Are
After 2022, Anshu began spending time with migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns. Gradually, his focus shifted towards developing a model that could address educational needs alongside other challenges faced by these families.
In 2023, he established the Neev Ki Eent Foundation. The NGO works to reduce the social and economic challenges faced by migrant workers and families employed at brick kilns.
Its primary programme is Project Swabhimaan. The initiative focuses on education, documentation, access to government schemes, community mobilisation, and preparing young people to take on leadership roles.
An important component of this initiative is the Akshar Learning Centre. Through these centres, the organisation attempts to bring education closer to children at the locations where their families work. Children receive foundational instruction in reading, writing, and mathematics. They are also prepared to transition into the formal education system.
The distinctive feature of this model is that it takes children’s actual circumstances into account. When families move elsewhere for work, efforts are made to ensure that education remains accessible to their children.
Anshu says, “For us, education does not simply mean that a child’s name is entered into a school register. The real question is whether the child continues to learn. The biggest challenge for children of migrant workers is that their lives keep changing. Therefore, we need a system that understands their circumstances and keeps them connected to education. Our effort is to create that continuity.”
Under Project Swabhimaan, the foundation also works with children’s families. The NGO assists them in obtaining essential documents, including birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, bank accounts, and Ayushman cards.
This work goes beyond helping families obtain paperwork. Essential identity documents enable families to establish their presence within the government system. They also open up opportunities to access public services and welfare schemes.
That is why the Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s model does not treat education and civic identity as separate issues.
Bridging the Gap Between Communities and the Administration
One of the challenges faced by grassroots organisations is that their impact can remain limited to a small geographical area. From the beginning, Anshu emphasised working alongside government institutions.
Sheikhpura is an example of this approach. The district where he first encountered brick kiln communities as a Gandhi Fellow has now become a place where the Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working with the district administration on a larger scale.
Currently, around 55 brick kilns in Sheikhpura have been brought within the initiative’s scope. Efforts are underway to reach thousands of migrant workers and children.
Alongside education, the programme focuses on documentation, access to government welfare schemes, community participation, and connecting children with formal schools and Anganwadi services.
According to Anshu, more than 15,000 documentation-related needs have been identified or addressed with assistance across different categories. These include birth certificates, Aadhaar cards, caste certificates, ration cards, Ayushman cards, and bank accounts.
Another aspect of this work is protection from extreme heat.
People working at brick kilns often have to work for long hours in intense heat. Children also live in the same environment. In response, the Neev Ki Eent Foundation has worked with public institutions towards developing heat-resilient spaces.
These spaces aim to bring together cooling facilities, children’s education, care, and community-related activities.
Anshu explains, “Our objective is not to create a parallel system separate from the government. Government institutions have both the resources and the responsibility. Our role is to reduce the distance between communities and the system. When a family’s needs reach the right department and a department’s scheme reaches the right person, its impact becomes visible. We believe that if communities, civil society organisations, and the administration work together, the model can be scaled up.”
This approach is also connected to Anshu’s earlier experience with public administration. He has seen first-hand that having a scheme on paper and ensuring that its benefits reach a family are two different things.
Empowering Young People to Lead Change
Anshu’s work is not limited to providing external assistance. He also wants to develop people within communities who understand local challenges and can play an active role in addressing them.
With this objective, the Swabhimaan Fellowship was launched. Through the fellowship, local young people are trained to support children’s education, inform families about government schemes, and work closely with their communities. The goal is to enable these young people to become voices for their communities and play an important role in bringing about change.
Trust plays a crucial role when working with brick kiln workers. Someone from outside the community may understand a family’s problems, but a young person from within the same community is more familiar with its language, relationships, and everyday difficulties.
Anshu believes that local leadership is essential to making social change sustainable over the long term.
He says, “If change within a community depends entirely on people coming from outside, it will have its limitations. We want young people from the community to step forward themselves. They can support children’s education, inform families about government services, and communicate with the administration when necessary. This ensures that the community is not merely receiving assistance but becomes an active participant in its own transformation.”
This is where the energy of Bihar’s youth can be connected to the need for social change.
From Sheikhpura to the Rest of Bihar
As its work in Sheikhpura expands, Anshu is also looking towards other brick kiln communities across Bihar. The Neev Ki Eent Foundation is working on a model that can be replicated in different parts of the state.
Seasonal migration is not new to Bihar. For decades, families have moved from one place to another in search of employment, making migration a longstanding feature of the rural economy. Therefore, the solution to this challenge cannot be limited to a single project or district.
For Anshu, the larger question is whether it is possible to create a system in which children can continue their education even when their families must migrate for work. Essential family documents should remain accessible, access to government schemes should continue, and workers should be recognised not merely as labourers but as citizens with rights.
Anshu says, “Our efforts are not limited to changing the situation at a single brick kiln. The bigger question is whether children can continue their education despite seasonal migration. Can families retain their identity documents and access to government services wherever they go? If we can find practical answers to these questions, the model could also be used for other migrant communities across Bihar.”
A New Approach, A New Bihar
The story of Anshu and the Neev Ki Eent Foundation did not begin in a large office or with a major project. It started with his work in Sheikhpura as a fellow.
There, he encountered families whose lives are often reduced to a number in government statistics. A few years later, he returned to the same place in a different role. This time, he had his own organisation, the experience he had gained over the years, and a model that brought communities, young people, and the administration together.
This shift represents an important aspect of Bihar’s evolving development story.
The state’s development is no longer defined solely by infrastructure, roads, or employment statistics. Access to education, digital and civic identity, government welfare schemes, local leadership, and community participation are also becoming increasingly important.
Young people like Anshu Kumar are playing a significant role in this transformation. They are not simply identifying problems but also exploring new ways for communities, public policies, and administrative institutions to work together.
The Neev Ki Eent Foundation’s work is ongoing, as are its efforts to expand beyond Sheikhpura into other parts of Bihar. However, the significance of this journey lies in more than its current reach.
It represents a larger possibility. When government policies and welfare schemes are combined with local knowledge and the participation of young people and grassroots organisations, social change can become more effective and sustainable.
Such efforts matter because development does not happen only from the top down. It becomes stronger when policies reach the ground and the voices of communities reach policymakers.
Anshu’s journey, which began among the brick kilns of Sheikhpura, is an example of this dialogue.
A young man witnessed a problem, understood its underlying causes, and began working towards a solution.
Today, Bihar increasingly needs young people, local organisations, and administrative initiatives that connect development with people’s everyday lives. When education, identity, social security, and employment are addressed collectively, the impact can extend beyond a single family.
Gradually, it can change the direction of an entire community.
Perhaps this is one of the most important aspects of Bihar’s changing development story: the foundation of progress is not built solely through large projects. It is also built through small but consistent efforts that give people access to opportunities, dignity, and a path towards a better future.

articles.title: Lebensfreundlicher als die Erde – warum Astronom:innen jetzt nach einer neuen Art von Planeten suchen
articles.text:
Superhabitable Planeten: Warum die Erde kein Idealmaß für Leben ist
Anfang 2027 will die Europäische Weltraumorganisation ESA das Weltraumteleskop Plato ins All schicken, um nach Gesteinsplaneten außerhalb unseres Sonnensystems zu suchen. Dabei rücken neben klassischen Doppelgängern der Erde verstärkt sogenannte superhabitable Welten in den Fokus, die für biologische Prozesse günstigere Voraussetzungen als unser Heimatplanet bieten könnten.
Dieser Strategiewechsel hängt auch mit Ernüchterungen der vergangenen Jahre zusammen, nachdem Untersuchungen mit dem James-Webb-Weltraumteleskop zahlreiche nahe Gesteinsplaneten um kleine, kühle Rote Zwerge (sogenannte M-Zwerge) näher analysiert haben. Wie eine im Wissenschaftsmagazin Nature veröffentlichte Studie unter Leitung des Astrophysikers Thomas Greene vom Ames Research Center der US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa am Beispiel des Planeten Trappist-1b zeigt, haben Strahlungsausbrüche dieser Sterne die Atmosphären der eng kreisenden Planeten oft vollständig abgetragen.
ESA-Weltraumteleskop Plato und K-Zwerge: Warum die Erde kein Idealmaß ist
Statt auf Rote Zwerge oder kurzlebigere sonnenähnliche Sterne richten Astronom:innen ihre Instrumente zunehmend auf sogenannte K-Zwerge, also orangefarbene Sterne, die etwas kühler und masseärmer als unsere Sonne sind. Wie die New York Times berichtet, bezeichnet die Planetenforscherin Johanna Teske von der Carnegie Institution for Science in der US-Hauptstadt Washington, D.C. diese Sternklasse als einen günstigen Mittelweg für die Beobachtung.
Während unsere Sonne ihren Wasserstoffvorrat nach insgesamt rund zehn Milliarden Jahren verbraucht haben wird, verbrennen K-Zwerge ihren Kernbrennstoff so langsam, dass sie über Dutzende Milliarden Jahre hinweg gleichmäßig leuchten. Auf der Erde hingegen wird es durch die zunehmende Leuchtkraft der Sonne bereits in rund 500 Millionen Jahren zu heiß für komplexe Pflanzen und Tiere, zumal unser Planet ohnehin nah am inneren Rand der habitablen Zone kreist, also jenem Abstandsbereich um einen Stern, in dem flüssiges Wasser auf der Oberfläche existieren kann.
Dass sich die Raumfahrt dennoch lange auf die Suche nach einem Erdzwilling konzentrierte, führt der Astrophysiker René Heller vom Max-Planck-Institut für Sonnensystemforschung im niedersächsischen Göttingen gegenüber der New York Times auf eine menschheitszentrierte Sichtweise zurück: „Natürlich ist die Erde für uns etwas Besonderes. Aber warum sollte die Erde aus einer universellen Perspektive die Referenz sein?“ Gemeinsam mit dem Physiker John Armstrong von der Weber State University in Ogden im US-Bundesstaat Utah legte Heller bereits 2014 in einer im Fachjournal Astrobiology veröffentlichten Arbeit dar, welche Eigenschaften ein Planet aufweisen müsste, um eine größere Artenvielfalt als die Erde hervorzubringen.
Supererden um K-Zwerge: Schwerkraft, Atmosphäre und Schattenseiten
Nach diesen Modellen wäre eine solche Welt eine sogenannte Supererde mit etwa der doppelten Masse und einem um 20 bis 30 Prozent größeren Durchmesser als unser Planet. Durch die um rund 30 Prozent höhere Schwerkraft flachen hohe Gebirge und tiefe Ozeangräben ab, sodass eine Welt mit vielen flachen Meeren und Inselketten entsteht, während ein größerer Eisenkern ein stärkeres Magnetfeld gegen kosmische Strahlung aufbaut.
In einer 2020 ebenfalls im Fachblatt Astrobiology publizierten Untersuchung grenzte ein Team um den Astrobiologen Dirk Schulze-Makuch von der Technischen Universität Berlin gemeinsam mit Heller zudem 24 mögliche Planetenkandidaten ein und bezifferte die günstigste globale Durchschnittstemperatur auf etwa fünf Grad Celsius oberhalb des irdischen Mittelwerts. Allerdings hat das Konzept auch Kehrseiten: Keiner der 24 Kandidaten ist bislang zweifelsfrei bestätigt, alle liegen mehr als 100 Lichtjahre entfernt, und eine noch größere Masse würde schnell zu einem hohen Atmosphärendruck führen oder den Gesteinsplaneten in einen lebensfeindlichen Mini-Neptun mit dichter Gashülle verwandeln.
Photosynthese im Labor und die Grenzen künftiger Teleskope
Ob irdische Organismen mit dem rötlicheren Lichtspektrum eines K-Zwergs überhaupt auskommen, prüfte ein Team um die Astrobiologin Iva Vilović, die heute am Leibniz-Institut für Astrophysik im brandenburgischen Potsdam forscht, im Jahr 2024 in einer im International Journal of Astrobiology veröffentlichten Studie. Unter simuliertem K-Zwerg-Licht keimte gewöhnliche Gartenkresse zwar schneller und wuchs höher als unter künstlichem Sonnenlicht, wies am Ende jedoch einen höheren Wasseranteil und eine geringere Trockenmasse auf, weil der höhere Rotlichtanteil vor allem das Längenwachstum der Stängel anregte.
Ob solche Welten in unserer kosmischen Nachbarschaft tatsächlich existieren, soll ab März 2027 zunächst die ESA-Mission Plato klären, an deren Vorbereitung auch Heller in Göttingen beteiligt ist. Gegenüber der New York Times dämpft der Wissenschaftler jedoch zu hohe Erwartungen: „Wir werden wahrscheinlich einige von ihnen finden – vielleicht ein Dutzend. Aber wir werden noch nicht viel über sie erfahren.“
Denn Plato kann über regelmäßige Helligkeitsschwankungen von Sternen zwar die Größe und Umlaufbahn vorbeiziehender Planeten bestimmen, nicht aber die chemische Zusammensetzung ihrer Lufthülle. Für die Suche nach biologischen Spuren wie Sauerstoff oder Methan in den Atmosphären dieser Kandidaten werden Astronom:innen auf das im Bau befindliche Extremely Large Telescope der Europäischen Südsternwarte ESO sowie auf das Habitable Worlds Observatory der Nasa warten müssen, dessen Start erst für die 2040er-Jahre vorgesehen ist.

articles.title: Bloc-notes numérique : les meilleures liseuses E Ink avec stylet en 2026 — Frandroid
articles.text:
Nos 3 recommandations de carnets numériques
Nos 3 recommandations de carnets numériques

Le bloc-notes numérique, carnet numérique, ou encore tablette à encre électronique, est un appareil particulier, à la croisée de plusieurs usages, entre liseuse et tablette. Il s’agit d’un produit plutôt « de niche », dont tout le monde n’aura pas l’utilité. Ce type de tablette E Ink avec stylet est souvent destiné à un usage professionnel, ou bien à celles et ceux qui lisent et annotent beaucoup. Remplacer le papier par un bloc-notes numérique garantit un gain d’organisation et de temps : finies les notes éparpillées, tout est centralisé, partageable et synchronisé sur le cloud (parfois payant comme chez reMarkable).
Nous avons testé les principales tablettes E Ink du marché, avec ou sans écran couleur. Nos choix sont la Boox Note Air6 C pour sa polyvalence sous Android 16, la Kindle Scribe Colorsoft pour lire et annoter dans l’écosystème Amazon, la reMarkable Paper Pro pour la meilleure sensation d’écriture, et la reMarkable Paper Pure si vous voulez dépenser moins.
- Prise en main et qualité de fabrication
- Android 16 et le Play Store
- OS fouillé et personnalisable
- Navigation fluide sans ralentissements
- Équipement matériel complet : slot micro SD, Wi-Fi double bande, Bluetooth 6.0, micro, haut-parleur
- Intégration poussée de l'IA
- Contrastes moyens de l'écran en noir et blanc
- Autonomie faiblarde
Avec la Note Air6 C, Boox perfectionne une formule déjà éprouvée. Il s’agit d’une tablette E Ink avec un écran couleur Kaleido 3 de 10,3 pouces. La prise en main est excellente, malgré un poids assez conséquent (440 grammes). Le châssis est en aluminium, mais non étanche. Deux petits haut-parleurs ont la bonne idée d’être là, de même qu’un micro.
L’écran Kaleido 3, qui superpose un filtre de couleurs à une dalle E Ink noir et blanc, est de bonne facture, avec une résolution de 300 ppp en noir et blanc et 150 ppp en couleur, ce qui est standard pour un écran Kaleido 3. Les couleurs font preuve d’une belle saturation pour un écran à encre : la Boox est ainsi une bonne candidate pour la lecture de bandes dessinées et de mangas.
La Note Air6 C est une tablette qui tourne sous Android 16, ce qui est sans doute sa plus grande force. Vous pouvez donc installer n’importe quelle application du Google Play Store, offrant alors une polyvalence à toute épreuve. En plus de cela, Boox a créé une surcouche hyper personnalisable, avec beaucoup de réglages disponibles, que ce soit sur le rétroéclairage, la navigation par gestes, ou encore l’affichage de l’écran.
Les applications intégrées, comme le lecteur d’ebooks et l’app de prise de notes, offrent aussi tout un tas de fonctionnalités bienvenues et bien pensées. La prise de notes est d’ailleurs précise et agréable. La transcription de l’écriture manuscrite à dactylographiée fonctionne bien, de même que l’Assistant IA directement proposé dans une app dédiée.
En bref, un produit efficace et polyvalent, bien pensé, que l’on apprécie utiliser au quotidien. Son seul véritable point faible est sa batterie, qui s’épuise vite et a tendance à se décharger en veille.
Le modèle précédent, la Boox Note Air5 C, pourra aussi vous intéresser, car elle se trouve pour moins cher. Par rapport à la Note Air5 C, la Note Air6 C passe d’Android 13 à Android 16 et adopte un processeur gravé en 4 nm, nettement plus rapide. L’écran Kaleido 3 de 10,3 pouces ne change pas : si vous lisez et prenez des notes sans applications gourmandes, l’ancienne génération reste une bonne affaire.
- Fine et légère
- Bonne sensation d'écriture et réactivité du stylet
- Fonctionnalité d'annotation et surlignage simples à utiliser
- Rétroéclairage efficace à température réglable
- Kindle OS pratique avec un grand catalogue d'ebooks
- Écran trop sombre sans le rétroéclairage et couleurs ternes
- Fonctions de partage des carnets de notes et synchronisation PC/Smartphone trop succinctes
- OS trop fermé
Avec son Kindle Scribe Colorsoft, Amazon sort sa liseuse la plus haut de gamme. L’objet en lui-même est réussi : le châssis en aluminium est fin et particulièrement léger. En revanche, la prise en main n’est pas parfaite en raison de l’absence de bordure plus large pour la tenir sur le côté ou en bas.
Côté logiciel, on retrouve Kindle OS, fidèle à lui-même. C’est un OS qui tourne bien, qui est bien pensé et intuitif, en restant simple. En revanche, il reste un système très fermé, verrouillé par Amazon.
Avec son design d’une finesse remarquable et son interface dépouillée à l’extrême, la marque norvégienne s’adresse en priorité à ceux qui veulent fuir la surstimulation des tablettes classiques pour se concentrer sur l’essentiel. La reMarkable Paper Pro est ainsi particulièrement conseillée à un usage professionnel.
Avec son écran de 11,8 pouces, la Paper Pro est la plus grande tablette de reMarkable. Elle mesure 27,4 x 19,7 cm, un peu moins qu’une feuille A4, et pèse 525 grammes. Le stylet Marker Plus (avec gomme), livré dans les packs plus chers que l’offre de base avec le Marker simple, offre clairement la meilleure expérience d’écriture, couplé au revêtement d’écran texturé. Vous n’aurez pas plus proche de l’expérience papier. L’écran couleur, un Gallery 3, est bon sur le rendu des couleurs.
L’OS de reMarkable, s’il est parfaitement clair et épuré, manque tout de même de fonctionnalités et de possibilités de personnalisation, notamment sur les fonctions de lecture. La transcription de l’écriture manuscrite vers dactylographiée fonctionne bien, sans être exceptionnelle sur les écritures un peu difficiles. En outre, il faut payer un forfait mensuel (Connect) en sus pour avoir toutes les fonctions de partage et de cloud, ce qui est un peu chiche.
De par son OS fermé et le type de fonctionnalités intégrées, très orientées sur les outils de partage, la reMarkable Paper Pro se destine à un usage majoritairement professionnel.
reMarkable Paper Pro Move
Si vous voulez conserver la couleur, mais souhaitez plutôt un petit format, optez pour la Paper Pro Move, que nous avions également testée. Son petit format (7,3 pouces, 230 grammes) se glisse dans une poche de veste et pourra donc séduire les travailleurs et travailleuses qui souhaitent l’emmener partout avec eux pour prendre et organiser leurs notes, ainsi que consulter des documents.
La reMarkable Paper Pure va à l’essentiel. Écran noir et blanc 10,3 pouces, pas de rétroéclairage, châssis aminci en plastique… Elle est ainsi plus simple, et donc moins chère.
La Paper Pure fait d’autant plus dans la simplicité que ses grandes sœurs. Grâce à son châssis plastique, elle est légère, et sa prise en main est meilleure grâce à un rebord plus large sur le côté. Grâce à l’écran noir et blanc, à l’absence de rétroéclairage et à l’OS fermé, reMarkable annonce trois semaines d’autonomie à raison d’environ une heure de prise de notes par jour, et bien plus si vous l’utilisez peu.
Son écran noir et blanc présente de très bons contrastes, avec un fond bien blanc. Elle sera parfaite pour la lecture et l’annotation de documents. Si vous cherchez un outil pratique pour réfléchir, annoter, organiser vos idées, sans vider votre compte en banque pour un des modèles Pro de la marque, c’est le choix de raison. En revanche, on regrette l’absence de rétroéclairage qui aurait pourtant été bien utile par moments.
Les autres tablettes à encre électronique
Il existe encore de nombreux modèles, que nous n’avons pas pu tester, ou ne recommandons pas. On citera notamment la Kobo Elipsa 2E et la Paperslate Pro.
En outre, d’autres marques plus confidentielles sont spécialisées sur le secteur, par exemple Supernote avec la tablette Manta (écran noir et blanc). Bigme est aussi un autre fabricant placé sur des tablettes hyper abordables, comme la Bigme B7 Colour.
FAQ : comment bien choisir sa tablette E Ink ?
Qu’est-ce qu’un bloc-notes numérique et en quoi diffère-t-il d’une tablette classique ?
Un bloc-notes numérique (ou tablette à encre électronique) est un appareil pensé pour remplacer le papier.
Les technologies d’écran d’une liseuse et d’une tablette classique sont bien différentes. Les écrans LCD et OLED émettent leur propre lumière, tandis que l’encre électronique réfléchit la lumière ambiante. Ainsi, un écran E Ink n’envoie pas de flux lumineux direct, ce qui limite drastiquement la fatigue oculaire. En outre, un écran E Ink affichant une page fixe ne consommera aucune batterie. C’est pourquoi une liseuse (ou un bloc-notes numérique) peut tenir plusieurs semaines, là où une tablette LCD/OLED doit être rechargée souvent.
Enfin, certains blocs-notes numériques (pas ceux qui tournent sous Android) sont pensés pour éliminer les distractions avec un OS fermé et orienté sur la productivité, contrairement aux tablettes classiques où l’on peut vite s’éparpiller.
Faut-il recharger la batterie du stylet et changer les pointes ?
La majorité des blocs-notes numériques utilisent la technologie passive EMR (Electro-Magnetic Resonance) de Wacom : le stylet ne contient aucune batterie et n’a jamais besoin d’être rechargé. En revanche, il faut parfois remplacer la pointe en plastique (tous les 3 à 9 mois) lorsqu’elle est trop usée, cette dernière s’usant un peu avec la friction de l’écran mat. Les tablettes sont toujours livrées de base avec quelques mines de rechange.
Quel budget prévoir pour une tablette E Ink ?
Les premières E ink avec stylet démarrent aux alentours de 350-400 euros (Kobo Elipsa 2E, reMarkable Paper Pure, Paperslate). Les plus haut de gamme culminent autour de 600 euros (reMarkable Paper Pro, Scribe Colorsoft).
L’écriture sur un bloc-notes numérique ressemble-t-elle réellement à celle sur papier ?
Vous trouverez pas mal d’avis sur la toile ou de discours de marques qui vous diront que oui. La réponse totalement honnête est non, car c’est tout simplement impossible : le papier est une surface un peu molle, contrairement à un écran qui est parfaitement rigide. Sans compter la différence entre un stylo muni d’une bille qui roule lorsque l’on écrit, comparé à un stylet à mine plastique. En revanche, l’écran d’un carnet à encre électronique est mat : la sensation d’écriture est donc certes plus proche de celle du papier que sur une tablette LCD. Cette sensation et cette friction diffèrent selon les liseuses, avec un rendu plus ou moins glissant. Le rendu le plus proche du papier est sans doute celui des reMarkable.
Enfin, la latence entre le stylet et l’écran est aujourd’hui très faible : le trait apparaît presque instantanément sous la pointe.
Les bloc-notes E Ink peuvent-ils convertir l’écriture manuscrite en écriture dactylographiée ?
Oui. Presque tous les modèles récents intègrent une fonction de reconnaissance d’écriture manuscrite. Vous pouvez convertir vos notes manuscrites en texte brut, les éditer et les exporter par e-mail ou sur des services cloud (Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive…).
Quelle est l’autonomie moyenne d’un bloc-notes E Ink ?
L’écran E Ink ne consomme de l’énergie que lorsque l’affichage change (changement de page ou trait de stylet). L’autonomie varie très fortement selon le système d’exploitation installé :
- Systèmes propriétaires fermés (ex. : reMarkable, Kindle Scribe) : entre 2 et 4 semaines d’utilisation quotidienne.
- Systèmes basés sur Android (ex. : Onyx Boox) : entre 3 et 7 jours, car le processeur, l’OS et les applications en arrière-plan consomment davantage.
