articles.title: Netflix : les meilleures séries d"horreur pour flipper un max pour Halloween 2026
articles.text:
Qu’on se le dise : regarder du véritable cinéma d’épouvante ne relève pas de la simple distraction du dimanche soir. C’est une expérience physique, une plongée volontaire dans des traumatismes intimes, des obsessions et des tensions qui vous prennent à la gorge sans jamais demander pardon.
Pour cette cuvée 2026, nous avons passé au crible le catalogue mondial de Netflix pour ne garder que la crème de la noirceur pour le meilleur Halloween 2026 possible. Nous avons aussi concocté pour vous la liste des meilleurs films d’horreur sur Netflix et des meilleurs films d’horreur sur Prime Video.
Dark
On ne va pas tourner autour du pot : Dark reste indétrônable au sommet de ce que Netflix a pu produire. Cette création allemande part d’un pitch en apparence classique, la disparition d’un gamin dans une petite ville paumée cernée par une forêt menaçante et une centrale nucléaire, pour dérouler un piège psychologique et temporel machiavélique.
Ici, pas de monstre ridicule qui surgit de l’armoire pour faire sursauter le spectateur naïf. L’ambiance est lourde, il pleut sans discontinuer, la musique stridente vous prend la tête et le scénario demande d’accrocher son cerveau dès les premières minutes. La série explore le deuil, les choix impossibles, les secrets de famille étouffants et la fatalité sans jamais prendre le public pour un imbécile. Si vous voulez une histoire complexe qui vous scotche au canapé et vous hante l’esprit pendant des jours, c’est le choix numéro un incontestable.
The Haunting of Hill House
Si vous n’avez jamais posé les yeux sur la série de Mike Flanagan, préparez vos nerfs. Hill House prend le cliché éculé de la grande demeure hantée et le transcende pour en faire un drame familial bien lourd, intime et profondément traumatisant.
On y suit la fratrie Crain, brisée par un séjour cauchemardesque dans un manoir maudit durant leur enfance, et poursuivie par ses démons à l’âge adulte. En plus de cacher des dizaines de spectres silencieux dans les coins sombres de chaque plan pour récompenser les plus attentifs, la série balance des révélations glaciales, comme la vision terrifiante de la Dame au cou tordu, et des scènes de confrontation qui fonctionnent à tous les coups. C’est flippant, c’est d’une tristesse infinie, et c’est surtout réalisé avec une maîtrise technique redoutable.
Stranger Things (Saisons 1 et 3)
Avant de devenir une machine commerciale XXL qui s’étale sur des années, Stranger Things était une excellente petite série d’angoisse aux relents de Spielberg et de Stephen King. La Saison 1 conserve toute sa force intacte : l’ambiance des années 80 dans une petite ville paumée, la gamine aux pouvoirs instables et dangereux, et la traque angoissante du Démogorgon dans les bois.
Pour fêter Halloween dans les règles de l’art, activez le mode VHS proposé sur la plateforme (saison 1) : l’image devient granuleuse, les couleurs bavent légèrement et la bande saute de temps en temps, exactement comme si vous veniez de louer une vieille cassette maudite au fond d’un vidéoclub de quartier. Et si vous voulez du sang, de la sueur et de la chair transformée, foncez sur la Saison 3 : sous ses airs de centre commercial coloré et insouciant, elle rend un hommage réjouissant, très gore et délicieusement régressif aux films de monstres baveux et visqueux des années 80.
Sermons de Minuit
Autre réussite marquante signée Mike Flanagan, Sermons de Minuit change totalement de registre en s’attaquant à un sujet brûlant : le fanatisme religieux et la peur panique de la mort. L’histoire se déroule sur une île isolée et en perdition, où l’arrivée d’un jeune prêtre charismatique s’accompagne de « miracles » étranges qui redonnent espoir à une population désespérée.
La série prend le temps d’installer ses personnages, de poser les bases de cette communauté insulaire soudée, puis fait monter la pression progressivement jusqu’à ce que la situation dégénère en un chaos sanglant. Les face-à-face verbaux sont tendus à l’extrême, le mystère s’épaissit à chaque épisode et le final apocalyptique est particulièrement marquant. C’est noir, intelligent, cynique par moments et terriblement bien interprété.
Marianne
Il serait criminel de faire ce tour d’horizon sans saluer le coup d’éclat français de la plateforme. Marianne est sans conteste l’une des séries les plus ouvertement effrayantes sorties sur Netflix ces dernières années, damant le pion à beaucoup de productions américaines au budget dix fois supérieur.
L’intrigue suit une autrice à succès de romans d’épouvante qui réalise avec effroi que la sorcière maléfique qu’elle a inventée dans ses livres existe pour de vrai dans son village natal, en Bretagne. L’ambiance des côtes balayées par les vents, les apparitions graphiquement dérangeantes et la performance absolument flippante de Mireille Herbstmeyer dans le rôle de la voisine possédée font mouche à chaque apparition. C’est brut, direct, ça ne prend pas de gants et ça ne cherche jamais à ménager les nerfs du spectateur.

articles.title: Les joueurs le soir, l’IA en journée : Shadow lance Blade pour rentabiliser ses 12 000 GPU
articles.text:
Shadow, le spécialiste français du PC dans le cloud, lance Blade, une plateforme GPU européenne dédiée à l’IA. Elle mobilise les cartes graphiques de son service de cloud gaming en journée pour proposer de l’inférence à prix réduit.
Connu pour son PC dans le cloud prisé des amateurs de cloud gaming, Shadow a dévoilé Blade jeudi 22 octobre une plateforme européenne qui met ses GPU, les puces électroniques chargées d'afficher les images, les vidéos et les jeux sur les écrans, au service de l'intelligence artificielle. L'idée relève presque du bon sens, car après tout, pourquoi laisser une partie de ses milliers de cartes graphiques se tourner les pouces pendant que leurs utilisateurs sont au bureau ? Le service s’appuie sur l’infrastructure qui fait tourner le PC dans le cloud de Shadow, nettement moins sollicitée en journée. Deux offres sont au programme, avec des tarifs annoncés sous ceux des géants du secteur et une option d’hébergement en Europe.
Des GPU Shadow au tarif des heures creuses
Shadow veut offrir à chacun un PC Windows complet, logé dans le cloud et accessible depuis n'importe quel écran. Pour animer ces ordinateurs virtuels, l'entreprise exploite quelque 12 000 GPU NVIDIA, au service de plusieurs dizaines de milliers d'utilisateurs en Europe et en Amérique du Nord. Or, de son propre aveu, la demande du grand public se concentre assez logiquement en soirée et le week-end. Dévoilée jeudi et accessible sur blade.sh, Blade remet ces machines au travail le reste du temps, pour le compte de développeurs, de start-up et entreprises qui veulent faire tourner des modèles d'intelligence artificielle.
Cette double vie a un effet très concret sur la facture, puisque Shadow affirme que Blade revient 25 à 40 % moins cher que les principaux acteurs du marché, à GPU équivalent, sans rien facturer pour la sortie des données ni pour des services annexes. Surtout, les prix fluctuent selon la capacité disponible, un peu comme l'électricité en heures creuses. Les tâches qui peuvent attendre, comme les traitements par lots ou la production de données synthétiques (des données artificielles générées par une IA), ont donc tout intérêt à être programmées aux périodes les moins chères.
L'entreprise sait de quoi elle parle, puisque depuis 2016, elle loue des PC dans le cloud et fait tourner des cartes graphiques à grande échelle. « Nous ne découvrons pas le GPU avec l'IA », insiste Boris Lecoeur, son directeur général. Le nom de la plateforme a d'ailleurs un parfum de retour aux sources, il ne vous a pas échappé que Blade était celui de la société à ses débuts. Aujourd'hui contrôlée par Octave et Miroslaw Klaba, les fameux cofondateurs d'OVHcloud, elle considère plus ce nouveau relais de croissance tourné vers les entreprises comme un complément à son activité historique, et non comme un remplaçant.
Une IA prête à l'emploi, version européenne
Concrètement, Blade se décline en deux offres. Déjà disponible, Blade Models ouvre par API l'accès à une vingtaine de modèles d'IA capables, entre autres, de rédiger du texte ou du code, d'analyser des images, de reconnaître du texte dans des documents, de créer des visuels ou de transcrire de l'audio, avec une facturation à l'usage. Ensuite, il y a AI Fabric, attendue courant novembre, qui va un cran plus loin. Depuis son environnement Python, ou en important un modèle depuis la plateforme Hugging Face, le développeur pourra déployer son propre modèle, son code ou son application sans jamais gérer de serveur. Il choisit les ressources, Blade les fournit et les orchestre, et la note se suit en temps réel.
Shadow ne prétend pas réinventer la roue. Blade mise sur l'inférence, c'est-à-dire l'exécution des modèles une fois prêts à servir, et sur la simplicité, avec une API compatible avec le standard d'OpenAI, une facturation lisible et la possibilité de changer plus facilement de fournisseur. L'entreprise se pose ainsi en contrepoint des grands clouds généralistefs comme Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure ou Google Cloud qui, selon elle, livrent surtout une infrastructure brute à configurer et administrer soi-même. « L'Europe ne manque ni de talents ni de modèles d'IA », estime Boris Lecoeur. Le blocage se situe selon lui au passage en production, quand la puissance de calcul s'avère coûteuse, complexe à exploiter et largement concentrée hors d'Europe. En étant débarrassées de ce casse-tête, les équipes pourraient alors « se concentrer sur leurs produits et innover plus vite ». Les entreprises les plus attachées à la souveraineté pourront aussi choisir des serveurs situés en Europe, hébergés chez OVHcloud.
La puissance de calcul ne règle toutefois pas tout. Un modèle d'IA, aussi rapide soit-il, ignore tout ce qui s'est produit après la date à laquelle ses données ont été figées. Pour y remédier, Blade intègre donc Staan, l'API de recherche web conçue par Qwant et Ecosia au sein de leur coentreprise European Search Perspective, qui permet aux modèles d'interroger le web pour obtenir des informations récentes et sourcées. Elle peut notamment alimenter des systèmes dits RAG, qui vont chercher des documents avant de formuler leur réponse. Ce mariage illustre la complémentarité entre Shadow et Qwant au sein de Synfonium, l'ensemble créé par les frères Klaba. De l'index de recherche à la puissance de calcul, l'Europe bâtit selon Boris Lecoeur « une alternative technologique crédible », dont elle maîtrise désormais, avec Blade, « un maillon essentiel ».

articles.title: Canal+ casse les prix : Netflix, HBO Max et du sport dans une offre à moins de 25€ par mois
articles.text:
Canal+ casse les prix : Netflix, HBO Max et du sport dans une offre à moins de 25€ par mois
Canal+ vient de dévoiler sa nouvelle offre d'abonnement Ciné Séries, proposant Netflix, HBO Max et Paramount+ à un prix imbattable. Mais faites-vite, celle-ci s'arrête dans quelques jours.
À l'heure où les tarifs des abonnements aux plateformes de streaming ne cessent d'augmenter, Canal+ revient à la charge avec une nouvelle promo. La généreuse offre Ciné Séries - avec Netflix, HBO Max et Paramount+ - de la chaîne cryptée est présentée à moins de 25 euros mensuels. Voici comment en profiter.
Du cinéma, du sport et des séries à prix réduit
Jusqu'au lundi 9 novembre inclus, Canal+ propose ainsi son pack Ciné Séries à seulement 24,99 euros par mois (au lieu des 29,99€ habituels) dans cette toute nouvelle offre intitulée "Pourquoi payer plus ?".
Dans le détail, celle-ci inclut les chaînes Canal+, Canal+ Box Office, Canal+ Grand Écran, Canal+ Sport 360, Canal+ Docs, Canal+ Kids et Canal+ Cinéma(s). À cela s'ajoute d'autres services de streaming aggrégés par la chaîne cryptée, soit Apple TV, HBO Max (abonnement Standard), Netflix (Standard avec Pub), Paramount+ (Standard), et Ciné+ OCS entre autres.
Une combinaison d'univers qui vous permet de profiter à la fois des derniers films et séries des plateformes les plus importantes du marché, tout en ayant également accès au meilleur du sport : football (Champion's League, Premier League), Formule 1, Top 14, MotoGP...
La chaîne cryptée française met ici en avant toute la force de son pouvoir d'aggrégateur, et le fait d'ailleurs bien savoir dans sa promo en rappelant que tous ces services coûteraient 74€ par mois s'ils étaient pris séparément. Une proposition particulièrement intéressante.
Soyez toutefois vigilants : il faut noter que cette offre vous demande un engagement de 24 mois, avec les 12 premiers mois au tarif réduit de 24,99€, avant que le tarif passe à 34,99€ par la suite.

articles.title: YouTube chamboule son interface et supprime un bouton présent depuis presque 10 ans
articles.text:
YouTube chamboule son interface et cela ne va clairement pas plaire à ceux qui avaient leurs habitudes bien ancrées depuis des années. La barre supérieure est ainsi complètement redessinée et l’application introduit la possibilité de créer des flux sur mesure en écrivant simplement ce que vous avez envie de voir.
La fin du bouton « Abonnements » sur mobile
Pendant près d’une décennie, le bouton « Abonnements » a trôné en quatrième position dans la barre de navigation inférieure des applications mobiles. Cette époque est révolue puisque le bouton se transforme en onglet et passe tout en haut de l’écran d’accueil, juste après l’onglet principal. Cela devrait casser pas mal de mémoire musculaire chez les habitués.
À côté de cet espace dédié aux créateurs favoris, la nouvelle barre supérieure accueille de nouveaux flux thématiques pour le direct, la musique et les films ou séries (ce dernier n’apparaissant que pour les personnes qui ont un abonnement payant pour y accéder). Cette refonte s’accompagne aussi de la suppression du panneau de navigation latéral sur mobile, ce qui a le mérite de simplifier la navigation.
Vous allez pouvoir créer des flux personnalisés
L’une des nouveautés les plus importantes est sans doute l’arrivée des flux personnalisés, que vous pouvez configurer en appuyant simplement sur le bouton « + » situé tout en haut du flux d’accueil. Il suffit ensuite d’écrire en quelques mots le sujet, les chaînes ou l’ambiance recherchés. L’exemple partagé est « Aide-moi à me détendre après le travail grâce à des méditations guidées de moins de 10 minutes ». Le flux sera alors personnalisé en fonction de votre recherche.
À lire : YouTube teste ces 3 nouvelles icônes pour son application
Ces flux personnels sont synchronisés entre les appareils et sont enregistrés directement sous forme d’onglets en haut de l’écran pour pouvoir y retourner facilement, avec une limite fixée à 3 flux actifs pour les comptes gratuits contre 8 pour les abonnés YouTube Premium, qui pourrait bientôt voir son prix augmenter. Cette fonction est pour l’instant uniquement disponible aux utilisateurs connectés de 13 ans ou plus aux États-Unis sur mobile et ordinateur, mais devrait être déployée dans d’autres pays prochainement.

articles.title: Microsoft Teams to get AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection
articles.text:
Microsoft says Teams will begin using AI-powered phishing detection in early November 2026 to detect malicious behavior in messages.
The rollout is part of a targeted release phase expected to end by mid-November, with the new security feature likely reaching general availability worldwide between early and mid-December.
Microsoft first revealed in a Microsoft 365 Roadmap entry last week that the AI-powered phishing detection will use conversation context (without retaining message content) to identify phishing and suspicious behavior in higher-risk messaging scenarios, such as external first-contact chats.
"Microsoft Teams is introducing AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection to help identify phishing, social engineering, impersonation attempts, and deceptive intent," the company said in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update on Wednesday.
"The capability analyzes conversation context to identify suspicious behavior that may not include traditional indicators such as malicious links or files."
Microsoft says IT admins won't need to take any action to enable this new security protection feature, which will focus on external first-contact chats for most users.
It also added that while the new Teams feature will analyze conversation context to discover suspicious behavior, it will not retain customer data for further AI training or other uses.
"This capability is used only for security protection and not for productivity, summarization, advertising, user monitoring, or other non-security purposes," Microsoft said. "Customer message content is not retained by the detection system for model training or other secondary uses."
This is part of a broader list of Teams security changes, with Microsoft announcing in December that admins could lock external users via the Defender portal starting in January to thwart cybercrime groups (including ransomware gangs) from abusing Teams in social engineering attacks that target victims' employees.
It also began rolling out a new Teams meeting protection policy in August that lets admins block all identified external bots automatically from joining meetings.
Last month, Microsoft also revealed that Teams will blur QR codes sent by external senders to better protect against fraud and phishing attempts, and that it will let users report suspicious guest invitations directly in Teams to help security teams block phishing attempts and other attacks abusing guest invitations.
More recently, in early October, the company announced plans to introduce support for third-party deepfake detection solutions and impersonation protection in Teams meetings.

articles.title: Alemania pone en aprietos el Modo IA de Google: cuando en el resumen no hay enlaces, la opinión es de Google
articles.text:
Cuando hacemos una búsqueda en Google, lo primero que nos aparece es un resumen generado por IA relacionado con esa búsqueda. Este resumen, denominado AI Overviews, generalmente comparte también una serie de enlaces para que nosotros podamos comprobar de dónde ha sacado la información. ¿Pero qué pasa cuando no hay enlaces? ¿Quién se debe responsabilizar cuando la IA de Google afirma algo sin esos enlaces como apoyo?
Un tribunal de Aquisgrán, Alemania, lo tiene claro: Google. Y es que ha ordenado a la compañía que impida que su modo de IA difunda afirmaciones falsas sobre un médico al que el resumen de IA de Google le había atribuido un delito de agresión sexual hacia su secretaria. El delito existe, pero fue atribuido a la persona equivocada. Ahora el tribunal, basándose directamente en una sentencia dictada en Múnich en mayo, considera las respuestas de IA de Google como declaraciones propias de la empresa. De momento es una medida cautelar y aún no es firme, por lo que Google todavía puede apelar.
El caso. Según el medio jurídico Beck-Aktuell, el demandante es un médico que trabajó como médico jefe en un hospital alemán hasta el pasado verano. A finales de agosto, un compañero le comentó que al buscar su nombre junto con la palabra “exención” en el modo de inteligencia artificial de Google, aparecía un relato sobre él bastante serio y en un tono preocupantemente elaborado. En él se afirmaba que había acosado a su secretaria en un viaje de negocios, que había sido despedido, que había recibido una condena condicional por agresión sexual y que se había marchado con una indemnización por despido de seis cifras.
Nada de eso era verdad. Y es que según cuenta Beck-Aktuell, los hechos parecen haber estado relacionados con otro antiguo miembro del personal directivo de la misma clínica, y de que los artículos de noticias enlazados por Google como fuentes nunca mencionaban el nombre del demandante. Según The Decoder, búsquedas adicionales con términos como “rescisión” y “procedimientos judiciales” también daban lugar a desinformación igual de detallada.
La respuesta de Google. El médico pidió a Google por correo electrónico que retirara el contenido a finales de agosto. Sin embargo, Beck-Aktuell cuenta que Google respondió que había revisado la reclamación y que no tomaría ninguna medida. Una carta de advertencia de sus abogados, el bufete de Colonia Höcker, enviada el mismo día, tampoco cambió nada.
Lo que decidió el tribunal. El tribunal de Aquisgrán dictaminó que los textos que generaba la IA vulneraban el derecho general de la personalidad del médico, debido a que le atribuían acusaciones penales y consecuencias laborales que afectaban a otra persona. Según el medio, emitió la orden en un procedimiento de urgencia, sin escuchar primero a Google, alegando los daños a su reputación profesional y social. Google se enfrenta a una multa de hasta 250.000 euros por cada infracción.
El precedente de Múnich. En el caso anterior, el Tribunal Regional I de Múnich dictaminó que Google puede considerarse directamente responsable de sus resúmenes de IA, según comparte DW. Los demandantes eran dos editoriales de Múnich a las que dicha función había vinculado erróneamente con estafas de suscripción y esquemas fraudulentos. Google argumentó que los usuarios podían comprobar las fuentes a través de los enlaces y sabían que no se debía confiar ciegamente en los resultados de la IA. El tribunal rechazó este argumento, al considerar que el resumen era una declaración autocontenida y no ofrecía a los lectores ningún indicio de que pudiera no ser fiable. Google declaró en su momento que recurriría la sentencia.
El medio The Decoder informa de que el recurso nunca llegó a resolverse, pues según la investigación, el caso terminó con un acuerdo extrajudicial, y ni Google ni la editorial quisieron aclarar si hubo contraprestación económica ni por qué se cerró el caso.

articles.title: Bolt’s annual plan is a long-term bet on customer habit
articles.text:
Bolt, the global ride-hailing and food delivery company, launched a paid membership called Bolt Plus in Kenya on 15 October. The service offers frequent users cashback on rides, free delivery on eligible food and retail orders, priority driver matching, faster food delivery and three free ride cancellations a month for KES 280 ($2.16), with the first month free. Bolt operates in nine Kenyan cities.
The more unusual figure is the yearly price of KES 899 (7), which works out to about KES 75 ($0.58) per month and sits well below the monthly price, even under the KES 119 ($0.92) introductory rate on offer for the first six months. The discount is so steep it looks like a mistake. Asked to confirm it, Bolt said the figure was correct and gave no explanation beyond wanting people “to consider the yearly subscription for better value”.
Bolt Plus enters a market where two rivals already sell memberships. Uber One, which Uber launched in Kenya in March 2025 after a pilot the previous November, covers rides, food and groceries and costs KES 280 ($2) a month or KES 2,800 ($22) a year, while Glovo Prime connects customers with restaurants, supermarkets and shops, and costs KES 400 ($3) a month for delivery only.
Read alongside the free first month and the introductory rate, the pricing suggests that Bolt cares more about securing a long commitment than about the fee itself. This strategy clearly appeals to customers but also creates trade-offs that the company’s announcement does not address.
Why the annual price makes sense
Annual plans generally favour the seller because the money arrives up front. A customer who has paid for the year has little reason to try rival apps, so a discount deep enough to win that commitment can pay for itself in loyalty, and at KES 899 ($6.92), Bolt’s yearly plan costs less than a third of Uber One’s.
The bundle adds a second layer to the logic, since Glovo Prime must recoup its fee on food and grocery orders alone, offering unlimited free delivery at participating outlets, with an average saving that Glovo puts at KES 150 ($1.15) per order. In contrast, Bolt Plus and Uber One combine rides and delivery, giving members two reasons to open the same app and the company two chances to recoup the discount cost. A customer who takes a ride to work and orders lunch through the same app is plausibly worth more than one who uses it for only one of the two.
Bolt also competes on service as well as price, adding priority driver matching, faster food delivery, and free ride cancellations, extras that don’t appear among the benefits Uber lists on its Kenya page.
The entry price also keeps the risk low for riders, because at about KES 75 ($0.58) a month, a regular user would not need to spend much on trips for the cashback to cover the fee. A single food order that earns the maximum free-delivery saving of KES 200 ($1.54) would repay nearly three months of that saving.
Where the benefits get harder to value
The size of the cashback is the first thing to pin down, because Bolt’s announcement promises 10% on every ride in its opening paragraph and in a company statement, but lists “5-10%” in its benefits section. Uber’s scheme is tiered, with 10% in credits on premium rides and 5% on economy rides. If Bolt follows a similar pattern, riders who stick to cheaper trips would earn about half as much as the headline suggests, making it harder to recoup the annual fee. The announcement does not say which rate applies.
Bolt Plus cashback stays in the app for future trips, tying its value to continued use, much like Uber’s credits, which are limited to eligible rides and orders. Bolt’s announcement doesn’t say what happens to a balance when a member cancels, a key detail for anyone who builds up credit and then wants out.
Priority matching comes with its own trade-off: faster matching during busy periods means other riders wait longer, and the announcement says nothing about how the scheme affects drivers’ earnings.
Free delivery is also more conditional than the headline suggests, applying only at outlets marked with a “+” and to orders within qualifying value ranges, with savings of “up to” KES 200 ($1.54) per order. Uber One imposes a KES 600 ($4.62) minimum at participating restaurants and non-grocery stores, so each scheme’s practical value depends on what a customer orders and how often they order.
A subscription of this kind rewards habits more than it creates them. The customers most likely to benefit are those who already use Bolt several times a month for both rides and food. At this price, the plan may end up subsidising customers who would have stayed anyway. A rider who checks several apps before booking, or orders from whichever platform has the better offer, will rarely spend enough with Bolt to make the cashback worthwhile, and Bolt is betting that its price is low enough to change that habit.
Bolt has not said whether KES 899 ($7) is a launch price or a standing price, or what a renewal will cost. At roughly KES 75 ($0.58) a month, customers risk little by signing up. What remains unexplained is Bolt’s economics, which leaves the annual plan looking more like a bet on habit than on margin.

articles.title: Mercado de criptomonedas: cuál es el valor de Bitcoin
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Costo de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El costo de la criptomoneda de bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 81554.06 dólares por unidad.
Esto quiere decir que la moneda digital registró un cambio del -0.29% en el último día, así como una variación del 0.0% en los últimos 60 minutos.
Actualmente, bitcoin se encuentra en el lugar #1 de popularidad en el mercado digital. Cabe mencionar que el máximo histórico que ha alcanzado esta criptomoneda es de 126.198 dólares por unidad.
El flujo histórico de inversiones impulsa a bitcoin a máximos nunca antes vistos
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: Bose acquires Skullcandy in surprise deal, looks to attract younger buyers
articles.text:
What just happened? There's a good chance that a random pair of Skullcandy headphones available at any store these days carries a "Sound by Bose" badge on the box. While that's been the most visible sign of their partnership so far, the integration may soon get a lot deeper. Bose has now acquired Skullcandy outright from a fund managed by Mill Road Capital. Neither company has yet said how much the deal is worth, though Mill Road paid roughly $196.6 million when it took Skullcandy private back in 2016.
Bose plans to keep Skullcandy running as its own brand, and its headquarters will stay put in Park City, Utah. It will sit inside Bose's Premium Consumer Audio business, gaining access to Bose's technology, global distribution, and retail partners while holding on to its own identity. Bose also says it plans to put money into growing the brand.
Quite a bit of that technology is already inside Skullcandy's lineup. The $129 Method 360 ANC earbuds, for one, use Bose drivers tuned for Skullcandy's bassier sound. Meanwhile, the $280 Crusher 1080 ANC headphones that launched in July pack the company's QuietControl noise cancellation and TrueSpatial head tracking. Skullcandy still added its adjustable "sensory bass" on top of all that – a feature that turns the low end into vibrations you can actually feel.
Bose's own announcement suggests Skullcandy's customers are a big part of the appeal. The company itself is better known for pricey noise-canceling headphones like the QuietComfort Ultra. Skullcandy, on the other hand, has long had ties to skate and snow culture, along with gaming, music, and fitness, and those are areas where Bose admits it has less of a presence today.
Bose has actually been chasing a younger crowd for a while, and just last month it started bringing back wired earbuds – its first in over a decade – as wired headphone sales crept back up.
Skullcandy is also the fourth company Bose has bought since November 2024. First came McIntosh Group, which owns the high-end McIntosh and Sonus faber brands. Bose also picked up Austrian streaming specialist StreamUnlimited in June this year and, earlier this month, Firelight Technologies, the Australian company behind the FMOD audio software used in plenty of video games.
Bose CEO Lila Snyder credits all of this to the company being privately held, saying it gives Bose "the freedom to make bold, long-term investments." Over at Skullcandy, CEO Brian Garofalow called the deal "a win for Skullcandy and our fans." Neither company has announced any new products resulting from the deal.

articles.title: CSIRO Uses Serverless Architecture to Query 100x More Genomic Variants on AWS
articles.text:
CSIRO has developed Serverless Beacon (sBeacon), a serverless architecture for querying genomic variant data without copying large genomic datasets into a central database. The system uses Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon Athena, and Amazon DynamoDB to provide an implementation of the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) Beacon standard, supporting genomic queries across large cohorts while keeping the underlying data in its original storage.
The architecture separates genomic data from the metadata needed to search it. Variant Call Format (VCF) files remain in Amazon S3, while metadata such as disease status, age, and location is indexed separately. During onboarding, sBeacon creates indexes and Athena tables for the metadata, while ontology terms are handled through CSIRO's Ontoserver to support queries combining genomic and phenotypic information.
sBeacon data onboarding architecture (Source: AWS Blog Post)
For variant queries, API Gateway routes requests to Lambda functions that identify relevant datasets and genomic regions. The Variant Querying Module uses bcftools and its htslib library to retrieve specific portions of VCF files through HTTP byte range requests. This allows the system to read the required genomic region without transferring the complete file. Results are aggregated and returned through the Beacon API.
Anuradha Wickramarachchi, Solutions Architect for Bioinformatics Products at CSIRO, highlighted data compression as an important consideration in the design,
One key consideration we have exercised carefully is having the data in the most compressed form. And querying while they are in the compressed form is greatly beneficial.
CSIRO evaluated the architecture using chromosome 1 from the 1000 Genomes Project, containing 2,504 samples in a 1.1 GB compressed VCF file. The dataset was onboarded in 18 seconds. A query covering 10,000 base pairs averaged 1.52 seconds at an estimated compute cost of USD 0.00013. Latency remained broadly consistent as matching variants increased from four to 400.
Lambda distributes genomic queries while S3 serves only the required compressed file ranges (Source: AWS Blog Post)
The design builds on earlier sBeacon research published in Nature Biotechnology, which reported support for up to 40 million individuals and 3 billion genomic locations. The original Beacon work described the federated model, while the GA4GH protocol was designed to operate across distributed data sources without prescribing an underlying storage technology. The original Beacon work described the federated model as a way for organizations to retain control of their genomic data while exposing standardized query interfaces. The 2026 implementation extends that model with cloud services that provide elastic query execution while retaining genomic files in object storage.

articles.title: Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning on Amazon SageMaker AI: A hands-on guide
Most fine-tuning teaches a model to produce a better answer to a single prompt. Agentic tasks are different. An agent that files an expense report or triages a support ticket takes a sequence of actions, and each step depends on what came before. There’s rarely one correct sequence to imitate, and the only reliable feedback is whether the whole sequence succeeded. Supervised fine-tuning has no labels for that, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit a decision made three steps before the outcome.
Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL) on Amazon SageMaker AI trains models on exactly that signal. SageMaker AI sends prompts to an agent you host on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, or on your own infrastructure, such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), or AWS Fargate, through an AWS Lambda forwarder. The example here uses AgentCore. The agent calls the policy model being trained, acts in your environment over as many turns as the task needs, and reports one reward when the episode ends. You don’t specify the right trajectory, only how to score the result.
This post uses Wordle, a game in which a player has six tries to guess a hidden five-letter word, as the example. After each guess, every letter turns green if it is in the right position, yellow if it’s in the word but in a different position, and gray if it isn’t in the word. The game suits MTRL because the rules are few, each guess depends on the feedback from the last, and the outcome is scored objectively. Wordle is a teaching example, and frontier models already play it well. In practice, you would use MTRL to make a small, low-cost model good at a multi-step task specific to your business, such as an internal workflow that public models were never trained on. The same pipeline applies to that setting.
In our run, MTRL took gpt-oss-20b from a 61 to an 84 percent solve rate on held-out words at its default reasoning effort, and from 15 to 69 percent at the low effort it trained at, for about $339 in training tokens. In this post, we walk through the pipeline end-to-end: deploying the agent and reward to AgentCore, preparing the dataset, training, monitoring in MLflow, and evaluating at serving settings. We also share the reward-design mistakes and training failures we hit. Your datasets, agent, and trained model stay in your AWS account and are not used to train the base models. All code is in the accompanying aws-samples repository.
Solution overview
The system has two halves. SageMaker AI owns the training job and the policy model. AgentCore hosts the agent, the Wordle environment, and the reward function. The following diagram shows how they connect.
For every rollout, the MTRL service invokes the AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with one training row, which holds one secret word. A Strands agent in the runtime calls the policy model through the SageMaker Job Runtime’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The model plays up to six guesses through one tool, guess_word, and after each guess the environment returns per-letter feedback and a summary of what is known. When the game ends, the agent returns one reward. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) uses the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word to update a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model.
Three design points matter for what follows:
- The agent and reward live in one place. A single Python file deployed to AgentCore holds the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.
- The dataset carries only the secret word. The word lists bundled with the agent are built from the open-source SCOWL word lists and are used only for scoring.
- The reward is outcome-dominant. A solve pays 1.05–1.55 depending on speed, a loss pays -0.5, and never making a valid guess pays -1.5. A small shaping term rewards good strategy within each tier.
Supported models and AWS Regions
MTRL is serverless: you pick a base model and the service provisions the training and sampling infrastructure. At the time of writing, it supports the following base models, each trained with a LoRA adapter:
| Base model | AWS Regions | 
| Amazon Nova 2 Lite | US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) | 
| GPT-OSS-20B | US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1), US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) | 
| Gemma 4 31B (instruction-tuned) | US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) | 
| Qwen 3.6 27B | US West (Oregon) (us-west-2) | 
We chose GPT-OSS-20B because it has the lowest per-token price of the four and its reasoning effort is controllable per request. See the MTRL documentation for the current list.
Pricing
You don’t choose instances or size a cluster. You pay per million tokens in three dimensions, priced by base model:
- Prefill: input tokens the policy model processes. These accumulate in a multi-turn task, because every turn re-reads the history.
- Sample: tokens the policy model generates, including reasoning tokens.
- Train: tokens processed in the backward pass that updates the LoRA adapter.
The 100-step run consumed 491.6 million prefill, 159.7 million sample, and 643.3 million train tokens across 105,486 rollouts in 12 hours 40 minutes. At GPT-OSS-20B list prices in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1) at the time of writing, that is about $339:
| Dimension | Tokens | Price per 1M | Cost | 
| Prefill | 491,616,806 | $0.12 | $58.99 | 
| Sample | 159,737,098 | $0.30 | $47.92 | 
| Train | 643,308,554 | $0.36 | $231.59 | 
| Total | 1,294,662,458 |  | $338.50 | 
The train dimension dominates and scales with trajectory length, so shorter games and less verbose reasoning cut the bill. The AgentCore runtime bills separately for the vCPU and memory the agent uses. For this run, that was about $79, from the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch usage metrics at us-east-1 list prices. DescribeJob reports the token counts under BillableTokenUsage. See Amazon SageMaker AI pricing for current rates.
Prerequisites
To follow this walkthrough, you need the following. See also the MTRL prerequisites.
- Python 3.10 or later, uv, Node 20 or later, and the AgentCore CLI (npm install -g @aws/agentcore). See Get started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for installation and the IAM permissions the CLI needs.
- botocore 1.43.37 or later, on the machine that launches the job. This is the first version that includes the AgentRFT CreateJob operation.
- Two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, described in Step 1.
- An Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket in the same Region as the agent. The training job must also run in that Region, because CreateJob rejects a cross-Region runtime ARN.
Step 1: Create the IAM roles
MTRL uses two roles, and one of them has a trust policy that the general SageMaker AI documentation doesn’t mention.
Agent runtime role. agentcore deploy creates this role for you. It trusts bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com and needs the AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess managed policy, which lets the agent call the policy model and report rewards. The CDK stack in the sample repository attaches this policy automatically.
Training job role. You create this one. It must trust job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com with both sts:AssumeRole and sts:TagSession, and it needs the AmazonSageMakerJobFullAccess managed policy.
Note: The trust principal is job.sagemaker.amazonaws.com, not sagemaker.amazonaws.com. With the generic principal, CreateJob fails with “Could not assume role,” and the message names the correct principal only after retries.
Step 2: Deploy the agent to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Clone the sample repository, set your account and Region in Wordle/agentcore/aws-targets.json, and deploy:
The CLI builds the agent’s dependencies for the runtime’s Linux ARM64 platform, creates the execution role with AmazonSageMakerJobRuntimeAccess attached, and deploys through AWS CloudFormation. We recommend it over uploading a code package on the console, where it’s common to get the roughly 700 MB of compiled dependencies or the policy attachment wrong. Note the runtime ARN in the output for the training job.
The runtime reads two environment variables from agentcore.json. REASONING_EFFORT=low sets reasoning_effort on every request to the policy model. In our evaluation jobs, low effort used 63 to 83 percent fewer sample tokens per game than medium. REASONING_PROMPT_HINT=true also adds “Reasoning: low” to the system prompt, which is how gpt-oss reads the setting in its Harmony chat format. Neither variable gives the model any hint about the secret word.
The agent is one file, main.py. Simplified, its entrypoint looks like the following. For your own task, you change the task parsing, the tools, and the reward:
Important: The sagemaker_rft_handler decorator does not start an HTTP server by itself. Wrap it with BedrockAgentCoreApp and @app.entrypoint, with the entrypoint decorator outermost. Without this, every invocation times out after 30 seconds.
Step 3: Verify the runtime
Before spending GPU time, confirm the whole chain works with a payload shaped like the one the training service sends. The repository includes one as Wordle/payload.json:
The fake job ARN is expected to fail, and the way it fails is the proof. Put your own account ID into it first: for a job ARN in another account, the service returns a 403 before it checks whether the job exists, which looks like a broken IAM setup. From the Wordle directory, run:
In the runtime’s Amazon CloudWatch logs, you see the agent parse the prompt, authenticate to the Job Runtime endpoint, and receive a 400 error reading “Could not find job.” That failure confirms that parsing, authentication, and error reporting work. The command itself prints {“reward”: -1.5}, because the agent never reached the policy model. A 403 reading “not authorized to access this resource” means the job ARN still names another account. A 30-second timeout instead means the HTTP server is not starting (see the Important note in Step 2).
Step 4: Prepare the dataset
The MTRL dataset has no target responses, transcripts, or labels. Each row is one task for the agent to attempt. Here are the first three rows of the training file:
The service reads the prompt column (or the first column) and passes the string to your agent verbatim, without parsing it. We made the string a small JSON object with three fields:
- prompt: the instruction the agent shows the policy model, identical on every row.
- answer: the secret word. Only the environment and the reward function use it. The policy model never sees it.
- id: a row ID for tracing a rollout in the logs back to its source row.
The sample repository’s make_dataset.py draws 640 training words (five full batches of 128) and 128 validation words from the answer list with no overlap, so the validation solve rate measures generalization. The service also accepts Apache Parquet, JSON arrays, and CSV. Upload both files to Amazon S3:
Because the service never inspects the prompt string, a production task can pack a full message list, tool configuration, or reward specification into it. See the MTRL documentation for examples, including how to protect sensitive content in the string.
Step 5: Launch the training job
The launcher uses the MultiTurnRLTrainer class from the sagemaker-train SDK. Point it at the runtime ARN from Step 2, the role from Step 1, the datasets from Step 4, and an MLflow app for metrics. The MLflow app is required, so if you don’t have one, create it first with aws sagemaker create-mlflow-app:
The launcher overrides three hyperparameters and leaves every other one at the gpt-oss-20b default. It sets sampling_max_tokens to 8192, the service maximum, because at the default of 4096 gpt-oss often ran out of tokens while reasoning, before its first tool call. It sets max_epochs to 20 and max_steps to 100: 640 rows at the default global_batch_size of 128 is 5 steps per epoch, and with the default group_size of 8, each step plays 1,024 games. The job moves through Starting, Downloading, and Pending before reaching Training. After it’s training, your AgentCore runtime begins receiving rollout invocations.
Important: Don’t redeploy the agent while a job is running. Redeploying restarts the runtime, in-flight rollouts see no sampling requests, and the service fails the entire job.
Step 6: Monitor training in MLflow
The service logs reward, token, and turn statistics at every step and runs validation every val_every steps. The metric to watch is val/reward/pass_at_1, the fraction of held-out words solved. Every solve scores at least 1.01, so it clears the service’s success_threshold of 1.0 and pass@1 counts it. The following chart is built from this run’s MLflow history:
Training reward climbs to about +0.57 within 15 steps and holds there. Validation reward stays lower, mostly because of temperature 1.0 versus 0 rather than overfitting (see Step 7). The validation solve rate jumps from 2 to 31 percent in the first 10 steps, then moves between 35 and 48 percent. With 128 words, those swings are mostly noise. We did not test whether more steps help at serving settings.
The runtime’s OpenTelemetry traces in CloudWatch record every model turn and tool call. Here is one game the trained model played during an evaluation job (medium effort, temperature 1.0), with the reasoning trimmed. The secret word was PASTE:
A trained-model rollout from the AgentCore runtime traces. The model keeps green letters in place, never reuses a gray letter, and uses each yellow letter to rule out positions, though nothing in the training data showed it how.
Step 7: Evaluate the trained model at serving settings
When the job completes, its page in SageMaker AI Studio shows the status and the model package group that holds the trained model. DescribeJob, with JobCategory set to AgentRFT, returns the output model package ARN and the billable token counts.
An evaluation job (JobCategory set to AgentRFTEvaluation) plays your evaluation prompts through the same AgentCore runtime and reward, on the base model or the trained package, and logs eval/reward/pass_at_1 to MLflow. Unlike training validation, you can set the temperature. The repository’s launcher runs evaluations back to back, because the default quota allows one evaluation job at a time (you can request an increase):
Each 128-word evaluation took four to seven minutes. Reasoning effort comes from the agent’s environment variables, so to change it you edit REASONING_EFFORT, redeploy, and evaluate. We evaluated both models at low and medium effort and at temperature 0 and 1.0:
The gray segment of each bar is the base model and the blue segment is the gain from training. The low-effort, temperature-0 pair is the training job’s validation at steps 0 and 100. The medium-effort, temperature-1.0 trained result is the mean of two runs (80 and 88 percent).
At temperature 0, both models often end the game without a solve, at either effort. With sampling on, medium effort adds 15 points for the trained model and 46 for the base model. The adapter adds 14–54 points in every setting, so what training taught transfers across settings.
The training job’s own validation curve in MLflow told a different story: it peaked at 48 percent at step 90 and ended at 37 percent, scored at temperature 0. The hyperparameters reference recommends temperature 0 for evaluation because greedy decoding makes curves deterministic and comparable across runs. We report temperature 1.0 because that’s how we serve the model. At medium effort and temperature 1.0, the trained model solves 84 percent of held-out words, up from 61 percent for the base model.
Tip: Evaluate at the settings you will serve at. The training curve says this adapter ends at 37 percent. At serving settings it solves 84 percent. The evaluation jobs that show this cost about $1.20 in tokens and took about an hour.
Step 8: Clean up
Training and evaluation jobs stop billing when they complete, but the AgentCore runtime, its IAM role, the MLflow app, and the S3 objects persist. From the project directory:
Because agentcore remove all rewrites the files under agentcore/, run git checkout -- agentcore/ if you want to redeploy later. Deleting the AgentCore-Wordle-default CloudFormation stack removes the same resources and leaves the files alone. The training job role and the model packages are not billed.
Deep dive: Designing the reward
Our reward needed one revision, and the mistake is a common one.
The first design summed the per-guess scoring from the wordle-lora-rl project over the whole game. That scoring works there because each guess is an independent training sample. Summed into one reward per game, it produced two inversions we found only by reading traces:
- A lost game paid positive reward. Six turns of bonuses added up to about +0.49.
- Solving on turn 1 scored below solving on turn 3. A first-guess solve earned +0.99 and a third-guess solve earned +1.61, because the extra turns collected more bonuses.
The fix separates a dominant outcome term from a small, bounded shaping term:
The outcome term is set entirely by how the game ended:
| Outcome | Value | 
| Solved on guess n | 1.05 + 0.5 * (6 – n) / 5, so 1.55 on guess 1 down to 1.05 on guess 6 | 
| Played all six guesses, unsolved | -0.5 | 
| Never made a valid guess | -1.5 | 
The shaping term is that per-guess scoring, summed over the game:
- Penalties for contradicting a known green, yellow, or gray letter, for repeating a guess, and for words outside the dictionary.
- An entropy bonus for a strong opening word.
- Bonuses for trying new letters and for shrinking the set of remaining possibilities.
The sum is clipped to [-1, 1] and scaled by 0.04 for a solve and 0.15 for a loss, so it separates games with the same outcome but never moves a game into another tier. With typical shaping values:
| Scenario | Reward | 
| Solve on guess 1 | +1.550 | 
| Solve on guess 3 | +1.375 | 
| Solve on guess 6 | +1.069 | 
| Lost after six guesses | -0.427 | 
| Never made a valid guess | -1.500 | 
A faster solve now always beats a slower one, every solve beats every loss, and never playing is the worst outcome. Our first fix used a single weight of 0.15, which let a guess-3 solve with full shaping (+1.45) outscore a guess-2 solve with the minimum (+1.25). Adjacent guess counts are 0.1 apart, so a smaller solve weight of 0.04 removes the overlap, and the worst solve (+1.01) still clears the 1.0 success threshold. Shaping still matters because GRPO learns from reward variance within a group, so two lost games that differ in clue consistency still teach the model something. As the SageMaker AI documentation advises, start with an outcome-based reward, add shaping sparingly, and check the reward on real trajectories.
Deep dive: What went wrong, in the order you will hit it
Each of these cost at least one training run.
- Bearer tokens under concurrency. Minting a token with a fresh botocore session per call starved the credential provider at 32 concurrent rollouts, and caching tokens for an hour returned 403 errors as credentials rotated. The fix is one self-refreshing session, a short cache, and a re-sign on 403.
- A rollout that never reaches the policy model fails the whole job. When every model call in a rollout failed authentication, the service ended the job with “No sampling requests were received.” Returning an error status fails it too, so always return a reward. A game where the model is sampled but never makes a valid guess is fine: it scores -1.5, and the 100-step run had 51 of them in about 105,000 rollouts.
- Tool calls drift into plain text. At too high a learning rate, the model wrote tool calls as text, every rollout got the same floor reward, and the gradient vanished. The agent now recovers guesses from raw text with a small formatting penalty.
- The plateau. Training reward stopped rising after about step 15 and validation stopped improving after about step 30, though at temperature 0 validation understates the model (Step 7). A curriculum that seeds games with prior guesses, or more rollouts per word than the default group_size of 8, is what we would try next.
Conclusion
MTRL on SageMaker AI trains a model on the outcome of a whole episode. That fits agentic tasks, where the right trajectory is unknown and only the result can be scored. We used a single episode-level reward. When intermediate steps can be scored too, MTRL also accepts one reward per turn through the UpdateReward API. In this post, an open-weight 20B model reached an 84 percent solve rate at serving settings, up from 61 percent, for about $339 in training tokens and about $79 in AgentCore runtime usage. The 37 percent the training curve reports is an artifact of how the training job scores validation, so evaluate at the settings you will serve at.
The same pipeline applies to internal procedures, tools, and workflows that public models were never trained on.
To get started, clone the sample repository, follow the preceding steps, and run the smoke test in Step 3 before committing GPU time. For the underlying APIs, see the SageMaker AI MTRL documentation.

articles.title: ICEYE strengthens Ukraine’s satellite communications ambitions while expanding wildfire monitoring capabilities | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Finnish SpaceTech unicorn ICEYE has announced two new partnerships aimed at expanding its satellite intelligence capabilities across defence and environmental monitoring.
The company signed a Letter of Intent alongside Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore sovereign satellite communications, while also announcing a collaboration with German startup OroraTech to develop an integrated wildfire intelligence solution.
This follows a period of notable growth for the Espoo-based scale-up. In June 2026, ICEYE secured €450 million in primary Series F funding, valuing the company at more than €10 billion, with a further €300 million revolving credit facility secured in May.
This funding activity can be placed alongside adjacent 2026 European SpaceTech funding announcements, including €51 million for Luxembourg and US-based Hydrosat to expand thermal satellite intelligence, €34 million for the UK’s SatVu to scale its thermal observation constellation, and €61 million for Switzerland’s SWISSto12 to develop satellite and communications infrastructure.
In Finland, Helsinki-based Kelluu also raised €15 million to expand its autonomous aerial intelligence capabilities.
Together with funding for France’s UNIVITY (€27 million) and Germany’s AIRMO (€5 million), these 2026 rounds account for approximately €643 million in the general SpaceTech sector, including ICEYE’s primary financing.
Founded in 2014 by Rafal Modrzewski and Pekka Laurila, ICEYE specialises in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite technology, providing Earth observation data and intelligence to governments, defence organisations, insurers and emergency management agencies.
The company originated from research at Aalto University and launched its first SAR satellite in 2018, becoming an early pioneer in miniaturised radar satellites.
The first of the two announcements centres on a Letter of Intent signed by ICEYE, Nokia and Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence to explore cooperation on secure satellite communications. Announced during the Finnish Prime Minister’s visit to Ukraine, the initiative aims to strengthen the country’s defence capabilities by developing communications infrastructure that Ukraine can independently own and control.
The agreement builds on an earlier partnership between ICEYE and Nokia, announced on October 1st 2026, to develop secure, high-performance broadband communications systems using low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites. Designed for governments, these systems would support defence, border security, emergency services and disaster response, while giving participating countries control over their satellites, ground infrastructure and terminals.
Rafal Modrzewski, CEO and Co-founder of ICEYE, said: “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls. We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today.”
ICEYE has supported Ukraine with satellite intelligence since 2022, making the proposed communications collaboration a potential extension of an existing relationship. The latest agreement remains exploratory, with no deployment timetable or financial commitments disclosed.
Alongside its defence-related developments, ICEYE has also partnered with Munich-based OroraTech to expand its wildfire intelligence services. The collaboration will combine OroraTech’s thermal satellite data with ICEYE’s SAR observations, creating a platform intended to help organisations monitor wildfires from their earliest stages through to damage assessment and recovery.
Founded in 2018 by Thomas Grübler, Rupert Amann, Florian Mauracher and Björn Stoffers, OroraTech develops space-based thermal intelligence for wildfire detection and monitoring. The startup has expanded its satellite network and provides information to governments and organisations managing wildfire risks worldwide.
As per our coverage, OroraTech secured a €37 million Series B extension in 2025.
Until now, ICEYE’s wildfire intelligence capabilities have primarily focused on assessing building-level damage during active fires. By incorporating OroraTech’s thermal observations, the company aims to extend its services to include identifying initial hotspots, tracking fire progression and assessing threats to communities and critical infrastructure.
The combination brings together two complementary technologies. OroraTech’s thermal satellites can detect heat anomalies and monitor active fires, while ICEYE’s SAR satellites can capture observations through clouds, smoke and darkness, helping assess damage to buildings and infrastructure even while a wildfire is ongoing.
Dr. Ignacio Zuleta, Chief Technology and Product Officer at OroraTech, commented: “Our thermal satellite intelligence provides that critical visibility from the earliest stages of an event, detecting hotspots and tracking fire activity as it develops. By bringing that intelligence together with ICEYE’s SAR capabilities, we can help decision-makers maintain a more continuous understanding of a wildfire, from first detection through its impact on communities, infrastructure and the surrounding environment.”
The integrated solution targets several sectors, including government emergency management, utilities and insurance. Emergency services could use the intelligence to inform evacuations and coordinate firefighting resources, while energy providers could monitor threats to electricity networks and other infrastructure. Insurers could also use the data to identify exposed properties, assess damage and prioritise claims.
According to ICEYE, the technology could help accelerate disaster response by providing more timely information on wildfire progression and its consequences. The company says its integrated approach could support damage assessments for disaster declarations within 24 hours, compared with processes that can otherwise take weeks.
Taken together, the two announcements are one of many examples of how ICEYE is expanding its satellite capabilities beyond Earth observation imagery into a broader range of intelligence and communications services.

articles.title: Government of Canada unveils proposed stablecoin regulations |
articles.text:
Canada has released a list of proposed regulations that will govern how stablecoins are used—bringing the country’s Stablecoin Act (SCA) one step closer to coming into force.
The news: The proposed regulations were published on Friday in the Canada Gazette, an online portal maintained by the Canadian government that publishes public notices, official appointments, and proposed regulations prior to them becoming law. The regulations are subject to a 60-day consultation period.
From the source: “This guidance should give the industry more certainty and stronger protections for payment use cases. At the same time, most issuers and platforms will still need to navigate both regimes with the Bank of Canada and the Canadian Securities Commission. This will create a burden to manage extra compliance work to be compliant with the current framework,” said Koleya Karringten, executive director of the Canadian Bitcoin Consortium, adding that joint guidance from both oversight bodies would benefit SCA-approved issuers looking for clarity on trading and listing requirements and exemption status for provincially regulated issuers.
RELATED: Stablecoins will eventually “leapfrog” real-time rail payments, finance leaders say
The context: Stablecoins are digital assets designed to hold steady value, and are usually one-to-one pegged to fiat currencies like the US or Canadian dollar. Canada’s SCA dates back to March when legislation to create the act first received royal assent. The regulatory framework is designed to govern stablecoins in Canada that have interprovincial or international applications and sets federal oversight of the digital currencies through the Bank of Canada.
Proposed regulations include requirements around reserve assets for issuers and where those assets can be held, as well as prohibitions on marketing stablecoins as legal tender, bank deposits, or publicly insured products, and from paying interest to holders.
The SCA will also enable the finance minister to assess stablecoin applicants for national security risks, and will establish enforcement powers for the Bank of Canada. The proposed regulations note that as digital assets are “rapidly evolving,” the act is designed to allow the Bank’s governor to make further regulations. A full description of the proposals can be found here.
Final thought: The global stablecoin supply is currently valued at more than $380 billion, and according to Visa, there has been more than $14 trillion in stablecoin transaction volume over the last year. But most of those stablecoins globally are currently pegged to the US dollar; Canada’s first CAD-backed stablecoin launched earlier this year. 
Feature image courtesy Wikimedia Commons under license CC BY-SA 3.0.

articles.title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
articles.text:
The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
Plus: Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises
Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?
In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
—Jessica Hamzelou
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science.
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
Help choose our next Roundtables topic
Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about?
Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs
Warhound says the dogs will detect explosives and protect troops. (Wired $)
+ It’s raised $200 million from investors, including Sequoia. (TechCrunch)
+ Colossal Biosciences will help clone and gene-edit the dogs. (Bloomberg $)
+ The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Donald Trump says Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s Starlink access
But Zelensky says Starlink speeds remained capped. (Reuters $)
+ Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift the speed limits. (WSJ $)
3 The newly disclosed PHP flaw is yet to yield successful attacks
Experts say the vulnerabilities are harder to exploit than expected. (NBC News)
+ Officials urged patches after the flaws forced websites offline worldwide. (BBC)
+ But publicly disclosed fixes can help hackers. (The Economist $)
4 Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death by 42%
The vaccine reduced melanoma patients’ risk of recurrence. (Ars Technica)
+ Federal health agencies are abandoning mRNA. (MIT Technology Review)
5 A powerful new gene editor has reached its first human patient
The prime editing technique rewrites DNA in liver cells. (Nature)
+ Companies are planning gene-edited babies. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Google will pay customers to free up power for data centers
Its virtual power plant will reward people for adjusting energy usage. (NYT $)
+ It’s also illegally felled 250,000 trees in Finland for a data center. (Guardian)

articles.title: What some of Anthropic’s backers are worth before its IPO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic’s public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company’s latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions.
Coatue, which first backed Anthropic in 2025 at a $183 billion valuation and co-led the AI lab’s last two funding rounds, has poured a total of $4.75 billion into the company. That stake, based on the last round’s price, is now worth roughly $7.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Coatue declined to comment.
Below is what some other backers of Anthropic are worth based on the last round’s price, according to Bloomberg:
Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic’s Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.
Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.
Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic’s Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.
Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.
Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in Anthropic’s 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into the company, resulting in a stake that’s worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm.)
Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than ninetyfold to $7 billion.
Updated to include Coatue’s returns.

articles.title: Everybody panic: A Valve developer said "HLX" in public
articles.text:
Gamers still hoping against hope for a true follow-up to Half-Life 2 (after so, so many years) may remember last year’s flurry of speculation that Half-Life 3 was finally nearing completion. Amid all those rumors, though, we never got any official sign from anyone inside Valve that a Half-Life project was currently in development.
That changed this week thanks to an apparent slip-up during a panel at GameSoundCon, an industry conference devoted to “the art, technology, and business of game audio.” In a panel devoted to Valve’s use of open audio engines (captured in this Vimeo clip), Valve composer and audio artist Mike Morasky let an interesting string of three letters slip while talking about the way the company implements high dynamic range (HDR) audio:
Our HDR system is basically that’s one of the three pieces that come together to make an HDR that you can easily optimize. And in fact, I think Deadlock has their own version of HDR. HLX has its own version, so on and so forth [emphasis added].
“HLX,” of course, has been widely reported as the internal code name for Valve’s next Half-Life project. The codename has shown up in Valve engine code since at least 2024, but it has never been referenced in public by a Valve employee until now (though Morasky was responsible for a close call in an interview last year).

articles.title: CyberCartel hacking gang used Claude and Grok AI agents to automate attacks on Latin American institutions — passwords and details stolen from over 400 institutions, including banks and payment apps
articles.text:
CyberCartel hacking gang used Claude and Grok AI agents to automate attacks on Latin American institutions — passwords and details stolen from over 400 institutions, including banks and payment apps
AI agents have been used to attack more than 400 institutions by a group called CyberCartel.
CyberCartel, a hacking group with a long history of targeting Latin American businesses, has been using AI agents, including SpaceX's Grok and Anthropic's Claude, to automate attacks on financial institutions such as banks and mobile payment apps. Passwords and customer data have been stolen, while individuals' bank accounts have also been accessed with little input from criminals in the latest example of criminals turning to AI-powered cyberattacks. That research comes from a cybersecurity startup called Straiker, with its findings shared by The Information.
While CyberCartel has been an active threat since at least 2012, its new leveraging of the power of AI has leveled up its attacks in recent months. Now, the research shows that the group can attack more businesses at a speed previously not possible when using human-powered hacks. Straiker shared its research with both SpaceX and Anthropic, and both firms are working to lock CyberCartel out of their services. The latter has already been able to block access to Claude. Chinese lab Moonshot AI's agent has also been used by the hacking group, but Straiker is still trying to get in touch with the company.
While it's true that AI models normally have protections in place to prevent them from being used to carry out cyberattacks, they've proven surprisingly easy to bypass. In this case, CyberCartel reportedly simply told the models that they were being used in test environments. If one model refused to proceed, the hackers used a different model. If that also refused, the AI agents would be tasked with deploying malware instead.
Notably, CyberCartel doesn't appear to be using Anthropic's Mythos for its recent attacks. The company caused a stir earlier this year when it announced the new model, warning that hackers could use it and models like it for attacks like those carried out by CyberCartel. Its release also saw security teams around the globe rush to address thousands of vulnerabilities that the model had identified.
This is far from the first time that Anthropic has been faced with the news that its AI is being used by bad actors. The company shared details of its AI being used to carry out a cyberattack in November 2025. Later, Claude was used to break the security of OpenAI, an Anthropic competitor in the AI space. That hack was carried out by researchers rather than criminals, at least.
Raiker's research on AI-powered attacks on Latin American financial institutions comes just days after news broke that South Korean authorities are investigating a similar issue affecting local banks. Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank are among the South Korean banks affected, with at least 25,000 Shinhan Bank customers having their personal credit information leaked.
AI companies are well aware of the risks their products pose. Nvidia, the graphics card company that now focuses on producing hardware for AI data centers, recently launched the Open Agent Safety Platform. The software platform and reference system design were developed to secure rogue AI agents via a new hardware and software security stack. It's hoped that it will go some way toward preventing agents from escaping their sandboxes, executing unauthorized code, gaining unauthorized access to critical infrastructure, or bypassing guardrails.
