articles.title: Milan’s Phononic Vibes secures €25 million to expand noise control tech used by Deutsche Bahn and Mercedes-Benz | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Phononic Vibes, a Milan-based noise management company that designs and manufactures noise and vibration products for rail, energy, industry, construction and mobility, has secured a €25 million financing round. The company has also launched its new identity and website today.
The round was led by Jolt Capital, a Paris-based private equity firm specialising in DeepTech growth companies, through Jolt Capital V, a fund targeting €1 billion and nearing final close. Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital SGR, and Simest SpA also participated in this round. The transaction includes the acquisition of 360 Capital’s stake, which it has held since the company’s Seed round. In 2020, the company announced the closing of a €2.3 million funding round.
Andrea Traversone, Managing Partner at Jolt Capital, said, “Noise control is reaching a turning point. Conventional products have hit their physical limit, and infrastructure needs quieter assets with less weight and space. Phononic Vibes is a company combining breakthrough science, a patented design engine and manufacturing at scale. We are excited to back the team in building a global leader in noise and vibration control. This is Jolt Capital V’s first investment in Italy, a country with an increasingly dynamic and vibrant deeptech ecosystem.”
Founded in 2018 by Luca D’Alessandro, Giovanni Capellari, and Stefano Caverni as a spin-off of Politecnico di Milano, the company manufactures in Italy and leads a group of established European manufacturers, including Matis, founded in 1979.
The company designs and manufactures noise and vibration products that do the same job with less material. According to the company, every noise barrier, enclosure, and silencer on the market obeys the mass law: more quiet means more material. Phononic Vibes claims to break it.
It designs metamaterials, structures whose shape does the work mass used to do. Its products weigh up to 30% less while delivering the same acoustic performance, or they perform better at the same weight.
At the core of the company is a proprietary design engine, protected by 18 patent families. “It turns the physics of metamaterials into certified products, drawing on application libraries that grow with every project, so each new market starts from proven designs rather than a blank sheet,” the company mentioned in the press release
The company highlighted that Deutsche Bahn certified its transparent noise barrier for the German rail network, the first see-through panel it rates as highly absorbing. Phononic Vibes. It also reports that Mercedes-Benz uses its technology in series production, which the company says is the first metamaterial in a series-production car. Contractors such as Webuild and Eteria choose its barriers because they install faster. Its revenue has doubled every year since 2018, reaching break-even in 2025.
Luca D’Alessandro, CEO and co-founder of Phononic Vibes, said, “Weight has always been the price of quiet. We have shown it is a design choice, with two of Europe’s most demanding customers. With Jolt Capital by our side in this new chapter, and the continued support of our existing investors Eureka! Venture SGR, CDP Venture Capital and Simest, we can accelerate our international growth, expand into new applications and make lighter noise control the standard across data centres, rail, energy and industry. I would also like to thank 360 Capital for believing in us from the early days, when we were still working at the desks of Politecnico di Milano, and for being part of the journey that brought us here.”
The company plans to use this capital to scale its proprietary design engine internationally, expand its technology into new applications and strengthen its delivery capabilities. Phononic Vibes also notes that targeted acquisitions will complement this strategy by extending the reach of its technology and bringing additional industrial capabilities to the group.

articles.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
articles.text:
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
A reporter’s unsettling takeaway from You Can See Everything.
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.
Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.
Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.
As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?
I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?
But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?
One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.
Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.
At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?
I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.
But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!
This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

articles.title: ‘Clayface’ es una pasable película de terror que no aporta nada al Universo DC
articles.text:
Clayface es una película de terror a toda regla. Y una, que hace un especial buen uso del body horror en los momentos correctos. No obstante, poco o nada tiene que ver con el Universo DC en construcción y ese es su gran problema. De hecho, esta película (basada en el clásico personaje con guion de Mike Flanagan) fácilmente podría ser solo una pequeña obra de autor del género. No en vano, su director, James Watkins, crea algunas secuencias escalofriantes y ciertamente deslumbrantes, que combinan efectos prácticos con digitales. A la vez, trabaja en una atmósfera cuidadosa y bien lograda, que profundiza en la oscura psicología de su personaje.
Pero el problema radica en que Clayface no se parece ni en tono ni en forma al resto del universo al que pertenece. Por lo que, a pesar de ser inquietante, repugnante y, a grandes rasgos, terrorífica, peca de genérica. Y lo es, porque el Tom Haggen de Tom Rhys Harries podría ser cualquier personaje atormentado de la reciente ola de terror gore. Mucho más, analizar los rigores del fracaso, el dolor y el miedo desde la popular perspectiva del terror elevado. Solo que la película se queda a medias en integrar todas esas evidentes bondades en la historia de origen de un villano comiquero. Uno además, cuyo enemigo tradicional es Batman.
Pero de esa conexión, hay poco o nada en toda la trama. Mientras Matt Hagen se convierte lentamente en un monstruo, en escenas a mayor gloria de Cronenberg, la cinta pierde la personalidad. En específico, porque la trama parece carecer de objetivo al narrar este relato tortuoso de caída a los infiernos, a la que parece faltarle una pieza. Más preocupante todavía, toda la película parece desvinculada, sin la menor línea de unión con Superman, o en cualquier caso, The Batman. Incluso, parece desligada por completo de la terrenal Linternas, con la que podría compartir tono y subtexto tétrico. Pero tampoco lo hace.
‘Clayface’, un villano trágico
El punto más alto de la cinta es, sin duda, el propio Matt Hagen. En particular, porque el personaje es interpretado con el tono de un villano cada vez más retorcido por Tom Rhys Harries. El actor logra captar la caída en desgracia de la maligna figura, sin exagerar ni llegar a la caricaturización. Más interesante todavía, logra hacer creíble su desplome. De ser una estrella naciente que sobrevive al mítico The Narrows de Gotham City, Matt se transforma progresivamente en una criatura fatídica. Y la cinta sigue esa transformación paso a paso, recreándose en la forma como el rostro y el cuerpo del personaje se convierten en territorio de pesadilla.
Lo más desconcertante de la cinta es que el contraste entre el antes y el después de Matt ocurre casi de manera súbita. Durante los primeros 15 minutos de la película, el personaje triunfa y se convierte en una luminaria. Solo para terminar siendo destrozado por el mafioso Markus Szabo (David Dencik), en un ajuste de cuentas motivado por celos. La película no se esfuerza en mostrar esa ruptura, sino que directamente Matt encuentra la tragedia en una escena sin mayor trascendencia. Y es parte de esa incapacidad para profundizar lo que juega en contra de Clayface como premisa.
En específico, porque no logra que la tragedia que envuelve a Matt resulte de verdadero interés. Todo por el simple motivo de que el guion no indaga en su personaje como para que resulte interesante o al menos cercano. En lugar de eso, la rápida transición entre ser estrella reconocida a figura desfigurada en una cama sabe a poco e importa menos. Mucho más, cuando la película utilizará todo el tiempo restante en construir una historia de horror a través del dolor de Matt. Pero no emocional. Tampoco en la forma astuta en que la sustancia jugó con el miedo a envejecer de sus personajes para hacer el terror incómodo.
En lugar de eso, Clayface pasa demasiado tiempo indagando en la maldad inherente al ser humano, sin otro motivo que el horror de Matt al perderlo todo. El guion muestra la degradación rápida del villano en una serie de pasos hacia el horror de la humillación. Matt pierde el empleo, termina en una habitación repleta de cucarachas, pero no hace lo mismo por su psiquis. Por lo que pasa muy por encima de lo que puede hacer semejante situación en la mente de cualquiera. Un error que le costará caro a la película cuando exija entender cada decisión cuando Matt intente recuperar lo perdido como sea.
Un error que costará caro a un villano de Gotham
Todo se vuelve peor cuando Matt parece dar con la solución a sus dilemas. Lo que implica ponerse en manos de la doctora Catelyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) y su cuestionable terapia celular. La película resuelve mal y de manera simple la decisión de Corr de ayudar y, de inmediato, Matt parece recuperar su rostro. Solo que, en realidad, la fórmula de la doctora termina por tener un efecto atroz. Uno que convierte el rostro de Matt en una máscara que se derrite y se deforma de manera aleatoria. Mucho peor, transforma su cuerpo en una sustancia maleable que cambia según sus emociones y, en última instancia, su horror.
Hasta este punto, Clayface logra sostener todo su vigor en la sensación de que todo lo que rodea a Matt empeorará a no tardar. ¿Qué es exactamente lo que ocurre cuando el personaje decide comenzar una travesía de venganza? Cada vez más repugnante, asquerosa y arriesgada, Clayface parece encontrar su punto más alto pronto. La de mostrar todas las habilidades de Matt, todo lo que su cuerpo retorcido y su rostro terrorífico es capaz de hacer. Mucho más, la promesa de que este monstruo furioso llegará pronto a un punto de no retorno que arrasará con Gotham por completo.
Pero en realidad, no ocurre nada de eso. Salvo tres o cuatro escenas realmente espectaculares, la cinta peca de genérica y de depender demasiado del impacto frontal. De resto, la batalla por la venganza se vuelve confusa porque la cinta nunca aclara del todo si Matt, en medio de su orgía de sangre, enloqueció. O que en realidad, toda su furia es una metáfora latente del mal en toda su extensión. Por lo que el argumento carece de toda profundidad, flota en mitad de escenas impactantes y, al final, naufraga en intrascendencia.
Dos películas en una en ‘Clayface’
Para su último tramo, Clayface parece dos películas en una. Por un lado, una mezcla audaz, pero deficiente y menor de La Mosca, La sustancia e incluso la saga Saw. De esta última, hereda su tono sucio, truculento y cada vez más sangriento. Por el otro, la historia de origen de uno de los exóticos personajes de Gotham, prácticamente la única referencia de la cinta al universo de Batman.
Ese lado caricaturesco y un poco menos retorcido es justamente el lado más flojo de la cinta. Sobre todo porque, al no haber conexiones con el universo DC, pareciera que la relación es solo incidental. Clayface pudiera ser la historia del archienemigo de Batman o solo la de un hombre cualquiera aterrorizado por su destino. Y esa falta de impulso, objetivo e identidad es justamente el elemento más genérico y poco atractivo de la película. Un giro lamentable para una película que más de una vez muestra todo lo que podía dar y se queda a medias.

articles.title: AWS Introduces Lambda Web Functions for Node.js Applications
articles.text:
AWS recently introduced Lambda Web Functions, allowing developers to run Node.js web applications using frameworks such as Express and Hono directly on Lambda, with support for concurrent requests and response streaming.
According to the Lambda Web Functions documentation, the new functions support concurrent HTTP requests and response streaming. They charge for active CPU time and memory, rather than CPU time spent waiting for downstream services. Multi-Region routing directs requests to the closest Region, while a single warm execution environment can handle multiple concurrent requests, significantly reducing cold starts. Existing Lambda functions are now called Lambda Event Functions, with no changes required. Micah Walter, senior solutions architect at AWS, summarizes the benefits and why it removes this complexity:
You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.
Endpoints use a Lambda-provided domain by default. To use a custom domain, edge caching, or AWS WAF, developers can use Amazon CloudFront in front, relying on Lambda Web Functions as the origin.
Lambda Web Functions target HTTP workloads, including full-stack web applications, REST and GraphQL APIs, and independently scaling microservices. They also support server-side rendering and streaming responses, such as incremental output from large language models, without requiring a separate hosting layer.
Lambda Web Functions currently support only Node.js; other languages, including Python, Java, and .NET, remain available through traditional Lambda functions. Earlier this year, AWS also launched Lambda MicroVMs, which provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments for running untrusted or user-generated code, with customer-managed lifecycles.
In their article "Exploring AWS Lambda Web Functions for Building Web Applications", Julian Wood, Kim Wendt, and Samrat Karak build a sample application to show how one execution environment handles many requests at once and how the application serves users globally. They summarize:
Lambda Web Functions bring the serverless operating model to web applications without adapter layers. You write a standard Node.js HTTP server, deploy it with one command or CloudFormation, and get a scalable, pay-per-use HTTPS endpoint with global routing built in.
Community reactions on Reddit and Hacker News have been largely positive, highlighting the simpler programming model and support for concurrent requests. However, discussions also raise questions about Python support and how the service differs from existing alternatives. User magnetik79 comments:
This is a big one - and nice to see something not entirely honed in AI. ☺️ What looks great: Many workloads can now skip API Gateway entirely (...) this totally changes the current Lambda HTTP programming model - now you're no longer working with one invoke/one request - now you might need to be sync/mutex aware.
In his article "Why I'm Excited About AWS Lambda Web Functions," Eric Johnson, principal developer advocate at AWS, highlights how Lambda Web Functions run standard HTTP servers and frameworks without modification, supporting REST, server-sent events, streaming responses, RPC, webhooks, and IAM authentication through a single managed endpoint.
AWS is not the only cloud provider offering this model: Google Cloud Run and Azure Container Apps also support web applications without adapter layers, scale-to-zero, and configurable concurrency, making them suitable for workloads with intermittent or bursty traffic.
Pricing for Lambda Web Functions is based on active CPU time and memory usage, potentially reducing costs for workloads that spend time waiting on databases or APIs. Memory is billed for the lifetime of the execution environment. This model may benefit I/O-heavy workloads, such as server-side rendering, API backends, and streaming AI inference. The service is currently available in five regions: Northern Virginia, Ohio, Oregon, Tokyo, and Ireland.

articles.title: 'Daddy's girl': Millicent Okumu’s road back to agriculture
articles.text:
Millicent Okumu doesn’t leave you wondering whether she believes what she is saying. She speaks with energy, with clarity about whom she is building for. Ask where the company is heading, and there is little hesitation; ask whether she will still be running it in ten years, and the answer is no.
By then, she expects Agriflex, the Kenyan agricultural business she co-founded, to be operating in at least five African countries, to be sustainably profitable, and to be led by somebody else. She might take an advisory role. For now, however, the company occupies even the hours she supposedly spends away from it. At family gatherings, unfinished tasks follow her into the room.
Her father, a civil servant and farmer, raised cattle and grew enough food to support relatives beyond his household. She was close to him, but less enthusiastic about the farm. She avoided agriculture at school and university, only to find herself back in it through a logistics job at iProcure in 2017.
Now she sells farm inputs, deploys spraying drones and listens to farmers explain why a clever piece of technology might be of little use to them. That last part has meant slowing down plans and turning away investors.
“We are in 2026,” she says. “We are no longer in 2006.”
She is impatient for progress, but increasingly particular about what counts as progress, and who benefits.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
If I had met you at ten years old and asked what you wanted to become, what would you have said? Would that girl recognise the woman sitting here today?
I wouldn’t have known exactly what I wanted to become, but I was already very determined and ambitious.
I was a daddy’s girl, always following my father around and taking an interest in whatever he was doing. Even when he was discussing serious matters, I wanted to be there. Although I wasn’t the firstborn, I was often the person he delegated tasks to.
I couldn’t have told you that I would end up doing what I do today, but I knew I would be powerful in one way or another.
What did money look like in the home you grew up in? Was it something people discussed openly, worried about quietly, or expected you to go out and find?
Money wasn’t something we discussed openly, but we didn’t have to go out looking for it either. My father was a civil servant who also loved farming. There was enough to take care of us.
That changed when he died, just after I had finished Form Four. Suddenly, I had to go out and find money. I started working at a young age and figuring out how to take care of everybody, including myself.
Money then became something we discussed openly because we had to work out how to make do with the little I was earning.
Your background is in logistics and supply chains. What happened that made agriculture personal enough for you to build a business around it?
Agriculture had always been part of my life. My father had a lot of cattle and land, and farming fed our family, our extended family and even other people in the village.
He was particular about getting certified seeds. He would bring them from Kisumu or travel to Homa Bay town to buy them. We all went to the farm, although I was the one who wasn’t particularly keen on it. My father knew that, but he also recognised that I had other strengths.
In high school, I avoided agriculture. At university, I avoided it again. Then, in 2017, agriculture came calling.
I had been working in logistics when iProcure approached me. The company had raised funding and needed someone to set up its logistics department. I joined in October 2017, and that changed everything.
The work exposed me to so much, and I grew to love it. By the time I decided to leave, I knew I wanted to continue working in agriculture.
Take me back to the first farmer you tried to persuade to work with Agriflex. What did they ask that your business plan hadn’t prepared you for?
To be honest, recruiting farmers and agro-dealers wasn’t particularly difficult because of the relationships we had built at iProcure. People knew us and understood what we could do for them.
But one farmer asked a question that stayed with us: “Millicent and Isaac, you know we need inputs, and you are giving us access to them and advice. But what happens after that?”
Isaac is my co-founder and handles commercial activities and operations. What the farmer was asking us about was the market for their produce. We were supporting production, but the challenges didn’t end there.
That made us think about how we could help farmers find buyers. We now have a plan to support some of them with that. We don’t want to help them through production and then leave them hanging, even as we continue rolling out other parts of the business.
You work with drones and traceability tools. How do you explain what you do to a relative who interrupts halfway through and asks, “But Millicent, what exactly do you sell?”
I start with what is easiest to understand: I sell seeds to farmers and agro-dealers. I also sell crop-protection products, including agrochemicals and foliar feeds. Those are things people recognise and use, even back at home.
Then I explain that we are helping farmers move away from manually spraying their farms. With a drone, we can spray an acre in a minute. Instead of using 100 litres of water per acre, we can use about 10 litres.
We are making the work easier, reducing the time farmers spend on these tasks and helping them farm more efficiently. We are in 2026. We are no longer in 2006.
Tell me about a time a farmer looked at something you were proud of and effectively said, “That is clever, but it won’t work here.” What did you do next?
That happened with the technology side of the business. Agriflex is technology-enabled, and we have been thinking carefully about how technology can complement our work and improve what we offer farmers.
Initially, we wanted to launch a mobile app with several features, including disease detection and recommendations on which inputs to use.
But when you go out to the farms, you encounter practical problems. The internet connection is poor, or there is no network at all. Many farmers also already recognise the common pests and diseases affecting the crops they grow regularly, such as maize and beans.
They told us: “If this is what your app will do, it won’t solve my immediate problem.”
What they wanted was access to basic, practical information about farming without having to wait for us to organise a training session or demonstration. They were already using WhatsApp. Could we make the information they needed accessible? Could we start there, register them and then build on that relationship?
That feedback made us slow down. We had wanted to introduce the technology immediately, but we listened to farmers and agro-dealers and only rolled it out this year.
It also meant saying no to some investors who wanted technology to be the priority. The feedback from the field was telling us something different, and we decided to follow that.
Who pays Agriflex, and for what? Where does the farmer’s gain end and your margin begin?
Two groups pay us: agro-dealers and farmers. A large proportion of our revenue comes from agro-dealers, whom we supply in bulk.
We want to reach as many smallholder farmers as possible, but we cannot reach all of them directly. Working through agro-dealers allows us to serve more farmers through businesses they already buy from.
Farmers can also walk into our two outlets, in Molo and Ol Kalou, and buy directly from us. Currently, they pay for inputs and drone services. We also introduced soil testing about a month ago.
We negotiate better trading terms with manufacturers, which allows us to offer affordable prices to farmers and agro-dealers while earning a margin.
Trust, reliability and affordability have been very important to us. Agro-dealers need to know that we will supply them reliably, and both they and the farmers need prices that work for them.
What is the most expensive assumption you have made in this business, and how long did it take you to admit it was wrong?
There was a project we took on early in the business that looked very lucrative. On paper, everything suggested it would work. Based on the information we had received and the assumptions we had made, it looked like a good opportunity.
But it didn’t work out as we expected.
It took us three months to agree that we needed to stop. We had to accept that it wasn’t working, cut it off and move on.
When people talk about empowering women farmers, the language can become very polished. Tell me about one woman whose experience forced you to change how Agriflex operates.
There is a woman farmer with about 50 acres that she plants every season. We were supplying her with inputs, but spending time on her farm showed us how much more support she needed.
Spraying even 20 acres involved several workers over several days. She had to be there supervising, and there was a 2,000-litre water tank on the farm. After all that work, the costs were still very high.
It made us ask what the support offered through empowerment programmes actually changes. Does it reduce the time a woman spends on the farm? Does it reduce the resources she has to put into it?
With the drone, we completed the spraying in about 30 minutes.
That experience made us pause and rethink our priorities. Instead of concentrating only on recruiting more customers, we needed to look more closely at how we supported the ones we already had. That applies to our agro-dealers too.
We have also supported her with finding a market for her produce, even though that is not the core of our business.
For me, empowerment means making someone’s life easier in ways they can actually see and experience.
Have you ever walked into a meeting and realised you would have to prove yourself before anyone would discuss your business? How did you handle the room?
Yes. Sometimes people say: “When you said you were Millicent, and we heard what you were doing, we expected someone older and bigger.”
They knew they were meeting a woman, but I still didn’t look like the person they had imagined. Then comes the question: why should they trust that I understand what I am doing?
What has worked for me is knowing my business inside out. I need to understand every aspect of it, including the numbers.
I also draw on my experience. I have done this work before, and I am proud of what I achieved. I am not going into it blindly. I have a blueprint and some understanding of what will work and what won’t.
When you can explain that clearly, people begin to listen. How you carry yourself into the room matters too. They may have arrived with assumptions, but you can give them reasons to reconsider.
What has been your closest encounter with giving up? What happened, who did you call, and what made you return the next morning?
There have been several moments, but I would focus on fundraising. My co-founder and I have considerable experience in the business itself. We understand the work. Funding has been more challenging.
Sometimes conversations progress very well, and you begin to expect a positive outcome. You have plans ready and are preparing to get things moving. Then the feedback comes: “Let’s pause. Let’s wait.”
You find yourself asking: wait until when?
It can leave you feeling so dejected that you wonder whether to continue and why you are doing it at all.
The person I call is always my co-founder, Isaac. I tell him things aren’t going as I thought they would, and we talk through it.
What brings us back is the people we have served. Despite the challenges, there has been so much joy in the journey.
One woman told us that previously, her farm hadn’t produced enough surplus to help with school fees. Last year, after putting aside food for her household, she had enough left to pay school fees for her two children. She was so happy.
Stories like that make us feel we have to keep going.
We also have to remain flexible and adjust quickly when things change. Having a co-founder who understands that we are building for the long term makes the journey easier.
What are you like when things go wrong? If I asked your co-founder, would he describe the same person you are about to describe?
Definitely. He would tell you that Millicent is very tough and very strict. But he would also tell you that I am the most positive person.
When something goes wrong, I am usually the one saying there must be a good side to it. We might not see it immediately, but perhaps we will understand it tomorrow.
Then I move quickly to the next question: what do we do now? We cannot stay in the same place, going over what has happened.
He would tell you I am tough, but also that I am the person who says: “This is temporary. Give it time. Let’s focus on what we can do next.”
What does the business get from you that the people closest to you sometimes have to go without?
My time. The business gets so much of my time.
Even when I am not working, it is at the back of my mind. I can be at a family event and suddenly remember something I was supposed to do.
These days, I keep notes. If something occurs to me when I am doing something else, I write it down so I can return to it later.
I might be somewhere doing something completely unrelated to Agriflex, but Agriflex is still there in my thoughts. It takes a lot of my time and mental energy.
You have received recognition for your work. After the photographs and congratulations, which problem is usually still waiting on your desk? Has an award ever helped you solve it?
The problem is always getting the right inputs to our customers at the right time. Whether I am in the field, receiving an award or speaking somewhere, that need remains.
You can never seem to have enough. The more you can supply, the more customers need from you.
Awards have helped by giving us recognition and credibility. Some investors understand how rigorous particular programmes or award processes are. When they know you have gone through those stages, it can make the conversation easier and the process faster, even if you don’t ultimately get the answer you hoped for.
Recognition has also helped us meet investors who are a better fit. One of our biggest fundraising challenges early on was being in the wrong rooms with the wrong investors.
Some awards and programmes provide continuing support. For example, the women entrepreneurs award we received through AGRA last month comes with support that continues beyond the award itself. These programmes can look at different aspects of the business and recommend things that help us improve.
Some awards also come with money, which goes into the business.
So yes, they have helped: through credibility, connections, financial support and ongoing guidance.
Suppose we meet again over lunch in ten years. What would have to be true about Agriflex, and about your life outside it, for you to say, “Adonijah, this was worth it”?
I think about growth differently now. We want controlled growth.
In ten years, I would like us to be operating well in at least five African countries. By then, I don’t expect to be the CEO.
I want the business to be running fully, with someone else leading it while I perhaps serve in an advisory role.
I would like Agriflex to be recognised in Kenya, across Africa and internationally as a company that has been resilient and become sustainably profitable.
That would give me joy: seeing someone else take the reins and continue building a great business.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: In Other News: Tor Exit Relays Hijacked, Banks Spot Rogue AI Agents, Self-Rebuilding macOS Ransomware
articles.text:
SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape.
This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment.
Here are this week’s highlights:
Heartbreaker macOS ransomware rebuilds itself from source
Researcher Patrick Wardle has analyzed Heartbreaker, a Rust-based macOS ransomware sample that was uploaded to VirusTotal in May 2025 and, as of his writing, was still undetected by every antivirus engine on the service. After attempting to set up a LaunchAgent for persistence, it encrypts files in the user’s Downloads folder. It then tries to change its hash by taking its own embedded source code, randomizing identifiers and adding junk functions, and recompiling itself (even trying to install Rust if it’s missing). Wardle believes it’s unlikely to be a major threat in its current form, as it uses a single hardcoded AES key that makes free file recovery possible, and its rebuild process depends on a Rust framework that’s no longer publicly available.
ISO/IEC standard targets AI data poisoning, model theft
ISO and IEC have published ISO/IEC 27090, guidance for detecting and mitigating threats specific to AI systems (including data poisoning and model theft) across their life cycle. The standard is meant to complement ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, and also flags the risk of corrupted operational data making its way into future model versions through retraining.
WhatsApp’s guarded evidence fails to prove NSO broke injunction
A federal judge has declined to hold NSO Group in contempt over WhatsApp’s claims that the spyware maker violated a 2025 injunction barring it from using WhatsApp’s infrastructure to target users. WhatsApp’s case relied solely on a Meta investigator’s declaration that 23 new accounts carried signatures previously associated with NSO testing, but the judge found it lacked clear and convincing evidence, noting that WhatsApp chose to limit the level of detail (to avoid exposing its detection methods).
Seized ShinyHunters chats put ransom negotiators under scrutiny
Federal investigators believe at least one executive at a US-based consulting firm helped operate Shinywire, a now-defunct ShinyHunters site used to pressure nearly 100 hacked organizations into paying, KrebsOnSecurity reports, citing sources close to the probe. Signal messages that authorities accessed when they arrested ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in the Netherlands reportedly show frequent contact with Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky and at least one executive at a US consulting firm, who sometimes knew about new victims before the victims themselves.
Bullhorn forces credential resets as it restores hacked platform
Bullhorn is restoring its ATS/CRM platform after a cyber incident forced it to disable access to its systems, but says it has not yet determined whether customer data was exfiltrated. As systems come back online, non-SSO users must reset their passwords and API users must rotate their API passwords. Bullhorn says there is no indication that Bullhorn Automation, Sourcebreaker, or VMS Sync were affected.
Conduent breach victims could get monitoring and cash under $80 million deal
An $80 million settlement has been proposed to resolve a consolidated class action against Conduent over its 2024 data breach, in which millions of people’s personal and health information was stolen. All class members can claim a year of credit or medical data monitoring and reimbursement of up to $3,500 for documented losses, while those whose data was stolen in a readily accessible format can also claim a pro rata cash payment. The settlement awaits court approval, and Conduent disputes the claims of wrongdoing and liability.
APT28 aims Hookedge backdoor at NATO shipbuilder, engine maker
Symantec has linked Russia’s APT28 (which it tracks as Swallowtail) to Hookedge backdoor attacks on a law enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and a military aircraft engine manufacturer in two NATO member states. At the shipbuilder, where the intrusion lasted at least two months, the attackers stole credentials using two different techniques, opened a persistent SSH tunnel into the internal network, and deployed a previously undocumented loader that decrypts and runs its payload in memory.
Hijacked Tor exits harvested SSH passwords
A researcher whose own SSH session was intercepted while using Tor found that 333 exit relays (roughly a tenth of all exits) were redirecting SSH connections to a dozen attacker-run servers, which captured the passwords of users who ignored SSH’s warning and then tried to infect the servers they were logging into with Ebury. The relays ran on servers already compromised with Ebury, and their exit policies had been changed to block encrypted email retrieval ports and allow plaintext ones. The Tor Project pulled the relays within three days, and one affected operator has traced its own breach to a reused password. The project has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment.
Railway customers told to rotate all secrets after suspected breach
Developer platform Railway says an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted customer environment variables (which can hold API keys and database and registry credentials) and obtained the decrypted contents of some of them. The company believes the incident is part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers, and has notified those providers to proactively revoke keys. Although the impact may be limited to a subset of users, Railway has paused all deployments and is urging every customer to rotate stored environment variables and private registry credentials.
Major US banks spot unsanctioned AI agents inside customer accounts
Major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some attempting actions that appear independent of user instructions, Axios reports, citing sources. The agents typically log in with the user’s permission and credentials, which goes against most banks’ rules, and many banks can’t tell whether agent activity is directed by the user. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents and JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi are also restricting them, while most banks are moving toward allowing read-only access.
PingCAP intruder copied customer records and source code over four weeks
TiDB developer PingCAP says an unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials between September 9 and October 7 to access some of its internal systems, copy data and obtain source code. Exported records included TiDB Cloud user names and email addresses, customer contacts, contract and billing details, and encrypted TiDB Cloud API key values, though the company has found no evidence that data stored in TiDB was impacted. PingCAP has invalidated all identified compromised credentials and fixed four vulnerabilities reported by an external firm, and is still determining which customers were affected.
Related: In Other News: ICS-Sniper Attack, Hacking XWorm Malware Operators, $250k Chrome Exploit

articles.title: The reactor meant to showcase nuclear’s comeback keeps hitting problems
articles.text:
US regulators have issued a warning to a nuclear project critical to Donald Trump’s efforts to revive the industry, after a contractor fell into a reactor cavity and a bundle of fuel rods nearly tipped over during refueling.
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission told Holtec International, a company racing to reopen a shuttered reactor at the Palisades nuclear power plant in Michigan, to address a “chilled work environment” that has made staff hesitant to raise safety concerns without fear of retaliation.
The warning has prompted concerns among critics that financial and political pressures to revitalize nuclear power as an answer to booming AI-driven energy demand are increasing risks of accidents.
The NRC performed an inspection at Palisades in July over concerns about safety awareness. It followed an incident last year in which a worker fell into the reactor cavity, ingested some water, and was sent off-site for medical attention. The individual was decontaminated by radiation protection personnel but had 300 counts per minute detected in their hair, according to an incident report.
In a second incident in August, a bundle of nuclear fuel rods tilted over during a refueling operation, delaying what was anticipated to be the first reopening of a shuttered nuclear reactor in the US.
The NRC also said nine of the 15 reactor operators at Palisades failed the test for an initial licence examination administered in July and August. Six individuals were issued operator licenses.
Holtec, which has never operated a nuclear power plant, has secured about $2.2 billion in government support for a project that has been touted as a symbol of US nuclear resurgence. The owners of two other nuclear plants slated for decommissioning—Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania and Duane Arnold in Iowa—announced restarts soon after Palisades began work.

articles.title: Questrade opens options trading outside market hours through Cboe
articles.text:
Questrade is opening up a way for options traders to jump on news outside of usual market hours.
The news: Toronto digital financial platform Questrade announced on Friday that equity trading on select US options is now available on its app before the market opens and after it closes. The new product is enabled through the options exchange Cboe, which extended its trading hours earlier this week.
Questrade users approved for options trading can begin making bids at 7:30 a.m. and end at 4:15 p.m. on a limited list of individual stocks and exchange-traded funds (ETFs). Its index options trading is also expanding.
From the source: “It gives our investors another way to respond to market-moving news,” Luca De Blasis, Questrade’s head of product, invest, and trade, said in an interview.
“Our customers wanted this. When news broke that Cboe would be offering this [trading] session, we got quite a lot of inbound from our customers that said, ‘we want to be active during these times.’”
The context: Instead of buying shares of a stock directly, options trading is when you purchase the right to later buy or sell an asset at a certain fixed price, before a given date. Options are becoming increasingly popular—according to a report by Cboe, average daily trading volume in the second quarter of 2025 was up more than 19 percent from the year before.
Questrade notes in its release that trading during extended hours is riskier because it involves lower liquidity, more price volatility, and wider bid-ask spreads. Through the new options trading hours, clients must buy limit orders—which set the price at which users are willing to sell or buy.
Final thought: Questrade is one of the first Canadian brokerages to offer this product, but others are following suit. In an email to BetaKit, Interactive Brokers confirmed that Cboe’s extended trading hours are available to its Canadian clients. BetaKit reached out to Wealthsimple, which offers 24/5 stock trading, about whether it offers Cboe’s extended options trading hours, but did not hear back by publication time. It comes as Questrade and other Canadian financial apps contend with more FinTech competition through international entrants like Robinhood. 
Feature image courtesy Questrade.

articles.title: It’s time to find a new browser
articles.text:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 149, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, happy It Actually Feels Like Fall Now At Least In My Neighborhood), and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
It’s time to find a new browser
Plus, in this week’s Installer: Call of Duty is back, Kindle Plus is sort of new, and you need to watch Wildwood.
This week, I’ve been reading about Demis Hassabis and computer chips and permafrost, enjoying the first episodes of Machine Gods,filming the next season of Version History (pet season!), seeing You Can See Everythingand then reading and listening to absolutely everything about it, painstakingly updating all the stuff in my 1Password, making tiny documents with Tiny Little Office, watching Conan O’Brien own Subway Takesthe way he once owned Hot Ones,finally getting properly good at CapCut, and blasting the soundtrack to The Mandalorian and Grogu all workday long.
I also have for you a new AI assistant, the most Duo-y new app for the iPhone Duo, my hunt for the next great browser, and much more. Let’s do this.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What are you playing / reading / watching / listening to / modding with Claude this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Obviously, Grand Theft Auto VI is the biggest game release of the year, but a new COD is always a big deal. This one doesn’t sound like some grand reinvention of the form, but rather an even more playable, even more powerful version of what works. I was particularly excited to hear that the campaign mode is a huge improvement this time.
- The Blink Mini 4K. Ring cameras get a lot more shine, but Amazon’s cheaper brand also makes some pretty good stuff. This one’s part of a whole new lineup of devices, but $80 for a 4K camera with two-way audio and plenty of smart security features? Not a bad deal.
- JustWatch TV. As streaming services get incessantly more expensive, I’m starting to bail on some paid services and spend more time on the free ones. JustWatch’s new service is surprisingly well-stocked out of the gate — I suspect they’ve been watching what people search for, and making some smart content bets.
- Claude Duet. Here’s Anthropic’s answer to Muse, Instinct, and Dots. Duet seems to be focused on helping you get stuff done at work by making to-do lists, coordinating meetings, and compiling data for you. Still waitlist-only right now, but it’ll be interesting to see if it’s as thirsty for attention as Muse is.
- Wildwood. Before you see this gorgeous, by all accounts excellent stop-motion movie, read everything you can about how it was made. Not a pixel of generative AI in sight, just an unbelievable amount of hard work and human creativity. Humans rock, artists rock, this movie rocks.
- The Teenage Engineering EP-35. When you go to buy this thing, it’s technically called “Life is fantastic!” Which, sure. This thing is a battery powered, multi-input, multi-instrument amp with lots of effects. As always, it is extremely cool-looking. I have no use for it, and I want it quite badly.
- Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. Nintendo basically hasn’t changed the formula here since Wii Sports from two decades ago, and I have absolutely no problem with that. Anything that gives me that super-active tennis and bowling (plus volleyball, boxing, thumb wrestling, and more) is a win in my book.
- Delta 2.0. The next couple of weeks are going to be full of interesting app updates as developers try to figure out what to make of Apple’s foldable phone. But one of the best is already available; Delta can now pretty successfully cosplay as any handheld console ever. (Plus the Sega Genesis!)
- Kindle Plus. This is mostly just a rebranding of Kindle Unlimited, but Amazon put a couple of interesting new features in its $12 monthly reading subscription, including AI-narrated audiobooks. I am dubious of those, but excited about expanding access to audiobooks. We’ll see.
Spotlight
The worst news of the week here in the Installerverse is that Arc is going away. This was obviously coming: The Browser Company bailed on Arc two years ago in favor of the more AI-centric Dia, and Arc has been in maintenance mode ever since. But now it’s not just being ignored, it’s going away. By Christmas, you won’t even be able to use the app anymore.
So now a lot of us are stuck looking for another browser. There are a million new ones out there, many of them somewhere between “heavily inspired by Arc” and “a direct copy of Arc I made in Codex this morning.” I need to test a lot of them. I don’t know exactly where I’ll land yet, but I figured I’d share a bunch of the ones I’m looking at:
- Dia. It has recently gotten a lot of Arc’s best features, and some of the AI stuff is pretty cool. (And mercifully easy to turn off.) The Browser Company’s attention to aesthetic detail remains the best in the biz, so I’m starting here.
- Zen. A total ripoff of Arc, and I mean that as a compliment. Zen runs on Mozilla’s Gecko engine rather than Chromium, which is a win for anyone looking for a little less Google influence in their lives. Last time I tried Zen it was a little buggy and unpolished, but I’ve heard it’s come a long way.
- Orion. I am a dedicated and very happy Kagi user, and I’ve heard good things about how simple and resource-friendly the company’s browser is. Given the seamless Kagi integration, I sort of hope this one wins for me.
- Vivaldi. I used Vivaldi for a while, and I love how customizable it is. I eventually got it set up exactly the way I wanted it. But right next to all that customization is just a feeling of fiddliness, and I couldn’t quite get comfortable in the browser. Might try again.
- Helium. The opposite of Vivaldi, this is a super minimalist, no-frills browser. It’s probably what I need, honestly.
- Firefox. Its confusing stance on AI aside, I like a lot of the recent design and feature choices Firefox has made. I’m also intrigued by some of the Firefox forks, like Waterfox and Floorp, which give it even more customization options.
- Brave. Brave has always felt too heavy to me, and like it’s always trying to convince me to use more of its own proprietary (and often underpowered) features. But it seems to always win in privacy comparisons, so I might need to give it a go again.
On mobile, it’s easy. Quiche is my favorite iOS browser by a mile. Arc was never great on Android, so I’m betting most of us never switched there in the first place.
There are also the default browsers, of course, like Chrome, Safari, and Edge. But each of those browsers continues to fail me in one way or another, and so my search continues. If you’ve found your browser of the future, tell me all about it! Otherwise, I’ll report back here periodically through my journey.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Youth is an absolute SCREAM on HBO Max at the moment.” — Jonathan
“Todoist has a stellar integration with Siri AI that has finally made me fully commit to just using it If you delete Reminders, Todoist becomes the default on Siri AI and you can add a to-do to any project with tag AND location support (using Apple Maps saved locations like home and work!). The best part is that it all works WITHOUT having to say ‘... in todoist’ at the end of each query!” — Sajishnu
“Apple added Sound Glow to existing HomePod models and it’s just kinda fun to watch the light on top of HomePod glow and flash. So I’m doing that with some of my favorite playlists.” — Connor
“I’m reading a book called How to Read a Book by Mortimer J. Adler because I want to get better at analysis and reading for understanding vs. absorbing basic information.” — Rhoades
“My girlfriend took a train ride up the west coast and reported that no less than four different people asked her if her 2024 Samsung Galaxy Z-Flip 6 was the new iPhone Duo.” — Nicholas
“I recently read Bodies of Magic by Freya Marske, and it was excellent. What if med school was magical, but everyone was still sleeping with each other and stressing over student loans? Then an unexpected dead body shows up during finals.” — Emmett
“I got a Framework Laptop 13 Pro running Ubuntu last month, and I’m really happy with it. (I haven’t done anything with Linux in maybe 20 years — it’s come a long way!) So now I’m trying to see if I can replace Capture One with Darktable. If I can, that would break my last tie to macOS, and I’ll replace my iMac with a Framework Desktop.” — Morgan
“Exploring the new Nektropos Castle dungeon in EverQuest Legends. The game has been such a nostalgia trip back to 1999, but new content in an ancient game is a bizarre delight.” — Alex
“Setting up Navidrome and having Claude build me a definitive ‘Songs From the Black Hole’ playlist from my Weezer MP3 collection. (It’s harder than first appears: is ‘Lisa’ track 12 or not!?)” — Micheal
“Best Buy had a pretty insane deal on a Bambu A1 Mini, so we got my 12 year old son a 3D printer for his birthday. It’s amazing how easy it was to put out a seemingly perfectly accurate PLA print, compared to horror stories from older printers.” — Jeff
Signing off
Last week, my wife and I went car shopping. Our plan was just to drive a bunch of cars — we knew we needed something with three rows, and really had no experience with any of them — and then go home. Somehow, a few hours later, we were the proud and slightly bewildered owners of a new Kia Carnival.
So far the car has been great, but wow are there a lot of weird tech ideas in cars now. I’m good with CarPlay and Android Auto. I hate how much everything has become a touchscreen. But I’m most thrown by how many features of my car now exist in a companion app. How do we feel about this? I almost miss when I had no idea what to do about the check engine light.
Anyway, I’m a minivan dad now. I think I’m okay with it. Send car tips! Send minivan tips! Send help! See you next week!

articles.title: ‘I don’t love it:’ Kindle+ is the new name for Kindle Unlimited, and it comes with extra audiobooks and some undesirable AI
articles.text:
Kindle Unlimited has been given a Kindle+ rebrand — complete with more audiobooks, unwanted AI, and fears of a price increase
A new name at the same price (for now)
- Amazon has rebranded Kindle Unlimited as Kindle+
- The rebrand also comes with additional audiobooks, though many of these are narrated by AI
- The price hasn't changed but some users worry it might go up soon
Kindle Unlimited is no more — instead, you’re now a Kindle+ subscriber, as Amazon has just rebranded its ebook subscription service.
The good news is that the price hasn’t changed, and all the features remain the same too. In fact, you’re actually getting more for your money, because — as reported by ZDNet — there are now significantly more audiobooks included.
The bad news is that many of these new audiobooks are narrated by AI, with Amazon’s Virtual Voice allowing authors to create AI-narrated audio versions of their books at no additional cost.
A worrying change
Aside from that, this is seemingly the same as Kindle Unlimited, but the name change has made some users wary that a price increase could follow.
Over on Reddit, one user said “I don’t love it. It’s a signal that things will change and it’ll most likely start with the price,” while in another thread about the change, comments included the likes of “wouldn’t be surprised if there is a price rise in the near future,” and “I’m just glad they didn’t Kindle plus on the price. I was scanning that email and just waiting for them to say there was a price increase. Or is this a soft launch on that later?”
Certainly, there’s reason to worry, especially with Amazon now being able to argue that you’re getting more with the subscription (even if much of that extra is AI-generated).
This could also potentially pave the way for tiered pricing — after all, ‘Kindle+’ sounds like a less complete service than ‘Kindle Unlimited’ before it, so maybe a pricier additional tier will be rolled out at some point.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
But on the other hand, Amazon might simply have wanted to get away from the arguably confusing ‘Unlimited’ name, since there were in fact limits to what books were available and how many you could access at once. So it remains to be seen whether this is a simple rebrand or something more insidious.

And of course you can also follow TechRadar on TikTok for news, reviews, unboxings in video form, and get regular updates from us on WhatsApp too.
James is a freelance phones, tablets and wearables writer and sub-editor at TechRadar. He has a love for everything ‘smart’, from watches to lights, and can often be found arguing with AI assistants or drowning in the latest apps. James also contributes to 3G.co.uk, 4G.co.uk and 5G.co.uk and has written for T3, Digital Camera World, Clarity Media and others, with work on the web, in print and on TV.
