articles.title: Lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics confirms patients' personal and health data was compromised during breach | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Medical lab testing giant Quest Diagnostics has confirmed a cyberattack and data breach affecting an as-yet unspecified amount of sensitive patient information stored in its systems, according to a legally required disclosure with U.S. regulators.
Quest said in an 8-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it learned of a cyberattack on Wednesday targeting one of its lab testing systems, Quanum, which allows doctors’ offices, hospitals, and healthcare practices to request lab tests for patients while also handling billing. The platform stores a large amount of patient health and medical records, as well as associated diagnostic and billing data.
The company said the unauthorized access included the accessing of “certain patient records.” Quest said it notified law enforcement and is investigating.
The cyberattack on Quest is the latest major cyber incident to affect the healthcare industry this year. A series of cyberattacks and data breaches have sparked weeks of disruption and allowed the theft of millions of patient electronic health records and other medical information. Health tech companies have become a major target for financially motivated cybercriminals, who aim to steal as much sensitive data as possible and threaten to publish it if they aren’t paid a ransom.
In recent months, a cyberattack resulted in the mass-wiping of employee devices at medical tech maker Stryker in March, and a hack on medical implant manufacturer Boston Scientific in August forced the company’s network offline for weeks, sparking “global disruption” to its operations. Meanwhile, separate hacks throughout the year caused massive breaches of patient data at medical recordkeeping company CareCloud, Scotland-based health tech provider Craneware, and U.S. pharmaceutical distribution giant McKesson.
The lab-testing giant has not yet said how many healthcare customers, or patients, had information stolen during the attack on its Quanum systems.
Quest’s website and materials say Quanum is used by about half a million clinicians in thousands of locations across North America. It’s unclear how many health records Quanum holds, but one 2026 case study on Quest’s website shows how a single health system with more than 6 million patients can hold hundreds of millions of related medical documents and charts.
Quest did not say when the breach began or whether any hacking group has contacted the company with demands, such as payment in exchange to not release the stolen data. Amanda Rivera, a spokesperson for Quest, did not answer TechCrunch’s questions about the incident and referred to its security notice.
In the notice, Quest said that some patients’ protected health information was taken, including “personal information and patient records,” but the company is still investigating what specific kinds of data were taken. (The website post currently contains “noindex” code, which tells search engines not to list the page in search results, making it far more difficult for people to find the page.)
This is Quest’s second known major data breach in a decade, after losing 11.9 million patient records in a cyberattack on a third-party billing company in 2019.
Do you work at Quest Diagnostics or know more about the data breach? We’d love to hear from you. You can reach this reporter on Signal at the username zackwhittaker.1337 or by email [email protected].
Updated with a response from Quest.

articles.title: Justiça Eleitoral: 4 apps que ajudam você no dia da votação
articles.text:
O segundo turno das eleições está chegando, e quatro aplicativos oficiais da Justiça Eleitoral podem facilitar a rotina de eleitores e mesários. Pelo celular, é possível consultar o local de votação, comunicar possíveis irregularidades, acompanhar informações dos Boletins de Urna e fazer o treinamento para atuar nas seções eleitorais.
e-Título, Pardal, Boletim na Mão e Mesário são gratuitos e estão disponíveis para Android e iOS. Embora tenham funções diferentes, os aplicativos cobrem etapas que vão da preparação para a votação ao trabalho realizado nas seções eleitorais.
e-Título e Pardal atendem o eleitor
O e-Título funciona como a versão digital do título eleitoral e concentra serviços para quem vai votar. O aplicativo permite consultar zona, seção e local de votação, justificar ausência, verificar a situação eleitoral e emitir documentos disponíveis ao eleitorado.
Quem tem fotografia cadastrada na Justiça Eleitoral pode usar o e-Título como documento de identificação durante a votação. Sem a foto no aplicativo, é necessário apresentar um documento oficial com foto.
Para evitar imprevistos, a Justiça Eleitoral recomenda baixar o aplicativo e fazer o primeiro acesso com antecedência, sem deixar essas etapas para a última hora.
Outra ferramenta voltada ao eleitor é o Pardal, usado para encaminhar denúncias à Justiça Eleitoral. Entre as situações que podem ser comunicadas estão propaganda irregular, suspeita de compra de votos e uso indevido da estrutura pública. O usuário também pode incluir descrição dos fatos, localização, fotos e vídeos.
O material recebido é direcionado aos órgãos responsáveis pela análise e pelas providências cabíveis. Em situações de ameaça, violência ou flagrante de crime, o Pardal não substitui o acionamento da polícia e dos serviços de emergência.
Boletim na Mão mostra os dados da urna
Depois do encerramento da votação, o Boletim na Mão permite consultar os Boletins de Urna, documentos emitidos em cada seção eleitoral. Eles registram a quantidade de votos atribuída a cada candidata ou candidato naquela urna.
Leia mais:
- Eleições 2026: candidatos à Presidência têm planos diferentes para IA, data centers e soberania digital
- Starlink será usada pelo TSE em locais remotos nas eleições 2026
- Eleições 2026: entenda a engenharia por trás da urna eletrônica
Para fazer a consulta, basta apontar a câmera do celular para o QR Code impresso no boletim afixado na seção. O aplicativo lê as informações e permite consultar os dados registrados no documento.
A ferramenta pode ser utilizada por qualquer pessoa. Não é necessário ser mesário, fiscal de partido ou trabalhar na Justiça Eleitoral para acessar os registros.
Mesário concentra treinamento e orientações
Quem foi convocado ou se ofereceu para atuar nas seções eleitorais encontra no aplicativo Mesário os recursos necessários para se preparar para a votação. A plataforma reúne o treinamento e materiais de consulta relacionados aos procedimentos do dia da eleição.
Durante a preparação, é possível acompanhar o progresso do curso, revisar orientações, receber notificações da Justiça Eleitoral e consultar listas de conferência para a abertura e o encerramento dos trabalhos.
O aplicativo também dá acesso à Declaração de Trabalhos Eleitorais (DTE), documento que registra os dias de atuação e a conclusão do treinamento.
Na prática, os quatro aplicativos cobrem necessidades diferentes:
- Antes da votação: consulta de informações eleitorais e preparação para o trabalho como mesário;
- Durante o processo eleitoral: comunicação de possíveis irregularidades;
- Após a votação: consulta aos registros dos Boletins de Urna;
- Em diferentes etapas: acesso a serviços e orientações diretamente pelo celular.
Os quatro aplicativos podem ser baixados gratuitamente nas lojas oficiais Google Play e App Store. Com funções específicas, eles oferecem ao eleitorado e aos mesários ferramentas para diferentes momentos da participação nas eleições.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Farben für Motherboard-Anschlüsse: Darum sind sie seit 1999 gleich
articles.text:
Rot, Grün, Blau: Warum sich die Farben für Motherboard-Anschlüsse seit 1999 nicht verändert haben
Auch wenn heute viel über kabellose Kopfhörer geht: Die drei farbigen Audioanschlüsse des Motherboards hat wohl jeder schon mal benutzt, der in den letzten Jahrzehnten einen PC besessen hat. Sie kommen standardmäßig in den Farben Rot, Grün und Blau daher.
Dafür stehen die drei farbigen Audioanschlüsse
Grün steht für den Audio-Ausgang für Lautsprecher oder Kopfhörer. Die Farbe Blau zeigt wiederum an, dass es sich um den Eingang für externe Tonquellen wie Diktiergeräte handelt.
Die Farbe Rot markiert den Eingang für Mikrophone oder Headsets. Meist sind die Buchsen eher in Rosa oder Pink gehalten, werden aber landläufig als rot angesehen. Bei allen drei Anschlüssen steht auch oft die Funktion daneben. Aber durch die Farben sehen kundige Nutzer:innen sofort, welcher Stecker wo rein muss.
1999 vereinheitlichte Leitfaden die Farbgebung
Doch warum ausgerechnet diese Farben? Das ist eigentlich völlig willkürlich. Welche Farbe für welchen Port steht, wurde zufällig zugeordnet. Wichtig ist nur die Einheitlichkeit. Denn vorher herrschte Chaos. Jeder Hardware-Hersteller markierte seine Anschlüsse anders.
Dies änderte sich erst im Sommer 1999. Damals erschien die dritte Version des PC System Design Guide. Dieser Leitfaden vereinheitlichte die Farbgebung der Anschlüsse. Dies betraf nicht nur die Audiobuchsen, sondern auch USB und mehr.
Das steckt hinter dem PC System Design Guide
Der PC System Design Guide wurde von Microsoft und Intel zusammengestellt. Er basiert auf dem Handbuch Hardware Design Guide for Microsoft Windows 95, das 1994 erschienen war. Das Buch und die Guides legten fast, was ein Rechner besitzen muss, um als sich als kompatibel mit Windows beschreiben zu dürfen.
Die erste Ausgabe des PC System Design Guide kam dann 1997 heraus. Darin wurde bereits festgelegt, welche Farbe der Anschluss für die Maus (Dunkelgrün) und für die Tastatur (Lila) haben muss. 1998, 1999 und 2001 folgten drei weitere Editionen, ehe das Projekt beendet wurde.
In der Version PC-99 wurden die Farben nicht nur für Audio, sondern für alle Anschlüsse festgelegt. Sie basierten auf dem international verbreiteten Farbsystem von Pantone.
Farbgebung heute eigentlich nicht mehr nötig
Auch wenn es heute natürlich auch digitale Audioschnittstellen wie S/PDIF gibt, hat sich an den meisten PCs mit den guten alten analogen Anschlüssen die klassische Farbgebung von 1999 gehalten. Dies liegt einfach daran, dass die Hersteller die Konventionen bedienen und die Nutzer:innen nicht verwirren wollen.
Dabei ist eine farbliche Differenzierung heute in der Regel nicht mehr nötig. Denn moderne Motherboards erkennen auch falsch eingesteckte Kabel. So ist es kein Problem, wenn man ein Mikrofon in die grüne Buchse steckt. Seit 2004 können dies Geräte, die mit dem HD Audio Standard von Intel ausgerüstet sind, erkennen und intern korrigieren.

articles.title: Kenyan startup StudyLabAI gives students an AI tutor built on their own course material - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Kenyan ed-tech startup StudyLabAI has built an AI-powered study platform that turns students’ own slides, lecture recordings and notes into interactive study tools, and has signed up more than 90,000 learners across over 100 countries without raising outside funding.
Founded in August 2024 by Abdulrahman Yunis and Anas Kali, StudyLabAI is aimed at students aged 14-25, and the teachers who teach them. Users upload a PDF, lecture recording, slide deck or other study material, and the platform turns it into study tools in seconds.
“Our mission is to give every student a personal tutor, whatever their background,” said Yunis, the startup’s lead engineer. “Everything is grounded in your own course material rather than the general internet.”
Students can turn a chapter into a narrated video lesson, practise with adaptive quizzes and mock exams, review flashcards scheduled through spaced repetition, and generate notes, mind maps and audio recaps. A lecture recorder and YouTube-to-notes tool round out the offering, alongside a 24/7 AI tutor.
“It answers questions about the student’s own material and points to the exact slide or recording timestamp it drew from. It also asks follow-up questions to check understanding,” Yunis said. “The app tracks how strong each student is on every topic and feeds weak areas into the next day’s study plan, so they always know what to study next.”
The platform works in most major languages, with notes, flashcards and tutor answers following the language of the source material.
A teachers’ edition, launched in January 2026, lets educators generate video lessons, lesson plans aligned to curricula such as IB, IGCSE, AP and SAT, and differentiated worksheets, while a dashboard tracks grades and flags students who are falling behind.
“We see AI as a force multiplier: it automates the routine work so students and teachers can spend more time on real learning and human connection,” said Yunis. “It supports teachers; it does not replace them.”
Yunis started the company in his final year studying Computer Science and Engineering.
“The idea came from our own late nights. At 2am in the library, we were drowning in hundreds of lecture slides and messy notes, and spending more time organising our material than actually learning it. The process was broken,” he said. “We realised every student deserved a personal tutor available around the clock, one that adapts to them and works from their own material.”
He built the platform end to end, including the web and mobile apps, AI features and cloud infrastructure, while Kali works on product and data engineering. The pair saw three problems in the market.
“Good tutoring is expensive. One-to-one help works, but most students cannot afford a private tutor, especially outside wealthy markets,” Yunis said.
“General AI chatbots are not built for studying. They answer from the whole internet, not from what a student’s course covers. They can be confidently wrong, and they make it easy to copy answers instead of learning. And most study apps are priced for students in rich countries.”
StudyLabAI sits in between, giving students the patient, personal help of a tutor, grounded in their own material, at a price students can afford. Students mostly compare the platform to general AI assistants such as ChatGPT, and to study tools such as Quizlet, Chegg and Google’s NotebookLM.
“Our difference is the combination of a voice tutor, video tutor, answers grounded in each student’s own notes, and pricing that works for students worldwide,” said Yunis. “We are careful not to build technology for its own sake. Many edtech tools are impressive but go unused. We start with conversations with real students and teachers, find where learning gets stuck, and only then decide how AI can help.”
StudyLabAI runs on a freemium model, with students and teachers paying a monthly or yearly subscription in local currency for unlimited generation and, for teachers, advanced analytics. The startup is bootstrapped and profitable.
“We have grown on revenue from paying students rather than outside investment, which has forced us to keep costs low and build features students will actually pay for,” Yunis said.
Uptake has been largely organic, with students finding the platform through TikTok, Instagram and Google search. Its largest markets are the United States, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and more than 1 million lessons have been created on the platform.
“We support international curricula such as IB, IGCSE, AP and the SAT, as well as custom syllabuses, which is part of why we travel well across borders,” said Yunis.
The journey has not been without its challenges.
“Every tutor session and summary costs us money in AI computing, so we have had to keep the product affordable for students while covering those costs,” he said. “Students also need answers they can rely on. Grounding every answer in the student’s own notes was our response to that.”
StudyLabAI is now offering free pilot programmes to schools and institutions so whole classes can use the platform with teacher dashboards, and plans to add more languages, including Arabic, as well as exam preparation for specific national curricula.
“Our growth so far has come from individual students and teachers,” said Yunis. “Now we want to bring StudyLabAI to whole schools.”

articles.title: Lubner’s iZinga Assist wants to rebuild trust in SA’s NGOs
articles.text:
After decades in philanthropy, Derek Lubner discovered that giving money was simple; verifying where it went was the real challenge. In conversation with PHATHISANI MOYO, the iZinga Assist co-founder explains how he plans to repair the trust deficit between donors and grassroots NGOs.
When Derek Lubner was managing his late parents’ foundation, Make an Immediate Difference, he routinely asked beneficiary non-profit organisations to submit wish lists for the upcoming year.
If an organisation wanted cricket bats and nets, a classroom or a soccer field, the co-founder and chairman of iZinga Assist, digital non-profit verification and support platform, would consider the request and agree to fund all or part of it. His only condition was that the organisation send him a photograph showing what the money had paid for.
Over the years, he estimates that barely a quarter of the organisations ever sent the requested pictures, leaving him with no straightforward way to confirm whether the equipment had been purchased or the project delivered.
For someone dedicated to supporting grassroots community initiatives across South Africa, the omission was frustrating. Yet it also forced him to reconsider the administrative burden traditional donors impose on frontline social workers.
“I could have blamed the organisations and cut their funding,” Lubner told TechCabal. “Instead, I realised we needed to help them meet those compliance requirements.”
That conviction spurred the creation of iZinga Assist, co-founded with chief executive Henk Swanepoel. The digital platform was designed to make grassroots non-profits more visible, structurally sound, and easier for donors to vet.
In a sector where registration alone does not establish whether an organisation is active, well-governed or accountable for its funding, the platform digitally checks NGOs’ documentation and offers resources to help them address administrative gaps. The goal is twofold: give donors reliable data before deploying capital, and prevent administrative paperwork from locking legitimate community leaders out of funding pipelines.
Lubner had seen first-hand that an organisation can be passionately rooted in its community while remaining ill-equipped to meet the rigorous reporting standards demanded by institutional philanthropists.
Learning to look beyond the donation
Lubner’s perspective had been shaped by nearly three decades in civil society, including a board seat at Mothers2Mothers since its inception in 2001. Founded in Cape Town during the height of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, the maternal health organisation pairs mothers living with HIV with pregnant women confronting new diagnoses, providing frontline guidance on treatment adherence and child protection.
The organisation demonstrated how social intervention succeeds when built around lived experience and backed by professionalised systems. Notably, Mothers2Mothers insisted on formally employing its mentor mothers rather than relying on unpaid volunteer labour, while resisting mission creep despite persistent donor pressure to chase unrelated grants.
Managing his family’s portfolio of 35 to 40 local non-profits provided the complementary funder’s perspective.
It made clear that the chronic reporting failures he witnessed were rarely acts of fraud; they were symptoms of severe under-resourcing. Small social initiatives simply lacked the administrative bandwidth to produce institutional-grade documentation.
That realisation informed the development of iZinga Assist during the COVID-19 pandemic. Rather than penalising under-staffed teams, the platform was conceived as an operational scaffold to help them structure their governance and become investor-ready.
“We wanted to shine a light on the under-served tier of the sector,” Lubner explained. “The objective is to make these organisations both verified and visible to prospective funders.”
Making organisations easier to trust
To secure verification, iZinga Assist requires non-profits to upload roughly 20 statutory documents spanning founding constitutions, board charters, tax compliance, and audited financial statements. Where documentation is missing or inadequate, the platform supplies standardised contract templates, governance guidelines, and direct coaching.
Onboarding and verification remain completely free for applicant organisations, a deliberate choice to ensure limited cash reserves do not prevent legitimate groups from demonstrating compliance.
“NGO leaders often do not know what they do not know,” Lubner noted. “We try to lift that administrative burden, including by maintaining a secure cloud repository for their files so they are always audit-ready.”
According to Lubner, the platform has onboarded more than 500 organisations, with roughly 110 achieving full verification. Completing the audit often takes months or even years, as many grassroots teams either have incomplete records or feel apprehensive about disclosing internal books.
South Africa’s non-profit register provides a count of registered organisations, but registration alone does not establish whether an organisation remains active, maintains its records or delivers the work described in its founding documents. The scale of the sector makes that distinction important.
iZinga Assist cited 289,852 organisations on the Department of Social Development’s register at the end of September 2025 and Trialogue’s estimate of R13.1 billion ($797.8 million) in corporate social investment spending in 2025. Those figures describe the wider sector, not funds verified or tracked by iZinga Assist.
For Lubner, the opportunity is to close the information gap between organisations seeking support and donors who need confidence in how their money will be used. That includes South Africans living abroad who want to support causes at home but may struggle to identify credible organisations.
He envisages donors being able to identify causes they care about and receive updates in line with their preferences. Someone interested in sport, for example, could support a community cricket programme and receive confirmation that equipment purchased with their donation reached the intended organisation.
The platform is exploring ways to make that process easier to track, including payment arrangements that could confirm when money has been spent on an agreed item. In one model Lubner describes, an NGO could use a payment card to purchase something specific, such as cricket bats, with the donor receiving confirmation of the transaction.
The objective is to replace philanthropic guesswork with verifiable paper trails. Yet Lubner readily concedes that proof of transaction is not synonymous with lasting community transformation.
“‘Impact’ is a term thrown around casually, but its definition varies wildly,” he explained. A community initiative might miss an arbitrary numerical target due to unforeseen local unrest or weather events without rendering its underlying mission invalid.
That distinction is vital: a photograph of soccer balls confirms procurement; it cannot determine whether youth delinquency declined or whether sports participation improved mental health. A credible verification mechanism must clearly delineate administrative compliance from long-term social efficacy.
Building trust without creating another barrier
iZinga Assist faces its own verification challenge: no external regulator currently audits its proprietary methodology, and remote document checks do not substitute for on-the-ground inspection.
“Donors have to place confidence in our vetting, and we recognise that scrutinising our own credibility is a fair demand,” Lubner acknowledged.
Digital document reviews confirm statutory registration and corporate governance, but they cannot prove that an organisation is actively running the clinics or food kitchens it claims. The platform’s forthcoming five-star rating index will have to clearly disclose where documentary verification ends and physical validation begins.
To solve this, Lubner is courting commercial banks and corporate donors to mobilise their workforce for volunteer field visits. Properly trained corporate volunteers could perform periodic on-site spot-checks, providing donor validation while connecting corporate personnel directly with local communities.
Lubner insists accountability must be mutual. Donors must communicate their metrics with clarity rather than imposing shifting reporting targets. “Too often, non-profits spray hundreds of proposals into the dark, while donors sit on capital because they cannot separate genuine operators from paper organisations,” he said. “We need symmetry in that relationship.”
Achieving platform sustainability is the next operational test. As core verification will remain free for non-profits, iZinga Assist must monetise by licensing its vetting infrastructure to corporate CSI teams, philanthropic foundations, and wealth managers who require compliance-as-a-service.
“I am not looking to make a fortune from iZinga Assist; the goal is operational self-sufficiency,” Lubner said. His five-year objective is to assemble an active network of several thousand verified non-profits that use the portal to source legal templates, professional development courses, vetted consultants, and verified funding leads.
What began decades ago as a quest for missing photographs has expanded into an ambitious structural intervention. Lubner is attempting to rewire an opaque philanthropic sector where well-intentioned donors and committed grassroots organisations remain divided by paperwork and mutual distrust.
Whether iZinga Assist succeeds will depend not just on the code it deploys or the documents it checks, but on whether it can command the same institutional credibility it is asking South Africa’s non-profits to prove.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Visualize points and routes with GeoJSON in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps
With Amazon Quick Sight layer maps, you can now plot points and routes, like store locations across a city or flights leaving an airport. Geospatial maps help businesses spot patterns that are tied to location, like how a region is performing or where customers are concentrated. Amazon Quick Sight supports this with multiple map types, including point maps, filled maps, and layer maps. When layer maps first launched, you could upload a GeoJSON file to draw custom shape layers, such as sales territories or districts, and join those shapes to a dataset. That handled regions and boundaries well, but it didn’t cover the individual locations inside them or the routes running between them.
Layer maps now support two more geometry types from the same GeoJSON workflow: Point and LineString. Points mark specific locations, such as individual store or facility sites. A LineString traces the route between locations, like a delivery path or a flight between airports.
Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence (BI) capability of Amazon Quick, is a unified BI service. It delivers modern interactive dashboards, natural language querying, pixel-perfect reports, machine learning (ML) insights, and embedded analytics at scale. Amazon Quick brings together AI agents for business insights, research, and automation in one integrated experience, helping you work smarter and faster while maintaining security and access policies.
In this post, we walk through the dataset and GeoJSON structure that layer maps require. We also explain how points and lines work in a layer map visual and when to choose each. Finally, we cover advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering geometries, and updating GeoJSON files programmatically.
Dataset structure considerations
A layer map gets its shapes from a GeoJSON file and its metrics from a Quick Sight dataset, and a shared key joins the two. How you structure each one determines what the map can show. This section covers what you need before you start and how a GeoJSON file is organized.
Prerequisites
The following are the prerequisites that you need before creating a layer map in Quick Sight:
- A GeoJSON file describing your geometry.
- A Quick Sight dataset holding the metrics and dimensions.
- A join key shared between the Quick Sight dataset and the GeoJSON file.
- The GeoJSON file must be saved in .geojson format, with a maximum supported file size of 100 MB.
Structure of the GeoJSON file
GeoJSON is a JSON-based format for describing geographic features such as points and lines.
The structure of the file is as follows:
- FeatureCollection is the whole file. It has a type of FeatureCollection and a features array.
- Feature is a single map element. It carries a geometry (the shape) and a properties object, which holds the join key.
- geometry has a type (Point, LineString, or Polygon) and its coordinates. The coordinates hold a single [longitude, latitude] position for a Point, and an ordered list of positions for a LineString.
Configuring the Quick Sight dataset and its GeoJSON
In Quick Sight, when you configure a layer in a layer map visual, there are two primary settings to consider. The first is the Geometry type to visualize, which sets which geometry from the GeoJSON file renders: Points, Lines, or Polygons. A layer renders one geometry type at a time, so when a file mixes types like the preceding example, only Features of the selected type appear on the map. The second is matching the Shape file key field to the Dataset key field, which links each Feature in the GeoJSON to a row in your Quick Sight dataset. The field names don’t need to be identical, but the values do. The following two examples show this end to end, first a LineString layer and then a Point layer.
Example: LineString layer
Consider example data showing a flight from JFK to a destination city like Los Angeles. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:
The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:
The route_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per route, and the dataset one row per route. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Lines.
Example: Point layer
Consider example data showing a retail store location like Long Island City. The GeoJSON structure for a single datapoint is configured as follows:
The corresponding row in the Quick Sight dataset contains the following information:
The store_id field is used to join the Quick Sight dataset with the GeoJSON file. The GeoJSON holds one such feature per store, and the dataset one row per store. The Geometry type to visualize is set to Points.
Lines on layer map visuals
Layer map visuals now support LineString geometry, connecting an ordered list of coordinates into a single path. As covered in the data structure section, each route is one feature, and its coordinates are the ordered positions the map connects in sequence.
Use lines when the relationship between locations is what you want to show, such as flight paths, delivery routes, shipping lanes, or pipeline segments. The visual draws each path from the coordinates in your GeoJSON file rather than generating it from your data at load time. A field from your joined dataset can determine the line color encoding, so you can group routes by whatever that field represents. In addition to color, you can customize lines with width and opacity controls to adjust visual prominence and clarity on the map. The join key in the GeoJSON properties object ties each LineString to the dataset row behind its tooltip and color.
For example, an airport operations team might map the flights leaving New York (JFK) on a given day. The GeoJSON file holds one LineString per route, keyed by a route ID that joins to the dataset. Each line starts at JFK and ends at its destination, such as Los Angeles, Chicago, or Miami. The dataset supplies the origin, destination, and carrier that show up in the tooltip.
Points on layer map visuals
Amazon Quick Sight offers a native point map visual type that geocodes location names automatically and refreshes with your SPICE schedule or Direct Query connection. It supports dynamic point sizing, color encoding, and point styles such as cluster points and heatmap density gradients. It works best with data that changes frequently and where you want the map to respond to those changes visually.
With the added support for GeoJSON point layers in layer map visuals, Quick Sight now offers a second point mapping capability with a few key differences. Layer map visual points use a uniform marker size and don’t support geocoding, so you provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file. In return, you can control the viewport precisely, locking the map to an exact geographic region, and disabling panning and zooming.
The following table summarizes the key differences:
| Feature | Point map | Layer map visual points | 
| Data source | Latitude/longitude values or geolocation names in your dataset | GeoJSON Point features joined to your dataset by a shared key | 
| Geocoding | Recognizes city, county, state, country, and postal code automatically | Not available. Must provide explicit coordinates in the GeoJSON file | 
| Location updates | Mapping updates automatically with SPICE refreshes or Direct Query as location values change | Visual uses a static GeoJSON file for point locations. Requires manual re-upload or API call to update geometry | 
| Viewport | Auto-fits to your data, panning and zooming always enabled | Auto-fits by default, can configure if panning and zooming is allowed | 
| Appearance | Size and color can be encoded from the dataset. Point style configuration available (basic, cluster, heatmap) | Customizable uniform marker size, fill opacity, border color and thickness. Color can be encoded from the dataset | 
Choose layer map visual points when:
- You require a locked, non-scrollable viewport.
- Your locations are fixed and curated (such as regional offices, distribution centers, retail stores) rather than changing with each data refresh.
- You plan to combine points with other geometry types (covered in the advanced use cases section).
Consider a retail brand whose regional managers use a Quick Sight dashboard to track store performance across a metro area. The GeoJSON file contains a Point feature for each store with a store ID property that joins to the dataset. The dataset holds the metrics (store type, monthly revenue, daily foot traffic) that drive the tooltip and color encoding. You position the map at the zoom level covering the metro area, then disable map navigation so the map renders at a consistent view on every load. Managers can’t accidentally zoom out to a national or global view.
Advanced use cases
The previous sections cover a standard layer map setup. Use the following techniques when you need more control over what readers see, want to combine geometry types in a single view, or need geometry that changes over time.
Controlling the viewport
When you need to control the viewport in layer map visuals, you can pan and zoom to the view you want manually. Then disable map navigation to lock it in place. For use cases where you need more precise boundaries or programmatic control, you can set the exact viewport coordinates through the visual definition using the Quick Sight APIs.
The layer map visual stores its viewport configuration in the MapState property within ChartConfiguration. This property accepts two fields:
- Bounds: The geographic coordinates defining the minimum visible area (North, South, East, West).
- MapNavigation: ENABLED or DISABLED to control whether readers can pan and zoom.
Although the bounds property is not exposed on the console, you can set these bounds when working with the dashboard definition JSON for programmatic asset management. For example, to define the bounds, modify the MapState block in the visual definition, then call the CreateDashboard or UpdateDashboard APIs.
The bounds define the minimum area that is guaranteed to be visible. The map zooms to make sure this entire area fits within the visual container. For the tightest fit with minimal extra space added to the map, match the aspect ratio of your bounds to the shape of your visual container.
Layering geometries
For use cases that require combining multiple geometry types into a single view, you can layer visuals on top of each other. For example, the following screenshot demonstrates plotting customer locations as points within US regional boundaries defined by polygons. This composition shows which territories have the highest customer density and can be used to correlate with other metrics present in the dataset like performance.
This second example demonstrates combining points as stops along a delivery route path. The LineString draws the planned route, and Point features mark each scheduled stop along the way.
To layer geometries, you stack multiple layer map visuals on top of each other, following these steps:
- Use free-form layout: Change the sheet layout setting to free-form so that visuals can overlap and stack.
- Create two layer map visuals: Create the two layer map visuals that you combine into a single view, such as one using a Point GeoJSON file and one using a LineString GeoJSON file.
- Use matching bounds: Using the approach previously described for controlling the viewport, verify all layer map visuals use identical bounds to have the same underlying map view.
- Disable panning and zooming: For each layer map visual, disable the panning and zooming under Map options so that alignment stays the same.
- Hide the base map and background on upper layer: Set the upper visual’s background to hidden under Display settings and disable the base map under Map options.
- Stack the visuals: Move the top visual on top of the base layer using drag-and-drop or by matching precise size and position coordinates under Display settings.
Layer ordering follows the visual stacking order in the free-form layout. To change a visual’s position in the stack, choose the menu icon (three dots) on the visual, then choose Send backward or Bring forward. Readers can access the tooltip of the topmost visual, so place the layer that readers need details from on top. Each sheet supports up to five layer map visuals.
Dynamically updating GeoJSON
Unlike other Quick Sight visuals where data refreshes through SPICE or Direct Query, layer map geometry lives in the GeoJSON file itself. When your dataset refreshes on schedule, the metrics update (for example, colors change and tooltip values refresh), but the geometry remains at its original position.
To update what appears on the map, like a new route, new point locations, or updated boundaries, you need to update the GeoJSON file and republish the dashboard. You can replace a GeoJSON file manually through the Quick Sight console by editing the layer map visual within the Analysis and uploading a new file. This works for infrequent changes such as updating territory boundaries quarterly or adding a new store location.
For automated, on-demand, or dynamic updates, the process involves Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the Quick Sight APIs outlined in the following steps:
- Upload the new GeoJSON to Amazon S3: Generate your updated geometry and save it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Custom solutions can use other AWS services such as Amazon Location Service to create the GeoJSON files.
- Reference the file on the dashboard definition: The dashboard definition contains a StaticFiles array with a SpatialStaticFile entry for each GeoJSON file. Modify the file reference to the S3 location of your updated file entry for each GeoJSON file.
- Call the UpdateDashboard API: Submit the updated definition with the new file reference using the UpdateDashboard API.
- Call the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API: Publish the change so it is visible to dashboard readers with the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API.
The following example uses this pattern to support on-demand map updates in an embedded dashboard to generate optimal routes between locations and waypoints. Although outside the scope of this post, this represents an advanced use case that combines each of the preceding approaches.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to use Point and LineString geometry in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps to plot specific locations and the routes between them. We covered the GeoJSON structure and dataset join that layer maps require, and compared layer map points with the native point map. We also walked through advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering separate visuals into one view, and refreshing GeoJSON files with Amazon S3 and the Quick Sight APIs.
To learn more about layered maps, refer to the Amazon Quick Sight layered maps documentation. Visit the Amazon Quick Community to connect with peers and stay updated on the newest features and resources.

articles.title: Canadian Startup Capital Association names new interim executive director | BetaKit
articles.text:
The Canadian Startup Capital Association (CSCA), a coalition for early-stage investors that launched this spring, has named a new interim executive director.
The news: On Thursday, the CSCA announced that Tara June (TJ) Misra had stepped into the executive director role. According to Misra’s bio, the Ottawa-based executive has a 15-year background in public-private partnerships for innovation ecosystems and has consulted for startups around the world. She is a co-founder of the SAIL Initiative, a non-profit organization that aims to help streamline the licensing and commercialization of publicly funded research. “With her strong commitment to innovation ecosystem development, we are excited to have her working on behalf of capital activation in Canada,” read a Thursday post on CSCA’s LinkedIn page.
From the source: Misra told BetaKit in an emailed statement on Friday that her focus will be on building CSCA into a coalition that consults with potential members so it’s structured to serve them, and that she looks forward to working with other organizations in the ecosystem. “The [CSCA] seeks to amplify expertise through policy recommendations on behalf of underserved and underrepresented parts of the country, as well as reduce barriers to investment and aid in the navigation of existing systems,” Misra said.
The context: The CSCA was founded in April by angel investor Jesse Wiebe with the intention of bolstering Canada’s early-stage investment ecosystem, supporting investors who focus on companies between pre-seed and Series A stages. At the time, it claimed to represent more than 3,500 active investors who had collectively invested more than $750 million into early-stage Canadian startups. In June, Wiebe was charged by Saskatoon police with unlawfully entering a home and committing an indecent act. He pleaded guilty in July, receiving a conditional discharge and an order to serve one year of probation. Misra said that Wiebe’s work to get CSCA up and running was “remarkable,” but that he’s “decided to step back from leadership to focus on his health and family.” BetaKit has reached out to Wiebe for comment.
Final thought: The CSCA launched with three key priorities: activating more early-stage capital by supporting first-time angels, family offices, and emerging fund managers; building a stronger national network for coinvestment and data-sharing; and lobbying the government for policies to grow the industry. The young organization may have helped lock an early win. On Thursday, the federal government announced it would allocate 10 percent of its $750-million Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy toward early-stage investment, and the remainder to growth—an allocation share the CSCA, among others, have advocated for. Misra, who attended the announcement, called the news “an important step forward.” The next test, she said, is how quickly that capital can reach investors.
With files from Josh Scott.
Feature image courtesy the Canadian Startup Capital Association.

articles.title: US banks have detected unvetted AI agents accessing customer bank accounts
articles.text:
US banks have detected unvetted AI agents accessing customer bank accounts
Agentic AI is threatening online banking security
- Customers are increasingly enlisting AI agents to handle banking jobs for them
- Banks are struggling to distinguish between human, legitimate AI and rogue activity
- Many are now preparing for worst-case scenarios when AI does go rogue
Several major US banks have detected third-party AI agents accessing their customers' bank accounts, sometimes even attempting to carry out actions beyond what users actually wanted them to do.
New Axios reporting has claimed banks are now said to be struggling to even distinguish between legitimate human activity and agentic activity – but especially between authorized and rogue AI agents.
Importantly, the concern isn't so much disconnected, rogue AI going after system vulnerabilities to obtain customer information – banks are currently worrying about AI agents that human users themselves are setting off on their behalves.
Banks are struggling to deal with an influx of customer-authorized AI activity
In many cases, customers are voluntarily providing their banking usernames and passwords to AI assistants to hand over some workflows and processes to them, however while customers may be prepared to share these sensitive details, it can often violate banks' policies – which require the customers themselves to log into the accounts.
Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citigroup have all started to restricted third-party agent access. Well Fargo is also said to be responding to potential threats.
Besides a lack of visibility and account security, banks are also worried about financial liability, because it's still unclear who's responsible for AI agents' activity if things go wrong.
Charles Schwab CEO Richard Wurster explained that he now expects a daily report about "how many times we've had to block one of the different agents" so that the bank has "control over authentication and the experience."

articles.title: Con este simple truco de Windows, olvídate de volver a “perder” el puntero del mouse
articles.text:
Si usas un PC con múltiples pantallas, seguramente has “perdido” el puntero del mouse en más de una oportunidad. Es bastante normal desorientarse al saltar de un monitor a otro y no encontrar la flecha del ratón, lo mismo al regresar al ordenador tras un momento de descanso. Lo que muchos no saben es que Windows tiene una función llamada Buscar mi mouse que hace que recuperar el puntero sea mucho más sencillo. Y lo único que necesitas es tener PowerToys instalado.
Como ya hemos explicado en otras oportunidades, PowerToys es el equivalente a una navaja suiza, pero de software. Se trata de una aplicación oficial de Microsoft que permite añadir un sinfín de funciones que no están disponibles de forma nativa en Windows, siendo Buscar mi mouse una de las más útiles y gratificantes.
Seguramente ya te imaginas de qué va esta característica. Al activar Buscar mi mouse en PowerToys, puedes usar un comando para disparar un indicador gráfico de dónde está el puntero del ratón. Así, si tienes un setup con varias pantallas, puedes evitarte un momento de frustración al tratar de encontrar dónde está la flecha.
Para invocar Buscar mi mouse en Windows se pueden configurar distintas opciones. La que llega definida por defecto es pulsar dos veces el botón Ctrl izquierdo. Sin embargo, se puede cambiar de forma fácil. Las alternativas disponibles son agitar el ratón, pulsar dos veces la tecla Ctrl derecha o establecer un atajo de teclado específico.
Cómo activar Buscar mi mouse en Windows a través de PowerToys
Lo primero que tienes que corroborar es tener instalado PowerToys en tu ordenador con Windows. Si todavía no lo has descargado, puedes hacerlo desde la web oficial. Posteriormente, ingresa en la aplicación y dirígete al panel izquierdo. Navega hacia Entrada y salida > Utilidades del mouse.
Una vez allí, encontrarás distintas herramientas entre las que se encuentra Buscar mi mouse. Actívala y define el comando de ejecución, y listo. En adelante, cada vez que necesites encontrar el puntero del ratón en cualquiera de tus pantallas, solo tienes que ejecutar el comando y verás que el software resalta su ubicación con un círculo imposible de no ver.
A primera vista puede parecer algo menor, pero si a diario trabajos con dos o tres monitores en Windows, verás que Buscar mi mouse es una herramienta salvadora. Y no olvides que PowerToys te da un sinfín de otras utilidades a las que seguramente también le sacarás provecho con facilidad; entre tantas, la que permite previsualizar el contenido de cualquier documento o archivo sin tener que abrirlo con su aplicación predeterminada.

articles.title: L’IA coûte 725 fois moins cher : pourquoi les géants de la tech ont des sueurs froides
articles.text:
Le prix de l’intelligence artificielle s’effondre à une vitesse spectaculaire. Une excellente nouvelle pour les utilisateurs, beaucoup moins évidente pour les entreprises qui investissent des fortunes dans leurs modèles et leurs infrastructures. Car derrière les progrès techniques, la question de la rentabilité devient de plus en plus pressante.
Faire travailler une intelligence artificielle coûte aujourd’hui une fraction de ce que les entreprises facturaient encore il y a dix-huit mois. Et la baisse est vertigineuse. Selon une étude publiée en septembre par Epoch AI, le prix nécessaire pour atteindre un niveau de performance donné a été divisé en moyenne par 13 chaque année depuis 2023. Sur certaines tâches, l’écart atteint même un facteur 725.
De quoi bouleverser l’économie d’un secteur où les investissements dans les centres de données battent pourtant tous les records.
Des performances comparables pour une fraction du prix
L’exemple le plus frappant concerne GPQA Diamond, un test de connaissances scientifiques de niveau doctorat. Au printemps 2025, le modèle o3 d’OpenAI dépensait environ 30 centimes de dollar par question pour atteindre 75% de bonnes réponses. Moins de dix-huit mois plus tard, GPT-5.6 Luna obtenait un résultat comparable pour seulement 0,0004 dollar.
Signalons qu’Epoch AI compare ici le coût d’utilisation des modèles sur des tests précis, pas le prix des abonnements à ChatGPT ni les dépenses nécessaires pour entraîner ces IA.
Cette chute des tarifs s’explique notamment par les progrès réalisés dans l’optimisation des modèles. La quantification réduit leurs besoins en mémoire, tandis que la distillation permet à des IA plus compactes de reproduire certaines capacités de modèles beaucoup plus imposants. Moins de puissance de calcul est alors nécessaire pour produire une réponse.
Pour les entreprises, cela change considérablement la donne. Traduction, analyse de documents ou assistance à la programmation deviennent accessibles à moindre coût. Certaines applications autrefois trop gourmandes en ressources peuvent désormais être proposées à grande échelle.
Des milliards investis dans des machines qu’il faudra rentabiliser
Pendant que le prix des réponses s’écroule, la construction des infrastructures nécessaires à l’IA, elle, ne ralentit pas. Alphabet prévoit ainsi 195 à 205 milliards de dollars de dépenses d’investissement en 2026, notamment pour développer ses centres de données et ses capacités informatiques.
Ces équipements coûtent cher à acheter, mais aussi à exploiter. Outre le prix des composants informatiques (GPU, mémoire, etc.), il faut alimenter les serveurs, les refroidir, les entretenir et les amortir sur plusieurs années. Avec un risque supplémentaire, celui de voir les nouvelles générations de puces rendre les précédentes moins compétitives avant même qu’elles aient été rentabilisées.
Pour les fournisseurs d’IA, toute la difficulté consiste donc à faire progresser les usages suffisamment vite pour compenser la baisse des prix. Une équation d’autant plus délicate que les concurrents se livrent une bataille tarifaire acharnée.
Et le développement des agents IA pourrait encore compliquer les calculs. Contrairement à un chatbot classique, ces assistants autonomes multiplient les requêtes pour accomplir une seule tâche (voir FAQ ci-dessous). Selon Gartner, le coût d’inférence d’un processus reposant sur des agents pourrait ainsi être multiplié par plus de cinq d’ici à 2028 et cela, malgré les gains d’efficacité des modèles. De quoi donner de sacrés nœuds au cerveau à ceux qui misent des milliards sur l’IA…
Le coût d’inférence correspond aux ressources (GPU/TPU, mémoire, électricité, temps de calcul) nécessaires pour générer une réponse une fois le modèle déjà entraîné. Il se mesure souvent « par requête », « par token » ou « par tâche » sur un benchmark, et reflète surtout l’efficacité d’exécution du modèle. Ce coût n’inclut pas les dépenses d’entraînement, qui sont des coûts initiaux très élevés (données, calcul, ingénierie) pour créer ou mettre à jour le modèle. Il est aussi différent du prix d’un abonnement grand public, qui agrège marge, support, fonctionnalités, et parfois des quotas. Dans l’industrie, la baisse du coût d’inférence peut faire chuter les tarifs facturés, même si les investissements d’infrastructure restent massifs.
La quantification consiste à représenter les poids et calculs du modèle avec moins de bits (par exemple 8 bits au lieu de 16/32), ce qui réduit la mémoire nécessaire et accélère certains calculs. En pratique, cela permet d’exécuter des modèles similaires sur du matériel moins coûteux, ou d’augmenter le nombre de requêtes traitées par un même serveur. La distillation entraîne un « modèle élève » plus petit à reproduire le comportement d’un « modèle professeur » plus gros, en apprenant à imiter ses sorties. Le gain vient du fait qu’un modèle compact demande moins de calcul pour une qualité proche sur des tâches ciblées. Ces techniques peuvent cependant introduire des compromis : légère perte de précision, dégradation sur des cas rares, ou besoin d’ajustements selon les usages.
Un agent IA ne se limite pas à répondre : il planifie, appelle des outils (API, navigateur, bases de données), vérifie des résultats et itère jusqu’à terminer une tâche. Chaque étape peut déclencher plusieurs requêtes au modèle, parfois avec des contextes longs, ce qui augmente mécaniquement le volume de tokens et le temps de calcul. Le coût total se raisonne alors « par objectif » (ex. produire un rapport, corriger un dépôt de code) plutôt que « par message ». Même si le coût unitaire d’inférence diminue, la multiplication des appels peut faire grimper la dépense globale par tâche. C’est un point clé pour les entreprises : l’autonomie et la robustesse d’un agent se paient souvent en itérations supplémentaires.

articles.title: Artefact AI Film Festival : comment l’IA accompagne la création d’un film
articles.text:
Créer un film est loin d’être une sinécure. Entre l’idée de départ et sa réalisation, les obstacles créatifs, techniques et financiers ne manquent pas. Pour donner forme à une histoire, il faut chercher, essayer et souvent recommencer. Un travail que les outils d’intelligence artificielle peuvent désormais accompagner : esquisser un storyboard, explorer une direction artistique ou générer les premières images d’une scène permet de tester des idées avant d’engager des moyens de production plus importants.
Pour sa troisième édition, l’Artefact AI Film Festival offre un cadre à ces expérimentations. Le thème retenu cette année, « (Dis)Connection », invite les participants à explorer les relations entre l’humain et la machine. Les candidatures sont ouvertes jusqu’au 2 décembre 2026.
De quoi donner envie de passer derrière la caméra, fût-elle virtuelle. Mais comment se lancer dans un tel projet ? Quels outils utiliser pour arriver à ses fins ?
Partenaires de cette édition, NVIDIA et LDLC accompagnent les créateurs à différentes étapes de leur projet : NVIDIA à travers ses technologies dédiées à la création et à l’IA, et LDLC dans le choix des équipements permettant de les exploiter.
Artefact AI Film Festival : une troisième édition pour explorer les liens entre cinéma et IA
Porté par mk2 et Artefact, en partenariat avec LDLC et Nvidia, l’Artefact AI Film Festival met à l’honneur des films créés à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle. L’idée n’est pas ici de se livrer à un concours de prompt : les outils doivent servir une histoire, une intention de mise en scène ou une émotion.
Ouvert aux participants du monde entier, le concours impose plusieurs contraintes. Chaque candidat peut soumettre un seul film, d’une durée maximale de 314 secondes, soit 5 minutes et 14 secondes.
Il doit également avoir utilisé au moins une technologie d’IA générative dans chacune des trois phases du projet : préproduction, production et postproduction. Du storyboard au travail sonore, en passant par la génération d’images, l’IA doit donc trouver sa place à plusieurs étapes de la création.
Après « Réalité(s) » et « (Dis)play », cette troisième édition propose un nouveau thème : « (Dis)Connection ». Les participants sont invités à explorer ce qui rapproche ou éloigne l’humain et la machine, l’auteur et son outil, le réel et le virtuel. De quoi nourrir aussi bien les récits que les choix de fabrication des films.
Lancé en 2024 par Artefact et mk2, le festival a d’abord été présidé par Jean-Pierre Jeunet, puis par Cédric Klapisch. Sa deuxième édition a réuni 265 candidatures venues de 52 pays, dont 20 films finalistes en compétition.
Cette année, le jury est coprésidé par Olivier Nakache et Éric Toledano, les réalisateurs, entre autres, d’Intouchables. Le premier prix est doté de 10 000 euros et s’accompagne de la diffusion d’une version de 30 secondes du film lauréat dans toutes les salles mk2 pendant une semaine. Trois autres récompenses de 1 000 euros chacune complètent le palmarès : le prix du jury, le prix du public et le Prix Artefact de la meilleure utilisation de l’IA.
Informations pratiques
| Étape | Dates annoncées | 
| Dépôt des candidatures | Du 2 septembre au 2 décembre 2026 | 
| Vote du public | Du 9 décembre 2026 au 13 janvier 2027 | 
| Délibérations du jury | Janvier 2027 | 
| Remise des prix | Février 2027, au mk2 Bibliothèque | 
Imaginer, itérer, créer : comment les GPU RTX de série 50 peuvent accompagner les cinéastes tout au long de leur projet
Puisque le règlement impose l’IA générative à chaque étape, de la préproduction à la postproduction, les participants doivent penser la place de ces outils dans toute la fabrication de leur film.
Partenaire du festival, Nvidia propose un écosystème matériel et logiciel permettant d’expérimenter avec l’IA sur son propre ordinateur. Avec un PC équipé d’une GeForce RTX de série 50 et un outil comme ComfyUI, il est possible d’installer des modèles compatibles pour générer des images ou des vidéos en local. Le calcul s’effectue alors sur la machine, avec des réglages que l’utilisateur peut conserver, modifier et réutiliser à l’envi.
Pour les cinéastes, l’intérêt est de pouvoir explorer plusieurs pistes : traduire une idée en proposition de décor, comparer des ambiances lumineuses ou préparer une image de référence pour guider la génération d’une séquence. Le choix des plans, leur cohérence et le rythme du récit restent l’affaire du cinéaste, mais ces outils lui donnent de la matière à sélectionner, retravailler et assembler.
Pour passer à la pratique, notre guide ComfyUI détaille l’installation et les premières étapes de génération d’images et de vidéos sur un PC équipé d’une carte Nvidia RTX.
La génération en local offre aussi davantage de maîtrise sur ses outils : en fonctionnement entièrement local, les images et les instructions ne sont pas envoyées à un service distant. Les possibilités dépendent néanmoins du matériel, des modèles installés et de leurs conditions d’utilisation.
Pour accélérer le processus, les GeForce RTX de série 50 s’appuient notamment sur leurs cœurs Tensor, spécialisés dans les calculs d’IA, et sur la prise en charge du FP4. Avec les modèles compatibles dans ComfyUI, ce format de calcul réduit jusqu’à 60 % les besoins en mémoire vidéo et rend la génération jusqu’à 2,5 fois plus rapide, selon Nvidia. L’intérêt, pour le créateur, est concret : moins d’attente entre deux versions pour comparer les résultats et affiner ses choix.
Une fois les images produites, il reste à monter et à finaliser le film. L’environnement Nvidia Studio accompagne également ces étapes, avec des pilotes dédiés et des optimisations dans les applications compatibles, comme Premiere Pro ou Blender. Selon les fonctions utilisées, le GPU accélère certains effets, le rendu 3D ou encore le décodage et l’encodage vidéo. Pour découvrir ces usages à travers les méthodes de professionnels, notre article consacré à Nvidia Studio revient sur le travail des monteurs de Mastu et Michou.
Enfin, pour aller plus loin, Nvidia propose de nombreux guides et tutoriels en ligne :
- Un tutoriel pour apprendre à générer des visuels IA (en anglais)
- Un tutoriel pas à pas sur Github pour générer des assets 3D IA sous Blender
- Le blog de Nvidia pour les créateurs regorge de ressources intéressante pour générer du contenu par IA
Quel équipement faut-il pour se lancer dans la création assistée par IA ?
Pour passer à la pratique, mieux vaut choisir sa machine en fonction des outils et des projets envisagés. Au-delà de la puissance du GPU, plusieurs caractéristiques méritent votre attention :
| Élément à regarder | Pourquoi c’est important | 
| GPU et mémoire vidéo (VRAM) | Exécuter les modèles IA choisis, avec une capacité adaptée à leurs besoins | 
| Mémoire vive (RAM) | Faire fonctionner les logiciels de création et travailler avec plusieurs applications | 
| Stockage SSD | Conserver les modèles, les rushs et les différentes versions du film | 
Côté format, un portable suit le cinéaste en déplacement, tandis qu’une tour offre une installation fixe plus facile à faire évoluer.
Partenaire du festival, LDLC propose de quoi s’équiper pour ces usages. D’un côté, l’enseigne propose une sélection de machines créées spécialement pour répondre aux exigences des profils créatifs et amateurs d’IA. De l’autre, une dimension conseil poussée pour tous ceux qui cherchent un équipement qui répondent à des contraintes précises. Choix du matériel, conception d’une tour personnalisée, conseils généraux : les équipes de LDLC sont là pour vous accompagner quelle que soit votre demande.
L’enseigne offre également cinq ans de garantie sur les ordinateurs éligibles vendus par ses soins, dont les PC intégralement assemblés par LDLC : deux ans de garantie légale, complétés par trois ans de garantie commerciale gratuite, hors batteries et consommables. Un avantage à considérer pour une machine destinée à accompagner plusieurs projets.
