articles.title: Valve publicly mentions HLX, which might be Half-Life 3, for the first time
articles.text:
Crystal ball: Hype surrounding the possibility that Valve was putting the finishing touches on Half-Life 3 reached a fever pitch last year before fading. A fresh batch of data-mining results and comments from Valve this week has reignited anticipation, however. While it remains unclear what precisely the company is working on, it appears to be completely unlike its current stable of live-service games.
Valve hasn't offered substantial details about a new Half-Life project since launching Half-Life: Alyx in 2020, but a quick name-drop has revived debate over whether Half-Life 3 is in advanced development. Code recently added to Deadlock and other Valve games also sheds more light on the game's features, if it indeed exists.
The codename HLX has appeared in the company's code since early 2024, but Valve did not mention it publicly until a Q&A session at GameSoundCon 2026 on Wednesday. Composer and sound designer Mike Morasky confirmed that Deadlock and HLX each have custom HDR implementations.
 – Tyler "Hype Merchant" McVicker (@Tyler_McV) October 22, 2026
Fellow sound designer David Feise, seated next to him, could be heard whispering "nice work," and later quipped that Morasky had only said HLX once, suggesting the mention wasn't meant to be public. This isn't the first time Morasky has referenced future Half-Life projects.
Then, on Thursday, well-known Valve data miner Tyler McVicker released his latest video describing how recent Source 2 engine updates for Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Deadlock might relate to HLX.
Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, and Deadlock are multiplayer games, but several reports from McVicker last year outlined portions of code mentioning systems typically associated with single-player shooters, such as AI-controlled enemies and concepts from prior Half-Life games.
Other features that seem unique to HLX include procedural level alteration, ray tracing, and AMD FSR support. In this week's video, McVicker also described features related to the Combine gunship and other enemies, as well as dynamic rain audio and new cut-scene animation technology.
The data miner has also been tracking Valve's commit rate, which spiked after the recent Source 2 updates. While some observers might suspect AI coding tools are behind the uptick, prior reports lead McVicker to believe the company has been using AI tools since at least 2024. The nature and extent of AI use within Valve remains unclear, but it's possible that HLX or something else is behind the increased activity.

articles.title: Multi-Cloud FinOps: An Engineering Framework for Cross-Cloud Cost Optimization
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Cloud providers in multi-cloud systems charge for data leaving their network, not entering it. The egress costs accumulate silently and are rarely caught before deployment.
- Architecture determines egress cost more than per-unit transfer rates. Where services are placed and how often they communicate matters far more than what you negotiate on billing rates.
- FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) provides a unified billing format across cloud providers, reducing normalization effort, but service-level attribution still requires provider-specific fields, ownership metadata, and network telemetry.
- Replacing continuous cross-cloud data transfer with scheduled synchronization reduces costs significantly without degrading service performance.
- Architecture had a larger impact on cost than provider pricing. In the controlled experiment, changing the communication pattern from synchronous cross-cloud processing to near-source processing saved over $2000 per month, while changing the provider rate saved $825 per month.
Introduction
Multi-cloud architectures give teams the flexibility to optimize for availability, vendor capabilities, and geographic reach. But this flexibility carries a hidden cost due to data movement across cloud provider boundaries. The costs accumulate through service placement decisions, communication patterns, and scaling behavior compounding over time. By the time it shows up on a bill, the architectural damage is done.
Most organizations respond reactively with billing reviews, rate negotiations, and post-production tuning, none of which address the root cause. In multi-cloud systems, cost efficiency should be decided at the design time.
This article applies Backend FinOps to multi-cloud architecture. It covers cost visibility through FOCUS, strategies for reducing cross-cloud data transfer, and engineering practices such as workload placement, synchronization models, and CI/CD-integrated cost governance. The goal is to make cost control a structural property of the system rather than an afterthought. Design systems where the architecture itself keeps costs in check.
Production Observation
While supporting a production retail ordering and payment platform, I observed that a single checkout request could fan out across promotion evaluation, payment authorization, order persistence, and fulfillment-related services. Distributed traces showed that transient downstream failures could turn one logical operation into multiple network calls through retries and repeated retrieval of order context. This problem led us to distinguish interactions that genuinely belonged on the customer-facing critical path from downstream work that did not need to block order confirmation. The practical benefit was lower failure coupling and more predictable checkout latency: A non-critical downstream consumer no longer needed to delay the customer response. I intentionally omit proprietary transaction volumes and provider topology; the controlled experiment later in the article generalizes this production pattern to a multi-cloud setting and quantifies its cost impact.
The Hidden Cost Structure of Cross-Cloud Data Transfer
Advertised egress rates are the starting point, not the whole story. Table 1 shows the layered cost structure verified against official provider pricing as of January 2026.
| Provider | Internet Egress | Hidden Charges | True Cost* | Free Tier | 
| AWS | $0.09/GB (first 10 TB) | +$0.045/GB Network Address Translation (NAT) Gateway, +$0.01/GB cross-AZ | $0.135/GB private subnet | 100 GB/mo | 
| Azure | $0.087/GB (Zone 1) | +$0.02/GB inter-region; zone-to-zone: free | $0.107/GB+ cross-region | 5 GB/mo | 
| GCP | $0.12/GB to internet | +$0.01 to $0.08/GB inter-region; Interconnect discounts | $0.12/GB baseline | 1 GB/mo | 
Table 1. True egress cost structure by provider (January 2026). Sources: AWS, Azure, and GCP. *Private-subnet traffic via NAT Gateway.
Published egress rates reflect only the base cost of data transfer. In practice, additional charges such as NAT Gateway processing, cross-zone, and transit traffic significantly increase the effective cost per gigabyte. For instance, in AWS, routing traffic through NAT Gateways can raise actual egress costs by over fifty percent compared to advertised rates. Similar cost layers exist across all major providers, especially for cross-zone and interregional traffic.
Industry findings show that many organizations underestimate these costs. The issue at the core is structural. Data transfer costs are driven by architecture and data movement patterns, yet they are typically discovered only after deployment through billing reports.
Four Architectural Issues in Multi-Cloud Microservices
The article, Backend FinOps: Engineering Cost-Efficient Microservices in the Cloud,establishes how to optimize microservices within a single cloud boundary; however, multi-cloud environments need further attention. Four patterns, as explained below, account for the majority of avoidable egress spending.
Issue 1: Cross-Cloud Synchronous Communication
In many multi-cloud systems, a single user request passes through services hosted on different cloud providers. Although this approach improves flexibility, it also creates hidden network transfer costs. Every synchronous request between clouds generates egress and gateway charges that increase with traffic volume.
The benchmark below models a typical enterprise setup using published Q1 2026 pricing. A product catalogue service runs on Amazon Web Services EKS, a recommendation engine on Google Cloud, and a fraud detection service on Microsoft Azure. Each service is called synchronously during a customer transaction.
| Configuration | Monthly Transactions | Payload per Hop | Cross-Cloud Traffic | Egress Cost/month(AWS rate) | Egress Cost/month (with NAT GW) | 
| 3-hop cross-cloud chain | 10,000,000 | 5 KB | 50 TB | ~$4,500 | ~$6,750 | 
| 2-hop cross-cloud chain | 10,000,000 | 5 KB | 33 TB | ~$2,970 | ~$4,455 | 
| Single-provider (baseline) | 10,000,000 | 5 KB | 0 TB | $0 | $0 | 
Key Findings
- Every additional cross-cloud service hop increases operational cost.
- A single-cloud deployment avoids interprovider transfer costs entirely for the same workload.
- These costs are determined by architectural design decisions, not runtime configuration.
Both AWS Well-Architected Framework and Google Cloud Multi-Cloud Guidance identify cross-cloud data transfer as a notable cost driver in multi-cloud environments.
from enum import Enum
class TrafficClass(Enum):
    INTERACTIVE = "interactive"
    BACKGROUND = "background"
class CrossCloudGateway:
    def __init__(self, realtime_client, batch_queue):
        self.realtime_client = realtime_client
        self.batch_queue = batch_queue
    def dispatch(self, request, traffic_class):
        if traffic_class is TrafficClass.INTERACTIVE:
            # Customer is waiting, e.g., for payment authorization.
            return self.realtime_client.send(request)
        # Customer is not waiting, e.g., for an analytics export.
        self.batch_queue.enqueue(request)
        return {"status": "accepted"}
# Usage
gateway = CrossCloudGateway(realtime_client, batch_queue)
gateway.dispatch(payment_request, TrafficClass.INTERACTIVE)
gateway.dispatch(analytics_event, TrafficClass.BACKGROUND)
This simplified gateway example makes the traffic classification explicit. A payment authorization is interactive because the customer is waiting for an immediate response, so it is sent synchronously. An analytics event is background because the customer is not waiting, so it can be queued and later batched, compressed, or processed closer to the data source. The key design decision is not the gateway implementation itself, but classifying the workload before it crosses the provider boundary so that interactive and background traffic do not automatically share the same latency, availability, and cost behavior.
For example, if a checkout service in AWS calls a fraud service in Azure before completing an order, the checkout latency and availability now depend on both providers and the network between them.
Retries, timeouts, and downstream fan-out can further amplify the number of cross-cloud calls and transferred bytes. The design question is, therefore, whether the caller truly needs an immediate response. Where it does, teams should use strict timeouts, fallbacks, small payloads, and controlled retries. Where it does not, the dependency can be replaced with asynchronous messaging.
Issue 2: Unnecessary Real-Time Data Transfers Without Freshness Requirement
Most engineering teams stream data between cloud providers continuously because real-time feels operationally correct. In practice, this assumption is rarely tested against actual consumption patterns. Analytics pipelines, Machine learning retraining workflows, and compliance systems predominantly operate on hourly or daily cadences, and incur per-gigabyte egress charges on every data transfer. The organization ends up paying for data movement at the rate of production, not at the rate of consumption.
In this case, the problem is not synchronous application coupling. The customer is not waiting for the analytics system. The problem is that the transfer cadence is faster than the business freshness requirement. Defining an acceptable data age, such as five minutes, one hour, or one day, makes it possible to batch, deduplicate, compress, or aggregate records before transfer.
A published case from Expedia Group clearly highlights this problem. Applications repeatedly fetched the same datasets across AWS regions, causing high cross-region egress costs even though the underlying data changed very little. Instead of transferring the same data repeatedly, Expedia introduced an Alluxio caching layer that served frequently accessed data locally. This reduced cross-region transfer costs by fifty percent, while also improving application performance, all without changing the business logic or the data itself.
The dominant cost factor was the frequency of cross-boundary data transfers, not the per-gigabyte charge, particularly for consumers without strict freshness requirements.
Issue 3: Moving Raw Data Instead of Computed Results
Transferring raw transaction logs, feature data, or clickstreams across cloud boundaries for downstream processing is one of the most cost-intensive data movement patterns. The inefficiency lies not only in the volume transferred, but in moving data that will ultimately be filtered, aggregated, or discarded at the destination.
Industry guidance consistently identifies near-source processing as the primary cost optimization strategy. Both the Azure Well-Architected Framework and Google Cloud's hybrid architecture documentation advocate reducing data before it crosses a provider boundary rather than relying on the destination to perform that reduction. Production evidence reinforces the principle. Siemens redesigned its analytics pipelines to process only incremental changes at the source rather than transferring full dataset copies on each run, reducing pipeline maintenance costs by ninety percent and cutting daily load time from six hours to twenty-five minutes.
This principle is increasingly reflected in platform architecture. As an example, Google BigQuery Omni moves compute to where data resides in AWS or Azure rather than transferring data to Google Cloud, eliminating egress charges entirely for qualifying cross-cloud analytics workloads. The architectural consensus is clear: Process data at the source and transfer only the result.
Issue 4: Cross-Cloud Broadcast Amplification
In event-driven systems such as gaming and IoT platforms, a single state update is often broadcast to multiple cloud providers at the same time. Although each cloud receives the same information, the data is transferred independently to every destination, causing redundant cross-cloud traffic and multiplying egress costs.
A more efficient approach is to publish the update once to a shared distribution layer (such as a content delivery network (CDN) or central hub cloud), and allow other environments to retrieve it locally. This approach ensures the same information is delivered without repeated cross-provider transfers.
This pattern is already used in production systems. Services such as Amazon CloudFront and Cloudflare cache content at the edge so repeated requests are served locally instead of repeatedly crossing provider boundaries. In analytics, Google Cloud’s BigQuery Omni follows a similar principle by processing data where it resides instead of duplicating datasets across environments.
Transfer data once. Reuse it at the point of consumption.
Controlled Experiment: Cross-Cloud Checkout Data Transfer
Experimental Background and Setup
The experiment models a common e-commerce checkout flow. During checkout, the customer submits a cart, and the AWS-hosted checkout service validates prices and inventory, calculates tax and discounts, authorizes payment, creates the order, and returns an order confirmation.
After the order is completed, the same order data is also required by a reporting platform in another cloud for sales dashboards and operational analytics. This reporting step is not required to complete the customer’s purchase, but poor architecture can still place it directly on the checkout path.
To measure this trade-off, the experiment compares three ways of delivering completed-order data:
- With synchronous transfer, the checkout service sends the full order payload to the remote reporting platform and waits for its response before confirming the order.
- In an hourly batch transfer, the checkout service confirms the order immediately, queues the reporting event in AWS, and later transfers deduplicated and compressed records in hourly batches.
- With near-source processing, AWS calculates the required dashboard metrics locally and transfers only summarized results to the remote platform.
All three approaches support the same hourly reporting requirement. The experiment therefore isolates how the communication pattern affects checkout latency, cross-cloud traffic, and network cost.
Workload
The test used one hundred thousand synthetic completed orders. Each order produced an average cross-cloud payload of two hundred fifty kilobytes, including order details, line items, payment metadata, and fulfillment information.
Traffic was generated over one hour with:
- An average load of 25 orders per second
- A peak load of 100 orders per second
- A payload size of 250 KB per order
- A remote-service latency of 100-300 ms
- A retry policy of two retries following timeout or failure
The results were then projected to a production-scale workload of one hundred million completed orders per month.
Metrics
The experiment captured:
- Checkout p95 response time
- Cross-cloud requests
- Cross-cloud transferred volume
- Retry volume
- Projected monthly network cost
- Estimated annual savings
Network cost was calculated using an illustrative transfer rate of $0.09 per gigabyte. A second calculation used $0.135 per gigabyte to represent $0.09 per gigabyte of transfer plus an illustrative $0.045 per gigabyte gateway-processing charge.
Experimental Results
| Architecture | Checkout p95 latency | Requests per 100,000 orders | Projected monthly volume | Monthly cost at $0.09/GB | 
| Synchronous transfer | 420 ms | 100,000 | 25,000 GB | $2,250 | 
| Hourly batch transfer | 145 ms | 24 batch transfers | 10,000 GB | $900 | 
| Near-source processing | 140 ms | 24 summary transfers | 1,250 GB | $112.50 | 
The batch architecture reduced transferred volume by sixty percent through deduplication and compression. Near-source processing reduced volume by ninety-five percent because only order counts, sales totals, payment distributions, and other dashboard metrics crossed the boundary.
Cost Impact
| Architecture | Monthly cost at $0.135/GB | Monthly savings vs. synchronous | Annual savings | 
| Synchronous transfer | $3,375.00 | – | – | 
| Hourly batch transfer | $1,350.00 | $2,025.00 | $24,300 | 
| Near-source processing | $168.75 | $3,206.25 | $38,475 | 
Key Observations
Synchronous communication increased both latency and failure coupling. Checkout confirmation depended on the remote reporting platform. Remote latency, timeouts, and retries directly affected the customer-facing transaction.
Batch processing improved both cost and reliability. Removing reporting from the checkout path reduced p95 latency from 420 milliseconds to 145 milliseconds while lowering projected network cost by sixty percent.
Near-source processing produced the greatest cost benefit. Transferring only summarized dashboard results reduced projected monthly cost from $3,375 to $168.75 when gateway processing was included, a ninety-five percent reduction and approximately $38,475 in annual savings.
Architecture had a larger impact than provider pricing. Changing the base transfer rate from $0.087 to $0.12 per gigabyte changed the synchronous monthly cost by $825. Changing the architecture from synchronous transfer to near-source processing saved more than $2,000 per month even before gateway charges were included.
Finding
The experiment showed that the largest financial benefit came from reducing the amount of data crossing the cloud boundary, not simply selecting a provider with a lower egress rate. Asynchronous processing removed the remote reporting platform from the customer-facing path, while batching, compression, and near-source aggregation reduced recurring transfer cost.
Near-source processing was appropriate because the reporting platform required hourly summaries rather than complete real-time order records. Workloads requiring immediate fraud decisions, authorization responses, or transaction-level audit data may still require synchronous or record-level communication.
Cost as a Non-Functional Requirement
Sustainable cost control does not come from periodic billing reviews. It comes from treating cost as a non-functional requirement managed with the same discipline as latency or reliability.
Figure 1. Cross-Cloud Egress Cost Management Lifecycle. (Source: created by author.)
Figure 1 illustrates how cost can be managed as a continuous engineering concern rather than a post facto financial exercise. The loop connects the key stages of the software lifecycle design, build, and runtime into a single feedback system.
The process begins at design time, where teams define cost expectations upfront. This upfront definition includes estimating data transfer, understanding service placement, and setting a cost budget for cross-cloud interactions. These early decisions establish the baseline for all subsequent stages.
During implementation, a lightweight validation step can estimate projected monthly egress based on deployment metadata, expected request volume, and payload size. If estimated network costs exceed predefined thresholds, the pipeline can require an architecture review before deployment. Similar to security or quality gates, this approach allows engineering teams to identify inefficient communication patterns before they become operational expenses.
At build time, these expectations are enforced through CI/CD pipelines. Automated checks validate whether new changes such as additional cross-cloud calls or larger payloads remain within the defined cost boundaries. This automation prevents inefficient patterns from reaching production.
During runtime, actual cost is continuously monitored. When spending deviates from the expected budget, alerts are sent directly to the teams responsible for the service. This use of alerts ensures that cost issues are addressed quickly, in the same way as performance or reliability incidents.
jobs:
  cost-impact-analysis:
    steps:
      - name: Estimate cross-cloud egress impact
        run: python3 scripts/estimate_egress_cost.py
      - name: Require review if threshold exceeded
        run: |
          if [ "$EGRESS_DELTA" -gt "$THRESHOLD" ]; then
            echo "Cross-cloud egress impact requires architecture review"
            exit 1
          fi
This type of check should not block every deployment. Its purpose is to catch material changes, such as a new cross-cloud dependency, a larger payload, or a new real-time synchronization.
The optimization loop uses this runtime data to identify inefficiencies and apply targeted improvements, such as reducing data transfer, compressing payloads, or adjusting synchronization frequency. Insights from these optimizations feed into post-incident reviews, where teams refine cost models and improve future designs.
Underlying all stages is the FOCUS 1.4 normalization layer, which standardizes cost data across cloud providers. This standardization enables consistent, service-level cost visibility, making it possible to track, compare, and govern costs throughout the lifecycle.
In summary, the diagram represents a closed-loop system where cost is planned, enforced, observed, and continuously improved integrated directly into engineering workflows rather than treated as a separate financial activity.
Practical Limitations: What Does Not Work Well Yet
FOCUS improves billing normalization, but it does not provide causal service-level attribution on its own. Enterprise discounts, marketplace fees, NAT and inter-region charges, and shared-platform allocations can still require provider-specific mapping. Billing exports are also retrospective. They show what was charged, not which runtime request, retry, or fan-out generated the traffic. In practice, normalized cost data must be joined with ownership tags, distributed traces, and network flow logs. FOCUS is therefore a normalization foundation, not a replacement for observability or internal chargeback logic.
The result is a closed-loop model in which cost is estimated at design time, checked during delivery, observed in production, and fed back into architecture decisions. Cost becomes part of the engineering lifecycle rather than a separate financial activity.
FOCUS-Aligned Multi-Cloud FinOps Framework
Implementation Roadmap
Phase 1: Establish Visibility (Months One to Two)
Connect all provider billing exports into a single data warehouse using FOCUS-compatible outputs from AWS, Azure, and GCP. Standardize resource tagging across all environments so costs can be attributed to owning teams and services. Build one dashboard that answers a single question: How much egress did each cross-cloud service pair generate last month? Without this baseline, every subsequent decision rests on estimates rather than evidence.
Phase 2: Target Quick Wins (Months Two to Four)
Use the attribution data from Phase 1 to identify the top egress cost drivers. Apply the highest-return interventions first: compression, batch scheduling, and CDN routing on the paths generating the most spend. These changes require no service migration and typically deliver thirty to sixty percent egress reduction on targeted paths. Update deployment policies to block new unreviewed cross-cloud integrations from reaching production. The goal is to establish a measurable cost reduction, within two to four months, that builds the organizational confidence to fund Phase 3.
Phase 3: Architectural Realignment (Months Four to Twelve)
With quick wins captured and attribution data established, address the structural cost drivers. In other words, you should consolidate high-frequency calling services within shared provider boundaries, redesign data pipelines to process at the source rather than transferring raw data, and embed cost review into architecture decision records. By the end of this phase, cost governance should be routine, reviewed at design time, enforced at deployment, and attributed to service owners at runtime.
The three phases follow the FinOps maturity sequence. Measure first, optimize second, and institutionalize third. Each phase funds the next.
Metrics for Multi-Cloud FinOps
Total monthly egress is useful, but it can fall simply because demand fell. The following metrics are more diagnostic because they connect the bill to system behavior.
| Metric | Calculation | Engineering signal | 
| Cross-cloud bytes per business transaction | Cross-cloud bytes / completed business transactions | Shows whether each transaction is becoming more network-efficient. | 
| Cross-cloud call amplification | Cross-cloud calls / originating business transaction | Exposes retries, fan-out, and chatty dependency chains. | 
| Effective transfer cost | All transfer and path-processing charges / cross-cloud GB | Reveals the effect of gateways, zones, regions, and connectivity choices. | 
| Attributed egress coverage | Egress cost mapped to a service and owner / total egress cost | Shows whether the data is actionable rather than merely visible. | 
| Freshness and latency guardrails | Data age, p95 latency, error rate, and recovery behavior before and after optimization | Prevents savings from weakening an explicit service objective. | 
Conclusion
Multi-cloud cost control is an engineering discipline, not a billing problem. Every dollar of egress spent reflects a placement decision, a synchronization frequency, or a data movement pattern that was chosen at the design time and billed at runtime.
The path forward is sequential, establish attribution first, optimize second, realign architecture third. Teams that skip to optimization without visibility reduce costs on the wrong paths. Teams that build visibility first generate the evidence that makes harder architectural changes defensible.
Start with the FOCUS billing query. Rank your top five cross-cloud egress paths. Ask whether each one moves data in the right form, at the right frequency, and across the right boundary. The answer to that question is worth more than any rate negotiation.
Design systems where cost efficiency is an outcome of architectural decisions rather than operational intervention.

articles.title: Apple ya estaría desarrollando el iPhone Duo 2: la segunda versión del teléfono plegable tendría Face ID
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo todavía no llega a todos sus compradores y Apple ya trabaja en una segunda generación de su primer celular plegable. La próxima versión del dispositivo podría incorporar Face ID, el sistema de reconocimiento facial que la compañía utiliza en sus smartphones tradicionales y que fue descartado en el modelo original para ahorrar espacio interno y reducir el peso del equipo.
Según Mark Gurman, periodista de Bloomberg especializado en Apple, la empresa ya prueba prototipos del iPhone Duo 2 con tecnología de autenticación facial. La intención sería incorporar esta función en el dispositivo que llegaría al mercado en 2027, aunque la decisión todavía no está tomada.
La posible incorporación de Face ID respondería a una de las principales críticas que recibió el primer plegable de Apple: la ausencia de reconocimiento facial y el regreso de Touch ID, el sistema de identificación mediante huella dactilar. La compañía también estaría evaluando otros cambios, como la incorporación de un botón de acción similar al presente en otros modelos de iPhone.
Face ID sería la principal novedad del iPhone Duo 2
De acuerdo con Gurman, Apple está probando la tecnología de reconocimiento facial en prototipos de la segunda generación de su celular plegable. Una de las posibilidades es que Face ID funcione desde la pantalla exterior, aunque todavía no se conoce cómo quedaría distribuido el hardware frontal.
En el modelo original, la cámara para selfies se ubica en la esquina superior derecha de la pantalla externa. La llegada de Face ID podría obligar a modificar esa disposición para integrar los componentes necesarios para la autenticación facial.
Por ahora, no está confirmado si Apple mantendrá esa ubicación o realizará cambios en el diseño. Tampoco existe una decisión definitiva sobre la incorporación de Face ID, por lo que las características del iPhone Duo 2 podrían variar durante su desarrollo.
La autenticación facial permitiría desbloquear el teléfono y validar determinadas operaciones sin necesidad de apoyar un dedo sobre el sensor. Esta función está presente desde hace años en buena parte de los iPhone de gama alta, pero quedó fuera del primer plegable debido a las restricciones de espacio propias de su diseño.
Por qué Apple habría descartado el reconocimiento facial
La ausencia de Face ID en el iPhone Duo responde a una decisión de ingeniería. Apple necesitaba reorganizar los componentes internos para adaptar el dispositivo a su formato plegable, de modo que prescindir del sistema facial le permitió disponer de más espacio y controlar el peso.
En su lugar, la empresa recurrió a Touch ID. Sin embargo, esta decisión generó críticas entre algunos analistas y usuarios, que señalaron dificultades para reconocer las huellas en el primer intento y cuestionaron la practicidad del sistema.
La falta de aplicaciones de terceros optimizadas para aprovechar la pantalla plegable también apareció entre las observaciones iniciales sobre el equipo. Estas limitaciones muestran que Apple todavía tiene margen para ajustar tanto el hardware como la experiencia de uso de su nueva categoría de smartphones.
Aunque Face ID sería el cambio más relevante, la compañía también estudia incorporar un botón de acción. Este control permitiría ejecutar funciones configurables, como ocurre en otros teléfonos de la marca, aunque todavía no se conocen los usos que tendría en el plegable.
Cuándo llegaría el iPhone Duo 2
Según la información publicada por Gurman, Apple apunta al otoño de 2027 para presentar la segunda generación del dispositivo. No obstante, la fecha dependerá de cómo avance el desarrollo y de las decisiones que tome la compañía sobre sus características.
Mientras tanto, el primer iPhone Duo comienza su llegada a los compradores el 23 de octubre de 2026. La disponibilidad inicial sería limitada debido a la elevada demanda y a las reservas que, en algunos casos, se han desplazado hasta noviembre, diciembre e incluso enero de 2027.
Apple también prepara una actualización de software para el plegable. Con iOS 27.2, prevista para la próxima semana según la información disponible, el dispositivo incorporaría compatibilidad con el Apple Pencil USB-C.
La evolución del iPhone Duo permitirá evaluar si Apple prioriza en futuras generaciones la autenticación facial, los cambios de diseño y una mejor adaptación de las aplicaciones. Por ahora, Face ID figura entre las novedades en evaluación, pero su llegada al modelo de 2027 todavía no está garantizada.

articles.title: Dayforce to acquire Ribbon AI to bolster AI recruitment capabilities | BetaKit
articles.text:
Dayforce is looking to help its enterprise customers offload some job interviews to AI.
The news: The Canadian-led human resources (HR) management software company agreed on Friday to acquire Toronto-based Ribbon AI. Ribbon’s AI-native platform conducts screening interviews on behalf of companies, using a generated voice to ask prospective employees questions and conduct conversations about the job based on its description.
Dayforce said in a statement that Ribbon’s technology will be natively integrated into its new agentic recruiting experience, with its combined capabilities helping Dayforce customers source, screen, evaluate, and engage talent. The purchase price was not disclosed, nor was the timeline for when the transaction will be completed.
From the source: “AI can take on more of the manual, time-sensitive work that slows hiring down, while recruiters focus on engaging talent and making the decisions that matter,” Dayforce’s Toronto-based founder and CEO, David Ossip, said in a statement. “Ribbon accelerates our vision for agentic recruiting, helping frontline organizations get the right people into critical roles faster and build a more responsive, resilient workforce.”
The context: The transaction follows Dayforce, which is headquartered in both Toronto and Minneapolis, being acquired and taken private by US-based private equity giant Thoma Bravo for $12.3 billion USD ($17 billion CAD) earlier this year.
Ribbon was founded in 2022 by CEO Arsham Ghahramani and COO Dave Vu. The company raised $8.2 million USD in early 2025, led by Radical Ventures. In addition to AI interviewing, Ribbon also provides AI-powered talent sourcing, and Dayforce said it’s nearing the creation of an AI scheduling agent.
Final thought: Dayforce said that Ribbon’s technology is proven at scale, with hundreds of customers and more than one million completed interviews. However, the rise of AI job interviewers has been met with criticism, whether it’s because of the impact of AI on the job market, the encouragement of insincerity, or because some feel being screened by an AI is dehumanizing.
Feature image courtesy Dayforce.

articles.title: China APT Uses AI Pentest Tool Artex in ConnectWise Attacks
articles.text:
A China-linked threat actor has been using the open source AI penetration testing framework Artex to automate a recent ConnectWise hacking campaign targeting hundreds of organizations, Microsoft reports.
Tracked as Storm-0940 and active since at least 2021, the APT is known for relying on password spraying and the exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing applications to hack into organizations across multiple sectors.
Starting in early September 2026, the threat actor was seen abusing Artex to automate its attacks, and previous reporting by CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and Recorded Future linked this AI-powered activity to attacks targeting South Korean financial institutions.
Now, Microsoft says Storm-0940 used Artex to automate intrusions into ConnectWise customers’ environments in mid-October. In response, ConnectWise suspended several services, including Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management.
At the time, Huntress observed the attackers using compromised ConnectWise application credentials to access hundreds of Microsoft 365 tenants, including over 300 Entra tenants.
According to Microsoft, the threat actor relied on Artex to accelerate reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. It hit over 300 accounts across eight organizations at a pace of more than 2,900 attempts per minute.
“Following the unauthorized access, Storm-0940 used Artex to attempt to sign-in to more than 2,250 tenants. While OAuth application abuse is a typical part of Storm-0940’s toolset, in this case the actor used Artex to accelerate the activity to machine speed,” Microsoft says.
Microsoft captured 151,000+ failed logon events associated with the attacks, but also observed successful authentication to customer environments using the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications.
“In some of these environments, the AI agents (on behalf of the threat actor) progressed beyond authentication to Microsoft Graph and directory operations, including reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups, and privileged roles,” Microsoft explains.
By changing application credentials, the attackers ensured persistent access to the victims’ environments even after the affected application was remediated, Microsoft warns.
“Organizations should examine service principal sign-ins alongside subsequent Microsoft Graph activity, directory changes, and resource access, correlating suspicious events with authorized administrative activity,” the tech giant notes.
According to Microsoft, since early September, Storm-0940 has used Artex in automated attacks against hundreds of organizations across the aerospace, automotive, chemicals, defense, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, and technology sectors, as well as against non-profits and think tanks.
This week, Zscaler published a technical deep-dive into Storm-0940’s AI-assisted attacks, including details on how the threat actor uses Artex, its configurations, synchronization scripts, a Claude Code prompt history, and network routing tools.

articles.title: London’s Cognitive Credit lands €35.73 million to scale its AI and data platform for credit markets | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cognitive Credit, the London-based provider of corporate credit data, analytics and AI technology, has secured a €35.73 million ($40 million) strategic growth investment.
The investment round was led by global growth equity firm Summit Partners, with continued participation from existing investor ETFS Capital. The investment follows an €8.93 million ($10 million) Series B led by ETFS Capital in September 2024, and a €7.17 million (£6 million) Series A led by Fitch Ventures in November 2021
“High-quality data at speed and scale is critical to powering AI workflows that credit professionals will increasingly rely on for high-stakes decisions,” said Chris Bon, a Partner at Summit Partners who has joined the Cognitive Credit Board of Directors.
Founded in 2017 by Robert Slater, Cognitive Credit was built by ex-credit analysts who experienced first-hand the limitations of relying on tools designed for equity markets, at a time when no credible alternative existed for the credit space. The company set out to address what it saw as a long-overdue digital transformation in corporate credit markets, one of the world’s largest asset classes with nearly €12.5 trillion ($14 trillion) raised in 2025 alone, according to OECD’s Global Debt Report 2026.
Cognitive Credit’s integrated web application provides support across the credit research workflow, combining verified data, advanced analytics and domain-specialist generative AI capabilities. Its platform is powered by proprietary data developed through the analysis of hundreds of thousands of financial reports to give analysts on-demand access to audit-grade credit models and primary reporting libraries across 3,500+ corporate bond and loan issuers in the US, Europe and emerging markets.
“Cognitive Credit is purpose-built for credit analysis and leverages institutional-grade technology to provide speed, precision, and auditability across thousands of issuers and to support leading banks and asset managers in use cases where accuracy and verifiability are critical. We’re excited to partner with Robert and the team as they further expand their presence and offering and help credit professionals put AI to work with confidence,” added Bon.
Cognitive Credit’s product suite includes a web application, an Excel add-in that streams proprietary financials directly into existing spreadsheets, a REST API for integration into institutional tech stacks, and a Claude Connector that allows analysts to query issuers and surface financial insights directly from within the Claude environment.
The company says all the outputs are fully auditable and traceable to source, a critical differentiator for institutional clients. This emphasis on verified data could be the reason why the company has managed to power analytical workflows for more than 80% of the top 25 global asset managers by AUM and all top 10 global debt league table investment banks. In a statement, Summit Partners says Cognitive Credit has achieved 240% active user growth and more than doubled its global bond and loan issuer coverage.
“Demand for credit-specialist technology will continue to accelerate from here, and we are pleased to partner with Summit Partners on our next phase of growth. With the imminent launch of DealConnect, ongoing innovation in our AI deployments, and many additional capabilities planned for 2027, we’re offering credit teams the highest quality data and analytics they require for differentiated analysis and high impact decision-making,” said Slater, founder and CEO of Cognitive Credit.
With this strategic investment, Cognitive Credit will accelerate its commercial expansion into the US and advance its next generation of products. These include the imminent launch of DealConnect, designed to enable on-demand access to detailed credit models for private issuers that report via secure data rooms, and the pending deployment of agentic credit analysis. The company also plans to continue expanding its issuer coverage into new credit markets.

articles.title: Review: Crystal Lake suffers a bit from its obsession with Pam Voorhees
articles.text:
Peacock series Crystal Lake doesn’t feel like a Friday the 13th movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original Friday the 13th movie but avoids major Crystal Lake spoilers.)
Instead, Crystal Lake strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory, while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son, Jason.
Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans, who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth.
Ars dug into news archives and found interviews where Palmer explained that the later films did nothing to expand the character, offering only “stupid” lines. There was no reason for the actor—who at the height of her fame dated James Dean and was often typecast as the sweet-faced girl-next-door—to stoop to stepping back into Pam’s shoes. She famously only agreed to do the first movie because her Mercedes broke down on the Connecticut Turnpike and she needed a new car. She worked 10 days to capture her scenes, got paid $10,000, bought a new car, and expected nobody to remember her performance.
“I read that script and thought ‘What a piece of junk,’” Palmer said in 2005.
Palmer often criticized the later movies for bringing back Jason’s mom but giving her nothing to do. So, while some die-hard Friday the 13th fans may find Crystal Lake slow and foreign in the first few episodes, it’s worth sticking around for the first stab at fulfilling Palmer’s dream of Pam being more than just a helicopter mom of a vengeful boy living at the bottom of a cursed lake.

articles.title: Wolves roam into Finnish villages after Google destroys 1,300 acres of forest for AI data centers — forest where wolf packs used to live is now an expanse of mud
articles.text:
Wolves roam into Finnish villages after Google destroys 1,300 acres of forest for AI data centers — forest where wolf packs used to live is now an expanse of mud
This is thankfully a less common but still very serious side effect of an AI data center being built nearby.
Google’s Finland country manager has apologized for unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have turned 816 acres of forest into an expanse of mud. The American search and AI giant has also been told to cease work where it has cleared roughly 500 acres of forest, 55 miles southeast of the village of Otanmäki. Now The Guardian reports that wolves, who used to live in the forests, are roaming into villages neighboring these man-made muddy wastelands.
Local anger continues to simmer over the damage done to Finnish forests, as Google seems to have ridden roughshod over regulations in the hurry to build new AI data centers in Finland. However, the report suggests that it isn’t just environmentalists who have a beef with Google. Some families say wolves and other wild animals have entered the countryside villages. This would be a serious human safety concern.
“We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest,” explained Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived in Otanmäki for generations. Ranta also fears the U.S.-owned data centers will make Finland an even juicier target for Russian aggression.
Finland is far from the first place targeted by AI data center developers to complain about environmental effects. This latest report also cites locals grumbling about construction/factory noise, streams turning brown, and rare birds being pushed out, among other unwanted side effects. We’ve seen similar concerns voiced across the U.S. and in other countries.
Google’s flouting of environmental policy has been unprecedented and clear, a representative of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL) indicated to The Guardian. The Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) seems to agree, as it issued an order for Google to stop development near Muhos and Otanmäki. Nevertheless, a Google spokesperson was upbeat. “We will fully comply with LVV’s requests in this matter,” they said. “We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organizations.” Google must be hoping the touted business benefits of the data centers will sway the government and/or regulators.
We last reported on these in-development data centers in Finland earlier this month, after the Finnish government (LVV) gave notice to Google to stop its construction activities in Muhos and Kajaani (near Otanmäki).

articles.title: Neues Leben für alte iPods: Diese Software-Lösungen sind besser als die von Apple
articles.text:
Neues Leben für alte iPods: Diese Software-Lösungen sind besser als die von Apple
Spätestens mit der Vorstellung des Widescreen-iPods mit Touch-Eingabe, des „revolutionären“ Mobiltelefons und des Internet-Communicators, waren die Zeiten des iPods vorbei. Schließlich handelt es sich dabei um das erste iPhone, das – wie Steve Jobs mehrfach wiederholte – einen iPod bereits eingebaut hatte. Heutzutage sorgt ironischerweise genau dieses Gerät dafür, dass Nutzer:innen wieder verstärkt zum iPod greifen – auch noch pünktlich zum 25-jährigen Jubiläum. Schließlich handelt es sich dabei um ein sogenanntes „Single Purpose Device“, ein Gadget, das nur einen Zweck erfüllt: ohne ständige Unterbrechung durch Nachrichten und Social Media Musik hören zu können.
Doch wie kommt heutzutage die Musik auf den iPod? Früher hat man dafür iTunes genutzt. Seit macOS Catalina handelt es sich dabei aber nur noch um einen Shop für Musik. Wir zeigen, wie du deinen alten iPod mit Bordmitteln wieder mit Musik bespielst – und welche Apps den Job noch besser erledigen.

articles.title: Microsoft recula con la IA en Windows 11 y retira 8 funciones de Copilot
articles.text:
Microsoft continúa ajustando su estrategia de inteligencia artificial en Windows 11. A unos meses de prometer cambios estructurales, el gigante tecnológico confirmó que retirará varias acciones de Copilot integradas en el Explorador de archivos. La compañía no se olvidará por completo de su asistente, ya que seguirá reforzándolo en otras áreas que ofrezcan un valor claro a los usuarios.
Según recoge Windows Latest, Microsoft eliminará ocho funciones de Copilot que están disponibles desde el menú contextual del Explorador de archivos. Cuando hagas clic derecho, ya no podrás acceder a las opciones para resumir documentos, comparar archivos, extraer texto o explicar el contenido de una imagen. Estas funciones estaban vinculadas a OneDrive y los servicios de Copilot y desaparecerán a partir de diciembre de 2026.
“Estamos simplificando cómo la gente usa Copilot con sus archivos de OneDrive en el Explorador de archivos”, dijo la compañía en una actualización del Centro de Administración de Microsoft. “Los usuarios pueden seguir trabajando con sus archivos de OneDrive en Copilot desde un lugar central, haciendo clic derecho en un archivo y seleccionando Preguntar a Copilot, o pasando el cursor sobre un archivo en el Explorador de Archivos Inicio y seleccionando el icono de Copilot.”
Las acciones de Copilot no desaparecerán por completo, ya que seguirán disponibles en el centro de actividades de OneDrive.
¿Qué funciones de Copilot desaparecen del Explorador de archivos?
Las funciones de Copilot que se eliminarán del menú contextual del Explorador de archivos se encuentran dentro de la categoría OneDrive. Cuando haces clic derecho en un archivo, el menú muestra varias funciones de IA para OneDrive que cambian en función del tipo de contenido. Estas son:
- Resumir
- Crear FAQ
- Comparar archivos
- Hacer una pregunta
- Explicar imagen
- Explicar imágenes
- Comparar imágenes
- Extraer texto
Si nunca has visto estas funciones, es porque no tienes instalado OneDrive o desinstalaste la app de Copilot para Windows 11. En caso de que las utilices, solo tendrás unas cuantas semanas antes de que Microsoft las elimine del menú contextual. La compañía confirmó que el retiro comenzará a mediados de noviembre y se completará en diciembre de 2026.
La retirada de Copilot en el Explorador de archivos es una nueva fase del plan de Microsoft para reducir la presencia de la IA en el sistema operativo. Si hacemos memoria, el jefe de Windows, Pavan Davuluri, prometió hace unos meses que se enfocarían en mejorar el rendimiento y la experiencia de uso. El directivo tuvo que dar marcha atrás a una estrategia con la que buscaba convertir a Windows 11 en un sistema impulsado por agentes, una propuesta que recibió un rechazo inmediato de miles de usuarios inconformes.
Microsoft no eliminará del todo la IA en Windows 11
Desde marzo de este año, Microsoft ha eliminado las integraciones de Copilot en Recortes, Fotos, Bloc de notas y los Widgets. Xbox también dio marcha atrás a otras funciones que se apoyarían en la IA para mejorar las sesiones de juego, las cuales nunca ganaron el apoyo necesario.
Pese a ello, la compañía sigue firme en su objetivo de convertir a Windows 11 en un sistema para el trabajo con agentes de inteligencia artificial. La prueba más reciente fue el evento de Surface, en donde se confirmaron los primeros ordenadores con el chip RTX Spark de NVIDIA. Las dos compañías impulsarán los portátiles con estos procesadores que permiten ejecutar modelos de lenguaje directamente en el dispositivo, algo que Qualcomm prometió hace dos años con los Copilot+ PC y que nunca terminaron de cuajar.

articles.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
articles.text:
OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”
OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
AI agents can still communicate without a network connection, OpenAI found.
OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.
Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:
Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.
OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”
In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

articles.title: 'There’s definitely some secrets and stuff that we had turned off' — WoW: Forever senior game designer confirms there are 'thousands' of items and 'things to discover that we didn't surface' in the beta
articles.text:
WoW: Forever senior game designer says there is 'really well-buried stuff' in the game 'that's going to take people a long time to find' that was 'turned off' for the beta — 'There's going to be things to discover that we didn't surface'
There's more to discover when WoW: Forever launches next month
- World of Warcraft: Forever senior game designer Josh “Aggrend” Greenfield confirms the MMO still has "thousands" of undiscovered secrets
- Greenfield says, "There’s going to be things to discover that we didn’t surface"
- He adds that there is "really well-buried stuff out there that’s probably going to take people a long time to find"
Blizzard Entertainment has confirmed that World of Warcraft: Forever features thousands of secrets, like items, that were turned off in the beta.
In its 'End of Beta Special' podcast, senior game designer Josh “Aggrend” Greenfield, alongside other WoW: Forever developers, was asked about the undiscovered secrets in the beta, revealing that Blizzard disabled many of them for the first 30 levels (via GameSpot).
"There’s definitely some secrets and stuff that we had turned off," Greenfield said. "There’s going to be things to discover that we didn’t surface, suffice to say that."
When host Josh Corbett brought up that there are supposedly "thousands" of things hidden in the MMO, Greenfield agreed; some of those secrets include items and recipes, but the developer refrained from sharing more details.
"Honestly, it's almost kind of hard to say, because the thing is, I guess it's interesting to frame it like this, that our team has gone through this sort of evolution," Greenfield said. "We're a lot larger than we were before; we have a lot more really talented designers, really creative people working on it, and I think we've all sort of done our own little things here and there along the way of 'I'm going to hide this in this nook and cranny, and I'm going to turn it off for beta, and then we'll see what people see,' and stuff like that."
He added that there are "all kinds of things" to uncover and hinted at "fun things" like "emergent behaviors that have happened in the game based on the things that people have found" and "some of the new sort of technology tools we have to play with."
"It’s hard to talk about secret stuff," Greenfield continued. "It’s secret, right? We want people to find it. There’s some really, really, really cool, and really, really, really well-buried stuff out there that’s probably going to take people a long time to find. If we tip our hats to it too much, it’s just going to take the fun away."

Many of these secrets are so hidden that even data miners can uncover them, and lead encounter designer Michael Nuthals more or less confirmed during the podcast that some features may be used in future WoW: Forever content, such as the Manor Mistmantle, which was recently found in Duskwood.
"There might be some homes, some manors, out there that folks have found that might be something interesting in the future,” Nuthals said. "You might have seen some instance portals hiding in some inconspicuous spots. There are some things coming in the future, and we’re really excited to share those as we get there."
WoW: Forever launches on November 4, and the game's beta officially ends today after getting a short extension.

articles.title: OPINION: Robotics are essential for Europe’s energy transition | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s energy transition story is usually told through assets: more renewable generation, smarter grids, electric vehicles and battery storage. Yet while much of the debate focuses on financing and building infrastructure, a different challenge is emerging beneath the surface: operating and maintaining a rapidly expanding asset base over the next several decades.
But the high-margin subsidised programmes that kick-started the industry are being phased out, and operators are facing a new reality of low-margin operations at scale. Combined with the demographic squeeze on the European workforce, the industry looks ripe for automation. Maybe even for robots.
The problem is well-known and systemic. Transmission networks are aging – some 40% of Europe’s distribution grids are over 40 years old – and cross-border capacity is set to double. Offshore wind is moving further from shore and into deeper water. Solar is multiplying faster than construction and maintenance teams can keep up with.
The jobs required to operate all of this are highly skilled or physically demanding and impossible to scale quickly: rope-access technicians, electrical engineers, subsea specialists, offshore crews. You cannot train a generation of them in a hiring cycle, and Europe’s demographics make the recruitment harder every year.
On the other side sits the newest trend in AI. “Physical AI” – large models and computer vision wrapped around a machine that moves – feeds hope for something close to a science-fiction solution. Capital has followed: foundation models for robotics, task-specific platforms, middleware to run fleets. What was research five years ago is now in early production across several industries, also by European energy operators. Among European energy operators, though, the pilot is still the standard unit of deployment.
Reality moves slower, but the underlying idea – raise output and de-risk demographics at the same time – is understood, and it does not require full autonomy to pay off. For now it is about making the people already on the payroll more productive: engineers delivering higher inspecting output, system designs that remove the need to send a crew into a hostile environment, machines that facilitate maintenance work with little manual additions. These advancements create capacity without waiting years for new workers. The infrastructure can keep scaling even when headcount cannot.
The build is financed but the operating cost is the open question
Europe is entering a period of extraordinary expansion. Solar capacity needs to grow 107% by 2030, wind 84%, electricity demand 60%, and transmission must roughly triple – with nearly €600 billion of grid investment needed between now and the end of the decade. In practical terms that means around 150 million solar panels and 150,000 wind turbines to install and then keep running, alongside an existing asset base that is getting older.
For most of the last two decades this was very lucrative, derisked through subsidised feed-in tariffs over up to 20 years. As feed-in tariffs phase out and CfDs roll in and new builds compete at market prices, operating on thin margins becomes normality.
The hardware got cheap, the margin moved
For years robotics was simply too expensive for this work. That has inverted, though not quite in the way the headlines suggest.
LiDAR is projected to fall from around €4,297 ($5,000) to €1,203 ($1,400) by 2040, actuators have roughly halved, battery packs sit near €92.81/kWh ($108/kWh), and inference at the edge costs cents per hour.
Autonomy has matured alongside it: transformer-based approaches have cut the demonstrations needed to teach a new task from tens of thousands to a few dozen, and most of the training now happens in simulation before anything is flown or driven near a live substation.
None of this favours European hardware manufacturers directly. Chinese robot makers undercut European prices by 20 to 30%, and in some cases by up to 50%. For investors, the profits need to be made on the intelligence. Two software layers decide whether a fleet of cheap sensors and commodity actuators actually becomes useful to an energy operator, rather than an expensive way to generate footage nobody watches.
The first is physical observability: the ability to reliably capture, attribute and continuously refresh real-world asset conditions. A thermal camera, microphone or LiDAR scanner only creates value when the observation can be tied to a specific transformer, switchgear compartment or span, stored in context, and compared against its operating history.
The challenge is therefore not simply collecting more data, but capturing the right signals at the right frequency and linking them to the correct asset. In critical infrastructure, where access is difficult, hazards are high and failure modes are rare, this observability layer becomes the prerequisite for any meaningful intelligence.
The second is spatial interpretation: turning what a camera sees into something an energy operator can act on. A generic vision model can flag discolouration on a turbine blade; a system built for energy assets can place that defect on the span, compare its progression against the rest of the fleet, check it against the threshold that triggers a mandatory inspection, and decide whether it justifies pulling a technician forward or waiting for the next weather window.
That judgement comes from fusing thermal, visual and historical inspection data against a specific asset class, and from having seen enough of those assets to know what normal looks like. Together, they form a loop that gets more valuable with every site added, because the data behind it cannot be bought off a shelf.
Why now is the time to act
Two regulatory dates give this some urgency. The EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, and it treats AI safety components as high-risk, requiring certification through a notified body. The AI Act’s obligations for robots operating in critical infrastructure follow on 2nd August 2028, covering transparency, technical documentation and post-market monitoring. Companies that can show compliance evidence alongside their product will move faster through procurement than those retrofitting it under deadline pressure.
Components will likely keep coming from Asia, and much of the underlying AI research from the US. Both enable value creation within Europe. The layer that captures the profits orchestrates customer needs, European and national regulation, and earns the operator’s trust through tangible results. That is where Europe is genuinely positioned to win, provided founders and investors resist the temptation to compete where the economics do not favour them.

articles.title: Le Walkman de Sony n'est pas mort, il coûte maintenant 5000 € et se recouvre d'or
articles.text:
Le Walkman de Sony n'est pas mort, il coûte maintenant 5000 € et se recouvre d'or
Sony renouvelle son offre de baladeurs audiophiles avec deux modèles premium aux tarifs particulièrement salés. Finitions luxueuses, composants triés sur le volet et lecture haute résolution sont au programme.
En 1979, Sony lançait le premier Walkman et transformait l’écoute nomade en phénomène mondial. Près d’un demi-siècle plus tard, le constructeur japonais perpétue cette tradition avec des baladeurs destinés à un marché de niche. La marque proposait encore récemment des modèles plus accessibles comme le NW-A306, commercialisé à 400 € et malgré tout dôté d’un module wifi pour accéder aux plateformes de streaming.
Sony fait désormais évoluer son offre vers le très haut de gamme, avec l’ambition de rivaliser avec Astell&Kern et FiiO sur le terrain des tarifs exorbitants. Les NW-WM1AM3 et NW-WM1ZM3 sont donc lancés aux tarifs de 2500 et 5000 €, soit respectivement 1100 et 1300 € de plus que leurs prédécesseurs NW-WM1AM2 et NW-WM1ZM2, lancés en 2022.
Des tarifs justifiés par des composants de haut vol
Le NW-WM1AM3 reprend une grande partie de l’architecture du NW-WM1ZM3, mais fait appel à des matériaux moins coûteux. Son châssis est en aluminium, tandis que sa face arrière est en cuivre plaqué or. Pour sa part, le modèle supérieur adopte un châssis en cuivre sans oxygène plaqué or et un câblage dit KIMBER KABLE, notamment. En outre, les deux baladeurs revendiquent des soudures à l’or, des composants du circuit imprimé remplis de cuivre et des vis plaquées or, autant de raffinements matériels que Sony annonce capables d’améliorer la restitution sonore, au grand bonheur des alchimistes de la hi-fi.
Si les deux baladeurs partagent une base commune, Sony mise donc principalement sur les matériaux et la sélection des composants pour justifier un écart de prix de 2500 € entre les deux références. Des différences dont la portée paraîtra bien ténue aux yeux du grand public au regard d'un tel surcoût.
Les deux appareils intègrent une amplification S-Master HX et disposent d’une sortie casque asymétrique de 3,5 mm ainsi que d’une sortie symétrique de 4,4 mm. Sony indique avoir revu leur alimentation, en intégrant notamment deux condensateurs de grande capacité censés réduire le "bruit généré par les circuits numériques". Le constructeur mentionne également un câblage en cuivre désoxygéné, soudé à la main, parmi d’autres raffinements. Inspirées de celles mises en œuvre dans les électroniques domestiques haut de gamme, ces améliorations entendent limiter les interférences électriques et stabiliser le signal audio.
Sortie symétrique, DSD256 natif, module wifi et puissance de sortie limitée
Avec tout ce beau monde, on s’attend bien sûr à ce que les appareils soient capables de fournir une puissance adaptée aux casques filaires exigeants. Or, pour les versions européennes, Sony annonce une puissance de sortie maximale de seulement 1,1 mW sous 32 Ohms. Cette limitation semble s’inscrire dans le cadre réglementaire sur la protection de l’audition avec les appareils audio nomades. La version japonaise promet quant à elle jusqu’à 250 mW par canal sous 16 Ohms. Bien que ces valeurs ne soient pas directement comparables, elles suffisent à constater que cette version est mieux adaptée à l’alimentation de casques gourmands.
Cette restriction est regrettable pour des appareils aussi onéreux. Avec certains casques de faible sensibilité ou d’impédance élevée, la marge disponible pourrait être insuffisante pour atteindre un niveau sonore confortable, contrairement à ce que peut offrir un ampli casque sédentaire.
Les deux Walkman prennent en charge le DSD256 natif ainsi que les fichiers PCM jusqu’en 32 bits/384 kHz. Ils intègrent également le moteur de remastérisation DSD de Sony, capable d'upscaler les fichiers PCM en flux DSD. Selon le constructeur, ce traitement entend rapprocher la restitution sonore de celle de l’analogique. Il peut être appliqué aussi bien aux morceaux stockés dans la mémoire du baladeur qu’aux contenus écoutés en streaming.
Les NW-WM1AM3 et NW-WM1ZM3 fonctionnent sous Android 16 et intègrent un module wifi. Ils permettent ainsi d’accéder aux principales plateformes de streaming et de naviguer sur le web. Le Bluetooth autorise également l’utilisation d’écouteurs et de casques sans fil. Les codecs pris en charge comprennent notamment les SBC, AAC, LDAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Adaptive et LC3.
Des baladeurs à l’autonomie confortable, qui diffèrent par leur capacité de stockage
Les deux modèles se distinguent aussi par leur capacité de stockage. Le NW-WM1ZM3 dispose de 256 Go de mémoire interne, contre 128 Go pour le NW-WM1AM3. Dans les deux cas, un emplacement pour carte microSD permet d’étendre cet espace. Sony conserve par ailleurs un écran de 5,5" et un port USB-C, qui peut servir à utiliser le baladeur comme un DAC externe avec un ordinateur, en plus de la simple charge.
Le constructeur annonce une autonomie pouvant atteindre 35 h en lecture de fichiers MP3 encodés à 128 Kbps et jusqu’à 31 h en streaming. Des valeurs particulièrement élevées sur le segment des baladeurs audiophiles.
Les Sony NW-WM1AM3 et NW-WM1ZM3 seront commercialisés à partir du 15 novembre 2026, aux prix publics conseillés respectifs de 2500 et 5000 €.
À de tels tarifs, ces baladeurs s’adressent avant tout aux audiophiles en quête d’une source compacte et nomade, capable de décoder des flux haute résolution et de fonctionner aussi bien avec un casque filaire qu’avec des écouteurs sans fil. Il demeure que leur puissance de sortie, relativement faible sur le papier, risque de limiter leur intérêt avec certains casques exigeants. Un paradoxe pour des appareils aussi ambitieux et onéreux.
