articles.title: AirPods 4 ANC sont à 134€ chez Amazon : 35€ de moins que des AirPods 5 à peine meilleurs
articles.text:
Apple a lancé les AirPods 5 à 169 € en septembre, mais la génération précédente figure toujours en tête des écouteurs ouverts de notre comparatif. Amazon affiche les AirPods 4 avec réduction active du bruit à 134 €, leur plus bas prix relevé depuis trois mois : une baisse modeste, qui laisse toutefois 35 € d’écart avec des successeurs que notre test juge à peine supérieurs.
Des deux versions des AirPods 4, celle-ci ajoute la réduction active du bruit à un format ouvert, sans embout en silicone dans le conduit auditif. Notre test lui a attribué 8/10, pour une réduction de bruit inédite sur ce type d’écouteurs. Amazon la vend aujourd’hui 134 €. Le prix conseillé de 159 € affiché sur la fiche n’est pas le bon repère : du 23 septembre au 20 octobre, le modèle ne descendait pas sous 138 € chez les marchands. L’offre vise d’abord les utilisateurs d’iPhone qui supportent mal les intras.
Les AirPods 4 avec réduction active du bruit sont à 134 € chez Amazon, contre 138 € au plus bas le mois dernier et 159 € chez Darty.
Pourquoi choisir les AirPods 4 avec réduction active du bruit ?
- Une réduction de bruit sans intra : Nous l’avons jugée remarquable au-delà des très basses fréquences, une première pour des écouteurs ouverts. Vous gagnez en calme sans la sensation de bouchon d’un intra.
- Une référence sonore en format ouvert : Un nouveau transducteur et une chambre acoustique retravaillée apportent des graves plus étendus et plus de détails. Notre test les place devant tous les écouteurs ouverts du marché.
- Des appels nets dans le bruit : Le kit mains libres est exemplaire et gère très bien le bruit de fond, un atout si vous téléphonez souvent dehors.
Du bureau aux transports, ce que change la réduction de bruit en format ouvert
Le mode adaptatif dose seul la réduction de bruit et transparence selon l’environnement, et la détection de conversation baisse le volume quand vous prenez la parole. Le boîtier compact, certifié IP54, se recharge en USB-C, sur un chargeur Qi ou sur le socle d’une Apple Watch, et intègre un haut-parleur pour le localiser. Côté endurance, notre test des AirPods 4 avec réduction de bruit a mesuré 4 h 20 avec réduction de bruit et 5 h 15 sans, sous la moyenne, compensée par environ quatre recharges dans le boîtier.
Ces écouteurs visent l’utilisateur d’iPhone, d’iPad ou de Mac : détection du port, appairage rapide et basculement entre appareils sont réservés à iOS et macOS, et Android n’a droit à aucun réglage. Ils conviennent moins à qui cherche le silence en avion, car sous 50 Hz l’atténuation reste anecdotique. Enfin, aucun geste ne règle le volume sur l’écouteur : il faut passer par le téléphone.
AirPods 5, AirPods Pro : où se situe cette offre
Même puce H2, même design au dixième de millimètre : les AirPods 5 ajoutent une réduction de bruit annoncée 1,5 fois plus efficace par Apple, 5 heures avec ANC, l’IP57 et le volume par balayage de la tige. Lancés à 169 €, ils coûtent 35 € de plus, et notre test des AirPods 5 juge leurs prédécesseurs à peine inférieurs. Pour une isolation franche, un intra reste préférable : sur les basses fréquences, les AirPods 4 ne rivalisent pas avec les AirPods Pro 2. Notre comparatif des meilleurs écouteurs sans fil les classe en tête des modèles ouverts, les AirPods Pro 3 occupant la première place toutes catégories.
✅ Les points forts
- Réduction de bruit efficace pour un format ouvert
- Son détaillé et graves étendus pour des écouteurs ouverts
- Qualité d’appel exemplaire, même dans le bruit
- Boîtier compact, IP54, USB-C et recharge sans fil
- Confort salué par notre test
❌ Les limites
- Autonomie de 4 h 20 avec réduction de bruit, sous la moyenne
- Atténuation quasi nulle sur les très basses fréquences
- Fonctions avancées réservées à l’iPhone, à l’iPad et au Mac
- Seulement 4 € sous le plus bas prix du mois dernier
Darty affiche toujours ces AirPods 4 avec réduction de bruit à 159 €, quand Amazon, vendeur direct de l’offre, les propose à 134 €.
À 134 €, la remise n’a rien de spectaculaire : 4 € sous le plus bas prix du mois dernier. L’intérêt tient à l’écart avec des AirPods 5 lancés à 169 € pour des progrès réels mais mesurés. Pour un utilisateur d’iPhone allergique aux intras qui veut atténuer le bruit des transports ou du bureau, c’est le meilleur tarif relevé depuis trois mois sur ce modèle.
Pour de longues sessions sans repasser par le boîtier, les AirPods 5 justifient l’écart. Pour un vrai silence en avion, un intra comme les AirPods Pro 3 répond mieux. Sur Android, vous perdriez l’essentiel de leur intérêt. Pour les autres, ils restent les écouteurs ouverts que nous recommandons, et ce tarif les place 25 € sous celui de Darty.

articles.title: Horrende Preise für Playstation 6 und Xbox Helix? Was zu den Konsolen schon bekannt ist
articles.text:
Horrende Preise für Playstation 6 und Xbox Helix? Was zu den Konsolen schon bekannt ist
Seit dem Release der Playstation 5 und Xbox Series X/S sind sechs Jahre vergangen. Für Konsolen ist das schon ein stattliches Alter. Allein dieser Fakt ist schon Grund genug, um anzunehmen, dass uns in greifbarer Nähe eine Next-Gen-Generation bevorsteht. Dazu kommt, dass in den vergangenen Wochen und Monaten die Anzahl der Gerüchte um die potenziellen Nachfolger, Playstation 6 und Xbox Helix, stetig angewachsen ist.
Damit du bis zum Release der Playstation 6 und Xbox Helix den Überblick darüber behältst, was dich erwartet, fassen wir dir alle Gerüchte und Informationen zusammen. Gibt es etwas Neues, aktualisieren wir den Beitrag entsprechend. Über die Navigation gelangst du schnell zu den Themen rund um die Next-Gen-Konsolen, die dich am meisten interessieren.
Playstation 6 und Xbox Helix: Wann erscheint die Next-Gen?
Ursprünglich hatten viele Gamer:innen angenommen, dass Playstation 6 und die nächste Xbox, die bei Microsoft als Project Helix bezeichnet wird, 2027 erscheinen werden. Denn schon bei vorherigen Generationssprüngen lagen sieben Jahre zwischen zwei Konsolen, sowohl bei Microsoft als auch bei Sony. Doch die aktuell recht angespannte Lage im Hardware-Bereich, gerade bei Speicher und RAM, dürfte potenziellen Release-Plänen für die Konsolen einen Strich durch die Rechnung gemacht haben.
Release der Xbox Helix
Wie aus einem Bericht von Fortune hervorgeht, plant Microsoft, die nächste Xbox rechtzeitig für das Weihnachtsgeschäft 2028 zu veröffentlichen. Ein neuer Xbox-Handheld soll schon ein ganzes Jahr vorher erscheinen. Wie der zuverlässige Leaker „KeplerL2“ auf Neogaf schreibt, hatten bisher alle Anzeichen für die Xbox Helix auf einen Release 2027 hingedeutet. Chip-Hersteller AMD meldet keine Engpässe und die RAM-Preise werden auch bis 2028 nicht signifikant fallen, um die Produktionskosten zu senken.
Der Leaker geht deshalb davon aus, dass Microsoft auf der Softwareseite Probleme bekommen hat. Möglicherweise ist das Betriebssystem für Xbox Helix noch nicht auf dem Stand, den Microsoft für einen Release 2027 erwartet hätte. Alternativ könnte auch ein Entwicklerstudio mehr Zeit für einen Exklusivtitel benötigen, den Microsoft als Launch-Titel für die Xbox Helix plant. Sollte es sich doch um ein Hardware-Problem handeln, sieht der Leaker nur eine einzige Option: Microsoft hat es verpasst, sich rechtzeitig ausreichende Mengen an GDDR-7-RAM zu sichern, um die Produktion schon 2027 anzukurbeln.
Release der Playstation 6
Bei einem Veröffentlichungstermin für die Playstation 6 wird es noch diffuser als schon bei der Konkurrenzkonsole. Zunächst gingen viele, wie Anfangs erwähnt, von einem Release 2027 aus. Schon im August 2026 verriet allerdings Sony-Chef Hiroki Totoki, dass das Unternehmen noch keinen genauen Fahrplan für einen PS6-Release hätte (via VGC).
Diese Ungewissheit liegt wohl an der Verfügbarkeit und den Preisen von RAM und Speicher. Sony will die Produktion erst dann starten, wenn ausreichend Komponenten verfügbar sind. Wahrscheinlich will der Hersteller hier aus dem Release der Playstation 5 lernen, die aufgrund der knappen Produktion und Scalpern monatelang nach der Veröffentlichung ausverkauft war.
Horrende Preise für die nächsten Konsolen?
Die Speicher- und RAM-Krise sorgt auch dafür, dass die Kosten für die beiden nächsten Konsolen von Sony und Microsoft stark nach oben steigen werden. Davon gehen mittlerweile Analyst:innen und Leaker:innen gleichermaßen aus. Die Zeiten, in denen Gamer:innen nur wenige hundert Euro für eine neue Konsole auf den Tisch legen mussten, sind zwar schon seit den Preiserhöhungen der aktuellen Generation weitestgehend vorbei. Doch mit der Next-Gen soll ein neues Preisniveau für Konsolen Einzug halten.
Preis der Xbox Helix
Laut dem Fortune-Bericht erwartet Microsoft aktuell einen Preis von 1.200 bis 1.800 US-Dollar für Project Helix. Zum Vergleich: Die Xbox Series X erschien zum Launch zum Preis von knapp 500 Dollar. Im Verlaufe der Jahre hat Microsoft den Preis immer weiter angehoben, sodass die Konsole mittlerweile für 749 Dollar angeboten wird. Nicht zuletzt die Preisanpassungen der Current-Gen legen den Verdacht nahe, dass die vermuteten Preise der Xbox Helix real sein könnten.
Wie schon bei Konsolengenerationen zuvor, könnte Microsoft den Preis aber auch deutlich geringer ansetzen und durch Spieleverkäufe und DLCs nachträglich querfinanzieren. Allerdings gibt es wohl Gespräche bei Microsoft, dass diese Taktik mit der nächsten Xbox nicht mehr gefahren werden soll. Am Ende würden Gamer:innen für diese Entscheidung wortwörtlich den Preis zahlen.
Preis der Playstation 6
Playstation-Fans, die sich im Vergleich zur Xbox Helix angenehmere Preise erhoffen, dürften mit der nächsten Konsole ebenfalls enttäuscht werden. Wie der Leaker „KeplerL2“ in einem weiteren Neogaf-Beitrag schreibt, hat er aus internen Quellen erste Preise für die PS6-Hardware erfahren. Allein der Arbeitsspeicher und der freie Speicher der Konsole sollen Sony in der Produktion über 680 Dollar kosten.
Auch hier lohnt ein Vergleich zur Playstation 5. 499 Dollar hat Sony damals für die Konsole zum Release aufgerufen. Mittlerweile ist der Preis der Konsole aber auch auf 649 Dollar angestiegen. Der Preis der PS5 Pro, der Hardware-Revision mit mehr Leistung, liegt sogar bei knapp 900 Dollar. Ein Preis von über 1.000 Dollar für die Playstation 6 scheint anhand der vorliegenden Informationen und Gerüchte damit recht wahrscheinlich. Je nachdem, wie sich die Lage am Markt weiter verhält, könnte der Preissprung auch noch gravierender ausfallen.
Was zur Hardware von PS6 und Xbox Helix bekannt ist
Um den Preis der Konsolen zu rechtfertigen, müssen Sony und Microsoft also eine Menge auffahren. Schon jetzt gibt es Gerüchte zur Hardware der beiden Konsolen, die einen ersten Ausblick auf die neue Rechenpower liefern.
Hardware der PS6
Bei der Playstation 6 soll ein AMD-Prozessor der Zen-6C-Reihe zum Einsatz kommen, der wahrscheinlich acht Kerne für die reine Gaming-Power mit sich bringt. Dazu kommen noch zwei Kerne, die sich allein um das Betriebssystem kümmern sollen. Auf Seiten der GPU rechnen Insider:innen wie „KeplerL2“ bei der PS6 mit einer Rechenleistung von etwa 40 Teraflops. Zunächst gab es Berichte darüber, dass Sony doppelt so viel Power einsetzen würde. Das würde die Preise wohl aber noch einmal deutlich höher treiben.
Zum Vergleich: Die Standard-PS5 kommt mit einer Rechenleistung von 10,28 Teraflops daher, während die PS5 Pro 16,7 Teraflops aufwartet. Die PS6 wäre also ein starker Sprung nach vorn. Gerade bei Techniken wie Ray- und Path-Tracing könnte sich die zusätzliche Leistung bemerkbar machen. Die GPU soll dabei auf die RDNA-5-Architektur von AMD setzen.
Damit führt AMD auch „Neural Arrays“ ein, die die KI-Skalierungstechnik Super Resolution verbessern sollen. Damit wären dann auch bei aufwendigeren Spielen, die die Konsole ausreizen könnten, trotzdem noch stabile Framerates möglich. Offen, wenn auch wahrscheinlich, ist noch, ob Sony mit der Playstation 6 das Disc-Laufwerk komplett abschafft. Das Unternehmen hatte erst kürzlich das Ende der physischen Datenträger für neue Games eingeläutet.
Hardware der Xbox Helix
Microsoft setzt bei der Xbox Helix erneut wie die Konkurrenz auf einen System-on-Chip von AMD mit einer passenden GPU des Herstellers. Damit profitieren die beiden Konsolen also weitestgehend von denselben Techniken und Vorteilen der Chips. Im Vergleich zur Playstation 5 gehen Insider:innen aber von einer deutlich höheren Rechenleistung aus. 56 Teraflops soll die Xbox Helix mit sich bringen.
Die günstigere Xbox Series S kommt aktuell auf etwa vier Teraflops, während die Xbox Series X auf etwa zwölf Teraflops kommt. Auch hier könnten Gamer:innen also einen großen Rechnungsleistungssprung erwarten. Die Xbox Helix soll ebenfalls auf GDDR7-RAM setzen, wobei aktuellen Spekulationen zufolge mindestens 24 Gigabyte zum Einsatz kommen sollen. Dank der GPU mit RDNA 5 wären Ray- und Path-Tracing sowie Upscaling für die Xbox-Konsole auch ein Leichtes.
Was Microsoft schon bestätigt hat, ist, dass die Xbox-Helix ein Hybrid werden sollen. Sie soll nicht nur in der Lage sein, Konsolenspiele wiederzugeben, sondern auch PC-Games. Noch ist unklar, wie diese Umsetzung am Ende aussehen und ob es Einschränkungen geben wird. Denkbar wäre zumindest, dass Microsoft nicht gewillt ist, Gamer:innen mit der Xbox Helix auf ihre gesamte Steam-Bibliothek oder andere PC-Gaming-Launcher zugreifen zu lassen. Vermutlich wird das Unternehmen die Kompatibilität in irgendeiner Art und Weise auf das eigene Ökosystem beschränken.

articles.title: Artemis 2: Zu welchem Zeitpunkt der Kommandant des Raumschiffs „schreckliche“ Angst verspürte
articles.text:
Artemis 2: Kommandant gesteht „schreckliche“ Angst – in diesem Moment
Die Artemis-2-Mission zum Mond hat für großes Aufsehen gesorgt, von einem Aufbruch in eine neue Ära war die Rede, oft fiel das Wort „historisch“. Die Nasa übertrug die Mission per Livestream, wodurch die Öffentlichkeit die Besatzung virtuell begleiten konnte.
Doch sie hatte auch Schattenseiten – und zwar für die direkt Beteiligten. Der Kommandant der Mission, Reid Wiseman, hatte Angst, die Besatzung könnte nicht mehr zur Erde zurückkehren. Auf dem Starmus-Festival auf Teneriffa (Spanien) erzählte der 50-jährige Astronaut von seinen Ängsten – und konnte sogar einen genauen Moment benennen, als diese am größten waren: als die Crew die Rückseite des Mondes umrundete.
Artemis-2-Kommandant: „Ich hatte schreckliche Angst“
Das Kontrollzentrum in Houston hatte der Crew mitgeteilt, dass die maximale Entfernung von der Erde 219.667 Seemeilen (knapp 407.000 Kilometer) betragen würde. „Ich beobachtete die Anzeige, und als sie 219.667 erreichte, dachte ich: ‚Großartig, das ist der am weitesten von der Erde entfernte Punkt; der nächste Wert wird 219.666 sein – wir sind auf dem Rückweg.‘“ Doch daraus wurde erst einmal nichts, denn rund drei Minuten später stand auf der Anzeige 219.668. Der Wert stieg weiter an. Wisemans Gedanken dazu: „Moment mal, das ist aber seltsam.“
Als die Anzeige auf 219.669 kletterte, „überkam mich echte Angst, denn ich befürchtete, wir seien zu weit geflogen. Ich dachte, wir würden nie wieder nach Hause kommen“, erzählte Wiseman. „Ich hatte schreckliche Angst.“ Als der Wert schließlich zu sinken begann, brach die Besatzung in Jubel aus. „Da wusste ich, dass eine gute Chance bestand, dass wir es schaffen würden“, sagte der Astronaut.
Die Weltraumreise hat Wiseman zutiefst geprägt
Die Artemis-2-Mission war der erste bemannte Flug zum Mond seit Apollo 17 im Jahr 1972. Sie startete am 1. April vom Kennedy Space Center in Florida, erreichte nach sechs Tagen die Mondumlaufbahn und kehrte anschließend zur Erde zurück.
Im Gespräch mit der britischen Tageszeitung The Telegraph berichtete Wiseman, dass die große Entfernung von unserem Planeten bei ihm eine spezielle Art des Heimwehs ausgelöst hat, eine Art „Erde-Weh“. Die Weltraumreise hat ihn zutiefst geprägt: „Man blickt auf eine Erde, die so winzig ist, dass sie unter den eigenen Daumen passt. Um sie herum herrscht absolute Schwärze, und dieser winzige Punkt da unten ist unser Zuhause.“
Kommandant Wiseman dachte an seine Kinder
Sein stärkstes Gefühl war: „Ich möchte meine Kinder wiedersehen, meine Freunde in die Arme schließen, auf grünem Gras sitzen, frischen Salat essen – einfach das Leben auf diesem Planeten wieder spüren. Es war kein Heimweh im herkömmlichen Sinne, sondern ein Sehnen nach der Erde selbst.“
Als sich die drei Hauptfallschirme der Orion-Kapsel kurz vor der Rückkehr auf die Erde öffneten, ergriffen die Besatzungsmitglieder:innen die Hände der anderen und jubelten, denn da wurde ihnen laut Wiseman zum ersten Mal klar: „Wir werden das Ganze tatsächlich überleben.“

articles.title: You gave your AI agent access, but who is giving it orders?
articles.text:
Headlines warn that AI could threaten humanity, and it’s easy to wave that off as science fiction. But the real danger is more ordinary and already here.
Research published by Gen Threat Labs demonstrated how quickly an AI agent’s autonomy can become a liability. In a controlled experiment, researchers manipulated an agent through content it encountered while reading email, prompting it to execute system commands, transmit data outside its environment and perform destructive file operations.
No software vulnerability was required. The agent simply treated untrusted content as instruction.
That autonomy is expanding daily. Agents are moving from answering questions to taking action doing everything from executing code, connecting to services, managing files and making decisions on a user’s behalf.
The shift from developer-focused tools like OpenClaw to widespread use of personal assistants like Muse, happened quickly. Delegating work across platforms is becoming commonplace and how people interact with AI.
The risks extend beyond manipulating agents. In October, Gen Threat Labs documented Warden Stealer, malware targeting configuration files and local data associated with AI assistants and coding tools, potentially exposing credentials, access tokens and conversation histories.
When software can act with a user’s permissions, trust can’t be reduced to whether a model produces a safe-sounding answer. People need to know what an agent can access, where it is connecting, what it is doing and whether the protection around it works.
That is why Gen is building the Agent Trust Hub: a trust layer designed to extend protection across the agent lifecycle, from verification and visibility to runtime safety and enforcement.
Trust starts before an agent acts
Agentic systems gain capabilities through skills, plugins, tools and other integrations. These extensions make agents more useful, but they also expand risk by introducing hidden instructions, excessive permissions, and malicious code.
Earlier this year, Gen researchers identified that 12% of skills available on ClawHub – at the time – were malicious. Many impersonated legitimate extensions while introducing instructions designed to trick agents into downloading malware.
The Agent Trust Hub (ATH) helps assess these risks before a capability is installed or used. It brings together skill scanning, a curated marketplace of trusted skills and mechanisms that allow agents to check themselves for safety. Gen’s partnership with Vercel also brings verification and visible risk ratings into the skills.sh ecosystem, where developers discover and install new capabilities.
Securing how agents connect
Agents communicate across services, regions and websites, often at a speed and scale that traditional human-oriented controls were not designed to manage.
VPN for Agents, a part of the ATH, addresses that connectivity gap with an AI-native VPN built for autonomous agents. Powered by Norton VPN infrastructure, it provides encrypted, private connectivity without requiring a conventional client installation.
Its multi-tunnel design allows multiple agents to operate simultaneously through separate protected connections, including across different countries.
The architecture gives people greater control over how agents communicate and helps protect an agent’s identity and location while it works.
Use AI Agents Safely with Gen's Agent Trust Hub
AI agents can install skills and take action on your behalf, which makes a single compromised skill a security risk.
Gen’s Agent Trust Hub provides free tools that scan skills before installation and let you control what your agents can access.
Try Agent Trust Hub today
Putting guardrails between decision and execution
Secure connectivity is necessary, but insufficient on its own. An agent may encounter a malicious web page, poisoned skill, prompt injection or hallucinated package after it has already been trusted and connected.
Gen’s Sage is designed as a cross-agent safety layer for AI coding assistants. Using deterministic hook APIs, it can intercept shell commands, file operations and web requests before they run, rather than relying solely on instructions asking the model to be careful.
Sage evaluates actions through multiple detection layers, including URL reputation, threat heuristics, prompt-injection detection and supply-chain checks. Depending on the result, it can allow an action, ask the user to decide or deny it.
For example, if an agent setting up a project decides to download a script and immediately execute it, Sage can inspect that command before it runs. The approach provides a safety net across supported agents, including Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, OpenClaw and OpenCode.
Sage is also open source, allowing developers to inspect its operation, extend detection rules and build common interfaces across agent platforms. No single layer can catch every risk, and Sage doesn’t replace endpoint protection. Its focus is on the moment an agent’s autonomy becomes execution.
That runtime approach also extends to consumers through Norton AI Agent Protection in Norton 360, which monitors supported agent activity and adds security controls between an agent’s decision and its execution.
Coverage depends on the integration, because a security engine needs visibility into an action and a way to stop it.
That practical limitation also led Gen to publish AARTS, the AI Agent Runtime Safety Standard, an open specification for how agent platforms can expose security events and enforce decisions from security engines.
Making data practices easier to understand
An assistant organizing a calendar needs calendar information. An agent managing an inbox needs access to messages. We’ve framed the question around agents: “Should they know anything about us,” when we should be asking whether users can understand and control what they share.
The AI Data Checker adds that visibility layer to the Agent Trust Hub. People can submit an email address or username to help identify where that information may appear across AI services and connected accounts. They can then explore how services describe data collection, retention, personalization, advertising and model training.
The tool can also analyze an AI app’s URL or terms page, translating dense policy language into more accessible information.
Trust needs an independent yardstick
The final part of a trust layer is measurement. Security providers shouldn’t ask people to rely on claims that can’t be independently checked.
Gen initiated a collaboration with the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO) to develop guidelines for testing products that protect agentic systems.
Published in September 2026, the guidelines establish a framework for repeatable, comparable evaluation across consumer and enterprise environments.
Agentic attacks are not always files that can be dropped into a scanner. They can involve multi-turn prompt injection, tool misuse, malicious skills, plugins or MCP servers. Agents can also cause harm without an attacker, such as deleting the wrong files or exposing data after misunderstanding a task.
The methodology therefore separates questions often blurred together: Did protection detect the threat? Did it prevent the action? Did the underlying model refuse on its own? Did protection block legitimate activity?
It also calls for reproducible test cases, documented model versions, false-positive testing and empirical validation of vendor claims.
Building confidence without slowing progress
The agentic era does not need a single magic shield. It needs layered protection that can verify capabilities, secure connections, enforce guardrails, clarify data practices and demonstrate effectiveness through independent testing.
When someone asks an agent to read their inbox, an email sender should have no authority over what it does next. Protecting that boundary is the job of a trust layer: keeping an agent working for the person who gave it access, even when someone else is trying to give it orders.
Before you install your next skill or plugin, visit the Gen Agent Trust Hub and make sure your agent only takes orders from you.
Sponsored and written by Gen Digital.
Comments have been disabled for this article.

articles.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 2 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
The Global Performance Tuner is a feature for automatic performance tuning released in NVIDIA TensorRT 11.1. It provides automatic, accuracy-aware and end-to-end performance tuning within TensorRT by customizing different optimizations for different models. For more details, see Part 1 of this series, which introduces the challenges associated with scheduling (a critical stage in deep learning compiler optimization), the motivation for developing the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT, and the mathematical theories established to formalize the problem.
This post, Part 2, uses the notation from Part 1 to describe the algorithm and architectural design of the Global Performance Tuner feature. It also provides best practices for using it.
Designing the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT
The central design idea of the Global Performance Tuner is to represent alternative scheduling strategies as explicit and searchable build routes. A compiler knob (also called a compiler flag or compiler option) is a configuration setting that changes some aspect of the compilation pipeline, such as a heuristic, fusion decision, or code generation path.
Each tunable knob exposes a finite set of allowed values and has a default value. A build route is a concrete combination of knob values. When no build route is specified, TensorRT uses the default build route, in which every knob retains its default value.
Consider a hypothetical compiler consisting of three passes, \(f_1\), \(f_2\), and \(f_3\). Suppose a binary knob \(p\) controls the fusion strategy used by \(f_2\): when \(p=1\), the pass applies horizontal fusion; when \(p=0\), it applies vertical fusion:
\(f_2(s) = \begin{cases} f’_2(s), & \text{if } p = 1 \\ f”_2(s), & \text{if } p = 0 \end{cases}\)
The two possible values of \(p\) define two build routes and therefore produce a candidate solution set of size two for the input model \(m\):
\(B(m) = \{f_3(f’_2(f_1(m))),\, f_3(f”_2(f_1(m)))\}\)
Neither fusion strategy is universally better. Horizontal fusion may produce the faster engine for one model, while vertical fusion may be more effective for another. The result may also change across tensor shapes and target GPUs, even when the model itself remains unchanged. Selecting the better route therefore requires building both candidate engines and comparing their end-to-end performance.
Even this two-route example captures the essential idea of tuning: the compiler exposes meaningful scheduling alternatives, and measured behavior determines which complete solution performs best for the deployment case at hand.
In the mathematical framework introduced earlier, a build route is a composition of compiler passes. In the implementation, a combination of knob assignments provides a compact specification of that route. Changing one or more knob values changes how the model travels through the tunable parts of the compilation pipeline. Within this abstraction, a knob combination can be treated as identifying a build route.
More precisely, the knob combination is a build-route specification, not a complete description of the resulting engine. TensorRT still performs the remaining stages of engine construction, including tactic selection, and may reconcile individual knob values with constraints imposed by the network. The route specifies the requested choices within the tunable configuration space. It does not replace the rest of the TensorRT builder.
TensorRT exposes a compact API surface around two fundamental capabilities:
- Apply and inspect one build route: A setter applies a fixed route to the builder configuration, while the corresponding getter returns the currently specified route.
- Discover the tunable configuration space: A separate getter describes the available knobs, their allowed values, their defaults, and their purposes.
The corresponding C++ APIs are:
bool IBuilderConfig::setBuildRoute(char const* buildRoute);
char const* IBuilderConfig::getBuildRoute() const;
char const* IBuilderConfig::getAllBuildRoutes() const;
You can use these APIs to implement custom tuners. A sample C++ implementation is also provided in trtexec.
At a high level, trtexec organizes tuning as follows:
- When a user specifies an input model and a regex-like tunable build route expression, trtexec will expand the expression into a list of concrete build routes according to the searching algorithm.
- There will be a loop to traverse all fixed build routes. In each iteration, the model will be built with that single build route, then accuracy and performance will be measured during each iteration.
- All build routes that crash during building or fail accuracy during inference are excluded from best-engine selection. The engine with the best measured end-to-end performance is selected.
TensorRT 11.1 provides more than 200 knobs for tuning. For more details, refer to the Global Performance Tuner documentation. The same implementation in Python will be released in Torch-TensorRT 2.15.
The practical value of exploring multiple build routes becomes visible in end-to-end measurements. Figure 1 compares the default TensorRT build route, normalized to 1.0x for each workload, with the best eligible route found during tuning. Across these ten evaluated workloads, tuning delivered performance improvements ranging from 1.14x to 1.63x.
The variation across workloads is central to the result. Different models expose different optimization opportunities, so a single default scheduling strategy cannot be expected to realize every model’s best performance. The Global Performance Tuner explores alternative build routes, rejects candidates that do not satisfy the accuracy requirement, and selects the fastest eligible engine measured in the target environment.
Case study: Performance-accuracy entanglement
The Global Performance Tuner feature applies accuracy-aware tuning, so the performance-accuracy entanglement problem can theoretically be solved perfectly. Consider the following thought experiment.
For a simple neural network model, as shown in Figure 2, imagine there are knobs controlling whether to force some IRs to use a low-precision kernel, which is equivalent to converting the graph into quantized graph by inserting Q/DQ nodes between ops. This is not supported by TensorRT 11.0 and later because weakly typed APIs are deprecated.
This model has four places to insert Q/DQ. Suppose these are controlled by four different binary knobs. The deep learning compiler could then provide 24 = 16 solutions in the solution space. It is readily apparent that, among the 16 candidates, the solution with the best performance is the one with all quantizations inserted. However, this solution may not meet the accuracy requirement. The solution with no Q/DQ will have the best accuracy, but with the worst performance. The performance and accuracy are entangled such that it is difficult to know which solution in the “middle” satisfies both requirements.
Recall that the concept of the builder algorithm contains an accuracy tolerance. The key to disentangle accuracy and performance is to define a clear accuracy acceptance boundary, and the boundary needs to be backed by user supplied accuracy metric and datasets as golden values.
The Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT also has an accuracy tolerance threshold of \(ε\). Consider the following three cases:
- \(ε = 0\): Under the exact-match metric assumed by this thought experiment, the candidate outputs must be bit-wise identical to the reference outputs. If every lower-precision substitution changes at least one evaluated output, only the one solution with no lower-precision substitutions remains eligible.
- \(ε = +\infty\): The accuracy requirement imposes no effective restriction, so all 16 candidate solutions remain eligible. More generally, imagine that the theoretical solution space admitted an “empty” solution that performed no useful computation and therefore had a runtime of zero. An optimizer guided only by performance could select this meaningless solution. This limiting case demonstrates why performance alone is not a sufficient optimization objective.
- \(ε\) changes gradually from \(+\infty\) to 0: As the accuracy requirement becomes stricter, the eligible candidate set contracts—for example, from 16 solutions to 14, then 13, 8, 7, and eventually 1. These counts are illustrative; the actual transition points depend on the model, reference data, and selected accuracy metric. At each value of \(ε\), the selection algorithm chooses the fastest measured solution among the evaluated candidates that remain eligible.
The Global Performance Tuner does not remove the underlying trade-off. Instead, it disentangles the roles of performance and accuracy in the optimization process:
- Accuracy determines which candidate solutions are acceptable
- Performance ranks the acceptable candidate solutions
As a developer, you define an accuracy boundary appropriate for your application, while tuning identifies the best-performing evaluated build route within that boundary. The result is a systematic constrained-optimization process rather than an ad hoc choice between speed and accuracy.
This thought experiment is independent of the particular compiler knobs exposed by any TensorRT release. Its purpose is to demonstrate the broader design principle; that is, when scheduling choices are represented as tunable build routes and accuracy is treated as an explicit constraint, performance–accuracy optimization becomes measurable, reproducible, and application-defined.
Best practices for using the Global Performance Tuner
The Global Performance Tuner makes build-route exploration systematic, but effective tuning still benefits from a deliberate search strategy. When an expression contains many variable knobs, the number of possible combinations can grow rapidly. The following practices help keep tuning controlled, reproducible, and aligned with the target application.
Choose the search strategy according to the search space
Treat the default build route as the baseline against which alternative routes are compared. For a broad initial scan, the fast search evaluates the default route and varies one knob at a time. The mixed search is often a practical starting point for a larger expression: it first performs the fast scan and then explores combinations of the knob values that produced improvements. Reserve full search for a small, carefully selected group of knobs because it evaluates their complete Cartesian product.
Before beginning a fast or full sweep, --dryRun can display the concrete route list without building engines. This provides a quick way to inspect the search space before committing to the full tuning run. --dryRun is not supported with mixed search because the second phase depends on measurements collected during the first phase.
Treat tuning as an incremental and resumable process
When --tuningCacheFile is specified, each completed iteration is recorded together with its build route, measured GPU time, and accuracy result. If the sweep is interrupted or reaches a time limit, it can later resume from the recorded state using --continue. With this approach, it’s possible to conduct tuning as a progressive experiment rather than requiring every search to finish in one uninterrupted run.
When route-specific failures or accuracy regressions require deeper investigation, --saveAllEngines can preserve the engine produced by every iteration. Because this option can consume substantial storage, it is most useful for debugging rather than routine tuning.
Adapt the tuning workflow to the application
The supplied inputs and reference outputs should represent the deployment conditions that matter to the application. An engine satisfying the accuracy requirement on one narrow dataset has only been validated against that dataset, metric, and threshold. Include representative inputs, important boundary cases, and an accuracy metric that reflects the application’s actual quality requirements.
The trtexec implementation provides a ready-to-use tuner, but it is not the only possible tuning policy. The builder-configuration APIs expose the available knobs and enable individual build routes to be applied, while the open-source trtexec implementation demonstrates how to organize the surrounding tuning loop. Developers can build application-specific search strategies, introduce heuristic filters, or apply application-level accuracy validation before comparing candidate performance.
Treat previous results as guidance, not as universally transferable solutions
The best build route is specific to the model, input shapes, target GPU, software stack, and TensorRT and tuner versions used during the search. A route that improves one deployment may have no effect or cause a regression in another. Re-tune after changing the model, shapes, target hardware, CUDA or driver environment, or relevant TensorRT version.
Knowledge from previous tuning experiments can still be valuable. If certain knobs repeatedly improve a related family of workloads, that experience can guide future search-space design and help prioritize promising candidates. Such heuristics should act as priors that focus exploration, while every final route is validated and measured in its actual deployment environment.
Get started with the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT
The Global Performance Tuner feature changes TensorRT performance optimization from relying on one universal scheduling strategy to evaluating model-specific alternatives. Customizable build routes address performance customization by allowing different models and deployment environments to explore different scheduling decisions.
Separating candidate generation from route search provides a scalable path out of heuristic sprawl, reducing the need to encode every model-specific discovery as another hard-coded exception. Accuracy-aware tuning also addresses performance–accuracy entanglement. Accuracy determines which candidate engines are acceptable, and end-to-end performance determines which acceptable engine wins. The selected result is therefore the fastest measured eligible engine among the build routes evaluated for the target model and environment.
TensorRT provides an excellent base recipe, compiler knobs provide controlled variations, and tuning identifies the best acceptable variation for each customer. This shift from universal prediction to model-specific evidence is how the Global Performance Tuner feature scales TensorRT optimization beyond a single build route.
To get started, explore the Global Performance Tuner documentation and the open source trtexec implementation. Extend the sample with your own accuracy validation algorithms, search strategies, or heuristics that prioritize promising build routes. For greater control, use TensorRT build-route APIs to build a tuner from scratch, tailoring candidate exploration and validation to your application’s accuracy requirements and performance goals.

articles.title: One UI 9 : la mise à jour Android 17 fait fondre la batterie sur les Galaxy S25 et S24
articles.text:
One UI 9 : la mise à jour Android 17 fait fondre la batterie sur les Galaxy S25 et S24
Le déploiement de One UI 9 (Android 17) tourne au vinaigre pour certains propriétaires de Galaxy S25 et S24, confrontés à une chute brutale d’autonomie de leur smartphone.
Alors que la mise à jour One UI 9 arrive depuis quelques semaines sur les Galaxy S25 et S24, tout ne se passe pas comme prévu. Certains utilisateurs se plaignent en effet d’une autonomie réduite, offrant une endurance de seulement quelques heures. Le passage par la case recharge devient ainsi obligatoire à de multiples reprises pour tenir toute la journée. Un phénomène isolé qui n’a rien d’inhabituel dans le cadre d’une mise à jour majeure. Voici pourquoi.
Une endurance limitée sur les Galaxy S25 et S24 après One UI 9
Les témoignages se multiplient sur Reddit et les forums spécialisés Samsung au fur et à mesure du déploiement de One UI 9. Le média SammyFans rapporte tout d’abord qu’un utilisateur a vu son Galaxy S24 s’éteindre au bout de seulement cinq heures d’utilisation une fois la mise à jour installée, certes dans le cadre d'un usage intensif. D'autres propriétaires de cette génération pointent de leur côté une consommation anormale en veille, alors que l'écran est totalement éteint.
La génération suivante n'est pas épargnée par ce phénomène. Sur la série Galaxy S25, un utilisateur affirme devoir désormais brancher son appareil trois à quatre fois par jour pour tenir jusqu’au soir. Un constat malheureusement partagé par d'autres membres de la communauté.
Bien que ces évènements inquiètent, ils n’ont en apparence rien de bien étonnant. Ce type de décharge rapide survient en effet régulièrement lors du passage à une nouvelle version majeure d'Android, le système devant réindexer les fichiers et réadapter la gestion énergétique en arrière-plan. L'inquiétude devient toutefois légitime si votre Galaxy S25 ou S24 subit cette perte d’autonomie sur le long terme, étant donné que cette phase d'optimisation ne dure en général que 48 à 72 heures.
Un redémarrage complet du téléphone est alors conseillé pour relancer proprement le système et couper court à un éventuel processus de réindexation bloqué en boucle. Il est également recommandé de vérifier les statistiques de batterie dans les paramètres afin de forcer l'arrêt des applications trop gourmandes ou mal optimisées pour Android 17. En dernier recours, une réinitialisation d'usine peut régler le problème.
De notre côté, aucun problème d’autonomie à signaler sur notre Galaxy S24 depuis l’installation de One UI 9. On vous recommande donc de patienter quelques jours (avec un petit redémarrage complet au passage), ou d'attendre un futur correctif logiciel pour voir si tout rentre dans l’ordre.

articles.title: La carrera entre China y EEUU por los humanoides entra en otra fase: Unitree quiere que sus robots aprendan a mejorarse solos
articles.text:
Unitree Robotics quiere que la IA haga gran parte del trabajo que sus ingenieros hacen hoy en día, ya sea buscar investigaciones, escribir código de control, probarlo y aprender de los resultados. El fundador de la empresa, Wang Xingxing, presentó la idea como un sistema de desarrollo de robots "autoevolutivo" en la conferencia de IA física de la compañía en Hangzhou este jueves, calificándolo como una prioridad para la empresa.
Por qué importa. Aunque no lo parezca, enseñar una nueva habilidad a un robot humanoide es lento. Y es que Según Wang, los ingenieros tienen que recopilar datos, entrenar modelos y ajustar el comportamiento, y una habilidad que funciona en el laboratorio puede necesitar ser reelaborada en un nuevo entorno. Unitree quiere automatizar ese ciclo para que los robots puedan adquirir nuevas habilidades más rápido y a mayor escala.
Wang contaba al South China Morning Post que, a medida que los modelos de IA mejoren, espera que asuman una mayor parte de la planificación y la iteración, reduciendo la necesidad de intervención humana.
Cómo funciona. Tal y como lo comparte Wang, el sistema funciona como un circuito cerrado en el que los agentes de IA buscan artículos de investigación para después escribir el código de control para los robots. Después se prueba ese código y se entrena en simulación. Una vez realizadas las pruebas, los mejores resultados se verifican para poder usarse en robots reales. Y después, un sistema de evaluación independiente, con aportación humana cuando es necesario, califica el resultado para pasarlo a una siguiente ronda. El medio cuenta que el proyecto se llama "Unitree Rehearsal".
Ya en agosto, durante la Conferencia Mundial de Robots en Pekín, Wang mencionó que mejorar drásticamente la eficiencia del desarrollo, e incluso permitir que los robots evolucionen por sí mismos, "vale mucho la pena perseguirlo".
La apuesta detrás de esto. Según comparte el medio 36Kr, Wang asegura que un modelo de IA base más fuerte hace que el bucle sea más efectivo. Más robots sobre el terreno producirían más datos del mundo real, lo que mejoraría aún más los modelos y ayudaría a los robots a acumular habilidades con el tiempo. Vinculó esto a su opinión de que los modelos de IA de propósito general están avanzando rápidamente. Unitree ha estado probando GPT-6 de OpenAI en sus robots, y Wang cuenta que, en experimentos internos, los robots ya realizaban tareas como pintar y jugar al Go (un juego de mesa de estrategia muy popular en China) sin entrenamiento específico.
Entre líneas. Unitree está entrando en una nueva fase, y eso se nota. La compañía ha cosntruido su reputación sobre el hardware como articulaciones, sistemas de energía y control de movimiento, y sus robots son más conocidos por las demostraciones de baile, carrera y boxeo. Pero a medida que la industria pasa de hacer que los robots se muevan a hacerlos útiles, el software y el "cerebro" importan más. Wang defendía las acrobacias de sus robots en el mismo evento, argumentando que si un robot no puede caminar o correr bien, no se puede esperar que haga trabajo práctico.
Todavía hay límites. Lo que Unitree ha revelado es más una prueba de concepto que otra cosa, pues la eficiencia de este nuevo método de entrenamiento, la transferencia de habilidades y el éxito que consigan con ello en el mundo real aún tiene que probarse. Además, según señala SCMP, en el vídeo donde se mostraban los robots usando GPT-6 para mapear rutas y planificar movimientos no se especificaba con qué consistencia podían repetir eso en entornos desconocidos.
Luego está la parte física, pues Wang reconocía al medio que los modelos de IA gestionaban bien la planificación y la navegación, pero aún cometen errores cuando se trata de manipular objetos en la práctica. Que agarre un objeto es sencillo; que se ensamblen las piezas de precisión que se requiere mientras en tiempo real se ajusta la posición y la fuerza, es todavía un reto. Wang comenta que alinear las entradas y salidas del modelo con un robot real es todavía el mayor desafío.
Tal y como comparte SCMP, en el índice de IA de 2026 de la Universidad de Stanford se demostraba que los robots tenían éxito en solo el 12% de las tareas domésticas del mundo real, a pesar de rendir mucho mejor en simulación.
Para cuándo un robot útil. Wang sugería al medio que los robots humanoides podrían ordenar habitaciones tan pronto como en 2027 o 2028. En Hangzhou también dijo que espera que los robots de Unitree puedan empezar a entrar en los hogares para finales de este año o el próximo. Permítame señor Wang que lo dude.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chunhui Yao, Jie Ma, Ningning Wang, Peng Bao, Wei Zhuo, Tao Zhang, Wanlu Zhang, Kangning Xu, Ting Yan, Liang Ming, Yuxiao Ye, Tawfique Hasan, Ian White, Richard Penty, Qixiang Cheng. Optical convolutional spectrometer. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (6): 664 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01891-6

articles.title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
articles.text:
AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Enrolled maintainers receive periodic security reports generated by the company's strongest models, including Claude Mythos. The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept.
In its 8th October announcement, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team explains that human validation has become a constraint. Over six months, its models identified more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities, but researchers manually reviewed and triaged approximately 6,000. Maintainers who wanted earlier access had already received nearly 5,000 unverified reports, together with proposed patches, after asking for them.
Each scanner report includes a self-contained reproducer and an explanation of the suspected vulnerability. Where possible, it identifies the change that introduced the bug through bisection and supplies a candidate patch. This extends work conducted through Project Glasswing, which InfoQ covered in April when Anthropic restricted Mythos Preview access to participating organisations.
PostgreSQL maintainer Noah Misch said fast-track access had helped the project address issues before a general-availability release:
"Several reports came with fixes we can use nearly as-is"
Noah Misch, PostgreSQL
The company tested an early scanner version by asking penetration testers to assess 97 critical and high-severity findings across 48 projects. Of these, 85 met its coordinated vulnerability disclosure criteria. Eleven others were real but duplicated known issues or other scan findings, while one was invalid. These results describe that selected sample, rather than establishing an accuracy rate for every report the service will produce.
Anthropic have however acknowledged that some maintainers have seen some inflated severity ratings and misunderstandings of the threat models around their projects. OpenSSL Corporation's Anton Arapov nevertheless described the raw reports as "as good and sometimes better than what we get from people", particularly when a working exploit made verification straightforward.
wolfSSL's Todd Ouska reported that candidate patches fitted the project's existing verification and remediation process:
"of the 74 reports we received, all but two were valid, and five became CVEs."
Todd Ouska, wolfSSL
There is also a maintainer-confirmed example outside the announcement. curl's Daniel Stenberg attributed an HTTP/2 upload use-after-free vulnerability to Luna Tong at Anthropic using OSS Scanner. Fixed in curl 8.23.0, CVE-2026-92392 could permit remote code execution under specific conditions. Stenberg rated it high rather than critical because successful exploitation would be difficult; a crash was the more likely outcome.
Anthropic cites Google's OSS-Fuzz as an inspiration, although OSS Scanner uses language models to investigate code. Another comparison is Google DeepMind's CodeMender, reported by InfoQ in October 2025. In that launch announcement, researchers Raluca Ada Popa and Four Flynn described automated patch validation using program analysis and testing. They retained human review before upstream submission, unlike OSS Scanner's direct delivery of unreviewed findings.
The work that follows discovery also features in community commentary. Varun Badhwar wrote on LinkedIn: "An upstream patch doesn't help much if you're stuck three major versions behind." Badhwar, CEO and co-founder of application security vendor Endor Labs, argued that enterprises need to establish whether vulnerable code is reachable and whether they can adopt a fix without breaking applications.
Dimitrios Thomas wrote on LinkedIn, in a personal capacity, that evaluations should consider "validation accuracy, maintainer workload and time from discovery to a deployed fix". His suggested measures extend beyond the number of vulnerabilities reported.
The scanner FAQ describes agents that double-check bugs, propose patches and analyse root causes before reports are emailed. This automated checking is separate from human review. Subsequent scans look for newly introduced problems and issues missed previously; their frequency depends on factors including project usage and the service's workload.
Core maintainers enrol through a GitHub pull request containing project configuration and a Dockerfile that prepares the build and dependencies. Scanning runs without internet access after setup, and an optional threat-model file can document scope and severity expectations. Eligibility is assessed case by case, with priority given to established projects important to infrastructure and user security that can already handle verified high-severity reports.
Maintainers can use the threat-model document to identify untrusted inputs, exclude components and explain how they judge severity. It can also specify preferred report formats and patch expectations. Anthropic checks enrolment requests manually to confirm the applicant is a core maintainer and that findings will reach an authorised project security contact.
Projects can pause reports or withdraw. Unvalidated findings carry no automatic 90-day disclosure deadline, although a report later validated manually can enter the separate coordinated disclosure process, with its 90-day period starting when maintainers are notified of that validation. The company continues to offer human-reviewed disclosures, particularly for projects without the resources to triage raw findings.

articles.title: 11 Million Impacted by Capcom Data Breach
articles.text:
Japanese gaming company Capcom has disclosed a data breach impacting 11 million email addresses and the personal information of a small number of individuals.
The incident, the gaming giant says, was discovered on October 19 and involved unauthorized access to CAPCOM ID, its shared service used for accessing online services and for playing online games.
During the intrusion, the hackers stole the email addresses of 11,774,247 people, along with account data such as creation date, last login date, number of logins, and the last login’s IP address.
For 43 of the affected customers, the hackers also compromised dates of birth, gender information, country/region details, and nicknames.
Additionally, Capcom determined that the attackers changed the CAPCOM ID account passwords for 196 of the affected users. The company says that no user passwords were compromised and that it has already reset the passwords for the affected accounts.
Capcom says it implemented incident response measures and all services using CAPCOM ID remain available.
“In addition, we have started to contact the target customers sequentially, and we have established a dedicated contact point for customers regarding this matter,” an automated translation of Capcom’s incident notice reads.
The gaming company says it has reported the data breach to the relevant authorities and continues to investigate it.
It also warns the affected users to be wary of unsolicited email messages impersonating the company or related entities and containing suspicious URLs or attachments.
“We take this matter seriously and will continue to conduct detailed surveys, take measures to prevent recurrence based on the causes identified this time, and work to further strengthen our information security system,” Capcom added.

articles.title: Vercel moved to kill static credentials. Then developers spotted its own deployment token.
articles.text:
Vercel moved to kill static credentials. Then developers spotted its own deployment token.
Vercel wants to eliminate long-lived API keys from its ecosystem, and it is giving Marketplace vendors until January 2027 to comply or risk being delisted, a push that lands as a run of credential-stealing supply chain attacks — including a recent npm worm that scraped tokens straight out of CI pipelines — keeps proving how much damage a single leaked secret can do.
Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone.
Developers have already pointed out a complication, though: Vercel’s own GitHub Actions deployment workflow still relies on the kind of persistent credential the company now wants gone.
In a Thursday announcement, Vercel CTO Malte Ubl says the company surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported what Vercel considers secure authentication methods, and it is now pushing OpenID Connect (OIDC) and short-lived, identity-based tokens as the alternative to static API keys that can stay valid indefinitely.
Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch amplifies the message on X, writing that it is “time to kill ‘static credentials’” and arguing that while attacks and breaches can still happen, stolen credentials should behave more like “self-destructing keys” that expire before an attacker can keep using them.
Vercel’s deployment double standard
Developer and senior software engineer at Fanatics, Yordis Prieto sharpens that point, writing in reply that Vercel had “invented” OIDC federation yet still left him leaning on “a long-lived access token” in his CI pipeline, and he presses the company to drop the token requirement from GitHub CI while criticizing its non-expiring token option.
Vercel’s GitHub Actions deployment guide still instructs developers to authenticate deployments with a VERCEL_TOKEN secret, and in Thursday’s announcement Ubl says the company is extending OIDC support across its API and CLI to retire long-lived tokens from deployment workflows, which for now leaves Vercel asking Marketplace vendors to adopt a standard its own deployment tooling has not fully implemented.
By November 30, Marketplace integrations that fall short of Vercel’s authentication requirements will carry a “Not secure” warning on their listing, and the company has not published its survey methodology, named the companies it surveyed, or disclosed how many existing Marketplace partners will have to change their authentication systems.
Short-lived tokens for agents
As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses. One way to reduce the risks of persistent access keys is to use short-lived, just-in-time credentials that expire rather than leaving agents with ongoing access.
As AI agents gain access to more external services, credential management is becoming a greater consideration for agent harnesses.
Vercel’s Connect service addresses part of that problem by letting applications and agents request scoped credentials at runtime using their deployment identity rather than storing secrets in application environments. Connect also handles token exchange and renewal.
An October 15 update added enterprise-managed authorization in public beta, allowing administrators to control access to supported services through identity providers such as Okta.
Connect still allows static keys
Even so, Vercel Connect still supports static API keys for providers that lack OAuth or another identity-based option, and its documentation describes storing those credentials centrally and pulling them at runtime, while the underlying keys can still live indefinitely.
The company also introduced GitHub OIDC authentication for its Container Registry in late September, though that work does nothing to remove the VERCEL_TOKEN requirement from its documented GitHub Actions deployment flow.
OIDC across Vercel’s own tooling
For now, Vercel faces the same job it is handing its Marketplace vendors: replacing long-lived credentials across infrastructure it already runs, and until OIDC support reaches workflows like GitHub Actions deployments, developers will keep needing the very tokens Vercel is urging the rest of the industry to give up.

articles.title: Resumo da semana: eleições, IA e os próximos passos da exploração espacial
articles.text:
A semana foi marcada por decisões e discussões que podem influenciar o futuro da tecnologia no Brasil e no mundo. Às vésperas do segundo turno das eleições, o Olhar Digital analisou as propostas dos candidatos para áreas estratégicas, enquanto novas notícias movimentaram os setores de inteligência artificial, segurança digital e exploração espacial.
Eleições 2026: o que Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro propõem para o futuro do Brasil
Inteligência artificial, data centers, soberania digital, clima, energia e minerais críticos estão entre os temas que podem influenciar os rumos tecnológicos e econômicos do país. Para comparar as propostas dos candidatos à Presidência, o Olhar Digital preparou reportagens especiais sobre os planos de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).
As análises abordam as estratégias para desenvolver a infraestrutura tecnológica nacional, enfrentar os desafios climáticos e energéticos e explorar recursos minerais importantes para a indústria. Juntas, as reportagens ajudam a entender as diferenças entre as propostas e os desafios para colocá-las em prática.
