Saiba mais (terras raras e minerais críticos).
NASA planeja próximos passos para voltar à Lua
A exploração lunar continuou entre os assuntos de destaque, com novidades sobre o cronograma do programa Artemis. Os planos da NASA envolvem testes e etapas preparatórias para levar astronautas novamente à superfície lunar, em meio à disputa internacional por avanços na exploração espacial.
Falhas críticas no PHP afetam sistemas públicos
Duas vulnerabilidades graves na linguagem PHP colocaram sistemas públicos em risco e provocaram a retirada temporária de serviços do ar no Brasil. O caso reforçou a importância de corrigir falhas de segurança e manter sistemas e servidores atualizados.
Segurança da inteligência artificial volta ao centro do debate
Novos episódios envolvendo sistemas de inteligência artificial reacenderam a discussão sobre os limites de autonomia dos agentes e a eficácia dos mecanismos de segurança desenvolvidos para controlá-los. O tema também levanta dúvidas sobre a responsabilidade das empresas à medida que seus modelos ganham novas capacidades.
Saiba mais sobre os testes com a OpenAI. Veja também o projeto da Anthropic e o teste com o Claude Mythos.
Elon Musk considera possível fusão entre Tesla e SpaceX
Uma possível fusão entre a Tesla e a SpaceX também chamou atenção. A combinação aproximaria os negócios de veículos elétricos e energia dos projetos espaciais de Elon Musk, embora a operação ainda dependa de decisões e negociações.
Calor extremo e conectividade via satélite também estiveram em pauta
A semana trouxe ainda notícias sobre eventos climáticos extremos e a expansão da conectividade via satélite, com a chegada da SpaceSail ao Brasil. Os assuntos mostram como mudanças ambientais e novas infraestruturas tecnológicas seguem influenciando a economia e o cotidiano.
Saiba mais sobre as ondas de calor globais. Confira também a estimativa de mortes na Europa.
Proteção de menores nas redes sociais segue em discussão
As medidas para proteger crianças e adolescentes no ambiente digital continuaram em pauta. O debate envolve a responsabilidade das plataformas, a exposição a conteúdos nocivos e os desafios de conciliar segurança, privacidade e acesso aos serviços digitais.
Saiba mais sobre a lei grega. Confira também a proposta da Noruega e a discussão sobre o design viciante no Brasil.
Ana Figueiredo é editora de tecnologia do Olhar Digital. É formada em Jornalismo pela Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU).

articles.title: Anthropic ofrece hasta USD 345.000 al año por un escritor humano para sus ejecutivos
articles.text:
Anthropic, la empresa detrás del chatbot de inteligencia artificial Claude, busca contratar a un escritor humano con un salario de hasta USD 345.000 al año. El aviso, publicado en su propio sitio de empleos, pide ocho años de experiencia en comunicación ejecutiva y capacidad para trabajar con información técnica bajo presión.
El puesto, llamado Escritor de Comunicaciones Ejecutivas, ofrece un rango salarial de entre USD 295.000 y USD 345.000 al año, según la publicación en la plataforma de empleos Greenhouse. La oferta incluye además la posibilidad de una compensación adicional en acciones de la compañía.
El trabajo consiste en redactar discursos, coordinar la respuesta de los directivos ante noticias de último momento y traducir conceptos técnicos complejos para públicos externos. Anthropic pide, además, experiencia previa en organizaciones de alto ritmo y buen criterio para manejar situaciones ambiguas.
A diferencia de un redactor de contenidos convencional, el cargo requiere ayudar a definir no solo cómo comunicar una idea, sino qué debe decir un directivo y en qué momento conviene hacerlo, de acuerdo con la descripción publicada por la empresa.
Anthropic busca, en particular, candidatos con experiencia en al menos un área ligada a sus directivos: investigación científica, arquitectura de productos de inteligencia artificial, estrategia comercial o narrativa visual de marca, según el texto de la convocatoria.
La empresa, con oficinas en San Francisco y Nueva York, exige que su personal asista de forma presencial al menos el 25% de la semana laboral bajo su política híbrida actual. El aviso aclara que Anthropic ofrece asistencia para tramitar una visa de trabajo, aunque no puede garantizarla en todos los casos.
La paradoja de pagar a un humano por escribir
Ann Handley, directora de contenidos de la firma de capacitación en marketing MarketingProfs, dijo al sitio Business Insider que cuando la velocidad de redacción se abarata, el criterio adquiere más valor. Según explicó, el trabajo de un escritor con experiencia puede incluir decidir qué debe comunicar un líder, no solo cómo redactarlo.
La búsqueda llega semanas después de que Anthropic publicara, el 16 de octubre, un informe sobre su propia dotación de personal técnico. El documento se basa en datos internos de la compañía y en entrevistas a 17 empleados.
Según ese reporte, el porcentaje de empleados de nivel inicial, conocido como personal junior, en las áreas técnicas bajó del 21% al 14% desde comienzos de 2025. La proporción de nuevas contrataciones técnicas junior, en particular, cayó del 27% al 9% en el mismo período.
El documento también señala que la compañía siguió sumando personal técnico en general, mientras que las áreas de ventas, finanzas y reclutamiento crecieron más rápido. Anthropic atribuyó parte del cambio a la expansión de su negocio y a que las herramientas de programación permiten que empleados sin perfil técnico desarrollen software.
Hacia abril, cerca de un tercio de los gerentes de aprendizaje automático y una quinta parte de los gerentes de ingeniería de software de la empresa dijeron que contrataban menos personal por el avance de sus propios modelos de inteligencia artificial.
Un puesto pensado para las crisis de comunicación
Entre las tareas del cargo figura también el apoyo presencial en eventos corporativos y la coordinación de las respuestas de los ejecutivos durante noticias que se desarrollan rápidamente. El aviso pide que el candidato sea, según sus propias palabras, un colaborador flexible capaz de manejar situaciones ambiguas.
Anthropic se prepara, según trascendidos recientes, para una posible salida a bolsa que podría valuarla en unos USD 2 billones. El nuevo puesto de comunicaciones ejecutivas se suma a su estructura mientras la compañía crece y multiplica su exposición pública.

articles.title: Berlin’s Cygrid exits stealth with €2.66 million to stop AI agents from accessing confidential company data | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cygrid, a Berlin-based cybersecurity startup, has exited stealth with a €2.66 million pre-Seed funding round for its identity-enforcement platform that controls access to confidential information.
The funding round was led by Atlantic, the pan-European pre-Seed fund, with participation from D11Z. Ventures, alongside angel investors including Boris Gorin, VP Product at Zscaler and founder of Canonic Security; Andreas Bermig, CEO of bonify; and Vlad Tropko of AmberVale Capital.
“Dmitry and Dekel are proven builders who combine deep cybersecurity experience with a real understanding of what enterprises need: security that stops the wrong action without slowing the business down. AI agents are widening the identity attack surface faster than any control can keep up. Intelligence-driven enforcement is the only answer that scales. The timing for Cygrid couldn’t be better,” said Marc-Olivier Lücke, General Partner, Atlantic.
Cygrid was founded in January 2026 by Dmitry Kharchenko and Dekel Paz, both of whom served in the Israeli Military Intelligence. The pair identified a security blind spot created by the rapid proliferation of AI agents inside enterprises, and Cygrid solves this by changing how identity and access management works at the enterprise level.
Unlike conventional identity and access management tools, which grant access at sign-in and stop there, Cygrid enforces limits continuously, checking each action an agent takes and blocking or narrowing it in real time. It also maps human, non-human and AI agent identities into a single intelligence graph, correlating what each identity is entitled to, what it actually does, and on whose behalf it acts. The company argues this approach lets it revoke a forgotten token in seconds and stop a risky AI agent command before it executes.
“Access control tells you who can log in. It says nothing about what they do next. Every identity in an enterprise can act, and once a token is valid, not one control in the stack can stop the action. Cygrid is the platform that does: it decides what each identity may do and enforces it before anything executes,” said Kharchenko, CEO and co-founder, Cygrid.
In just nine months after incorporation, Cygrid is already serving 19 design partners across FinTech, e-commerce, and SaaS verticals, with six in production. In one early deployment, a Berlin-based D2C company discovered AI agents and third-party app connections its own security team was unaware of, and used Cygrid to remediate more than 100 risky findings.
The fundraise follows a rise in attacks on trusted identities. According to Palo Alto Networks, machine identities now outnumber human ones by 109 to 1, with 79 of those being AI agents. A CrowdStrike report from 2026 found that 82% of cyber detections involve no malware whatsoever; the attackers simply exploited trusted identities such as leaked tokens or compromised agent providers.
With more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies already deploying AI agents and nearly a third of employees using connected agents without organisational approval, according to Microsoft’s Cyber Pulse report 2026, Cygrid sees an urgent, wide-open opportunity.
The startup will use the fresh capital toward expanding its enforcement capabilities, growing its team, and scaling go-to-market operations across Europe. It aims to become the European alternative to US and Israeli providers of AI identity security.
“This funding allows us to scale that approach and help organisations move from reactive identity security to continuous, real-time enforcement, so they can adopt AI agents at full speed without losing control of what those agents can do,” added Kharchenko.

articles.title: Q&A: Why economist and author Kyla Scanlon thinks the AI bubble will pop slowly | BetaKit
articles.text:
Will the AI bubble pop with a bang, or go out more like a sad balloon?
Anthropic was preparing to soon hold a record-breaking IPO, just months after Elon Musk’s SpaceX held its own. But Reuters reported on Tuesday that the San Francisco-based AI giant is now lowering its valuation target amid dramatically widened net losses. It’s yet another symptom of the AI bubble spectre, as investors question when, if ever, AI demand will justify the cost of the associated buildout.
To understand that question for ourselves, BetaKit brought in the big guns: economic commentator and New York Times best-selling author Kyla Scanlon. She joined the BetaKit Podcast earlier this month to help us finally understand what’s going on in the AI and labour markets, as well as ease (or intensify) the AI bubble fears.
An excerpt from that conversation is below.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
BetaKit editor-in-chief Douglas Soltys: About a month ago, BetaKit walked through a series of our favourite AI bubble red flags on this podcast. Do you have a preferred AI bubble red flag, or are you optimistic?
I’m really watching the debt markets. The companies are borrowing quite heavily; they’re spending a ton of money, and I worry about that because once you involve debt, that’s when things get really serious. That’s when systemic risk can start to spread because of who owns that debt. If insurers are buying up that debt, that exposes them, therefore, it exposes households to the AI bubble bursting.
BetaKit managing editor Sarah Rieger: That was something we definitely wanted to talk about today; KKR issued a warning last week. Do you think we’re at the point where all this over-leverage is close to tipping?
There was a really good paper out of Brookings called Financing the AI Buildout. The author said that the AI companies are going to need to make, like, $10 trillion by 2032. It’s really hard to conceptualize that much money. Jared Bernstein, who is the former chair of [former US president Joe] Biden’s council of economic advisors, summarizes it as Amazon and Google would have to build a whole other Amazon and Google on top of the existing Amazon and Google just for AI within the next 10 years in order to make the app buildout work.
RELATED: “The math is not mathing”: How AI bubble fears are changing Canadian VCs’ investment approach
If you think about it, it took 30 years to build Amazon and Google the first time. We’re not totally sure who’s going to be paying for all these AI products. All of a sudden, they’re just spending all this money, and you can’t even plug in some of the data centers. There’s just not enough power, particularly in the United States. So it just seems like the AI industry is a little bit over its skis.
DS: Do you think AI is propping up the stock market?
I think the stock market is not even the stock market. The stock market is AI companies. Like, 75 percent of companies in the S&P 500 are below their 50-day moving average. So, it’s really just a couple of guys pulling this thing up. If you look at the S&P equal weight, that thing’s down four percent. So the S&P is really being driven by these AI companies.
I think it’s just the classic signs of a bubble, where people are like, ‘Okay, cool. This is really exciting and awesome, and I’m going to put money into this buildout because I think that there’s no other alternative because of the weak points in the other parts of the economy.’ The United States’ economy definitely has a cold right now, one might say, and when the US sneezes, the whole world catches a cold, and we’re certainly seeing that.
DS: With AI, we’re seeing both people spinning up companies fast, as well as young people having the worst possible time finding their way into the labour market. How does that play into all of this?
I think for young folks right now, there’s this sense that you studied really hard in school, you did everything right, and it didn’t matter. We haven’t really provided much guidance for anybody to navigate this new economy, and I think for a lot of corporations the number one goal seems to be saving money, and the way you save money is by not investing in the future, it seems, in terms of your employees. I think it’s creating downstream effects that a lot of companies are underpricing. If you don’t hire juniors now, you’re not going to have seniors later.
RELATED: Waving the AI bubble red flags
At the end of the day, somebody else has to buy your product, and ideally you want people employed so they can buy your product, just from a functional perspective.
SR: If we are in a bubble, is there a possibility here of a managed release of air from that bubble, or could this all just pop? Is there a way out that is less dramatic than that?
If the bubble does pop—if it is a bubble—it seems like it’s going to be pretty slow just because of how the money is wrapped up and because there are so many big banks involved. People are trying to protect against the downside here, so it seems like it would be a slow release of air.
I think the highest probability scenario is that AI demand doesn’t totally match what the buildout expected; we have a bunch of empty data centers, and the companies have to figure out how to pay back all that debt. Some of them might not be able to. They’ll go bankrupt and default on those loans. I don’t think it’s going to be like a big implosion, but who knows? That could change depending on how much more they borrow and who they borrow from. Once you get life insurance involved, that gets dicey real fast.

With files from Douglas Soltys and Sarah Rieger.

articles.title: Extremely rare and 'previously undocumented' Pokémon Red prototype cartridge surfaces at auction, starting at $25,000 — Nintendo Game Boy dev board from 1998 features 32KB of readable memory, fully identical to the final game release
articles.text:
Extremely rare and 'previously undocumented' Pokémon Red prototype cartridge surfaces at auction, starting at $25,000 — Nintendo Game Boy dev board from 1998 features 32KB of readable memory, fully identical to the final game release
A piece of gaming history, with a big price tag
A rare, prototype copy of Pokémon Red for the Nintendo Game Boy, originally released back in 1998, is on sale at auction, with a single bid of $25,000 currently registered so far. This prototype, spotted by Retro Dodo, is "incredibly rare" and features 32KB of readable data. According to the Goldin auction page, the cartridge has been authenticated by specialists at PSA, who examined the card. According to them, while a "complete data read" wasn't possible, the first 32KB of data was, a "technically unique" result. The PSA notes, however, that the game data is otherwise "completely identical" to the U.S. release version of the game, with PSA "expressing confidence" that the rest of the data, if it were readable, would match.
The PSA report does note two changes to the ROM's header data that don't affect the game data. According to PSA, "the difference is at offset 0x014C, which denotes the Mask ROM version and is incorrectly set to 55 when it should be 00. This has the effect of changing offset 0x014D, which is a calculated header checksum, to CB instead of 20."
This prototype development cartridge has a sticker reading DMB-MBC-16M-FLASH, with a part number DMG-(F)KGDB-01. DMB likely refers to Dot Matrix Game, the original internal codename for the Game Boy, while MBC likely means Memory Bank Controller, a custom chip that allowed games to use more than the Game Boy's 32KB ROM limit. 16M likely refers to a 16 megabit limit of flash-writable memory. Retro Dodo notes that the cartridge is longer than a standard Game Boy cartridge, too.
The auction notes that this uses a "previously undocumented" development board, although the DMG-(F)KGDB-01 part number has been seen before. The Rare Gaming Dump wiki, for instance, lists the same part number for a development cartridge from 2000. It, too, had a 16 megabit Sharp flash chip, with U1 FLASH MEMORY printed on the board. Close-up views from the Goldin auction page show an almost identical design, although the wiki entry shows a slightly different DMG-MBC3-16M-FLASH cartridge sticker.
Pokémon Red is a gaming classic that helped kickstart the global Pokémon franchise in the 1990s, along with Green and Blue. Combined with Blue, Pokémon Red is reported to have sold more than 31 million copies. There are several days left to go on this auction, so while the single bidder may secure this piece of gaming history for $25,000, it may sell for an even higher price before the auction process ends.

articles.title: Faster OpenVPN, P2P on every server, and fewer commands: NordVPN 6.0 lands on Linux
articles.text:
Faster OpenVPN, P2P on every server, and fewer commands: NordVPN 6.0 lands on Linux
Version 6.0.0 moves obfuscated servers to NordWhisper, speeds up OpenVPN on modern kernels, and clears out legacy commands
- NordVPN 6.0.0 for Linux moves its obfuscated servers onto the in-house NordWhisper protocol.
- OpenVPN connections should get faster on newer kernels, and P2P now works on every standard server.
- Several legacy commands have been retired, so anyone relying on scripts should check before updating.
NordVPN has pushed out version 6.0.0 of its Linux app, dated October 22, 2026, and the jump to a new major version number feels earned.
The update reworks how obfuscation works, speeds up OpenVPN on newer kernels, and trims a handful of legacy commands from the CLI.
It’s the latest in a long run of Linux upgrades from the provider. Back in August, version 5.3.0 began installing the GUI app automatically alongside the command-line daemon.
NordWhisper takes over obfuscation
The biggest change is that NordVPN’s obfuscated servers now run on NordWhisper rather than OpenVPN XOR. Choosing NordWhisper switches obfuscation on automatically, so the old nordvpn set obfuscate command has been removed entirely.
NordWhisper is NordVPN’s own censorship-resistant protocol, launched in January 2025 and aimed at networks that actively block VPNs, such as some workplaces, schools, public Wi-Fi, and heavily censored regions. Until now, using obfuscated servers meant switching to OpenVPN.
The nordvpn set protocol command now picks the technology and protocol in one go; for example, nordvpn set protocol openvpn_udp.
Faster OpenVPN and P2P everywhere
OpenVPN has been bumped to version 2.7.7, and Data Channel Offload (DCO) now works out of the box on Linux kernel 6.16 or newer. DCO hands OpenVPN’s data handling to the Linux kernel itself, avoiding slow transfers between kernel space and user space, and the driver was upstreamed into the 6.16 kernel.
OpenVPN still has ground to make up on NordLynx, NordVPN’s WireGuard-based protocol. In TechRadar’s testing, NordLynx consistently hit 780-950+ Mbps, while NordVPN’s OpenVPN implementation managed 109-173 Mbps.
The dedicated P2P server group has also gone, because every regular server now supports P2P, so torrent users can simply pick a location. NordVPN has stopped labelling virtual servers too, explaining that “sometimes a server is just a server."
Check your scripts before updating
The cleanup is where power users should pay attention. The outdated threatprotectionlite, tplite, tpl, and cybersec aliases have been removed, along with the old whitelist alias for allowlist. Real-time protection is now enabled with nordvpn set protection on. Auto-connect also can no longer target a specific server number, so you’ll need to choose a country, city, server group, or the fastest server instead.
On the fixes front, port forwarding on dedicated servers now works with Meshnet and LAN discovery enabled, nordvpn set defaults properly restores every setting, and the tray Pause menu on Linux Mint works again. LAN discovery also gains multicast and SSDP support, and screen reader navigation has been improved further.
Unlike NordVPN’s other apps, the Linux version doesn’t update automatically. On Debian-based distros, run sudo apt-get update followed by sudo apt-get install nordvpn. If you’re shopping around, our best Linux VPN guide has more options.

Monica is a tech journalist with over a decade of experience. She writes about the latest developments in computing, which means anything from computer chips made out of paper to cutting-edge desktop processors.
GPUs are her main area of interest, and nothing thrills her quite like that time every couple of years when new graphics cards hit the market.
She built her first PC nearly 20 years ago, and dozens of builds later, she’s always planning out her next build (or helping her friends with theirs). During her career, Monica has written for many tech-centric outlets, including Digital Trends, SlashGear, WePC, and Tom’s Hardware.

articles.title: Sony abandona su último reproductor Blu-ray y se despide del formato físico
articles.text:
Sony ha puesto punto final a una de las categorías de dispositivos que ayudó a popularizar durante las últimas dos décadas. La compañía japonesa confirmó que dejará de fabricar el UBP-X700/K, su último reproductor Blu-ray Ultra HD que todavía se vendía en Japón. Con ello, Sony saldrá del mercado de reproductores dedicados, una jugada que forma parte de una estrategia para alejarse del formato físico.
Según recoge FlatpanelsHD, el UBP-X700/K dejó de distribuirse el 22 de octubre de 2026 y desaparecerá una vez que se agoten todas las unidades. Este modelo llegó como una actualización del UBP-X700 y era compatible con discos Ultra HD Blu-ray, HDR10, Dolby Vision, Dolby Atmos y DTS:X. Sony no ha revelado si habrá un sucesor, pero todo indica que no ocurrirá, puesto que la compañía ha dejado de invertir en este tipo de reproductores debido al auge del formato digital.
Hace más de un año que la japonesa anunció que dejaría de fabricar discos Blu-ray grabables y que no tenía planes de un nuevo formato. Aunque Sony aclaró que la medida solo se aplicaría a los discos vírgenes y no a las películas o videojuegos, la realidad es que la empresa ya tenía planes de alejarse de este negocio. En junio de este año, PlayStation dio la estocada final al formato físico al anunciar que ya no lanzarían juegos en disco a partir de 2028, generando rechazo por una buena parte de la comunidad de jugadores.
En el caso de los reproductores de películas, Sony también ha dejado sin opciones a los entusiastas. Al discontinuar el UBP-X700/K, la PlayStation 5 será la única alternativa para reproducir discos Ultra HD Blu-ray, aunque sin compatibilidad con Dolby Vision.
Sony se aleja del Blu-ray y el formato físico
El fin del UBP-X700/K podría pasar desapercibido para las nuevas generaciones que crecieron con Instagram y Netflix, pero para el resto no. Sony fue una de las principales impulsoras del formato Blu-ray y participó activamente en el desarrollo de Ultra HD Blu-ray.
Aunque el Blu-ray llegó al mercado en junio del 2006, este formato no se convirtió en el sucesor inmediato del DVD. En esos tiempos existía una batalla entre el Blu-ray y el HD DVD para definir cuál sería el formato que ofrecía la mejor experiencia para los videos en HD. Empresas como Sony, Panasonic y Philips apoyaban al Blu-ray, mientras que Toshiba, NEC y Sanyo impulsaban el HD-DVD. La misma Microsoft apoyó a este último con un reproductor externo para la Xbox 360.
Al final, el Blu-ray ganó gracias al apoyo de los grandes estudios de Hollywood y a sus capacidades tecnológicas y. Sony fue una de las compañías que más se benefició, ya que la PS3 incluía un reproductor compatible con juegos y películas de este formato, algo similar a lo que ocurrió con el DVD en tiempos de la PS2. Tras dos décadas de dominar en el mercado, ahora Sony dice adiós porque las descargas digitales y el streaming se han comido el mercado.
Con con la salida de Sony, Panasonic quedará como la única que ofrece una alternativa para quienes desean montar un cine en casa. También existen Magnetar o Pannde, aunque estos van dirigidos a quienes no tienen problemas en pagar más de 2500 euros por un reproductor de Blu-ray.

articles.title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
articles.text:
Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny.
Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
You have got to listen to these conversations with Block’s new Dessa AI model.
Take this one, for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”).
Here’s a video of Dessa playing a guessing game over voice:
The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video.
On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.
Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.
AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.
The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

articles.title: Samsung arruina la batería de los Galaxy S24 y S25 con la actualización a One UI 9
articles.text:
Mucho ojo con la actualización a One UI 9 y Android 17 en tu móvil Samsung. Usuarios de los Galaxy S24 y S25 reportan drásticos problemas con la duración de la batería tras instalarla, lo que da a entender que un bug en el nuevo software podría ser la causa detrás de este fallo.
Según recoge Android Authority, los casos de usuarios impactados por esta situación se han replicado con rapidez tanto en Reddit como en foros dedicados a dispositivos de Samsung. Por lo pronto, la firma coreana no se ha pronunciado respecto de lo que está sucediendo, aunque considerando la gravedad de algunas situaciones no sería raro que ya lo esté investigando.
Los problemas de batería tras instalar One UI 9 no se limita a los Galaxy S24 y S25 base. También hay reportes de situaciones similares en las versiones Plus y Ultra de los dispositivos en cuestión.
Uno de los casos más notorios es el de un usuario del Galaxy S24, cuya autonomía se degradó notoriamente tras instalar One UI 9. En una captura de pantalla se observa que tras cargar el móvil al 100 %, la batería se descargó hasta el 5 % en solo 5 horas y 2 minutos. Del total, el tiempo con la pantalla activada fue de 3 horas y 15 minutos.
One UI 9 estaría drenando la batería de los Galaxy S24 y S25
Que los Galaxy S24 y S25 se queden sin batería en un puñado de horas tras instalar One UI 9 es, sin dudas, una enorme molestia. No solo porque obliga a los usuarios a recargar el móvil de forma continua, sino también porque la actualización que llega junto con Android 17 era muy esperada.
Todavía no se sabe qué fallo puede estar provocando que los móviles de Samsung tengan una autonomía prácticamente nula. De todas maneras, la repetición de los incidentes en foros y Reddit da a entender que no es un problema que esté golpeando a un número ínfimo de personas.
Más allá del caso extremo del Galaxy S24 que vacía su batería en solamente 5 horas, otros reportes menos drásticos también mencionan un marcado incremento en el consumo de energía con la pantalla apagada tras instalar One UI 9. Un usuario incluso ha aseverado tener que cargar su móvil unas 4 o 5 veces al día para llegar hasta el final de la jornada.
Considerando que Samsung está desplegando One UI 9 a un gran número de dispositivos, incluyendo los de la serie Galaxy A, es lógico pensar que una solución a este problema no debería demorarse demasiado. Estaremos atentos a cualquier novedad en tal sentido.

articles.title: Calls and texts no longer the main priority for young Australian smartphone users - Tech Guide
articles.text:
New research by Samsung shows calls and texts are no longer the primary use of smartphones for almost a quarter of Australians aged 18 to 24.
For 22 per cent of young Australians between 18 and 24, calls and texts – the first features enabled when mobile phones became a popular consumer product – is now not the top priority.
For everyone else, calls and texts as the main use of their device have fallen from 67 per cent in 2019 to 53 per cent in 2026.
This is a significant shift in how Australians use mobile phone technology.
The study shows smartphones are increasingly becoming more work-centric but also designed for entertainment, creativity, and everyday life.
As a result Australians are demanding more from their mobile devices than ever before.
The change in behaviour in the past seven years has coincided with the period when Samsung released its first foldable phone.
In fact, foldable phones have emerged as the new all-in-one solution for productivity, creativity, and entertainment.
Apple has also just entered the foldable market with the release of the iPhone Duo.
It will certainly bring a lot more attention to the category and attract more customers to adopt the new form factor.
Social media recorded the biggest increase as a primary smartphone usage, rising from 17 per cent in 2019 to 24 per cent in 2026.
Meanwhile smartphone use for work purposes increased by more than 50 per cent in the same period.
“In just seven years, Australians have shifted from using smartphones primarily to call and text to relying on them as all-in-one tools for work, payments, navigation, social connection and AI-powered assistance,” says Gary Mortimer, Queensland University of Technology, Professor of Marketing and Consumer Behaviour.
“The smartphone has evolved from a communication device into a digital life hub.”
The research also showed 60 per cent of Australians say smartphone productivity is more important today than it was in 2019, while 63 per cent see the improvement in smartphone photography as a key feature.
Another 40 per cent say they their smartphone replacing their wallet, keys, and ID is also an important smartphone innovation that they didn’t know they needed seven years ago.
The findings also play into the growing appeal of a foldable smartphone.
Earlier this year Samsung introduced the Galaxy Z Fold8 – a passport-shaped foldable smartphone which has been a huge success around the world.
It was also joined by the Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra and the Galaxy Z Flip8 which expanded Samsung’s portfolio to support different customers and different lifestyles to suit their productivity, multitasking, creativity and entertainment needs.

articles.title: Les banques sont « horrifiées » : des IA ont fait irruption dans des comptes bancaires
articles.text:
Une enquête d’Axios lève le voile sur un phénomène inquiétant. Le média a découvert que plusieurs grandes banques des États-Unis ont identifié des agents IA au sein des comptes de leurs clients. Interrogés sur la question, plusieurs responsables pointent du doigt une « situation effarante ». L’un des dirigeants précise que le secteur bancaire nourrit de « graves inquiétudes » à l’idée que des agents IA prennent des mesures « susceptibles d’affecter les finances des utilisateurs ».
À lire aussi : Deux ChatGPT ont pris des initiatives inquiétantes, et OpenAI ne comprend pas pourquoi
Une infraction aux règles bancaires
Comme le rapporte le média, l’intrusion commence lorsqu’un internaute confie ses identifiants à un assistant IA. Sans surprise, l’internaute veut déléguer certaines tâches à l’assistant. En se faisant passer pour le client, l’agent IA se connecte alors au compte, ce qui viole les règles de la plupart des banques. Les établissements bancaires exigent en effet que chaque personne se connecte elle-même à son propre compte.
Sur le papier, il n’est pas autorisé de déléguer l’accès à une IA. Dans certains des cas épinglés, les agents IA ne se sont pas contentés de consulter les transactions. Certaines IA ont contacté les centres d’appels de la banque et ont pris « des initiatives indépendamment des instructions de l’utilisateur ». En clair, des IA se sont mises à improviser diverses actions alors qu’elles avaient le contrôle du compte en banque
À lire aussi : Arnaques en ligne : malgré la nouvelle loi, votre banque peut encore refuser de vous rembourser
Les banques prennent des mesures
Les banques n’arrivent pas à distinguer les opérations réalisées par une IA de celles initiées par un être humain. Un cadre dans une banque américaine admet ne pas savoir si un agent « a été autorisé par un utilisateur ou s’il est devenu incontrôlable » après son irruption sur le compte.
Face au phénomène, la riposte des banques a pris des formes variées. Morgan Stanley a bloqué purement et simplement les agents sur ses plateformes. Plus modérés, JPMorgan, Bank of America et Citi se sont contentés de restreindre l’accès accordé à un agent. La plupart des banques s’orientent vers un accès « en lecture seule ». En clair, l’agent pourrait consulter les informations financières du client, sans réaliser la moindre transaction de son propre chef. Un porte-parole de Chase rappelle que « les clients ne doivent communiquer leurs identifiants et mots de passe à personne », y compris à un assistant IA.
Reste un équilibre délicat à trouver. Gareth Davies, Chief Product Officer d’Auth0 (Okta), résume le dilemme des banques : « Les banques ont tout intérêt à mettre en place des garde-fous autour des agents IA, car, en définitive, ce sont elles qui doivent assumer les conséquences financières lorsqu’une fraude survient. Cependant, elles ne peuvent pas traiter les risques liés aux agents IA comme elles traitent la fraude traditionnelle, en se contentant de bloquer les activités suspectes après coup. Si elles bloquent les agents IA, elles bloquent aussi l’avenir du commerce. »
L’affaire a fait réagir le monde politique. Sur X, Bernie Sanders, sénateur indépendant du Vermont et figure de la gauche américaine, s’est emparé du sujet : « C’est insensé. Nous ne pouvons pas permettre aux agents d’IA d’accéder à votre compte bancaire et d’agir de manière indépendante sans votre autorisation. Mais c’est précisément ce qui se passe en ce moment. »
L’élu élargit aussitôt le propos à tout le système : « Laissé sans contrôle, l’IA pourrait mettre en danger l’ensemble du système financier mondial — y compris votre compte bancaire. » Avant un appel sans détour : « Stoppez l’IA maintenant ! »
Les dérives de l’IA se multiplient depuis quelques mois. Plusieurs versions de ChatGPT, Claude et Gemini ont orchestré des cyberattaques en toute autonomie, piratant des entreprises, des plateformes et des particuliers. Ces incidents à répétition ont poussé une grande partie de la Silicon Valley à réclamer un moratoire d’urgence sur la recherche et le développement des IA.

articles.title: The original Apple iPod debuted 25 years ago today — Steve Jobs’ $399 device fit 1,000 songs into a package the size of a deck of cards with 5 gigabytes of storage
articles.text:
The original Apple iPod debuted 25 years ago today — Steve Jobs’ $399 device fit 1,000 songs into a package the size of a deck of cards with 5 gigabytes of storage
The chunky little original iPod packed a 1.8-inch Toshiba HDD, and used FireWire because the USB of the era was too slow and didn't offer charging.
On this day in 2001, Apple CEO Steve Jobs unveiled the original iPod. He began the presentation by teasing “a breakthrough digital device that’s not a Mac.” Ultimately, the iPod that was revealed that day became a pocket-sized digital music player phenomenon, and would be many gadget fans' favorite always-carry device before smartphones matured enough to make such things redundant. The key claim iPod launched with was that it could put your entire music library in your pocket for $399.
In October 2001, when the iPod launched, Steve Jobs had successfully steered Apple beyond the beige into the Mac OS X era, with iBooks and iMacs well established. A revival of the Cupertino company's fortunes was well underway, with these iDevices doing well among consumers – at a difficult time, not long after the dot-com bubble burst.
Jobs predicted that the “Mac could become the center of your digital lifestyle.” It would do so as a hub uniting digital cameras, digital camcorders, DVD players – and the portable music player. Apple decided to go down this avenue as everyone loves music and it’s a huge target market, without a market leader, reasoned the CEO.
Small companies like Creative and Sonic Blue, and the much larger Sony, already had portable digital music players, acknowledged Jobs. However, “none of them has really found the recipe yet, for digital music,” he told the crowd at the iPod unveiling. At the time of Apple’s iPod announcement, there were four mainstream portable digital music solutions: CD players, MP3 CD players, flash players, and hard disk-based jukebox players. Jobs saw that last one as the optimal choice for market entry.
After this long preamble, the iPod was introduced as an MP3 music player, offering CD-quality sound, capable of playing all the popular formats of the time (MP3, WAV, AIFF). Its 5GB capacity meant that it could hold 1,000 songs. Specifically, that meant 1,000 typical pop-song length MP3s at 160Kbps. “For most people it’s their entire music library,” enthused Jobs.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The Apple CEO then sketched out three big claims that would make the iPod a winner. First, its ultra-portable form factor made it desirable. This aspect of the design was aided by Toshiba’s newest ultra-compact and ultra-thin hard drive at 1.8 inches in diameter and 0.2 inches thick. The actual device would be the size of a deck of cards – 2.4 x 4 x 0.78 inches, with a weight of 6.5 ounces, “lighter than most cell phones.”
Despite its compact size, the iPod offered advanced features like 20-minute skip protection, fast file transfers, and charging via a single FireWire 400 cable. The iPod was heralded as the “first and only music player with FireWire.” The connection was fast enough to transfer an entire CD to the device “in five to 10 seconds,” according to Jobs’ presentation. The USB connections of the same era would keep you waiting around five minutes for the same single CD of MP3s data transfer to complete, it was claimed. To fill the iPod (1,000 songs), it was estimated it would only take 10 minutes vs. five hours for a USB digital music player.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
A rechargeable lithium-polymer battery in the first iPod offered 10 hours of continuous music playback. An empty battery could be recharged to 80% in one hour, Apple said.
Secondly, the iPod benefitted from “an amazing Apple design,” with minimal and durable back and sides, noted Jobs. It was touted to offer “Apple’s legendary ease of use” in a portable music player. Its specially designed controls were single-hand friendly, with an accelerated scroll wheel using a piezoelectric clicker for tactile feedback. It enabled the fast location and playback of music by playlist, artist, or song. Quiz fans – the first song demoed on stage was 'Building a Mystery' by Sarah MacLachlan.
The third breakthrough for the iPod claimed by Jobs was its Auto-Sync with iTunes digital music libraries feature. iTunes 2 launched on the same day with several advanced features like MP3 CD burning and syncing support for the new music player. However, the Auto-Sync meant that the libraries you created, customized, and curated on your Mac would always be synced with your pocket player when you connected to transfer music or charge. The iPod also doubled as a FireWire HDD.
The first iPhone launched over five years later, in early 2007. Both devices would sit alongside each other in the Apple product stack for over a decade. However, the iPod’s star inevitably faded, with the final model being the 7th-generation iPod Touch in May 2019. The product line was left unmaintained but was only officially discontinued in May 2022.

Here's our pick of the top five NFL Week 7 games – and who's showing them
Who'd have imagined that the Rams' season would be hanging by a thread as early as Week 7 of the NFL 2026 campaign? That the reigning champion Seahawks would be staring down the barrel of a losing record? That the Packers would steady the ship so rapidly? Or that the Ravens could still be throwing away fourth-quarter leads?
That last one, perhaps, was acutely predictable, but otherwise the NFL is doing an impossibly good job of keeping us guessing from week to week.
Scroll down for our pick of the top five NFL Week 7 games – and who's showing them.
Steelers vs Saints
- Sunday, 9.30am ET, NFL Network/ESPN Unlimited (US) | FREE on Virgin Media Play (IRE)
The Steelers have been a model of consistency this season compared to the Saints, so nobody quite knows what to expect from the first ever NFL game in France. Taking place in Paris against a backdrop of serious unrest, there's a sense that the teams really ought to put on a good show. Both defenses came to the fore in victory last weekend, Pittsburgh racking up five sacks to complete a remarkable late turnaround and New Orleans registering four of their own, along with three interceptions, so there's every chance this could get physical.
Bengals vs Ravens

The Bengals have a shoddy recent record against their AFC North rivals, but Lamar Jackson's injury issues might just turn the tables at the Bank. articles.title: Scaling NVIDIA TensorRT Performance Optimization Beyond a Single Build Route with the Global Performance Tuner, Part 1 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Deploying a trained neural network involves more than translating each operator into a GPU kernel. It is a compilation problem with many legitimate answers. For example, when NVIDIA TensorRT builds an engine, it makes interdependent decisions about graph-IR transformations, fusion, implementation selection, memory placement, and quantization. This process is called scheduling. Different scheduling choices can preserve model semantics yet produce very different inference performance, making scheduling central to deep learning compiler optimization.
No single scheduling strategy is best for every model and deployment environment. A transformation that accelerates one network may slow another. A kernel that is faster in isolation may interact poorly with fusion, tensor layouts, or memory traffic elsewhere in the graph. Aggressive scheduling may improve performance while violating an application’s accuracy requirement. These coupled, model-dependent effects often appear only after the complete engine is built and measured, making the right strategy increasingly difficult to predict.
This post is Part 1 of a two-part series that is intended to develop a clearer way of reasoning about performance optimization. It explores questions such as: What makes one compiled engine better than another? Why can individually promising decisions fail end to end? How should accuracy constrain performance optimization? It introduces the Global Performance Tuner, a feature for automatic performance tuning released in TensorRT 11.1, and explores these questions through an intuitive example and mathematical framework.
What challenge does the Global Performance Tuner feature solve?
The following analogy illustrates the motivation for building the Global Performance Tuner feature in TensorRT.
Imagine a chef with one excellent dish that has pleased three regular customers for years. One likes spice, another sweet-and-sour flavors, and the third extra salt. The chef combines chili, syrup, lemon, and salt in one standard recipe that satisfies all three. One day, a new fourth customer arrives who dislikes spice. Keeping the chili disappoints the newcomer; removing it risks losing the first customer.
The root cause of the chef’s dilemma is the method of adding the seasonings does not scale out: the number of interacting exceptions grows with the customer base, and a change for one customer can degrade the meal for another.
A scalable approach keeps the base dish but makes the seasonings configurable. The chef records an appropriate combination for each regular customer. For a new customer with unknown preferences, the chef offers free samples with different combinations, rejects unsuitable variations, and keeps the one the customer likes best.
Mapping this analogy to deep learning compilation, TensorRT is the chef, its shared pipeline the base recipe, tunable compiler configurations the seasonings, and the compiled engine the finished dish. Each ONNX model is a customer. Performance tuning offers samples, and end-to-end performance reflects customer satisfaction.
Historically, TensorRT performance optimization has started with internal KPI models. Engineers study these workloads, identify optimizable patterns, and encode their findings as heuristics in the TensorRT default scheduling strategy. Each heuristic captures expert knowledge and allows users to benefit automatically from optimizations discovered on representative models.
As models and deployment environments diversify, this approach leads to a scaling problem similar to the one described in the analogy. A heuristic inspired by one internal KPI model joins the shared strategy and may help familiar patterns while causing a regression for an unseen external model. Adding another check or exception may protect that model, but repeating the process makes the scheduling logic increasingly difficult to extend.
The problem appears in three related forms:
- Heuristic sprawl: Each new model-specific heuristic introduces another rule whose interactions with existing rules must be understood and maintained. As these rules accumulate, the code becomes unmaintainable, and improvements for one family of models can unintentionally affect another.
- Performance-accuracy entanglement: Reduced-precision kernels and other aggressive optimizations can improve performance while introducing numerical differences that exceed an application’s acceptable tolerance. Higher-precision choices may reduce that risk but sacrifice performance. Performance and numerical acceptability therefore cannot always be optimized independently.
- Performance customization: Scheduling choices that work well for one model or GPU may not work well for another. Encoding every successful choice into one universal scheduling strategy makes it difficult to specialize TensorRT efficiently for a continually expanding range of external models, hardware platforms, and application requirements.
Tuning provides a scalable complement to heuristic optimization.
Mathematical theory for deep learning compiler performance
This section develops an abstract mathematical model of deep learning compiler performance. The purpose is to separate two fundamental questions:
- What executables a compiler can construct for a model
- How the compiler selects one from those possibilities for optimal performance
Concept: Model, model space
Let \(m\) represent a model and \(M\) represent the collection of all models under consideration, called the model space:
\(m \in M\)
Here, a model is an abstract description of the computation to be compiled. Its concrete representation may be an ONNX graph, a network created through the TensorRT API, a PyTorch model, or another frontend representation that fully specifies the model computation.
Concept: Solution, solution space
Given a model \(m\) as input, a deep learning compiler constructs an executable output for the target hardware, defined as a solution. The same model can generally be compiled into different solutions under different scheduling policies. Let \(s\) represent one such solution, and let \(S\) represent the collection of possible solutions, called the solution space.
A solution is an abstraction of executable computation on the target hardware. Concretely, a solution may be a TensorRT engine or a cubin of serialized sequence of GPU kernels. More abstractly, it may also be a compiler’s intermediate representation (IR), provided that the representation uniquely determines the final executable under the remaining compilation process.
Each solution also defines a function from the model’s input domain to its output codomain:
\(s : X \rightarrow Y\)
\(s(x) = y\)
Here, \((x,y)\) is an input-output pair for the sequence of GPU kernels that implements the neural network. At this level of abstraction, the model describes the intended computation, while a solution describes one particular way of realizing that computation on the target hardware.
Principle of determinism
Statement: When both a deterministic program and its complete execution environment remain fixed, the program has a fixed underlying run time.
This principle serves as a modeling assumption for performance analysis. Under a rigorous interpretation, the environment includes the input data, target device, software stack, GPU frequency, temperature, power state, system load, and other execution conditions that may influence runtime. In practice, not every environmental variable can be controlled perfectly, so repeated runtime measurements exhibit noise. If this disturbance is modeled as independent Gaussian noise, the average of repeated measurements is the maximum-likelihood estimation of the underlying mean run time.
Once the execution environment has been fixed at the level required by the abstraction, each solution can be associated with one characteristic runtime. This association enables runtime to be represented as a mathematical function.
Concept: Run time function
The run time function \(T\) maps each solution to its runtime on a specified target device under a fixed execution environment:
\(T(s_0) = t_0\)
The environment is treated as fixed and is therefore omitted from the notation.
Concept: Builder algorithm
A builder algorithm (also called a performance scheduler) is a mapping from the model space to the power set of solution space. When given a specific model as input, the builder algorithm will output a solution space with a given accuracy requirement.
In the accuracy condition shown above, the input–output pairs \((x, y)\) are treated as reference values, and \(ε\) represents the accuracy tolerance threshold. The reference data, comparison metric, and tolerance are treated as fixed context and are therefore suppressed from the arguments of \(B\).
Ideally, the builder algorithm should generate a sufficiently rich set of solutions to contain \(s^*\), the optimal solution: the fastest feasible solution in the modeled solution space.
Concept: Searching algorithm
A searching algorithm (also called a solver of solution space) is a mapping from the power set of solution space to the solution space. When given a set of candidate solutions as input, the searching algorithm will pick one solution from it as the output.
\(A(S) = argmin_{s_i \in \underline{S}} T(s_i), \underline{S} \subseteq S\)
Note that in the real world, a searching algorithm may pick a suboptimal solution from the solution space. In TensorRT, this suboptimality can arise from at least two sources:
- Heuristics used during searching: A heuristic may remove candidates before they can be evaluated as part of a complete engine. For example, the builder may filter certain convolution tactics according to a channel-dimension threshold in a certain layer of the input model. If a filtered tactic would have participated in the fastest end-to-end solution, the searching algorithm can no longer discover that optimal solution.
- A mismatch between local profiling and end-to-end execution: During engine building, kernel candidates may be profiled individually during tactic selection, however, performance is measured across the complete engine when inference. A kernel running in isolation and the same kernel running as part of a larger graph do not share an identical execution environment (for example, the adaptive grid sizing technique used in an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU). Consequently, the sum of individually measured kernel runtimes does not necessarily equal the end-to-end runtime.
In the ideal case, the builder algorithm generates a candidate set containing \(s^*\), and the searching algorithm reliably selects it:
A deep learning compiler can therefore be represented by an algorithm tuple \((A, B)\), where \(B\) generates candidate solutions and \(A\) selects among them. In an actual implementation, however, candidate generation, pruning, profiling, and selection may be tightly coupled. The boundary between \(A\) and \(B\) may therefore not be explicit in the compiler architecture.
Let \(B^*\) denote the optimal builder algorithm among the builder algorithm family, and \(A^*\) denote the optimal searching algorithm in the searching algorithm family. The ideal compiler would implement the tuple \((A^*,B^*)\). For any input model, this tuple would generate a candidate set containing the global optimal solution and then reliably discover it:
At the level of the mathematical abstraction, one possible implementation of \(A^*\) is brute-force algorithm—evaluate every solution in the candidate set and select the one with the lowest runtime:
\(A^*(S) = argmin_{s_i \in S} T(s_i)\)
Though applying the brute-force searching algorithm will not always be acceptable when the build time budget is limited, there could be trade-offs between build time and inference performance. \(A^*\) is used to represent the searching algorithms that will definitely return the optimal solution given any input model.
Constructing \(B^*\) is the more fundamental challenge. Even an ideal searching algorithm cannot select a solution that the builder never makes reachable. Rather than expecting to construct \(B^*\) in a single step, it’s possible to progressively approximate it by expanding and improving the build routes available to the compiler.
Global Performance Tuner modeling
This section models compilation as a sequence of compiler passes, then shows how customizable build routes provide a foundation for accuracy-aware performance tuning.
Deep learning compiler modeling
Like a traditional compiler, a deep learning compiler can be viewed as a sequence of passes, each of which transforms one IR into another. As previously mentioned, IR has a one-to-one mapping to the final executable binary; thus IR could be thought of as a solution. For this abstraction, let \(f\) represent an IR self-map from the solution space to the solution space:
\(f : S \rightarrow S\)
\(f(s) = s’\)
The builder algorithm of a deep learning compiler can be modeled as a series of passes to convert one solution to another solution:
The builder algorithm \(B\) is a function composite that looks like a route that the model walks through and gets transformed into a solution space, so \(B\) can also be called a build route.
Note the following:
- Strictly speaking, at least one compiler pass (such as the final code-generation transition) maps from model space \(M\) into executable solution space \(S\). However, compiler passes are not always perfectly decoupled, and an IR can be treated as uniquely identifying the engine produced by the remaining fixed pipeline. Modeling the passes as transformations over a generalized solution-state space therefore provides a useful simplification.
- Some compiler passes are functionally indispensable while not participating in the performance choices under study. Such performance-irrelevant passes can be treated as identity mapping or omitted from the tunable portion of the route because they do not distinguish one route from another.
- At first glance, the composition above may appear to imply that one build route generates only one solution (that is, the built engine). In practice, the TensorRT compilation pipeline may consider and filter many potential tactics before producing the final engine. Much of this candidate-generation process remains implicit in the composition because algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) are tightly coupled. The formula describes the selected solution, not every candidate that was considered or discarded along the way.
Customizable build route
Experience from performance analysis and optimization shows that effective scheduling is model-dependent. Different models can benefit from different choices in individual compiler components, even when they run on the same target GPU. Consequently, the optimal solutions for all models do not necessarily originate from one universal build route.
A build route should therefore be customizable, allowing scheduling decisions that adapt to the model and its deployment environment. Such a tunable builder algorithm can be called a customizable build route.
For example, consider two models, \(m\) and \(m’\), and a family of available build routes:
\(\{B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_n\}\)
The two models need not share the same optimal route. Model \(m\) may achieve its best result through \(B_3\), while model \(m’\) may achieve its best result through \(B_1\):
\(A^*(B(m)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m)} \{T(B_1(m)), T(B_2(m)), \ldots, T(B_n(m))\} = B_3(m)\)
\(A^*(B(m’)) = \arg\min_{B_i(m’)} \{T(B_1(m’)), T(B_2(m’)), \ldots, T(B_n(m’))\} = B_1(m’)\)
The Global Performance Tuner begins with the idea of customizable build routes. For each candidate solution, it validates the outputs against the specified accuracy criterion and measures end-to-end inference performance. Among all solutions that meet accuracy requirements, the searching algorithm selects the minimum-runtime feasible solution from the expanded solution set.
The following three principles define the framework:
- Accuracy-aware tuning: Use end-to-end accuracy as a constraint that guides performance tuning.
- Customizable build route: Make build routes customizable so that scheduling can adapt to each model and deployment environment.
- Large solution space: Construct a rich feasible solution set, then select the fastest candidate whose numerical difference remains within the specified tolerance.
The mathematical representation of the Global Performance Tuner can be written as:
Learn more
To learn more, check out the Global Performance Tuner documentation and read Part 2 of this series, which describes the algorithm and architecture design of the Global Performance Tuner and best practices for using it.

articles.title: AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan.
articles.text:
AI jobs are waiting while GPUs sit idle. Kubernetes has a new plan.
Welcome to another edition of Road to KubeCon! We’re tracking movements in the Kubernetes and cloud-native ecosystem as we count down to KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 November 9–12 in Salt Lake City.
Half of our column this week focuses on untangling Kubernetes as we add the demands of agentic AI: automating pod-restart troubleshooting, syncing communication between the scheduler and autoscaler, and maturing how we distribute inference across a cloud-native stack.
The other half goes deeper into what we need to look at closely in Kubernetes environments: What context’s missing, what slips through the gaps in metrics, and whether the AI agents you already use are really worth their salt as SREs.
Let’s get into it.
HPE on automating pod restarts in AI development
As more enterprises turn to Kubernetes for large-scale AI and machine learning jobs, they’re hitting a common obstacle: pod restarts. This is something that HPE has noticed as customers utilize its HPE Private Cloud AI (PCAI) to host long-running AI/ML workloads on inherently ephemeral container-based infrastructure like Kubernetes.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) is a presenting sponsor of Road to KubeCon. HPE Software helps IT organizations modernize infrastructure, streamline operations, and accelerate AI initiatives across hybrid, multi-vendor environments.
According to HPE system software engineer Guoping Jia, Kubernetes provides some troubleshooting commands out of the box, but it still requires extensive manual investigation. “This operational workflow does not scale effectively in PCAI’s large-cluster environment,” writes Jia on the HPE blog.
His solution involves smarter automation for troubleshooting, using an open-source Kubernetes troubleshooting tool, k8s-pod-restart-info-collector, to automatically gather details and send diagnostic information straight to a Slack channel. It’s one helpful strategy to improve usability for Kubernetes operators.
Will the scheduler and autoscaler unite?
There’s been a lot of talk recently about how Kubernetes is evolving to meet AI’s new demands. This week, AWS senior software development managers Sajjan Gundapuneedi and Neelendra Bhandari weighed in with this blog post on how AI is reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling.
The core problem they highlight is friction between the scheduler, which places pods on existing nodes, and the autoscaler, which adds new ones, when managing GPU accelerators on Kubernetes. Often the two sides aren’t on the same page, leaving pods pending and pricey GPUs sitting idle. Capacity reservations, device topology, and GPU sharing complicate things further.
“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it.”
“A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it,” the authors write. “Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node.”
To them, solutions are already taking shape: dynamic resource allocation (DRA)-aware autoscalers, workload-aware scheduling, and a companion mechanism, provisioning requests, to bridge the two sides. Still, they expect the autoscaler to grow into “a more scheduler-aware partner.”
Deeper integration is underway, too. A public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling group sketches APIs that would let the two loops talk directly, so the scheduler could see capacity that could be provisioned, express placement preferences across it, and request it explicitly.
Distributed AI inference grows up with llm-d v1.0 release
On Tuesday, at PyTorch Conference North America, the CNCF sandbox project llm-d reached v1.0. The project now bridges AI application developers in the PyTorch ecosystem and the production cloud-native stack.
Carlos Costa, co-founder and lead maintainer of llm-d, and a distinguished engineer on IBM’s hybrid cloud platform for AI, says the v1.0 release signals maturity.
“This is the moment open source AI serving crosses from experimental projects into dependable infrastructure you can build on,” Costa tells The New Stack. Whereas earlier versions focused on proving state-of-the-art performance, v1.0 is about sustaining that performance in production, he adds.
llm-d has already seen plenty of use at Tesla, AWS, Oracle, Google, and beyond. Costa adds that a recent IBM Research demonstration found that an agent factory exploring quantum error correction hardware ran at 11.5x lower inference cost on open models with llm-d than on an all-proprietary configuration.
“This demonstration shows where llm-d really shines: agentic workloads,” he says, adding that it absorbs bursty agentic traffic and, in IBM’s test, pushed cache reuse to about 98%.
From building models to operating frontier intelligence at scale
For a taste of the type of discussion to expect at KubeCon NA, let’s briefly visit the East. Chris Aniszczyk, CTO at CNCF, set the stage very well at last month’s KubeCon + CloudNativeCon + OpenInfra Summit + PyTorch Conference China 2026 in Shanghai, in the talk Operating Frontier Intelligence at Scale with Xiao Zhang.
As he puts it, it’s not just about models anymore. It’s about putting them all to work. “AI is essentially moving from just purely about building the greatest models [to] how do we actually make this run at scale, stitch it all together and run in different types of environments,” says Aniszczyk.
Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince recently declared that bot traffic, driven by AI agents, has passed human traffic online for the first time. Aniszczyk says that shift is putting tremendous pressure on systems, pointing to recent GitHub outages. As inference becomes the predominant workload, everything shifts.
“It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career.”
This shift is causing all sorts of side problems, he notes, from building new infrastructure to building more data centers to ensuring enough power is available. “It’s the craziest kind of technology change that I’ve seen probably in my career,” says Aniszczyk.
Still, he’s an optimist, framing it as a fun problem and challenge for the cloud-native community to tackle together.
Promoting your AI agent to the SRE role
Plenty of AI site reliability engineer (SRE) platforms are emerging. But according to Roy Libman, CPO, Radar (Skyhook.io), your next SRE hire might be right under your fingertips: the AI coding agent you already use. The trick is giving it the right context.
“The coding agent your engineers use, whether that’s Claude Code, Codex or Cursor, can already investigate a Kubernetes cluster,” writes Libman on the CNCF blog. “What it usually lacks is context: what’s failing right now, and what changed before it broke.”
In his benchmark of 50 injected faults on a live cluster, Claude Code, given read-only context through MCP tools, diagnosed slightly more accurately than with shell and kubectl access. The bigger difference was speed: with context, it reached a correct diagnosis within two minutes on 86% of faults, versus 60% with a shell.
It’s an interesting sign that context is king for diagnosing complex errors, and that you might not need to shell (pun intended) out for another AI subscription just to triage issues.
Industry take: what goes undetected in Kubernetes
A previous Road to KubeCon asked what’s still missing with OTel and Prometheus. Well, one gap is state that isn’t a time series, like slowlog entries, client lists, and access control list (ACL) changes, shares Kristiyan Ivanov, former engineering manager at Redis, current contributor to Valkey, and founding CTO of BetterDB. “These get lost between scrapes,” he tells The New Stack.
“Metrics count, but they don’t explain.”
Metrics count, but they don’t explain.” According to Ivanov, much goes undetected in Kubernetes because Valkey and Redis keep evidence in in-memory buffers, which Prometheus reduces to lengths and counters. “Kubernetes makes this even worse in several ways,” he says, noting that pod restarts, failovers, and ephemeral pod IPs worsen tracking.
“Almost everything in the ecosystem is an INFO scraper,” he says. “Missing across the board: durable history across restarts and failovers, attribution to a service or ACL user, an audit trail of ACL and config changes, and aggregation across shards.”
Emerging approaches are helping cloud operators see these gaps. He points to improvements in Valkey’s detection capabilities and OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation to enable granular tracing. But eBPF can’t see evictions, ACL denials, or configuration changes, he says. Those require engine-level collection.
As Kubernetes evolves, so do the demands on the teams running it. Presenting sponsor HPE helps teams address that complexity with software spanning virtualization, cloud management, observability, and automation.
Half can’t measure AI agents effectively
Eighty-seven percent of respondents say monitoring AI is a priority, yet over half admit they can’t effectively measure AI quality, like LLM response quality, or control AI costs, found Splunk State of Observability 2026, which surveyed 2,050 ITOps and engineering professionals and was released Oct. 20.
The report also found 83% are concerned about the unintended consequences of AI agents. This tracks with agentic AI’s tendency to take unexpected actions and create bursty traffic patterns, both of which are driving major infrastructure changes.
“Most companies will soon have far more agents at work than people,” said Jeetu Patel, president and chief product officer at Cisco, in the press release. Monitoring AI is also driving more collaboration between observability and security teams, according to 81% of respondents.
More updates from the cloud-native universe
The excitement around cloud native never sleeps. Here are a few more community, project, and vendor updates from the past week or so.
- Congratulations to Anish Bista, the first Golden Kubestronaut from Nepal!
- Kubernetes v1.38.0 is targeted for release on Wednesday, December 16.
- Per the release schedule, Kubernetes 1.34 hits end of life October 27.
- Fairwinds shares lessons from running n8n in production on Amazon EKS.
- Broadcom’s AAI v26 adds cost tracking and Kubernetes support; see EMA’s impact brief.
- Splunk now lets teams remotely configure OpenTelemetry Collectors on Kubernetes.
- New Relic shipped v4.8.2 of its Kubernetes integration with dependency updates.
One more stop on the Road to KubeCon
Road to KubeCon is an eight-part series presented by HPE. Before you go, explore how HPE Software helps IT teams do more with less complexity.
This series is almost over — only one edition remains.
We’ll be here next week to round things off with a special sign-off for Road to KubeCon. In the meantime, you can catch up on previous editions in the Road to KubeCon archive.
Bill Doerrfeld, the writer of this series, is open to community pitches. Feel free to share interesting takes, new releases, or tips on the best dive bar in Salt Lake City.
He accepts direct messages on LinkedIn, or you can reach him through his personal contact page.

articles.title: Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product?
articles.text:
Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%; What sells? The celebrity or the product?
Food and grocery delivery platform Swiggy has narrowed its net loss by 15.6% year on year in the second quarter of FY27. Its revenue rose 36% during the same period.
Dear Reader,
Shiprocket expands into the food commerce market.
The company’s AI-native commerce platform fastrr has partnered with Vegorama Group, which operates Punjabi Angithi, and Bikkgane Biryani, to help the restaurant brands manage direct orders, customer engagement, and hyperlocal deliveries.
In recent times, restaurants have been exploring ways to drive orders through their own digital channels instead of relying solely on third-party food aggregators. Direct channels give restaurants greater access to customer data and more opportunities to engage with diners after a purchase.
Meanwhile, Bengaluru-based digital trust company eMudhra has decided to exit its global website security certificate business, following a security incident involving weak cryptographic keys that prompted action from Google and Mozilla.
In a regulatory filing on Thursday, the company said its board had decided to voluntarily withdraw from the business, citing rising compliance costs, increasing data sovereignty requirements and diminishing commercial returns.
In other news, rural healthcare platform CureBay has raised Rs 100 crore in a pre-Series C funding round led by IvyCap Ventures. The round comprises Rs 69 crore in equity from IvyCap Ventures and existing investors, and more than Rs 30 crore in debt from Trifecta Capital, Alteria Capital, and VentureSoul Partners.
CureBay will use the funds to expand its operations across India, strengthen its healthcare delivery network, and develop its technology and AI capabilities.
Amid increasing AI threats, here’s a new one.
Major US banks have detected AI agents lurking inside customer accounts. Some of these unauthorised third-party agents are even attempting to act independently, Axios reported. Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Wells Fargo are working to curb these risks.
Lastly, what’s PHP and why did companies worldwide scramble to fix flaws in the programming language used to build websites? Here’s the lowdown.
In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Swiggy’s Q2: Net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%
- What sells? The celebrity or the product?
Here’s your trivia for today: Who was awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize for Literature? (Scroll down for the answer)
Earnings
Swiggy’s Q2 net loss drops nearly 16%, revenue rises 36%
Food and grocery delivery platform Swiggy narrowed its net loss by 15.6% year on year (YoY) in the second quarter of FY27. Its revenue rose 36% during the same period.
The company reported a loss of Rs 922 crore in Q2 of FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 1,092 crore in the same period a year ago. Revenue for the quarter was Rs 7,571 crore, up from Rs 5,561 crore a year ago.
Key takeaways
- Losses at Instamart, Swiggy's quick commerce business, widened to Rs 764 crore, compared with Rs 739 crore a year ago, thus impacting the overall numbers of the company. Instamart’s revenue for the second quarter was Rs 1,306 crore, up from Rs 980 crore in the corresponding year-ago period.
- The gross order value of the food delivery business grew 17.7% YoY to touch Rs 10,054 crore for the second quarter. The adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was Rs 341 crore, an improvement of Rs 101 crore over the last one year.
- In comparison, Swiggy’s rival Eternal reported a 92% rise in net profit at Rs 125 crore, while revenue grew 78% to Rs 24,138 crore in the second quarter of FY27.
TechSparks
Celebrities don’t sell, the product does: Ananth Narayanan
The froth has gone out of D2C, and brands that want to last will have to play the patient game. This was the key message from Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME, at the 17th edition of YourStory’s TechSparks event.
In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Narayanan said, without product-market fit, merely scaling, which a lot of D2C brands used to do, is not valued anymore. “You need real cash flows, you need real product love, which is very hard,” he said.
Key takeaways
- A celebrity may add recall to a brand, but it’s the product that sells, said Narayanan. “A face can give you initial momentum, but I don’t think it can get you repeat consumers.”
- He advised founders to build with heart. “Build products that you love. Otherwise you are becoming a bit of a machine that churns out unit economics.”
- On India as a brand, Narayanan said the country stands for talent and should now move on to culture, from yoga and Ayurveda to mindfulness. “Why can’t we make the Indian way of living the most important thing in the digital age?”

News & updates
- PHP patch: Companies and governments worldwide rushed on Thursday to patch critical flaws in the widely used PHP programming language, as a cybersecurity company reported millions of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. This came after governments in Europe and elsewhere took websites offline as a precaution on Wednesday while website operators scrambled to secure systems running the software.
- Nasdaq slide: The tech-heavy Nasdaq slid more than 1% on Thursday as growth stocks weakened after earnings from mega-caps Tesla and Meta failed to allay AI-related concerns, with a recovery in oil prices further adding to market unease, Reuters reported.
- Job cuts: Barclays is cutting around 5,000 jobs or 5% of its workforce this year, as it uses technology such as AI to slash fixed costs and improve returns. The job cuts were revealed as Barclays reported a third-quarter profit of £2.3 billion ($3.08 billion), up 12% from a year ago but undershooting analysts’ forecasts as its fixed income trading business underperformed.
