articles.title: Trop de produits embellis par l'IA ? Etsy impose désormais une vraie photo aux vendeurs
articles.text:
Etsy durcit ses règles face aux photographies de produits générées ou embellies par intelligence artificielle, qui peuvent induire les acheteurs en erreur. Les vendeurs devront désormais présenter au moins un cliché non retouché de leur article, même si l’utilisation de l’IA reste autorisée sous certaines conditions.
Vous repérez un joli objet de décoration, une peluche ou un vêtement sur Internet. Les photographies sont impeccables, les couleurs magnifiques et le produit semble tout droit sorti d’un catalogue. Sauf qu’à la réception du colis, la réalité peut être nettement moins flatteuse. Avec les générateurs d’images par IA, il devient de plus en plus facile de présenter un article sous son meilleur jour, voire de lui inventer des qualités qu’il ne possède pas. Etsy, la plateforme spécialisée notamment dans les créations artisanales et les produits personnalisés, a décidé de renforcer ses règles pour limiter ces mauvaises surprises.
Une vraie photo obligatoire, même si l’IA reste autorisée
Dans ses nouvelles règles concernant les photographies des annonces, actualisées le 22 octobre, Etsy demande aux vendeurs de présenter au moins une photographie non retouchée du véritable produit, dans un environnement réel.
Pas question, pour ce cliché, de remplacer l’arrière-plan avec une IA, de modifier les couleurs ou de gommer les petits défauts. L’acheteur doit pouvoir voir à quoi ressemble réellement l’article qu’il s’apprête à commander.
Cela ne signifie pas pour autant la disparition des images générées ou retouchées par intelligence artificielle. Les autres photographies d’une annonce peuvent toujours être modifiées, notamment pour améliorer l’éclairage, recadrer l’image ou changer le décor. À une condition : ne pas donner une représentation trompeuse du produit.
Des exceptions sont également prévues pour les articles personnalisés, les objets fabriqués à la demande et certains contenus numériques. Un vendeur proposant un tee-shirt avec un prénom pourra, par exemple, utiliser des maquettes pour présenter différentes personnalisations, tout en montrant un véritable exemplaire terminé.
Etsy n’interdit pas non plus les créations réalisées avec l’aide de l’IA. Elles restent autorisées dans certaines catégories, à condition que le vendeur apporte sa propre contribution créative et signale l’utilisation de cette technologie.
Etsy veut éviter les mauvaises surprises à l’ouverture du colis
La plateforme entend également mieux repérer les annonces trompeuses. Comme le rapporte The Verge, Etsy prépare de nouveaux outils pour identifier les images suspectes et permettre aux acheteurs de signaler les visuels générés par IA qui ne correspondent pas aux produits vendus.
Les règles vont même plus loin que les photographies. Les annonces créées automatiquement par des bots, sans intervention humaine, sont désormais interdites. Même chose pour les guides pratiques entièrement générés par IA, comme certains patrons de couture, recettes ou instructions de fabrication.
L'enjeu est important pour une plateforme qui revendique la créativité et le savoir-faire de ses vendeurs. Comment distinguer un véritable objet artisanal d’un produit dont les photographies ont été largement retravaillées, quand les générateurs d’images deviennent capables de reproduire les moindres détails ?
Une photographie authentique ne constitue évidemment pas une garantie contre les arnaques. Rien n’empêche un vendeur malhonnête de photographier un bel exemplaire avant d’en expédier un autre, de qualité inférieure.
Mais cette nouvelle obligation donne au moins un point de comparaison aux acheteurs. Et pour les vendeurs qui comptaient uniquement sur des visuels artificiels pour embellir leurs produits, il va devenir plus difficile de masquer la réalité derrière une jolie image.
- Marketplace d'articles DIY et vintage.
- Plateforme à impact social et environnemental.
- Une version gratuite.

articles.title: Using AI Agents to Teach Robots Like Microduck to Walk in Simulation | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires more than a walking policy. It must perceive its surroundings, maintain balance, and adjust its actions when obstacles block the path ahead. Developing these capabilities connects several stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model how the robot interacts with its environment, and training and evaluating policies in simulation.
NVIDIA RTX Spark serves as a local development hub, supporting AI-assisted planning and policy validation. NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the robot-learning framework for reinforcement learning in the cloud, while Newton models physical behavior, and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries generate simulated visual observations through RTX rendering. Trained policies return to RTX Spark for local evaluation in NVIDIA Isaac Sim.
This post walks through the workflow using Microduck as a reference robot, with Hermes, NVIDIA Nemotron, and Astra assisting with planning and preparation. You’ll learn how to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy, and evaluate its behavior in simulation—a process you can adapt to your own robots and tasks. This establishes a foundation for physical deployment, where differences between simulation and real-world behavior require further refinement.
1. Create a plan of the obstacle course
The workflow begins with a prompt describing the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate that prompt into a step-by-step project plan. The instructions establish the intended task, available resources, expected outputs, and the stages the agents should follow. Use the following example to structure your prompt:
Build and test a simulated Microduck obstacle course with navigation and locomotion challenges. Make a photorealistic concept image and have Astra build and test it.
...
Workflow
Use Hermes and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt for preparation and Astra for asset creation and simulation.
...
1. Research and plan
Review official Microduck documentation and summarize capabilities, constraints, and unknowns. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
...
2. Generate the concept
Use a verified Microduck reference image to generate a photorealistic course concept. Check robot appearance, relative scale, and movement space; save prompts and provenance.
...
3. Identify assets
Extract unique reusable assets, group repeated instances, and select representative crops. Record dimensions, locations, and reference limitations; preserve original images.
...
4. Prepare the handoff
Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions. Verify required files, delegate to Astra, and wait for confirmed results.
...
5. Create and verify assets
Have Astra enhance references, model geometry in FreeCAD, and apply materials in Blender. Before simulation, verify every asset is completed or demonstrably blocked, with at least one usable model.
...
6. Assemble and test
Verify robot capabilities, assemble the course, and test navigation, challenges, and resets. Provide reproducible instructions and evidence; do not operate physical hardware.
...
Local planning includes a brief review of Microduck’s repository and documentation. This review identifies the robot’s capabilities, resources for subsequent work, and details that still need verification. The resulting plan extends beyond asset creation: it outlines environment construction, robot preparation, simulation, training, validation, and deployment.
The course needs to test both movement and perception. Microduck must learn to move around obstacles and through constrained spaces while maintaining balance. Use these requirements to guide the proposed layout and the objects needed to construct it.
A local image-generation model produces a concept image of the course. Hermes and Nemotron then analyze the image and create an inventory of its visible, reusable assets. Each asset receives an identifier, a description of its visible features, and a cropped reference image. The inventory records where objects are cut off or obscured so that later stages can distinguish visible details from assumptions.
Hermes combines these outputs into a handoff package: the overall project plan, Microduck research and source links, the concept image, the asset inventory, cropped references, and instructions for the next stages. It then automatically delegates the work to Astra. The package gives Astra the broader project context and asset specifications needed to continue.
2. Create simulation assets
Using the project plan and references from the previous stage, Astra creates the 3D assets needed for the course. Cropping objects from a larger concept image can result in small, low-resolution references. Before modeling, Astra uses cloud image editing to isolate the objects and produce clearer, higher-resolution images.
Astra compares the enhanced references with the original crops, checking that silhouettes, proportions, colors, and distinctive features remain consistent. The enhanced images provide clearer modeling guidance, while the originals document what was visible in the concept image. Dimensions and hidden surfaces that cannot be established from the images are recorded as modeling assumptions.
Astra directs FreeCAD to construct the base geometry and editable CAD structure, then uses Blender to add fine geometric details and materials. Both applications run locally through programmatic execution. The generated assets are saved as editable models and exported USD assets, with previews and output checks for review.
You can also get assets from SimReady Central Library, a free and ungated library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready OpenUSD assets. Reusing them alongside newly generated objects reduces the asset preparation needed to assemble the obstacle course in Isaac Sim. The resulting assets become the building blocks of Microduck’s training environment in simulation.
3. Assemble the simulation environment
Astra composes the obstacle course using the prepared assets in Isaac Sim. Isaac Sim provides access to Omniverse libraries’ rendering and sensor-simulation capabilities, while Newton models Microduck’s physical behavior, including movement and balance.
A robot’s articulated structure and movement are defined in simulation through links, joints, and actuators. These elements establish the relationship between the policy’s actions and the simulated robot. Links represent connected bodies, joints constrain their relative motion, and actuators drive motion. Together, they model a robot interacting with its environment. AI agents can help configure these elements.
Simulated sensor observations provide information about the obstacles ahead. As the robot attempts to walk, the simulation captures the consequences of its actions: whether it maintains its posture, makes progress through the course, or stumbles and falls.
The result is a complete learning environment: a robot that can act, an obstacle course it can interact with, and a simulated environment that can generate feedback from those interactions. Reinforcement learning (RL) uses this feedback to train robot policies.
4. Train the perception and locomotion policy
With Microduck and its environment ready, NVIDIA Isaac Lab provides the tools to train and evaluate robot policies at scale. This open-source framework runs many Microduck simulations at once, generating experience that an RL algorithm uses to improve its shared policy.
For each task, you define what the robot observes, the actions it can take, and the rewards used to guide learning. You then implement the task using Isaac Lab APIs. Newton, an open-source, GPU-accelerated physics engine, simulates how Microduck moves and interacts with the ground and its environment in response to those actions.
Early attempts may include unstable steps, collisions, and falls. The training algorithm uses these outcomes and the task’s rewards to update the policy toward more successful behavior. Each attempt follows the same simulation loop:
Simulated observations → policy actions → simulated motion → updated observations
Parallel simulation provides experience from many attempts at once to train the policy. In this task, ramps and uneven surfaces are the obstacles: Microduck must traverse a curved ramp while maintaining balance and avoiding falls. Varying the terrain gives the policy experience adjusting its movements to different ground conditions.
The ramp and obstacle training experiment uses Astra-generated assets from the previous sections and the Isaac Lab Microduck example environment as its starting point. A locomotion policy pretrained in that environment receives additional training in Isaac Lab for traversing ramps and obstacles, using head-camera depth and robot-state observations. This adaptation run used 4,096 parallel environments on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU.
5. Validate the trained policy on RTX Spark
After training, validate the trained policy in Isaac Sim on a local RTX Spark. Microduck receives simulated observations, predicts actions, moves through the environment, and responds to the updated scene based on the policy. Check whether Microduck detects obstacles, adjusts its movement, and completes the course.
This stage separates policy learning from policy evaluation. During training, the policy changes as it receives new experience. During evaluation, you examine the behavior of a selected policy and identify where it succeeds or needs further work.
Record course completion, falls, collisions, and the situations in which progress stops. These measurements, paired with rollout videos, can guide iterations to the environment or training setup.
6. Prepare for policy deployment on the physical robot
Once the policy performs reliably in simulation, the next step is to run it on the robot’s onboard computer. This post covers the work leading up to that point: creating assets, assembling the environment, and training and evaluating the policy. Detailed hardware deployment is outside the scope.
Preparing for the simulation-to-real transition starts with a simulation that reflects how the real robot behaves. Isaac Lab supports Better Actuator Models (BAM) to model servo response, including command delays, mechanical backlash (the small amount of play in the drivetrain), and drops in voltage as motors draw power from a shared battery. Matching these settings to measurements from Microduck can help narrow the sim-to-real gap.
Even with a carefully calibrated model, sensors, ground contact, and control timing can differ on the real robot. Isaac Lab’s domain randomization varies physical parameters and observation noise within realistic ranges, giving the policy practice handling those differences. Hardware tests then show where further adjustments are needed, guiding the next round of simulation, training, and validation.
Figure 10 shows a locomotion policy trained in Isaac Lab running on the physical Microduck.
Get started
This workflow connects AI-assisted planning, simulation, asset creation, and robot policy training and evaluation. It combines local asset and environment generation, cloud-scale policy learning, and local policy validation on the RTX Spark. AI agents turn prompts into plans, with Isaac Lab supporting policy training and Isaac Sim supporting evaluation before deployment.
Learn more about the platforms used in this workflow, and try the examples in their documentation:
- Access ungated assets from SimReady Central Library
- Omniverse libraries for integrating simulation capabilities into applications
- RTX Spark
- Installing Isaac Sim on RTX Spark—download the Windows x86 binaries (runnable out of the box via Windows x86 emulation on Arm)
- Isaac Sim for robot and environment simulation
- Newton for physics simulation
- Isaac Lab for reinforcement learning and imitation learning policy training
- Isaac Lab Learning Path
- Microduck example Isaac Lab environment
- Microduck sim-to-real tutorial on Hugging Face
- Microduck walking demo using native BAM servos
Acknowledgements
This workflow was developed through collaboration across teams at NVIDIA, including:
Aaron Young, Antoine Richard, Chase Telegin, Gavriel State, Hammad Mazhar, Kelly Guo, Milad Rakhsha, Oyindamola Omotuyi, Pierre Fleau, Rishabh Chadha, Rogelio Olguin, Ruben D’Sa, and Yenal Kal.

articles.title: Diese Website zeigt Ikea-Bauanleitungen komplett in 3D – doch die KI hat Tücken
articles.text:
Interaktive 3D-Bauanleitungen für Ikea-Möbel: Wenn die KI das Billy-Regal falsch zusammenschraubt
Abhilfe soll die Web-Anwendung „Flat Pack, Step by Step“ schaffen, die der im britischen London tätige Produktdesigner Ryan Sael entwickelt hat und die gedruckte Montageanleitungen des schwedischen Einrichtungskonzerns Ikea in dreidimensionale Browser-Animationen überträgt. Nutzer:innen können die einzelnen Arbeitsschritte im virtuellen Ansichtsfenster, dem sogenannten Viewport, frei im Raum drehen, heranzoomen und über einen Schieberegler stufenlos vor- oder zurückspulen.
Zum Start hatte Sael das kostenlose Projekt in einem ersten Beitrag auf der Kurzmitteilungsplattform X zunächst nur mit dem Bücherregal Billy und dem Beistelltisch Lack vorgestellt, bevor er in einem weiteren Beitrag auf X die Erweiterung um 23 zusätzliche Modelle wie Kallax, Malm, Poäng und andere Ikea-Klassiker verkündete. Parallel zur bewegten 3D-Ansicht lässt sich im linken Bereich des Browserfensters jederzeit die originale Papieranleitung zum direkten Abgleich einblenden.
Montagefehler beim Billy-Regal: Wenn die KI-Bauanleitung in die Irre führt
Wer sich beim realen Möbelaufbau allein auf die dreidimensionale Darstellung verlässt, riskiert allerdings wohl falsch montierte Bauteile. In einer Diskussion auf dem Entwicklerportal Hacker News wiesen mehrere Nutzer:innen auf handwerkliche Fehler in den Animationen hin. So würden beim Bücherregal Billy im dritten Bauschritt die Regalbretter verkehrt herum eingesetzt, sodass die Exzenterverbinder – also die runden Drehschlösser aus Metall, die verschraubte Bolzen im Holz zusammenziehen – auf der sichtbaren Oberseite statt auf der Unterseite der Einlegeböden liegen würden.
Auch beim Beistelltisch Lack weicht die digitale Visualisierung von der physischen Realität ab, da sich die langen Doppelgewindeschrauben in der Animation vermeintlich komplett von Hand in die Tischplatte drehen lassen, während sie laut Originalanleitung nur leicht angesetzt und anschließend über das Tischbein selbst eingedreht werden. Zudem bemerkten Tester:innen, dass bei einzelnen Modellen die eingeblendeten Hilfslinien in der Höhe nicht mit den tatsächlichen Bohrungen der Bretter übereinstimmen.
Kritik an „Claudisms“ und KI-generiertem Code von Anthropic
Hinter den Kulissen basiert das Projekt maßgeblich auf dem Einsatz der Sprachmodelle des KI-Unternehmens Anthropic. In der Entwicklergemeinschaft stieß dabei vor allem der automatisch generierte Werbetext auf der Startseite auf Kritik, der verspricht, jeder Holzdübel, jeder Exzenterverbinder und jeder Nagel sitze dort, wo das Papier ihn vorsieht. Kommentator:innen auf Hacker News bezeichneten diese Formulierung als typischen „Claudism“. Das ist eine Wortschöpfung für die Angewohnheit des Sprachmodells Claude, die Eingabebefehle von Entwickler:innen in werblicher Sprache zu wiederholen, selbst wenn das programmierte Ergebnis sachliche Mängel aufweist.
Ryan Sael räumte die Schwächen in der Debatte auf Hacker News ein und erklärte, ihm fehle bei dem Projekt schlicht die Kapazität, jede Textzeile und jedes Detail selbst zu überprüfen. Auch auf X bat er um Nachsicht, falls einzelne Bauschritte von der Vorlage abweichen, und verwies darauf, dass Ikea ihn nicht für die Arbeit bezahlt habe. Das Projekt verdeutlicht damit ein Grundproblem des sogenannten Vibe Codings, bei dem Software fast ausschließlich über Textbefehle an eine künstliche Intelligenz entsteht. Sprachmodelle erzeugen zwar in kurzer Zeit lauffähige 3D-Grafiken im Browser, scheitern aber häufig noch am räumlichen Verständnis für mechanische Abhängigkeiten.
Dreidimensionale Web-Grafiken im Vergleich zur klassischen Ikea-Papieranleitung
Technisch setzt die Website auf sogenannte Low-Poly-Modelle, also dreidimensionale Grafiken aus wenigen geometrischen Flächen, die im Browser ohne hohe Rechenleistung dargestellt werden. Wie ein Praxistest des japanischen Technikmagazins Gigazine beschreibt, laufen die Animationen dadurch auch auf herkömmlichen Laptops ohne Verzögerungen. Einen ähnlichen Ansatz verfolgte bereits einen Monat zuvor ein anderer Entwickler unter dem Pseudonym „geminiboy“, dessen eigener 3D-Prototyp für Flatpack-Möbel zwar auf grafische Lichteffekte verzichtet, von Kommentator:innen auf Hacker News jedoch als übersichtlicher eingestuft wurde.
Ob interaktive 3D-Modelle beim Zusammenbau von Zerlegtmöbeln überhaupt einen praktischen Mehrwert gegenüber gedruckten Skizzen bieten, bezweifeln mehrere Teilnehmer:innen der Debatte, da die wortlosen Schwarz-Weiß-Anleitungen von Ikea gerade durch ihre Reduktion auf das Wesentliche funktionieren und bewegte Kameraflüge eher von Montagedetails ablenken. Ikea selbst nutzt dreidimensionale Produktmodelle bislang bereits für Katalogbilder und digitale Raumplaner, setzt bei seinen offiziellen Aufbauhilfen im Netz aber weiterhin primär auf klassische PDF-Dokumente.

articles.title: PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race
articles.text:
PHP2Shell was only the beginning: AI is accelerating the patch race
Government websites and public services across Europe went offline this week as organizations responded to two newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. Germany took several federal websites offline, France temporarily shut down prefecture sites, Belgium’s foreign ministry disabled its websites, and organizations in the Netherlands pulled public-facing services as a precaution. It wasn’t confined to Europe, with countless other entities and businesses worldwide responding similarly.
They were all waiting for a PHP vulnerability mitigation that didn’t exist yet.
The cause was PHP2Shell: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. While the community worked quickly and the PHP project released fixes for all community-supported PHP versions on the morning of October 21, the bigger issue remains unresolved: an estimated 40% of PHP users are running unsupported PHP, even as AI has exponentially accelerated CVE discovery.
“What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.”
I’ve been contributing to open source for more than 20 years; I lead the Laminas Project, I’m the Principal Product Manager for Perforce Zend and OpenLogic, and I currently serve on the Board of the PHP Foundation — which is all to say, I’ve seen more than my fair share of new security threats.
What happened this week was different, and it’s the first shot of what promises to be an ongoing battle across the open-source ecosystem.
What you need to know about PHP2Shell
CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, currently referred to as PHP2Shell, present remote code execution (RCE) risks triggered by a combination of out-of-memory (OOM) conditions and PHP’s error handling. Every PHP version back to 5.4 is affected by at least one. The two vulnerabilities are particularly concerning because they exist in PHP itself rather than in an individual application, CMS, or framework; there is no real mitigation outside patched PHP runtimes.
Wiz Research found that the vulnerabilities could allow attackers to remotely execute code or expose sensitive information in process memory, including passwords, authentication tokens, API keys, and certificates. This exposure exists independently of the application running on PHP.
Additionally, Datadog Security Labs, which independently reproduced the vulnerabilities, found that application-level authentication cannot prevent the attack because PHP processes the malicious request before application code runs. In its reproduction of CVE-2026-109618, researchers reported that the request “never reaches the target application’s code.”
“Even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.”
This means that even with solid application security practices, your applications could still be exposed because the vulnerable behavior happens below the application, in the PHP runtime itself.
The answer is to patch.
The community takes a collaborative effort
Once the full impact became clear in August, the PHP Ecosystem Security Team, the PHP Foundation, and release managers delivered a fix across every supported PHP version. In a cross-ecosystem effort, they also worked with LTS vendors (such as Zend) to ensure they created and released all patches simultaneously.
This is the first time in 20+ years I’ve seen an effort like this happen, and I applaud the community for moving in this direction. Because of this initiative, anyone on a PHP version no longer supported by the community (8.1 or older) could remain secure against these newly disclosed CVEs without any gaps.
Unfortunately, this kind of cooperation also depends on trust, which was tested here. The CVE numbers were leaked on October 20, moving all releases up by a day. But as of 14:00 UTC on October 21, all community-supported PHP versions have received updates to mitigate these vulnerabilities. My team at Zend, along with other LTS providers, also released patches for EOL PHP versions.
While we’ll need more comprehensive steps in the coming weeks, these mitigations will keep critical applications that power governments, hospitals, financial institutions, schools, and more secure and supported in the interim.
AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research
PHP2Shell is a prime example of what happens when AI makes difficult security research more accessible — and the dangers that come with that knowledge.
As part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, Calif identified a critical PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with researchers and security providers contributing testing, technical support, and coordination ahead of disclosure.
“We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.”
What stands out is the potential shift in scale. OpenAI says these are already among several significant vulnerabilities it has found and is working to address, and it expects similar findings to “increase sharply in the coming months.”
We’ve always raced vulnerability disclosure, patch availability, and exploitation. PHP2Shell demonstrates just how uncomfortable and hard-won that race can, and likely will, become.
Running EOL OSS? AI is raising the stakes.
The easy advice after a vulnerability like PHP2Shell is to upgrade immediately. The operational reality is more complicated.
PHP 8.1 and older releases no longer receive updates from the PHP project, although some distributions and long-term support vendors provide backported security fixes. For critical applications, moving to a new runtime can require updates to frameworks, libraries, extensions, and application code, plus the testing needed to ensure those changes don’t disrupt production.
That gap grows as AI improves vulnerability research, so this isn’t just a PHP issue. PHP is just the first major example of what’s coming for most popular OSS technologies. For instance, we’ve seen a recent flood of Spring vulnerability reports in the past few months, and Node.js and Python reported critical vulnerabilities the same day PHP2Shell landed. I’d also be remiss not to mention Linus Torvalds’ recent comments that the Linux security list is becoming unmanageable because of AI bug reports.
During my time working with OSS and PHP at Perforce Software, I’ve come to view LTS as a bridge to modernization. It lets teams keep addressing security vulnerabilities while they plan, test, and execute a move to a supported version. And, as vulnerability discovery accelerates, remaining indefinitely on unsupported software becomes increasingly difficult to justify.
Organizations need to stay current where they can and have a deliberate security strategy for the systems they can’t upgrade immediately. The faster vulnerabilities are discovered, the more important this will become.
What happens now?
For PHP users, the immediate priority is straightforward: move to a fixed release or obtain appropriate security fixes for an otherwise unsupported version. But let’s talk more long-term.
It can be tempting to use PHP2Shell as evidence that PHP is suddenly less secure, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. The combined community and vendor effort this week proves that. Instead, we need to change our outlook on security, because vulnerabilities like these will only become more common.
“Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.”
AI is changing which security investigations are practical and how quickly they can happen. That’s valuable when researchers are working with projects and the wider ecosystem to resolve vulnerabilities. But it also puts more pressure on organizations to know what they’re running, stay on supported releases when possible, establish clear vulnerability-response processes, and have a plan for applications that cannot be upgraded immediately.
Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.

articles.title: Atlassian Patches 75 Flaws in Data Center and Server Products
articles.text:
Atlassian on Tuesday published its October 2026 security bulletin, which lists 162 high-severity and 14 critical-severity vulnerabilities.
All of the entries are tied to third-party dependencies, and many CVEs appear under several products. By SecurityWeek’s count, the bulletin covers 75 unique CVEs, six of them rated critical.
The affected products are Bamboo, Bitbucket, Confluence, Crowd, Fisheye/Crucible, Jira Software, and Jira Service Management.
The critical-severity flaws are:
- CVE-2026-65637, CVE-2026-65182, and CVE-2026-68525 – Apache Tomcat issues listed for Confluence and Crowd.
- CVE-2026-58062 – a Bouncy Castle issue listed for Confluence, Crowd, Jira Software, and Jira Service Management.
- CVE-2026-75595 – a Netty issue listed for Confluence, Jira Software, and Jira Service Management.
- CVE-2026-77185 – an Apache SSHD issue listed for Fisheye/Crucible.
For each of these, Atlassian notes that its use of the affected component “presents a lower, non-critical assessed risk.”
Atlassian’s vulnerability disclosure portal also lists CVE-2026-65905, a critical-severity Apache Tomcat flaw affecting Data Center and Crowd, among the issues disclosed on October 20. However, the CVE doesn’t appear in the bulletin, and the portal lists fewer unique CVEs than the bulletin does.
The remaining high-severity flaws affect widely used open source libraries, including Apache Tomcat, Netty, Bouncy Castle, Jackson, Axios, Spring, Apache Struts, and Apache ActiveMQ.
Many of them are denial-of-service (DoS) issues. Others are described as cryptographic weaknesses, authentication and authorization problems, server-side request forgery (SSRF), information disclosure, and code execution bugs.
“CVEs reported in monthly Security Bulletins have been assessed as presenting a non-critical risk to Atlassian customers,” the company says.
Atlassian makes no mention of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in attacks. It recommends updating to the latest product versions or to the fixed releases listed in the bulletin.
Organizations should keep their Atlassian products up to date, as threat actors often quickly exploit vulnerabilities. One example is CVE-2026-21589, a critical flaw in Atlassian’s self-hosted Data Center products that attackers began targeting within hours of a PoC being published.
Related: Atlassian Patches Critical Vulnerability Affecting 8 Products
Related: Critical One-Click Vulnerability in Atlassian’s Rovo AI Exposed Enterprise Data
Related: Atlassian, Splunk Patch Dozens of Critical, High-Severity Vulnerabilities

articles.title: Más de 30 grandes empresas despidieron personal este año mientras redirigen su inversión a la IA
articles.text:
Más de 30 grandes empresas de sectores tan distintos como la banca, el comercio minorista y la tecnología anunciaron despidos este año mientras redirigen inversión hacia la inteligencia artificial, según un relevamiento de la agencia Reuters actualizado el 22 de octubre.
La lista, que la agencia actualiza a medida que surgen nuevos anuncios, incluye recortes que van desde unos pocos cientos de puestos hasta decenas de miles, y abarca compañías de Estados Unidos, Europa, Australia y Brasil.
El banco HSBC encabeza la lista: evalúa un recorte de hasta 20.000 puestos, cerca del 10% de su plantilla, en medio de una reestructuración que la entidad vinculó a la adopción de IA. Amazon confirmó en enero 16.000 despidos corporativos como parte de una reorganización que la empresa atribuyó a la eficiencia y a la inteligencia artificial.
La banca, uno de los sectores más golpeados
Standard Chartered anunció en mayo el recorte de más de 7.000 empleos a lo largo de cuatro años, en un plan de optimización operativa impulsado por IA. Mizuho informó en febrero que eliminará hasta 5.000 puestos en una década como parte de una estrategia de largo plazo.
Barclays se sumó en octubre con el recorte de unos 5.000 empleos, el 5% de su plantilla, con impacto en áreas de soporte. Danske Bank y DNB, dos bancos escandinavos, también anunciaron reducciones de 420 y cerca de 400 puestos, respectivamente, que atribuyeron al mayor uso de automatización.
Los gigantes tecnológicos también recortan
Microsoft despidió en julio a 4.800 empleados, el 2,1% de su plantilla, con impacto en sus áreas comercial y de Xbox. La empresa dijo en un memo interno, citado por Reuters, que la IA cambió la forma en que se ejecutan tareas rutinarias, aunque enmarcó los recortes como un reordenamiento de recursos.
Meta eliminó más de 1.000 puestos en su división Reality Labs en enero, en un giro desde el metaverso hacia los dispositivos de IA, y sumó otros 600 recortes en octubre dentro de su laboratorio de superinteligencia. La compañía además advirtió en marzo que su plantilla podría reducirse hasta un 20%, mientras planea invertir USD 600.000 millones en centros de datos para 2028.
Block, la empresa de pagos que dirige Jack Dorsey, recortó en febrero más de 4.000 puestos, cerca de la mitad de su plantilla, en una reestructuración centrada en IA. Cloudflare, Snap, Pinterest y Autodesk también anunciaron reducciones de entre varios cientos y mil empleos vinculadas a su apuesta por la automatización.
De la industria pesada al software
La química Dow despidió en enero a 4.500 personas, el 13% de su plantilla, como parte de una automatización de sus procesos de punta a punta. La cadena de supermercados Kroger confirmó en octubre recortes corporativos de alrededor de 3.000 puestos, también enmarcados en una reestructuración de eficiencia e IA.
La australiana WiseTech Global, que fabrica software de logística, eliminará 2.000 empleos, casi un tercio de su plantilla global de 7.000 personas, para integrar IA en su software y en sus operaciones internas. La compañía afirmó que algunos proyectos que antes tardaban seis o siete meses ya se completan en un día, según informó Reuters.
British American Tobacco anunció en junio el recorte de 5.500 puestos, con el traslado de otros 3.500 roles a terceros, dentro de un plan de reducción de costos basado en IA que afecta a cerca del 20% de su plantilla. Intuit, HP, SEB, Allianz, Atlassian y Fair Isaac (FICO) completan la lista con reducciones de entre 500 y 3.000 empleos cada una.
La consultora de finanzas personales Intuit recortó en mayo unos 3.000 puestos, el 17% de su plantilla, como parte de una reestructuración operativa con mayor foco en IA. FICO, la firma que calcula puntajes crediticios en Estados Unidos, anunció en octubre el recorte del 15% de su plantilla, unos 570 puestos, para simplificar su estructura con flujos de trabajo de IA.
Meta mantiene uno de los plazos más concretos de la lista: la compañía deberá definir antes de 2028 si cumple con la inversión de USD 600.000 millones en centros de datos que anunció junto con la posible reducción de hasta el 20% de su plantilla.

articles.title: Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
articles.text:
Last week, Starshield — the version of SpaceX’s Starlink used by the Ukrainian military — was throttled to block terminals traveling above certain speeds from accessing the service. The Ukrainian army’s interceptors, which counter Russian drones carrying bombs, suddenly stopped working at high speeds, making it easier for Russia to attack the country’s energy infrastructure and leading to a reported two deaths and at least 17 injuries.
Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
As SpaceX throttles Ukraine’s Starshield, experts warn that Elon Musk’s de facto monopoly over launch and satellite tech poses a major threat to global security.
Elon Musk’s dangerous grip on outer space
As SpaceX throttles Ukraine’s Starshield, experts warn that Elon Musk’s de facto monopoly over launch and satellite tech poses a major threat to global security.
The Ukrainian military reported receiving no advance warning about the Starshield speed restriction. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was a direct message from the US amid rising tensions between himself and President Donald Trump. The abrupt nature of the cutoff and its potentially dangerous military and humanitarian ramifications led to widespread public outcry focused both on Trump for pulling the rug out from under Ukraine and on SpaceX CEO Elon Musk for enabling him.
Since then Musk and Trump have traded denials back and forth. Musk first said that SpaceX has no control over Starshield and decisions are made by the US military, while the White House denied taking action. Then reports emerged that Musk was the one who suggested the slowdown tactic to Trump, who then accepted it, followed by a further report that Musk himself unilaterally ordered the restrictions.
The finger-pointing is of little interest to Ukrainians, who are focused on trying to defend their country from a brutal ongoing Russian invasion. Zelenskyy is well aware that he is being used as a scapegoat as Trump flails around attempting to blame Ukraine for the rising oil prices caused by his unpopular war with Iran.
But Ukraine needs to play nice to some extent, given how dependent it is on US technologies like Starlink/Starshield that enable it to mount a defense against Russian attacks. Starlink access has been deliberately restricted there before, including in 2022, when coverage was not extended to cover a counterattack operation in Crimea. If Musk decided to pull the plug completely, the effect on Ukraine could be devastating.
This amount of geopolitical power being wielded by an unelected tech oligarch is the direct result of consolidating so much of the space industry into just one company, and one man’s hands. And the scope of Musk’s control goes well beyond Ukraine. From the defense of nations to the ability of NASA to launch its astronauts into space, SpaceX has been irreplaceable — and that means Musk has the space industry in his grip.
A de facto monopoly
SpaceX’s recent IPO positions it as one of the most valuable companies in the world. And while the company has generated most of its recent revenue from its Starlink service, it made its name as a company that launches rockets into space.
SpaceX’s Falcon 9 is the most successful rocket in history, and its “rideshare” program, which lets small satellite operators share space on a rocket, has dropped the price of launches to historic lows. This has helped organizations from small startups to university research departments launch their own satellites and has been hailed as a democratizing force in the space industry.
However, that success has come at a cost, which is that SpaceX now holds all the cards when it comes to access to space.
“For all intents and purposes, SpaceX has a monopoly on launch right now,” said Wendy Whitman Cobb of the School of Advanced Air and Space Studies at Maxwell Air Force Base, Alabama. “There are competitors out there,” she said, such as United Launch Alliance, Blue Origin, and Rocket Lab, “but nobody comes even close to SpaceX in terms of frequency, mass, scale, cost. I mean, they’ve got everything in the bag.”
Space economist Oğuz Karasu of the Oxford Space Initiative concurred. SpaceX doesn’t have a monopoly on launch in the legal sense, he said, but in practical terms it does. And that gives the company tremendous pull over the industry as a whole.
“The rocket launch industry is around 8 percent of the entire [space] industry,” Karasu said, “but without that 8 percent, you can’t have the rest of it.”
The gatekeeper for space
SpaceX, which didn’t respond to a request for comment, has a tremendous advantage in providing space-based services like satellite internet. The company has been able to build out its network of over 10,000 Starlink satellites currently in low Earth orbit by launching them cheaply and efficiently using its Falcon 9 rockets.
“This is almost like an antitrust issue,” said defense expert Andrew Reddie of the University of California, Berkeley. “The issue is that SpaceX launches support Starlink constellations that are owned by SpaceX. There is no incentive for a SpaceX launch to be used to provide constellations for other countries that would compete.”
Interestingly, SpaceX has previously launched Amazon Kuiper (now Leo) satellites on a handful of missions — arguably as a preemptive defense against antitrust complaints. Or perhaps SpaceX is simply so confident in its position that it can afford to be magnanimous (or to flex a little on its rival) by launching a few competitor satellites.
The downside of a monopoly, at least for the customer, is that eventually prices rise.
SpaceX doesn’t share prices for its launches publicly, but both Whitman Cobb and Karasu say they’ve heard complaints that Falcon 9 launches are getting more expensive, particularly for low Earth orbit deployments. And the Starlink service has seen considerable increases in price since its beta launch in 2020.
Of course, there are plenty of reasons for a company to increase its prices, from inflation to rising costs, but when a company has enormous market dominance (and now shareholders to please) there isn’t much incentive against raising prices to increase profits.
If this business model sounds familiar, it’s because it’s one of Silicon Valley’s favorite and most destructive tactics. Uber perfected the art of predatory pricing, whereby investor cash is used to artificially lower prices so that a company can corner a market and push out competition. Then, with the monopoly safely in place, the company can jack up its prices and lower the quality of its product or service, secure in the knowledge that customers no longer have any other viable alternatives.
The unseen power of space
This might sound like an obscure problem, something that might make life more difficult for a few high-tech operations but has little relevance to the day-to-day lives of most people. But space infrastructure is now embedded in the mechanisms of our most essential technologies, in the form of satellite communications and GPS data.
“If GPS goes down, you’re not going to be able to get gas at the gas pump, you’re not going to be able to get money out of the ATM,” said Whitman Cobb, “let alone not be able to do financial transactions or get an ambulance to the right place on time.”
It’s not that space experts are realistically worried that Elon Musk is going to lose his mind and cut off Starlink access worldwide, or cause a collision that could take down GPS. It’s that the space industry is woven, unseen, into so many parts of our everyday lives that allowing one company or one person to control access to space hands them enormous power.
“All of our current economic activities are based on space technologies right now,” said Karasu. “Giving this much control, or this much power, to one person is not good for society’s future.”
Even huge agencies like NASA and the Space Force face risks from being too dependent on SpaceX. With the company deciding to retire its workhorse and extremely reliable Falcon 9 rocket, reportedly not taking any new missions from 2028, the Space Force is struggling to find launch options for its military satellites, and NASA now faces a potential future in which it doesn’t have access to the Crew Dragon capsule for carrying its astronauts to and from the International Space Station.
History has shown the dangers of having only one launch option. After the Space Shuttle Columbia disaster in 2003, which cost the lives of seven astronauts, the entire program was canceled and no humans were launched into space from the US from 2011 until 2020.
That’s why NASA is continuing to support beleaguered Boeing in its slow and troubled development of the Starliner capsule, because dependence on a single launch provider means putting all of your very expensive and delicate eggs into one precarious basket. That was demonstrated in February this year, when issues with the usually rock-solid reliability of the Falcon 9 temporarily grounded it, leading to concerns that NASA’s launch of the Crew-12 mission to the space station could be delayed.
This was a timely reminder that even the most impressive and reliable of technologies — and, to be clear, the Falcon 9 is both an incredible feat of engineering and outstandingly successful — can have failures or outages. NASA continues to contract with smaller companies like Rocket Lab and Blue Origin, and has repeatedly stressed its desire to have multiple commercial providers for services like transporting astronauts to the space station.
“Even NASA is realizing, okay, we are putting all our bets on a single player,” said space business expert Michele Scataglini of the Oxford Space Initiative and University of Oxford. “The market needs to have more competition, otherwise it’s not a market.”
Whether any of these companies will be able to catch up and provide a meaningful, affordable alternative to SpaceX remains to be seen. It will be hard for any company to keep pace with SpaceX’s sister companies developing complementary technologies as well.
“The complementarity of the assets that SpaceX has built — artificial intelligence, the batteries, the launch capabilities — these are all self-reinforcing capabilities for the firm, that I would say none of the other players alone possesses,” said Scataglini.
Too much power in too few hands
For now, with Starlink access restored in Ukraine, the country will continue to walk the tightrope of trying to defend itself using technology it does not ultimately control. Unlike previous restrictions of Starlink usage there, which were arguably more about limiting offensive capabilities, “what seems to have been impacted in this most recent episode is Ukrainian defensive capability,” said Reddie, the defense expert. “And then you end up with all the harrowing images of apartment blocks on fire and people getting pulled out of the buildings.
“And so that’s the major security challenge, that you’ve effectively got a non-state actor making decisions as if they’re a government.”
Scataglini concurred, describing the events in Ukraine as a global wake-up call. “There’s a single entrepreneur that has more power than governments in deciding how strategic defense capabilities can be used,” he said.
In times of stress and uncertainty — and between ever-climbing costs of living, a decimated social safety net, fears about AI coming for our jobs, and rising global populism and extremism, there’s plenty to be stressed and uncertain about — it is tempting to turn our gazes inward, to look out for our own interests and prioritize the needs of our own nations.
But space does not respect national boundaries, and what happens in orbit around our planet affects us all. The risk, Scataglini said, is that “we are moving into one firm dominating the launch market and deciding who goes up, and who doesn’t. Which country has access to space, and which one does not, because not all nations around the world, especially if you think about the Global South, will have easy access to these capabilities.”
Looking to the future, experts hoped that out of the brutal events in Ukraine could come more public awareness of the dangers of too much power held in too few hands.
“I’m cautiously optimistic that, at least in this case in particular, it is highlighting the dangers of being reliant on a single company, a single individual,” said Whitman Cobb. “It took something bad happening — people dying — for people to realize, oh, wait, maybe there’s a problem here.”

articles.title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
articles.text:
Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale.
So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%.
Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests, a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule, and Cloudflare handles the rest.
A request for part of a file
An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header:
GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Range: bytes=1048576-2097151
If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range:
HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content
Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000
Content-Length: 1048576
Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it.
The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it.
The range-size problem
Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration.
The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post: each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone.
The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key.
This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming, a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range.
The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology.
Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently.
Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora-based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers.
Fixed-size cache chunks
The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache already thinks in chunks, the range size doesn't need to be a setting at all, it can just be the chunk!
For a range request, Cloudflare checks which requested bytes are already cached. It serves those bytes directly. For missing bytes, it fetches origin ranges aligned to the cache's fixed-sized-chunk boundaries, stores the result in the same chunks used for ordinary cache storage, and returns only the bytes requested by the client.
For example, a request for bytes 150-250 can cause Cloudflare to fetch the aligned chunk containing those bytes. The downstream response still contains only 150-250.
This does not eliminate extra work for requests smaller than our chunk size — such a request can still require fetching the whole chunk containing it. We also are taking on the cost of more work for non-aligned ranges. The difference is that the extra work is bounded and predictable, and no longer determined by a customer-selected range size that can cause unpredictable effects on us and origins.
Coordinating cached and in-flight data
Parsing the Range header is straightforward. The harder problem is producing one correct response when the requested bytes are split across cached data, an origin response, and downloads already in progress.
At a high level, the edge:
- Looks up the asset headers and range-coverage metadata.
- Reads whatever part of the asset it can from disk or streaming in memory.
- Fetches missing coverage from the origin using aligned ranges.
- Writes the new bytes and records the completed range in metadata.
- Combines the pieces and sets Content-Range and Content-Length for the client response.
This is a coordinator, not a single cache lookup. One request can use a cached prefix, an in-flight download, and a newly fetched suffix. The internal origin response can be larger than the downstream response, but the downstream status and headers describe only the requested range.
If an existing download covers another request's bytes, the second request can attach to that download instead of starting another origin fetch. This shares work during bursts for popular large files.
The design uses the existing cache data model. Headers identify the asset version, the body is stored in bounded chunks, and metadata records which ranges were written successfully.
Validate before composing
Composed range responses are valid only when all bytes belong to the same representation. The coordinator checks that each origin response matches the requested range, that the total asset size is stable, and that the entity tag remains consistent across subrequests.
The If-Range header lets a client request a range only if the representation still matches a known validator. If it does not match, Cloudflare returns the full representation instead of combining bytes from different versions.
Cloudflare also avoids composing ranges for a representation it is about to decompress because the range over a set of compressed bytes would be different from those selected by the range in a decompressed response. In these cases, Cloudflare serves the transformed full response rather than advertising a range it cannot honor correctly.
The resulting behavior is standard HTTP:
- A satisfiable range receives 206 Partial Content with an accurate Content-Range.
- An unsatisfiable range receives 416 Range Not Satisfiable.
- A response that cannot safely be ranged is served as the complete representation.
What changed in production
Before opening Origin Range Requests to everyone, we moved existing users of the old range-caching feature onto the new implementation, starting with the workloads that hurt us most.
Those workloads had a lot of concurrent range requests against very large files, often on very spiky traffic. Configured range sizes on the old system ran from tens of kilobytes to tens of gigabytes. With a large range size, a request that wouldn't fill a floppy disk could make us download a few DVDs' worth of data from the origin and move it across several data centers, sometimes after the client had already given up and gone elsewhere. With a small range size, one request turned into a long line of tiny origin requests, each holding memory while it waited. Both patterns caused real operational incidents for us.
R2 was the largest internal user. Its configured range size was 64 MiB, so a small read that crossed a range boundary could cost us 128 MiB of transfer between data centers. After moving R2 to the new implementation, we saw:
- Faster responses. Across R2's storage regions, p99 time to first byte dropped by roughly half on both cache hits and misses.
- Fewer bytes on our network. Our most recent change taught the coordinator to combine bytes already on disk with bytes fetched from upstream in a single response. Before, a request was served either entirely from cache or entirely from upstream. After we turned this on for R2, tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads dropped about 6% week over week, which is petabytes less data moving between our data centers every day.
Getting started
Once the cache no longer depended on a customer-selected range size, the product configuration could not be simpler. Customers select matching traffic through Cache Rules. Cloudflare handles the chunking and cache coordination.
Origin Range Requests is intended for traffic where clients naturally request parts of a large cacheable object:
- Progressive and seekable video such as MP4
- Resumable large downloads
- Software distributions and package repositories
- Disk images, archives, and other multi-gigabyte objects
- AI training and inference workloads that transfer large model files or fetch selected regions of model artifacts
- Clients that fetch metadata or a small region of a larger file
We intend to make this the default way certain file types are served on our network, modifiable by cache rules.
This feature does not change normal cache eligibility. Enabling it does not make an otherwise uncacheable response cacheable. The origin also needs to support byte ranges for partial origin fetches to be useful.
To turn it on, create a Cache Rule that matches your large-file traffic and set Origin Range Requests to On. You can do this in the dashboard under Caching > Cache Rules, or through the API with origin_range_requests: { "mode": "on" }. Customers choose the traffic; the edge handles the cache coordination and correctness requirements.

articles.title: Meta diz ao TSE que canal “Exército do Lula” não viola regras do WhatsApp
articles.text:
A Meta afirmou nesta sexta-feira (23) ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) que não encontrou violações das regras do WhatsApp no canal “Exército do Lula”, criado para divulgar publicações de apoio à candidatura à reeleição do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). A manifestação foi apresentada após o presidente da Corte, ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, solicitar uma análise técnica do funcionamento do canal.
Segundo a empresa, a avaliação concluiu que o canal não desrespeita as políticas da plataforma. A Meta também afirmou que o relatório técnico encaminhado ao tribunal detalha as regras consideradas e a metodologia utilizada para identificar conteúdos que violam suas diretrizes.
O pedido de análise foi feito após uma solicitação da campanha de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), que alegou haver indícios de que as plataformas da Meta não estariam cumprindo o plano de conformidade apresentado à Justiça Eleitoral para garantir a integridade do processo eleitoral.
Canal já havia sido suspenso pelo TSE
- A disputa em torno do “Exército do Lula” envolve decisões distintas dentro do próprio tribunal;
- Em 11 de outubro, Nunes Marques determinou a suspensão do canal após considerar que publicações reproduziam conteúdos anteriormente classificados como inverídicos pela Justiça Eleitoral;
- Posteriormente, o ministro Ricardo Villas Bôas Cueva derrubou a suspensão. Nunes Marques voltou a determinar a interrupção do canal, argumentando que ele teria vínculo com a campanha oficial e deveria, portanto, ser registrado no TSE;
- O funcionamento foi liberado depois que o canal passou a ter registro oficial na Justiça Eleitoral;
- Nesta sexta-feira, o ministro Floriano de Azevedo Marques decidiu que o canal não poderá ser suspenso ou restringido novamente por decisões individuais de integrantes da Corte. Segundo ele, uma eventual nova decisão sobre o tema deverá ser tomada pelo plenário do TSE;
- A medida foi adotada após a campanha de Lula apresentar um mandado de segurança preventivo para impedir nova suspensão.
Leia mais:
- Meta é processada na Austrália por suposto vício de crianças em redes sociais
- Meta: parlamentares dos EUA cobram Zuckerberg por atuação nas eleições do Brasil
- Seu Direito Digital: quem decide o que você consome sobre política nas redes?
Meta afirma não ter encontrado irregularidades
A análise apresentada pela Meta responde ao pedido de investigação sobre o funcionamento do canal, incluindo possíveis ações coordenadas entre contas, padrões de engajamento e atividades publicitárias.
A empresa declarou que não identificou violações de suas políticas na avaliação realizada. A conclusão diz respeito às regras da plataforma e não substitui a análise da Justiça Eleitoral sobre eventuais infrações à legislação brasileira.
O caso ocorre em meio à disputa entre as campanhas de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro sobre a atuação das plataformas digitais durante a eleição presidencial.
A campanha de Flávio questiona o funcionamento do canal de apoio ao presidente, enquanto a campanha petista já havia apresentado questionamentos sobre decisões e procedimentos relacionados à circulação de conteúdo político nas redes sociais.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
articles.text:
CHIPS Act $389M to power chips, vertical GaN, materials; Micron’s memory roadmap; Nvidia expands supply chain capacity; Tenstorrent raises $1.5B; China NAND fabs; 800V power for AI data centers; Intel advances Arizona fab; China orders +$35B in Nvidia GPUs.
The U.S. Commerce Department signed letters of intent for up to $389M in semiconductor R&D funding to four companies working on power devices and critical materials, including vertical GaN and ultra-high-purity quartz technologies. Under the proposed agreements, the government will receive minority, nonvoting equity stakes as a condition of the awards.
Amkor to expand advanced packaging capacity in S. Korea, bringing the companies’ combined Arizona and S. Korea agreements to $3B. The expansion targets more than a fourfold increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028.
UMC and AP Memory announced a technology and manufacturing collaboration to develop silicon-capacitor power-delivery solutions for AI and HPC systems, using UMC’s deep-trench-capacitor technology to move capacitance from the board into the interposer, substrate, or landside of advanced packages.
As advanced packaging scales, a new report examines the challenges of moving from wafer to panel, including warpage, yield, process control, and equipment limitations.
Siemens and Nvidia expanded agentic AI for 3D-IC electrothermal co-design, with Siemens reporting up to 95% less engineering effort and 50× more design alternatives. The companies are also developing a PCB inspection digital twin using virtual boards and synthetic defect data to reduce manual engineering effort by up to 85% and false calls by more than 40%.
Fig.1: Agentic 3D IC engineering workflow aimed at power and thermal challenges. Source: Siemens
AI data center power delivery
Infineon and Nvidia expanded their collaboration on 800 VDC power architectures for AI data centers, focusing on GaN-based intermediate bus converters (IBCs) designed to improve power efficiency and density for high-power AI systems.
Accellera released Functional Safety Language Standard 1.0, providing a common data model for exchanging and reusing functional-safety information across design tools and teams, with an initial focus on standardizing FMEDA data exchange.
China
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix reportedly are upgrading their China NAND fabs to produce more advanced memory, with Samsung targeting 286-layer V9 NAND production in Xi’an and SK hynix moving toward 240-layer or higher NAND in Dalian, despite U.S. restrictions on chipmaking equipment exports, according to Reuters.
ByteDance, Alibaba, and Tencent have reportedly placed more than $35B in orders for Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX PRO 5500 GPUs, according to Reuters.
China’s access to AI computing power could nearly double to 8.8M Nvidia H100 equivalents by the end of 2027, IFP estimates, although tighter chip export controls and restrictions on overseas data-center access could slow growth.
Memory
Micron outlined a memory technology roadmap featuring vertical HBM stacked directly on logic, targeting volume production in 2028. Its 1δ DRAM and 400-plus-layer G11 NAND are slated to ramp in the second half of 2027, with G11 targeting twice the bit density and up to 1.5× the I/O speed of G9.
Samsung reportedly will use TSMC’s 3nm process for the base die in Nvidia’s custom NVHBM, while continuing to manufacture the DRAM dies itself. Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to standardize NVHBM base dies on TSMC’s process to simplify performance validation.
Indium is expanding its Rome, New York, operations to restart U.S. processing of high-purity critical materials used in advanced memory manufacturing, backed by an investment and long-term supply agreement with Micron.
Funding
Tenstorrentraised $1.5B in Series E funding to scale manufacturing and deployment of its Galaxy servers and advance its AI and RISC-V CPU IP.
Notable: Lam Research reported record quarterly revenue of $8.2B, up 54% YoY, with systems revenue rising 62% to $5.7B amid strong AI-driven wafer-fab equipment demand.
Quarterly Revenue: Besi (up 114%), JCET (up 13%), MaxLinear (up 72%), Nordic (up 32%), and TI (up 28%).
By the numbers
Global wafer shipments are forecast to grow almost 12% in 2026, per SEMI.
Server CPU shipments are expected to grow more than 40% in 2027, per TrendForce.
Intel Foundry said construction and tool installation are underway at Fab 62 in Arizona, its sixth high-volume manufacturing fab at the Ocotillo campus. Operations are expected to begin by the end of 2028.
SpaceX and Tesla are aiming to begin volume production in Q3 2028 at their planned Texas Terafab, which is intended to combine advanced logic and memory manufacturing, packaging, and test. An SRAM test chip is targeted for May or June 2027.
UnternehmerTUM Accelerator, Infineon, and others announced plans to launch the Physical AI Growth Lab, a new equity-free development accelerator initiative for European physical AI, robotics, and industrial AI startups.
Cadence launched sovereign cloud infrastructure in Munich for semiconductor, system and advanced-packaging design, allowing European customers to run EDA, simulation, and AI workloads while maintaining data residency within Europe.
Asia
Japan’s NEDO is backing two post-5G projects: NTTInnovation Devices will lead a four-company effort on optical-chiplet mass production, and Preferred Networks and Tenstorrent will develop AI processors using chiplets, photonics-electronics integration, and advanced packaging.
Japan’s METI is seeking ¥400B ($2.5B) in additional government investment for Rapidus as the company works toward 2nm mass production in the second half of fiscal 2027.
TSMC halted some structural-steel construction work at new fab sites across Taiwan following an accident that killed four workers at its Fab 22 project in Kaohsiung, reports CNA. Authorities are investigating the incident.
Synopsys reported new GPU-acceleration benchmarks, including a 12× speedup in 3D power-device breakdown simulation at Infineon and up to a 40× speedup for S-Litho on an imec model of DUV, EUV and High-NA EUV processes.
Infineon added an AI coding assistant to its ModusToolbox development environment.
Rambus is adopting ChipAgents’ agentic AI platform companywide, including across its chip and silicon IP design and verification workflows. The companies also will collaborate on AI-assisted chip design and IP integration, and Rambus became a strategic investor in ChipAgents.
Hyundai Mobis is working on automotive semiconductor system projects alongside 19 other South Korean companies, with 13 chip collaborations already in development.
Research
Northwestern University-led researchers demonstrated current-induced switching in antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions using octupole-driven spin-transfer torque. The nanoscale devices achieved 363% tunnel magnetoresistance at room temperature, pointing to a potential approach for nonvolatile antiferromagnetic memory.
Institute for Basic Science and POSTECH researchers developed 2D transistors through selective conversion of WSe₂ into WTe₂ contacts, WS₂ semiconductor regions, and WOₓ insulating layers. The technique enabled integrated transistors and complementary logic without separately assembling different 2D materials.
UC Berkeley, Samsung Electronics, and Intel researchers introduced a nanoelectromechanically gated gain-cell architecture for embedded DRAM to address limited data retention, parasitic coupling, and the need for boosted write voltages in conventional gain-cell designs. The approach explores an alternative embedded-memory architecture as SRAM scaling slows.
University at Albany and other researchers designed and demonstrated a 15-kV silicon carbide insulated-gate bipolar transistor, becoming the first U.S. academic institution to demonstrate this class of ultra-high-voltage device. A single switch could replace multiple lower-voltage devices in high-power systems, potentially reducing circuit complexity, equipment size, and energy losses.
Security
New offerings
Infineon expanded its PSOC Control family with PSC3M/P6 microcontrollers for multi-motor control and power conversion, featuring post-quantum firmware security capabilities.
Nvidia introduced Confidential Bare Metal, extending confidential computing across Grace Blackwell and Rubin systems.
Alerts of the week
Two critical vulnerabilities were discovered in the widely used open-source programming language PHP. The flaws could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers.
OpenAI disclosed that two internal AI agents weakened misalignment monitoring while performing coding tasks, including suppressing alerts to its security team and removing a monitoring integration.
Siemens confirmed active exploitation of a vulnerability in Siemens Software Center, in which attackers paired a genuine signed copy of the software with malicious DLL files that were loaded at startup. Siemens said its systems, products, and update channels were not breached and issued a fix.
OpenCode reported a breach related to a large-scale distillation attack affecting 1.4% of OpenCode Console users. Third-party OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google API keys stored by affected users may have been exposed.
NIST, NSA, and CISA published 10 voluntary practices for responding to incidents during super-intelligence training and evaluation, including cases where agents take significant uninstructed actions that compromise security controls or human oversight.
DHS ordered federal civilian agencies to stop procuring and remove DeepSeek products, including products from affiliated entities and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.
Institute for AI Policy and Strategy says honeypots could help detect insider threats from AI agents by using decoy credentials, servers and other traps to flag unauthorized actions. Detection has the strongest evidence base, though honeypots only cover paths where defenders deploy them.
Scaling Data Movement For Physical AI: Physical AI poses a host of new challenges for chip engineers. These systems contain a mix of compute elements, which collectively must process a stream of real-time data, analyze it, make decisions, and still function long enough on a battery to be useful. The key here is deciding what data gets processed where, and how to minimize the movement of data.
Quantum Hardware
Quantinuum reported 99.9995% logical memory fidelity per error-correction cycle on its Helios trapped-ion system using a distance-7 color code.
Alice & Bob built and operated three cat-qubit demonstrators — two using 6-qubit chips and one using a 12-qubit chip — demonstrating noise-biased CNOT gates, repeated error-correction cycles, and a non-Clifford gate. Its measured logical error rate has not yet fallen below the error-correction threshold.
UW and PNNL researchers developed a hybrid gallium-phosphide-on-diamond photonic platform for coupling photons to silicon-vacancy qubits. They fabricated more than 600 nanophotonic cavities with a 99.5% yield and demonstrated single-shot electron-spin readout.
DGIST, Tokyo University of Science, RIKEN, et al., demonstrated a protected cat-qutrit manifold using a three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator. The team observed three-photon Rabi oscillations, three-component cat states and an energy gap separating the qutrit manifold from excited states.
McKinsey says scaling fault-tolerant quantum hardware is becoming a manufacturing challenge, requiring major expansion in lasers, cryogenics, control electronics and fabrication capacity. The firm also noted that no single qubit technology has yet emerged as the clear winner.
Workforce, Education
Qualcomm will begin notifying employees in November about global job cuts following its annual performance reviews, reports Reuters, but the company has not disclosed how many positions will be affected.
Micron will introduce quarterly profit-linked bonuses for employees worldwide beginning in fiscal 2027, following an agreement with its Taichung union in Taiwan. The company also plans salary adjustments, increased retirement contributions and additional paid leave for Taiwan employees.
Hoover Institution senior fellow Paola Sapienza argues that tighter U.S. high-skilled immigration policies, including new H-1B restrictions and proposed limits on student visas, could make it harder for the chip industry to recruit specialized engineers and researchers as countries including the UK step up efforts to attract technical talent.
Malaysia said 22,849 people have been trained for the semiconductor sector through the third quarter of 2026, toward its goal of developing 60,000 highly skilled semiconductor engineers by 2030. Training covers IC design, advanced packaging, wafer fabrication, embedded systems and automation, while the government is establishing a semiconductor academy in Penang focused on IC design, fabrication and advanced packaging.
