articles.title: OpenAI réclame encore 30 milliards de dollars, mais les investisseurs commencent à tiquer
articles.text:
Les milliards continuent d’affluer chez OpenAI, sans que la rentabilité soit encore au rendez-vous. Le créateur de ChatGPT préparerait une nouvelle levée de fonds avant son entrée en Bourse, mais aurait dû revoir ses ambitions à la baisse face aux réticences de certains investisseurs.
Chez OpenAI, les levées de fonds se suivent à un rythme presque aussi soutenu que les nouvelles versions de ChatGPT. À peine sept mois après avoir annoncé un financement historique de 122 milliards de dollars, l’entreprise de Sam Altman serait déjà sur le point de réunir 30 milliards supplémentaires. Selon CNBC, le fonds américain Coatue et plusieurs investisseurs des Émirats arabes unis participeraient aux négociations, avec une valorisation envisagée de 1 250 milliards de dollars, avant l’apport de cet argent.
Un montant vertigineux, qui masque pourtant une première difficulté. D’après le Financial Times, OpenAI espérait initialement être valorisé à 1 400 milliards de dollars, mais les investisseurs n’auraient pas tous suivi.
Des milliards levés à un rythme effréné
Les investisseurs accompagnent OpenAI depuis longtemps. Microsoft avait ouvert le bal en 2019, avant de remettre au pot en 2021 puis en 2023. Le financement a ensuite changé de dimension, avec 6,6 milliards de dollars levés en 2024, puis 40 milliards l’année suivante.
En mars dernier, OpenAI annonçait encore 122 milliards de dollars de capitaux engagés, pour une valorisation de 852 milliards. Attention toutefois, ces engagements ne correspondent pas nécessairement à autant d’argent immédiatement disponible.
La nouvelle opération porterait sa valorisation à près de 50 % au-dessus de ce précédent niveau. Mais le fait qu’OpenAI ait dû revoir ses prétentions témoigne d’une certaine prudence chez des investisseurs déjà très sollicités. La perspective d’une introduction en Bourse en 2027 pourrait aussi les inciter à regarder de plus près les comptes de l’entreprise.
ChatGPT rapporte beaucoup d’argent, mais en coûte encore davantage
Le succès commercial d’OpenAI ne fait guère de doute. Selon Reuters, son chiffre d’affaires de septembre, extrapolé sur douze mois, approcherait désormais 50 milliards de dollars. Il s’agit cependant d’un rythme annualisé, pas de recettes effectivement encaissées sur une année entière.
Le problème vient surtout des dépenses. Entraîner les modèles demande des infrastructures informatiques gigantesques alors que leur utilisation quotidienne mobilise elle aussi des milliers de GPU. Plus ChatGPT attire d’utilisateurs, plus OpenAI doit investir pour suivre la demande.
D’après des projections internes révélées par le Financial Times, le groupe pourrait ainsi consommer 278 milliards de dollars de trésorerie d’ici à 2030. Une estimation qui illustre l’ampleur du pari financier, même si ces prévisions restent susceptibles d'évoluer.
Pour les investisseurs, tout repose donc sur la capacité d’OpenAI à transformer sa croissance en bénéfices. Si les marchés jugent sa valorisation excessive lors de son introduction en Bourse, les actionnaires pourraient subir une sévère déconvenue.
Anthropic et Mistral dépensent aussi des milliards
OpenAI est loin d’être le seul laboratoire à brûler autant d’argent pour développer ses modèles. En mai, Anthropic a levé 65 milliards de dollars, portant sa valorisation à 965 milliards. Le créateur de Claude prépare lui aussi son arrivée en Bourse avec des besoins croissants en puissance de calcul.
Google dispose d’une situation plus confortable grâce aux bénéfices d’Alphabet, mais cela ne l’empêche pas de solliciter les marchés. Sa maison mère a notamment levé 49,6 milliards de dollars en juin pour financer ses activités et ses infrastructures.
À une autre échelle, le français Mistral AI a obtenu 3 milliards d’euros en septembre, pour une valorisation supérieure à 21 milliards. L’entreprise mise notamment sur les services aux professionnels et la souveraineté technologique pour poursuivre son développement. Bref, l’IA ressemble plus actuellement à un puits sans fond qu’à une cash machine.

articles.title: Mysteriöse Nachricht in Super Mario 64: Wurde sie nach 30 Jahren endlich entschlüsselt?
articles.text:
Super Mario 64: Fan knackt nach 30 Jahren das Rätsel der geheimnisvollen Plakette
Schon 1996 haben Zocker:innen auf der ganzen Welt in Super Mario 64 auf ein seltsames Detail geschaut. In einem Hinterhof des Schlosses steht die Statue eines Sterns. Darunter ist eine Plakette mit einer Inschrift angebracht. Die Auflösung von 32 x 32 Pixeln hatte es bisher aber unmöglich gemacht, die genauen Wörter zu entziffern. Doch das hat Gamer:innen nicht aufgehalten, Theorien aufzustellen.
Super Mario 64: Theorien zur Plakette
Seit Jahrzehnten hält sich hartnäckig die Theorie, dass die obere Zeile der zweizeiligen Inschrift „L is real 2401“ zeigen würde. Die kryptische Nachricht soll laut einigen Gamer:innen ein versteckter Hinweis der Entwickler:innen sein, dass Luigi (also „L“) sich doch im Spiel befindet. Die Zahl 2401 soll indes ein Hinweis sein, wie er freischaltbar ist.
Im Laufe der Jahre hatte Nintendo diese Theorie aber schon zerstört. Damals hieß es in einem Schreiben an einen Fan, dass die Nachricht bewusst unleserlich ist und niemand genau wüsste, was da überhaupt steht. Doch jetzt will ein Fan endlich Licht ins Dunkel gebracht haben. Unter dem Nicknamen „Supermochi64“ hat er auf GitHub eine ausführliche technische Analyse der mysteriösen Plakette veröffentlicht.
Was sagt die Inschrift wirklich?
Um das herauszufinden, hat der Mario-Fan nicht einfach KI genutzt, um die niedrigaufgelöste Plakette hochzurechnen. Er hat den umgekehrten Ansatz gewählt und eigene Plaketten erstellt, die er dann auf die Größe von 32 × 32 Pixeln geschrumpft hat. So konnte er Font und die geschriebenen Wörter mit dem Original vergleichen und die Phrasen mit der höchsten Wahrscheinlichkeit finden. Das ist möglich, weil die Buchstaben trotz der geschrumpften Größe ein Muster hinterlassen. Die Plakette benutzt insgesamt 32 verschiedene Grautöne.
Am Ende bekam „Supermochi64“ für eine Reihe von Phrasen einen Mismatch-Score. Je niedriger dieser ist, desto besser stimmen die Ergebnisse mit dem Original aus Super Mario 64 überein. Allein für das erste Wort ließ der Mario-Fan mehr als 1,2 Millionen Optionen vom System analysieren. Dabei kristallisierte sich „Eternal“ als klarer Sieger heraus. Andere Wörter dahinter waren lediglich Varianten von „Eternal“ mit Schreibfehlern. Erst auf dem 13.217. Platz landete das nächste fehlerfreie englische Wort „Sternal“.
Denselben Vorgang wiederholte er auch für die anderen Wörter und Phrasen. Am wahrscheinlichsten steht auf der Plakette in Super Mario 64 demnach „Eternal Star / We hope so“. Bei der zweiten Zeile gibt es noch andere Kandidaten mit ähnlichen Resultaten wie „We hope he“ oder „We hope as“. Da sie mit dem Rest aber keinen Satz ergeben, geht „Supermochi64“ davon aus, dass sich lediglich das Schriftbild ähnelt.
Um sein System zu überprüfen, versteckte der Mario-Fan anschließend noch 50 andere Wörter in der Plakette und ließ sie analysieren. Bei 38 von ihnen befand das System aus über 1,2 Millionen Kandidaten das korrekte Wort als bestmögliches Ergebnis. Bei den anderen zwölf Wörtern schnitten Varianten mit Schreibfehlern (wie „Dnration“ bei „Duration“) nur geringfügig besser ab.
Zu guter Letzt prüfte „Supermochi64“ auch noch andere Theorien, die sich im Laufe der Jahre angesammelt hatten. Seine Phrase erreichte einen Gesamt-Mismatch-Score von 1.129 über beide Zeilen. „L is real 2401“ hat einen deutlich höheren Mismatch-Score von 2.031, der auch nur die erste Zeile umfasst. Denn die Theorie hat nie eine Phrase für die zweite Zeile geliefert. Und auch der Satz „A Secret Star / lie here“, der seit Jahren in der Community kursiert, kommt auf einen hohen Mismatch-Score von 4.304.
und was lernen wir daraus ?
Mario Fans haben viel Freizeit?

articles.title: Iran’s Prince of Persia APT Hosts C&C in US for First Time Since 2016
articles.text:
Prince of Persia, a threat group sponsored by the Iranian government, ran one of its command-and-control (C&C) servers from the United States this year, after a months-long lull in its operations, according to Semperis.
The APT actor, also tracked as Infy, has been operating for close to 20 years. Its targets are mostly Iranian dissidents, along with government and private entities in the US, Europe, and the Middle East.
Tomer Bar, AVP of security research at Semperis, tracked the group in his previous role at SafeBreach. He says that within a week of SafeBreach’s February 2026 report, the hackers took a C&C server offline and later relocated the rest of their servers.
Prince of Persia then halted operations for three months, a longer silence than any other in its nearly two-decade history. The pause overlapped with the war between Iran and the US and Israel, which broke out on February 28.
Semperis told SecurityWeek that this is the longest downtime it has confirmed, as its researchers were monitoring the group’s infrastructure the entire time. Earlier quiet periods reflected gaps in researchers’ visibility into the group’s operations rather than confirmed inactivity.
Prince of Persia’s operations restarted on May 27 with the deployment of a new C&C server, and data theft resumed. Within seven days, Tonnerre, one of the group’s malware families, had siphoned over 1,800 files from a single victim.
Bar says the victim count is still small, possibly a sign that the group is either running targeted attacks or struggling to compromise new systems.
In August, Bar identified a new server, likely built on July 7, that supports the second stage of Tornado. Tornado is the group’s latest malware family, and its capabilities include stealing files through a Telegram bot.
The server was located in the US, the first time since 2016 that the group has hosted a C&C server inside the country, Bar says.
“It is not unusual for nation-state–sponsored threat groups to hide C2 servers inside the United States using cloud infrastructure and web hosting providers, but it is unusual behavior for this threat actor,” Bar notes.
For this server, the attackers switched providers. They also abandoned virtual private servers (VPSs) in favor of Namecheap shared hosting, home to thousands of domains, including legitimate sites and some operated by other threat actors.
“This is the last place we expected to find Prince of Persia hiding,” Bar said.
On August 24, the group began setting up another Tornado second-stage server hidden behind Cloudflare. Semperis suspects the hackers had realized that their US-hosted server was exposed.
Semperis has shared IoCs tied to Prince of Persia’s infrastructure. It advises organizations to add them to their security tools and watch for suspicious Telegram traffic.
Related: In Rare Move, Alleged Iranian State Hacker Extradited to US
Related: US, UK, Dutch Agencies Expose Iranian ‘Chosen Brick’ Surveillance Malware

articles.title: Après PHP, une autre brique essentielle du web doit être mise à jour d'urgence
articles.text:
C’est la panique sur Internet depuis ce 21 octobre 2026. La raison : deux failles critiques ont été repérées dans le langage informatique PHP, utilisé par des centaines de millions de sites web à travers le monde. La situation se révèle être un vrai casse-tête pour l’Internet mondial, étant donné qu’il est souvent difficile de repérer le langage PHP, omniprésent, mais souvent invisible. En attendant les correctifs, certains sites ont tout simplement décidé de suspendre leur accès, craignant des cyberattaques. C’est notamment le cas d’Orange qui, après avoir connu une panne majeure, a annoncé la suspension temporaire de certains de ses sites et applications par mesure de sécurité. Et la situation ne semble pas vraiment s’arranger pour l’Internet mondial, étant donné que le projet Node.js vient de publier en urgence une série de correctifs de sécurité.
Node.js corrige 10 failles de sécurité, dont quatre critiques
Node.js est un environnement d’exécution qui permet de faire fonctionner du JavaScript en dehors d’un navigateur web, notamment sur des serveurs. Node.js est bien moins répandu que le langage PHP, mais il occupe tout de même une certaine place dans l’Internet mondial. Selon les données de W3Techs du 9 septembre 2026, Node.js est utilisé comme serveur web par 7 % des sites dont le serveur est identifié. Cette proportion atteint toutefois 22 % parmi les 1 000 sites les plus fréquentés. Les risques de perturbation du web mondial sont donc réels en cas de cyberattaque.
Justement, le projet Node.js vient de publier trois mises à jour de sécurité qui corrigent dix failles, dont quatre sont classées de gravité élevée. L’une de ces quatre failles permet l’exécution de code à distance sur un serveur vulnérable. À l’heure où nous écrivons ces lignes, aucune exploitation de ces failles dans le cadre d’attaques n’a été signalée.
Node.js recommande aux administrateurs de mettre à jour leurs serveurs sans attendre
Les trois correctifs de sécurité publiés par Node.js sont les suivants : Node.js 22.x (version 22.23.4), Node.js 24.x (version 24.22.1) et Node.js 26.x (version 26.12.1). Il faut donc bien s’assurer que la version correspondant à sa branche est installée.
Pour les applications exécutées dans des conteneurs, une simple mise à jour de la machine ne suffit pas. Il est également nécessaire de reconstruire les images utilisées, puis de redémarrer les services concernés. Par ailleurs, les versions de Node.js arrivées en fin de vie, comme Node.js 20, ne bénéficient plus de correctifs de sécurité. Elles restent exposées aux vulnérabilités découvertes.

articles.title: VPN, antivirus, protection de la navigation : NordVPN réunit tout dans une seule application — Frandroid
articles.text:
Une promo trop belle sur une boutique inconnue, un logiciel gratuit récupéré sur un site obscur : même en étant vigilant, difficile de savoir au premier coup d’œil si une page ou un fichier est fiable. Un outil de sécurité peut alors faire ce tri à votre place, sans compliquer la navigation.
NordVPN a lancé fin mai 2026 son antivirus nouvelle génération. Intégré directement à son application, il réunit plusieurs outils capables d’intervenir pendant la navigation, sans avoir à multiplier les logiciels. En ce moment, pour le Black Friday, l’éditeur propose jusqu’à 78 % de réduction et 3 mois offerts sur ses abonnements.
Un antivirus nouvelle génération qui va au-delà des virus
Quand on pense antivirus, on imagine généralement un logiciel chargé de repérer les programmes malveillants qui auraient pu infiltrer votre ordinateur. Les risques ne se limitent cependant pas aux fichiers infectés. Une fausse boutique en ligne ou un site qui imite celui de votre banque peuvent aussi suffire à compromettre vos données personnelles.
L’antivirus nouvelle génération de NordVPN cible justement ces menaces. Il repère les sites soupçonnés de phishing et en bloque l’accès. Vos identifiants et vos coordonnées bancaires restent ainsi à l’abri. Pour détecter ces pages frauduleuses, NordVPN s’appuie sur plusieurs modèles d’apprentissage automatique développés en interne, chacun entraîné sur un type de menace précis.
Cela permet à NordVPN d’intervenir directement pendant la navigation, avant même qu’un fichier malveillant ne soit téléchargé.
Selon NordVPN, son antivirus nouvelle génération a bloqué 4,8 millions de menaces au seul mois d’avril 2026, dont plus de 3 millions de logiciels malveillants.
Une protection qui surveille aussi vos téléchargements
En plus des sites suspects, l’antivirus nouvelle génération de NordVPN surveille les fichiers que vous téléchargez et bloque certains éléments qui gênent la navigation.
Vous récupérez par exemple un logiciel, un document ou une archive sur Internet ? Pendant le téléchargement, NordVPN analyse le fichier à la recherche d’éventuels programmes malveillants. Si une menace est détectée, le service place le fichier en quarantaine avant que vous ne l’ouvriez, ou le supprime directement si vous avez activé l’option dédiée. Vous n’avez donc pas besoin de lancer vous-même une analyse après chaque téléchargement.
NordVPN s’attaque également aux publicités intrusives et aux traqueurs publicitaires utilisés pour suivre votre activité lorsque vous passez d’un site à l’autre. En bloquant une partie de ces éléments, le service contribue à préserver votre vie privée, tout en rendant la consultation des pages web plus agréable.
Autant de protections qui fonctionnent en complément les unes des autres, directement depuis l’application NordVPN.
VPN et antivirus : deux protections réunies dans une seule application
L’intérêt de NordVPN est aussi de réunir plusieurs outils de sécurité au même endroit. D’un côté, le VPN chiffre votre connexion Internet pour protéger les données échangées. De l’autre, l’antivirus nouvelle génération s’occupe des menaces rencontrées pendant la navigation, notamment les sites frauduleux et les fichiers malveillants.
L’antivirus nouvelle génération n’a d’ailleurs pas besoin du VPN pour fonctionner. Il reste actif en permanence, que le VPN soit activé ou coupé.
Plus besoin de jongler entre plusieurs logiciels pour profiter de ces fonctionnalités. Leur disponibilité dépend toutefois de la formule NordVPN choisie et de votre appareil.
L’antivirus nouvelle génération fonctionne sur Windows 10 et 11, ainsi que sur macOS 12 et versions suivantes avec l’application téléchargée sur le site de NordVPN. Sur Android, iOS et dans les extensions de navigateur, NordVPN propose sa protection en temps réel, qui bloque publicités, traqueurs et sites dangereux.
Pour en profiter à moindre coût, NordVPN propose actuellement et pour le Black Friday jusqu’à 78 % de réduction et 3 mois offerts sur ses abonnements. Une bonne occasion de s’équiper à prix réduit, avec en prime une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours.
Elle concerne notamment la formule Premium, qui ajoute ces protections à la connexion VPN. Son prix passe à 4,79 € TTC par mois sur 27 mois, soit 129,28 € TTC au total, contre 5,39 € TTC par mois auparavant.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

articles.title: Los países están considerando prohibir las gafas inteligentes por preocupaciones de privacidad
articles.text:
Varios países están estudiando prohibir las gafas inteligentes por el riesgo de que puedan grabar a otras personas o captar información confidencial sin que se advierta. Su uso ya está prohibido en determinados lugares, mientras que otras restricciones se consideran en diversos países.
Restricciones en espacios públicos y tribunales
Noruega se comprometió el 5 de octubre de 2026 a presentar un proyecto de ley para prohibir de forma temporal las gafas inteligentes en espacios públicos. Entre los lugares sujetos a esta consideración se incluyen los parques, las playas, los museos, los centros comerciales y los eventos deportivos.
El Gobierno también está considerando incluir en la propuesta de normativa a las escuelas y los hospitales. El anuncio no equivale a una prohibición nacional en vigor: en agosto de 2026 se prohibió su uso en las escuelas de Oslo.
En Australia, el Gobierno federal está reuniendo opiniones con respecto a limitar el uso de las gafas con cámara en sus lugares de trabajo. En septiembre, la ministra de la Función Pública, Katy Gallagher, le pidió consejo a la Comisión de la Función Pública sobre una posible prohibición en estos centros y las excepciones. En Inglaterra y Gales se han prohibido las gafas de Meta en los tribunales por las restricciones a hacer fotos y grabar vídeos en esos recintos.
En los cines de Gran Bretaña está empezando a restringirse el empleo de gafas inteligentes con cámara, según una declaración de la UK Cinema Association, la asociación del sector. La entidad declaró el 20 de agosto que las preocupaciones sobre la privacidad y la piratería habían llevado a muchos operadores de cines a prohibir las gafas o, al menos, a limitar el uso de las gafas con cámara. Esta entidad explica que las gafas inteligentes pueden ayudar a personas con necesidades de accesibilidad.
El Sistema Unificado de Tribunales de Nueva York ha prohibido la entrada con gafas inteligentes a sus instalaciones desde el 20 de julio de 2026. Esta prohibición también se aplica a las gafas graduadas capaces de grabar sonido o vídeo. Los visitantes deben entregarlas al personal antes de acceder. El aviso de los tribunales insta a las personas que llevan gafas de corrección visual a traer otras gafas como sustituto.
También existe un encargo de un informe sobre la aceptación social de las gafas inteligentes en la UE y de la petición de la eurodiputada Veronika Cifrová Ostrihoňová para que Europa considere la cuestión.
El software y la responsabilidad de quien graba
Las precauciones contra las grabaciones indeseadas ya han llevado a reforzar los avisos de grabación. En la página de explicación de sus funciones, Meta explica que desactiva la cámara cuando detecta que el LED que indica la grabación está cubierto, desde la segunda generación de gafas, y que ha anunciado mejoras para detectar su manipulación o destrucción. Esta función se aplica a la captura de fotos y vídeos para guardarlos en la galería.
El control de las gafas en Australia también se extiende al software. El 7 de octubre, la Oficina del Comisionado Australiano de Información (OAIC) abrió una investigación formal sobre Shenzhen Qingcheng, fabricante de una aplicación que funciona con modelos económicos.
El nombre de la aplicación es HeyCyan, y las Anko de Kmart son un ejemplo de gafas inteligentes de bajo precio que la usan. La OAIC le había pedido a Qingcheng que explicara cómo podían grabar, quién podía acceder a la información grabada y dónde podría almacenarse, según el regulador. Qingcheng no respondió a esas consultas preliminares. La mera apertura de la investigación no prueba ninguna irregularidad.
El Comité Europeo de Protección de Datos publicó el 13 de octubre de 2026 una declaración sobre las gafas inteligentes. El Comité explica que utilizar las gafas para publicar fotos en una cuenta pública o con fines profesionales puede hacer que uno sea responsable del tratamiento de los datos, de acuerdo con el Reglamento General de Protección de Datos (RGPD).
Puede quedar excluida la aplicación del RGPD si una pareja graba a su cónyuge o un padre a su hijo, siempre que se trate de un uso estrictamente personal o privado. El Comité advirtió al mismo tiempo que pueden aplicarse otras leyes, tanto civiles como penales, o normas laborales. El Comité recordó además que quienes fabriquen o proporcionen el servicio, cuando actúen como responsables del tratamiento, seguirán sujetos a dichas obligaciones y no pueden trasladarlas a sus usuarios.
Se insta a proporcionar avisos que indiquen claramente que se está grabando. Aunque el dispositivo pueda utilizarse en un lugar, difundir públicamente el material grabado o utilizar las gafas para trabajar también puede generar obligaciones de protección de datos.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
articles.text:
We gave the iPhone Duo a 7 /10. But that wasn’t always the score we planned, and it might not be the right score forever. Such are the challenges of reviewing — and assessing — a big, new idea about the most popular smartphone in history.
The iPhone Duo should have been an iPad
On The Vergecast: Notes on an iPhone Duo review, a PHP scandal, Brendan Carr, and more.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay debate whether the Duo deserved the score it got, and try to work through how this device might change over time. Is the outer screen, as Daring Fireball’s John Gruber suggested, the worst iPhone ever? Would it be a better product if it started as an iPad rather than an iPhone? Would we feel differently about this thing if it were simply called the iPad Duo? It’s easy to see how the Duo will improve over time, but will it ever be the phone for everyone?
After that, the hosts talk about the huge PHP cybersecurity flaw that rocked the web this week and what it means for the future of the web, AI, and everything. It was a strange week for the web in general, as the ongoing increase in AI shopping has forced retailers everywhere to figure out how they want to interact with customers — and by customers, we mean Muse agents. Then it’s time for Brendan Carr Is a Dummy, an impending reboot inside of Netflix, and some very confusing Gemini news.

articles.title: A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines.
articles.text:
A few engineers asked IT for Linux. Then it spread to 200 machines.
Linux is already part of the AI developer’s desktop toolkit. Nvidia’s DGX Spark, which became available to order on October 15, 2025, runs the Ubuntu-based DGX OS. OpenAI’s Codex CLI already supports Linux, another example of AI tools meeting developers where they work.
There’s just one problem. Developers can fall in love with Linux at home. Getting enterprise IT to let them use it at work is another matter.
Angelo Huang, founder and CEO of Swif.ai, a platform that manages and secures employee devices, wants to change that. Huang tells The New Stack that giving developers Linux machines starts with giving IT teams the controls to manage and secure them.
Huang says that starting this past week, Swif began expanding its Linux device management and compliance capabilities, adding Omarchy and Linux Mint support to its roster. Swif is also optimizing the onboarding process across supported Mac, Windows, Linux, iOS, and Android environments. They claim that it now takes under 10 minutes to set up device compliance standards such as SOC 2, ISO 27001, and HIPAA.
“Linux already runs much of the infrastructure behind AI,” Huang says. “Increasingly, developers want it on their desks too. The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working for their compliance requirements. That’s the gap we’re closing.”
“The problem isn’t that Linux can’t be secure. It’s that enterprise IT needs to be able to manage it, enforce controls, and prove those controls are working…”
Swif lists support for Linux distributions including Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, openSUSE, Arch Linux, Manjaro, MX Linux, Pop!_OS, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, NixOS, and Universal Blue.
According to Swif’s Omarchy guide, the tested configuration (version 4.0.2) for x86_64 machines supports device enrollment, inventory tracking, application blocking, and selected OpenClaw logging and tool policies. (The guide flags limitations around login, home encryption, remote desktop, and updates.)
Linux Mint’s status is less straightforward, though.
“Linux Mint works today because it’s built on Ubuntu, and we have customers running it,” Huang says, “but it isn’t on our officially supported list yet. Requests for new distributions come in through support tickets and our customer success team. A customer with a real deployment, the number of seats involved, and how far it diverges from a distribution we already support move a distribution up the priority list. For an Ubuntu- or Fedora-based distribution, initial support typically takes one to two weeks.”
Swif’s software-management guide lists Mint for APT-based application installation, although its Linux enrollment list does not name Mint. That documents a specific capability, rather than full validation of every management policy.
Mint also offers a Debian-based edition, LMDE; shared ancestry alone does not establish compatibility across editions and versions.
Making Linux manageable for enterprise IT
Swif’s Linux management capabilities cover familiar IT needs: policy enforcement, LUKS encryption recovery, and automated remediation. Support varies by distribution and policy; the recovery policy manages access to an already encrypted disk rather than encrypting an unencrypted one.
Swif sends Linux device evidence to the governance, risk, and compliance (GRC) platform Vanta hourly.
It also offers a Drata integration with hourly syncing. Still, Swif’s Drata guide is inconsistent on Linux: it lists Linux evidence fields, but its device eligibility list names only macOS and Windows. Linux teams should confirm Drata coverage with Swif before relying on it.
These records support compliance assessments; they do not, by themselves, establish compliance.
The New Stack asks how a developer might, for example, run Wayland on a Framework laptop, and how this leaves IT to determine which management functions work with that setup.
“Our agent runs in user space and relies mainly on systemd, the package manager, and standard kernel interfaces, so hardware like a Framework laptop is rarely the issue,” Huang says. “The display server is where it gets interesting. Wayland support through PipeWire and xdg-desktop-portal is in development. Our rule of thumb: if it affects whether our agent can enforce policy, report inventory, or prove compliance, it’s ours to fix.”
User space does not mean unprivileged: Swif’s Linux management commands can run as root. PipeWire and desktop portals handle functions like screen sharing; this is distinct from basic device inventory or policy enforcement. Swif’s Omarchy guide flags its RustDesk-based remote desktop policy as having experimental Wayland support.
Let the developers have Linux
“The argument inside companies doesn’t need to be Mac versus Windows versus Linux,” says Huang. “If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no. Give developers the tools they want to get the job done. Give security the controls it needs.”
“If your AI team wants Linux, the answer from IT shouldn’t automatically be no.”
Swif focuses on enterprise IT, but developers also have a stake in how IT manages their machines. The New Stack asked if it ran a Linux development community.
“The usual story is that a few engineers ask IT to get off Windows, and it grows to 50, 100, sometimes 200. IT then needs a way to manage those machines that a GRC platform will accept as evidence, and that’s when they come to us. We also hear from developers directly, through shared Slack channels with customers, onboarding calls during rollouts, and support tickets filed by end users. We don’t run a community for Linux developers today, but it’s a good idea.”
AI oversight: Documented features and roadmap
“Right now,” Huang says, “we have MCP server management, agentic security, Claude Compliance integration, and Data loss prevention in beta. On the roadmap is integration with OpenAI’s compliance API and agentic compliance.”
After enrolling a Linux machine, Swif’s MDM agent is installed for device management, while installing the Agentic Security agent provides visibility into supported AI-agent activity.
Its Claude compliance integration collects organization-level audit events, while its documented DLP beta uses a browser extension and requires organization-level beta opt-in.
Its email documentation covers Gmail and Outlook on the web, excluding native desktop mail clients. Those features have a different scope than monitoring local agent activity.
“It’s bringing oversight of AI agents on employee endpoints into the device management layer. The problem is simple. Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.
“Agents run on employee endpoints with access to code, credentials, and customer data, and almost nobody oversees them.”
“When OpenClaw first launched, many customers asked us to block it outright. As more people use agents at work, companies have too much to lose from a data breach or IP theft to leave that unmanaged,” Huang says.
OpenClaw’s own security documentation warns that untrusted content can carry prompt injections. The risk depends on the agent’s permissions, tools, and isolation.

articles.title: El furor por el iPhone Duo llega a las tiendas: horas de espera para adquirir el plegable de 2.300 euros frente a los acampados de Sol
articles.text: Personas aguardan frente a la tienda de Apple de la Puerta del Sol, este viernes 23 de octubre de 2026. La fiebre por el nuevo iPhone Duo ha llegado a la Puerta del Sol. Decenas de personas han hecho cola por el primer modelo plegable de Apple desde la primera hora de la mañana de este viernes, a tan solo unos pocos metros de los manifestantes que el 26 de septiembre decidieron instalar sus tiendas de campaña en el kilómetro cero de Madrid , tras el desahucio de Maricarmen Abascal y en protesta por la crisis de la vivienda. La expectativa ha sido tal que algunos han decidido esperar frente a la tienda casi 24 horas antes. Es el caso de Anthony Bravo, de 31 años, el primero en llegar para adquirir el nuevo móvil. “Estuvimos aguardando desde las diez de la mañana de ayer jueves. Es el primer iPhone de la generación plegable. Es un poco caro, 2.300 euros, pero creo que el precio es justo por la innovación”, aseguraba poco después de haber sido recibido con aplausos por parte de los trabajadores de la marca, 10 minutos antes de la apertura oficial de la tienda, a las ocho de la mañana. articles.title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
articles.text:
Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography.
While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography.
Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later.
For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work.
The evolution of GeoKey Manager
Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security (TLS) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager. This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network.
GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key.
That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel. This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries.
Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping
In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all of them depend on the region where a customer’s private key can be unwrapped, because TLS traffic can only be decrypted where that key is available.
During initialization, the edge key service (the component on each Cloudflare edge server that unwraps customer private keys and uses them to serve requests) verifies that it has loaded every regional root key required by its configuration. If a configured key is missing or malformed, the service does not start. After initialization, an individual request also fails closed (Cloudflare rejects it rather than risk unwrapping a key out of region) if its metadata identifies a regional root key that is not locally available. If a request for Germany was somehow trying to decrypt in Spain or France it would fail, since neither Spain nor France have the regional root key for Germany. This guarantees that a regional root key never leaves its region, no matter what.
Cloudflare needs to maintain high performance while keeping our customers’ regionalized data secure at scale. This is where the next version of GeoKey Manager comes in. We are enabling fast performance while logically separating our network by using post-quantum cryptography to restrict where customers’ private keys are unwrapped. Most of our regions will be available for customers to regionalize their workflow, and there may be product specific caveats. Customers select a region and Cloudflare manages everything else needed to unwrap their private keys within the region’s boundary.
How GeoKey Manager ensures that keys are only available in a region
GeoKey Manager controls where wrapped private keys can be unwrapped and used on the data plane. It does not control where requests are forwarded or routed (that’s Regional Services), where tunnels terminate, or where traffic inspection happens (also Regional Services).
GeoKey Manager separates globally distributed wrapped private keys from the regional root key required to unwrap it. Quicksilver, our global configuration distribution system, distributes wrapped private keys and its metadata across our network. It does not distribute regional root keys; that happens through a separate provisioning service that stores regional root keys and delivers them only to edge servers authorized for each region. Regional root keys follow a separate, controlled path. On the data plane, a node’s regional configuration, which region a node belongs to, determines which nodes can receive which regional root keys.
Defining key hierarchy and application-specific keys
Every wrapped customer private key carries metadata identifying its service context, regional boundary, and epoch.
The service context is the Cloudflare service that uses the key, such as Tunnel or Gateway. The regional boundary is the approved set of Cloudflare data centers where the key may be unwrapped and used, such as data centers in Germany or the European Union. The epoch identifies which generation of the regional root key the key belongs to; each rotation creates a new epoch.
For example, Acme Co. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (acme0001) and another for Gateway in Germany (acme0002). Road Runner Inc. might have one key for Tunnel in Germany (runner0001) and another for Gateway in the European Union (runner0002).
Keys with the same service context, regional boundary, and epoch use the same application-specific key pair. Therefore, compromising the Tunnel-Germany application-specific private key could expose both acme0001 and runner0001, but not the Gateway keys. Compromising the Germany regional root key could affect every application-specific key derived from that root for the same epoch, including acme0001, acme0002, and runner0001.
In the current architecture, the application-specific key pair is asymmetric. The public component wraps the customer's private key material, while the private component is required to unwrap it. The resulting wrapped private key is distributed with its service context (Access, Gateway, Tunnel, Cloudflare One client), region, and epoch.
Provisioning regional root keys
When Cloudflare/Admin configures a region for a CF1 use case, key management service (which also derives application-specific key pairs and wraps customer private keys) creates a regional root key and associates it with a regional boundary and epoch and sends it to provisioning service for storage and distribution which under the hood uses Vault, which is managed by us on-premises.
Authorizing edge servers for a region
Before an edge server can receive a regional root key, provisioning service evaluates three inputs:
- Trusted Platform Module (TPM) proves that the server possesses a registered hardware identity
- Zinc, Cloudflare's server inventory system, maps that identity to a data center and location
- Provisioning service determines which regional root keys the server may access
Zinc updates its membership records for each edge server. This asynchronous process adds new servers as the network grows and removes servers when they are decommissioned. As Cloudflare performs maintenance on data centers in Germany, the definition of which data centers belong in Germany changes in Zinc. That definition is swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver so that our edge is up to date. The reverse also works. As we add capacity to our network, the definition of Germany, or any other region, is updated in Zinc and that is also swiftly propagated through our network with Quicksilver.
Zinc also associates a registered hardware identity with a server and physical location, which supports FIPS 140-3 compliance. TPM-backed identity, server inventory data, and regional configurations determine which region an edge server belongs to and what regional root keys it can access.
Each edge server calls the control plane’s provisioning service, and provides its registered hardware identity. After verifying the server’s hardware identity and regional membership, the provisioning service issues a token that permits the server to retrieve only the regional root keys authorized for its location. Each edge server receives its token and uses it to fetch the regional root keys.
Authorized edge servers load regional root keys into the kernel keyring rather than persisting them on disk. Process level access controls limit which services can use them. Because this memory is volatile, a machine restart removes the keys and the server must authenticate and provision them again. This adds operational complexity in exchange for reducing persistent key material which could be an attack vector for adversaries.
Wrapping private keys for global distribution
When the key-management service receives a customer's private key material with a service context and regional boundary, it will use the request’s regional boundary to get the regional root key and its latest configured epoch. It will then derive the corresponding asymmetric application key pair and use its public component to wrap the private key. The result is a wrapped private key and its metadata.
Quicksilver will then distribute the wrapped private key and metadata across our network. Since the wrapped key requires the specified region to decrypt, global wrapped key distribution does not grant edge servers global access to the private key because unwrapping still requires the corresponding regional root key and service context.
Unwrapping using application-specific keys on the data plane
Why we chose this cryptographic design
Symmetric roots with asymmetric key wrapping
Regional root keys are 256-bit symmetric secrets. GeoKey Manager derives application-specific keys from each regional root key. For the current Cloudflare One path, the control plane’s key management service derives an application-specific Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) key pair.
HPKE with hybrid post-quantum KEM
The Cloudflare One path uses HPKE, as defined in RFC 9180. Its key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) combines ML-KEM-768 with X25519, while HKDF-SHA-256 provides key derivation and AES-256-GCM provides authenticated encryption. Combining post-quantum and classical components preserves confidentiality as long as at least one component remains secure.
Designing for rotation
The validated design supports two types of key rotation: soft rotation and hard rotation.
A soft rotation creates a new epoch for the regional root key while retaining controlled access to a limited number of previous regional root-key epochs — let’s say one previous generation, as an example. The customer’s new private-key material is wrapped using the latest epoch, while older wrapped private keys are still usable during the transition. This is a similar concept to when a credit card company allows you to use a previous version of your credit card for recurring payments from an authorized retailer. In this case, the number of epochs we support determine how many generations of previously wrapped private keys — credit cards — are usable. This allows customers to preserve their service uptime while they transition.
A hard rotation instead rewraps affected customers’ wrapped private keys under a replacement epoch so access to the previous epoch can be removed. In this case, it would be like the credit card company not allowing you to use the previous credit card for a transaction under any circumstances.
Security and availability tradeoffs
Failing closed is a very intentional design choice. Failing open would mean unwrapping a customer’s private key outside its allowed region rather than rejecting the request. We never do that: if any required check fails (service context, region, epoch, etc.), the request is rejected. At startup, each edge’s key service loads every configured regional root key from its Linux kernel keyring. Missing or malformed root keys prevent the edge key service from initializing. Once running, the edge key service uses in-memory copies so that it can’t be tampered with, preventing out of region or cross-region unwrapping. In practice, an edge server serves requests for a region only once its configuration and key provisioning are complete.
The trust boundary (all services that can access the regional root key) includes the key-management service, the provisioning service, and authorized edge key services because each can access regional root keys. The key-management service uses them to derive application-specific keys, the provisioning service stores and distributes them, and edge key services use locally authorized copies of them. Quicksilver remains outside this boundary because it receives only wrapped private keys and associated metadata.
Operating GeoKey Manager
Cloudflare’s network is constantly changing. As servers enter or leave service, Cloudflare’s fleet inventory updates regional membership. This means the list of data centers that make up a region like Spain is not static. GeoKey Manager’s provisioning layer refreshes that membership several times each day, granting or removing access to regional root keys as the network changes. This process is separate from key rotation and requires no customer action.
When regional membership changes, the provisioning service immediately synchronizes the server’s Linux kernel keyring with the latest authorized regional root keys. The edge key service caches these keys in process memory until it restarts or the cache expires. It then reloads the current authorized set from the kernel keyring.
What’s next: Cloudflare One integration and CDN
GeoKey Manager is the basis for an improved Regional Services offering for Cloudflare One; these new capabilities will be announced in a few months.
Older versions of GeoKey Manager already provide geographic controls for private keys associated with CDN certificates. We are developing a separate integration that will bring this new post-quantum GeoKey Manager described here to that existing CDN capability. We will share testing and transition details when that work is ready.
Getting started
If you are a current DLS customer who is regionalizing CDN traffic, you can register intent to test this feature before it’s generally available for CDN traffic here.
Thank you to everyone who made this product a reality. It was a huge effort across the Data Localization Suite, Cloudflare One, and Cloudflare Research teams.

articles.title: OpenAI corta internet de suas IAs mais avançadas após falhas de segurança
articles.text:
A OpenAI passou a treinar seus modelos de inteligência artificial (IA) mais avançados sem acesso à internet aberta após identificar falhas que permitiram a agentes de IA ultrapassar barreiras de segurança e acessar sistemas externos. A medida busca impedir que modelos em desenvolvimento explorem vulnerabilidades durante o treinamento e causem danos fora dos ambientes controlados pela empresa.
Em publicação feita nesta sexta-feira (23), a companhia explicou que reforçou os mecanismos de isolamento de seus ambientes de pesquisa e criou um sistema offline no qual os modelos podem interagir com conteúdos da web previamente indexados e armazenados em cache, sem acessar diretamente servidores externos.
A empresa havia suspendido o treinamento e a avaliação de seus modelos mais avançados em setembro, após um modelo interno explorar uma configuração incorreta e conseguir acesso limitado à internet. Depois de implementar novas proteções, a OpenAI retomou o treinamento por aprendizado por reforço e o uso interno desses modelos em 1º de outubro.
Segundo a companhia, a decisão de manter o treinamento sem acesso à internet aberta continuará em vigor até que avanços nos mecanismos de segurança justifiquem uma flexibilização.
Agentes de IA encontraram formas de contornar barreiras
- Para avaliar a eficácia das proteções, a OpenAI colocou grupos de agentes de seus modelos mais avançados para tentar identificar falhas na própria infraestrutura de pesquisa. Os testes procuraram três tipos de vulnerabilidade: caminhos para acessar a internet, brechas que permitissem atravessar limites de segurança e formas de comunicação entre agentes que deveriam permanecer isolados;
- A campanha identificou vulnerabilidades inéditas em componentes de software de código aberto e configurações incorretas em serviços internos. Algumas falhas permitiam escapar de ambientes isolados, movimentar-se entre sistemas e alcançar a internet;
- A empresa afirmou ter corrigido os problemas encontrados e trabalhado com os responsáveis pelos projetos de código aberto afetados para viabilizar a divulgação e a correção das vulnerabilidades;
- Os testes envolveram um volume de processamento expressivo: a OpenAI afirma ter utilizado centenas de bilhões de tokens durante os experimentos de segurança.
Leia mais:
- IA da OpenAI desativou mecanismos de segurança e negou ter feito isso
- OpenAI amplia presença na nuvem e chega ao Google Cloud
- OpenAI negocia rodada de R$ 162 bilhões com investidores dos Emirados Árabes
IAs conseguiram trocar informações sem conexão de rede
Um dos resultados mais relevantes surgiu quando a empresa tentou descobrir se agentes poderiam trocar informações mesmo sem acesso à internet, sem arquivos compartilhados e sem canais de comunicação autorizados.
Em um experimento, agentes executados em máquinas virtuais separadas conseguiram transmitir informações usando o cache do processador, memória de acesso rápido que armazena dados utilizados recentemente.
O método explorava a diferença de tempo entre acessar informações presentes no cache e recuperá-las da memória principal do computador.
Um agente alterava o estado do cache para codificar uma mensagem. Outro media o tempo necessário para acessar determinados dados e interpretava as diferenças como sinais. Depois de estabelecerem um protocolo de codificação e decodificação, os agentes conseguiram trocar informações sem abrir uma conexão de rede ou modificar um arquivo compartilhado.
A OpenAI também identificou outros possíveis canais de comunicação, incluindo o uso de armazenamento compartilhado, competição por tempo de processamento e um cache de certificados TLS na infraestrutura web offline da empresa.
Segundo a companhia, muitos desses canais transmitem informações lentamente e são difíceis de explorar. Ainda assim, eles representam brechas potenciais em sistemas projetados para impedir que agentes isolados se comuniquem.
A empresa afirma ter acrescentado verificações aos mecanismos de monitoramento para identificar tentativas de comunicação por esses meios.
OpenAI reforça isolamento e monitoramento
A estratégia de segurança da companhia combina diferentes camadas de proteção, incluindo ambientes restritos de execução, máquinas virtuais, monitoramento de atividades e controles de rede e infraestrutura em nuvem.
A ideia é impedir que uma falha isolada permita que um modelo ultrapasse todas as barreiras. Mesmo que um agente consiga escapar de um ambiente restrito, outras proteções devem impedir que ele alcance sistemas externos.
A OpenAI também informou que continuará usando seus modelos mais avançados para procurar vulnerabilidades nos próprios ambientes de pesquisa. Os resultados desses testes passaram a integrar as avaliações de segurança utilizadas para decidir se novas rodadas de treinamento podem prosseguir.
A companhia reconheceu, porém, que modelos futuros poderão encontrar vulnerabilidades ainda desconhecidas. Por isso, pretende manter os testes contínuos e aprimorar os mecanismos de detecção e interrupção automática de atividades consideradas arriscadas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
articles.text:
Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment.
The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications.
The announcements below — coinciding with a visit to Astana by NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang — point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing, along with its growing demand for what comes next.
On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the Alem.AI program.
Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI
In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy.
Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models.
Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said.
He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.”
The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems.
Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture.
Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people.
“If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.”
Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally.
Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity.
For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI.
“I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.”
The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling
The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace.
Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027.
A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships.
Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials.
“What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.”
Kazakhtelecom, the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty.
Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale.
An Honorary Black Belt for Huang
At the end of their meeting President Tokayev presented Huang with the Order of Dostyk, First Class, for his contribution to the development of artificial intelligence in Kazakhstan. Dostyk means friendship and the Order honors peace, friendship and cooperation.
Later that day, also at the Akorda Presidential Palace, the president of the International Judo Association presented Huang with an honorary black belt in Judo. The belt, embroidered in gold stitching, was a special thanks for Huang’s support of Kazakhstan’s AI ambition and for leadership aligned with the spirit and rigor of the martial art.
AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute
And that development is accelerating. The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them.
Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow.
inDrive and Pony.ai are also collaborating to explore robotaxi services in Kazakhstan, with Astana as the first deployment city. The companies will assess the feasibility of bringing Pony.ai’s seventh-generation robotaxis to the inDrive app, supported by NVIDIA AI infrastructure, built on the NVIDIA Hyperion sensor and compute platform with the NVIDIA Halos safety system.
More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute.
Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications.
That was at the core of the discussion the NVIDIA team had with hundreds of developers from across Kazakhstan during a reception later in the evening. The gathering in this self-proclaimed AI nation was inspiring because of the ideas shared, the clear drive to build and a collective ambition to share it with the world.
Today’s announcements represent different layers of the AI stack in Kazakhstan— infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale.
