articles.title: Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking
articles.text:
Microsoft’s new voice AI can start working out what you want before you finish speaking
“I think you said, ‘representative.’” It’s the fastest way to bypass automated speech recognition chatbots that fail to route human callers to the service they need. Achieving a human handoff to a living, breathing representative still feels like a badge of honor.
Microsoft wants to change that dynamic.
Naomi Moneypenny, senior director of product development at Microsoft Foundry Models division, blogged on October 1 to introduce three new Microsoft AI (MAI) models in Microsoft Foundry, Redmond’s app and agent model catalog and platform.
“A voice agent has to do more than hear a request and produce a reply. It has to keep the interaction moving while it listens, reasons, uses tools, and speaks. A delay at either end can turn a conversation into a series of awkward pauses,” writes Moneypenny.
Available now in Microsoft Foundry, the latest voice-centric models include MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming, which turns live speech into text as it is spoken; MAI-Voice-2.1, an expressive multilingual text-to-speech model; and MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash, optimized for responsive, high-volume voice applications.
Partials drive incremental speech recognition
Instead of waiting for a person to finish speaking before returning text, the technology (which has automatic language detection) produces its first hypotheses (known as partials, associated with the field of incremental speech recognition) within the “low hundreds of milliseconds” of receiving audio. The model then refines the partials as more context arrives, before committing to a stable transcript once an utterance ends.
“A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken.”
“That distinction matters when an application needs to act while someone is speaking. A customer-service agent can begin identifying a caller’s request before the sentence is complete. A voice assistant can start reasoning or preparing a tool call sooner. A live transcription experience can surface words almost as quickly as they are spoken,” writes Moneypenny.
MAI-Voice-2.1-Flash is proposed as “a natural fit” for live support agents, voice assistants, and other applications that generate spoken responses. Moneypenny suggests developers can choose MAI-Voice-2.1 when “expressive fidelity” is the priority, or Flash when they need to balance natural speech with responsiveness and cost at scale.
Moneypenny is bullish about the benchmarks thus far. Her post noted that MAI-Transcribe-2-Streaming “debuts at #1 for accuracy” on both partial and final transcripts on the benchmark-based Artificial Analysis leaderboard.
Time for voice to speak up?
All said and done then (pun intended), does this mean that across the spectrum of human-machine input methods, voice is now ready for wider use and adoption? CEO of voice-agent platform company Phonely, Will Bodewes, tells The New Stack he sees these developments positively.
“Voice AI is ready for prime time, if Microsoft’s entry into the market is any indication,” Bodewes says.
Microsoft is hardly new to speech, though: Azure Speech has been on the market for years, and it ships the new MAI models. “For an AI developer, that’s an opportunity to build on that momentum, so expect more players to follow suit. But the model is only the beginning. Voice agents need to learn from every call and measurably improve over time. For companies to see real results, their voice AI must be ready for prime time in theory and in practice.”
“In the early days, a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up.”
From an infrastructure-operations perspective, there’s a clear advancement here. Bodewes, whose company builds its own voice-agent LLM, notes that in the early days (and he means back from the mid 2010s onwards in the initial cloud-based speech API era, such as the Google Cloud Speech-to-Text API, Azure Speech Services, Amazon Transcribe, etc.) a speech request to a hosted model could sit behind a thousand others for 30 seconds, which, on a phone call, is a hang-up.
“We built routing infrastructure just to find the least-loaded endpoints. Owning the model meant owning the queue, and that’s how we got to 120-millisecond responses,” explains Bodewes. “Every sentence you add to a prompt adds another chance of failure. So we enforce the critical steps in code. If an agent needs a name, email, and date of birth before it issues a refund, the codebase guarantees it. Leaving that to the LLM is how you ship incidents.”
The front end (speech) isn’t the hard part
Phonely machine learning researcher Amit Kiran Rege tells The New Stack he agrees the developments are positive, but warns of deeper nuances (speech pun intended, again) in the wider rollout.
“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out, which tells you it’s betting on a cascade effect for contact centers, the same as we did. But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part. The hard part is the silence in the middle where the model is deciding whether a caller is done or taking a breath before the next word,” explains Rege.
What surprised Phonely when scaling this type of service to millions of calls is that speeding up the data pipeline makes the agent interrupt callers more.
“Microsoft shipped the two ends of the voice agent pipeline, speech in and speech out … But in our work, we found the ends aren’t the hard part.”
“Two-thirds of the time our agent decided to jump in too early, and nobody heard it, because the caller resumed before the first syllable and we canceled the reply. Cut your latency in half, and those become audible interruptions. Thus, the lesson is that latency and turn-taking have to improve together,” cautions Rege.
Talking our way into future interfaces
Microsoft’s position on these technologies states that developers can embrace these same models and toolsets to build customer-service agents, multilingual assistants that recognize a spoken language and reply in a consistent voice, what it defines as “interactive learning experiences that move between languages, speakers, and conversational exercises” and live captions and voice-driven interfaces.

articles.title: Preethi Ashwath Went From Chip Lab to Center Stage
articles.text:
Many engineers are more comfortable working behind the scenes developing technology than speaking to consumers about products. But Preethi Ashwath has learned to take center stage, talking about the “hearable” and wearable devices she has had a hand in developing as an analog integrated circuit designer in the consumer electronics division at Analog Devices of Wilmington, Mass.
The IEEE member is one of the few women who work in the specialized field, where about 11 percent are female, according to career platform Zippia.
Preethi Ashwath
Employer
Analog Devices, in Boston
Title
Integrated circuit designer
Member grade
Member
Alma maters
SJB Institute of Technology in Bengaluru, India; University of California, Irvine
Ashwath stepped out from behind the scenes last year to meet with attendees at the Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. She demonstrated Analog’s new earbuds, which track people’s heart and lung health through vibrations in their ear canals.
After she demonstrated her ability to explain the technology to consumers in simple terms, Analog selected her to represent the company at other events. She says she has “come to see speaking as part of contributing to the field, rather than something separate from technical work.”
She also gives technical talks on various aspects of electrostatic discharge (ESD) and other topics, as well as participates in panel discussions, she says, because they “reach engineers well beyond my immediate team.”
Ashwath is an active volunteer with the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society.
“Whether through designing semiconductor products, publishing technical articles, reviewing conference papers, or speaking at industry events, I try to contribute to the growth of the engineering community and the advancement of the field,” she says.
Discovering circuit design at Intel
Ashwath, who grew up in Bengaluru, India, learned about electronics engineering from her high school physics tutor.
That introduction led her to take electronics as one of her core courses in her final years there. At the time, Ashwath’s older sister was pursuing an engineering degree.
“Between my interest in electronics and seeing her already on that path, it became clear to me that engineering was the way to go,” Ashwath says.
After earning a bachelor’s degree in electronics and communications engineering at the SJB Institute of Technology, in Bengaluru, she wanted to pursue a career in very-large-scale integration. But that changed once she moved to the United States and began her master’s program in electrical engineering at the University of California, Irvine.
She discovered her passion for circuits and devices during an internship at Intel in Santa Clara, Calif. She learned about circuit design, package design, and reliability verification tools such as Ansys Totem.
“Seeing every layer of the chip development process gave me a more complete picture of what goes into building a semiconductor product,” she says. “Through that experience, I realized I felt most connected to design.
“It was the hard work and creativity that drew me in. You start with a specification, build a circuit, simulate it, then wait for the chip to come back from fabrication. When your design works, it’s a real feeling of satisfaction. It teaches you patience and perseverance.”
After attaining her master’s degree, she was hired by Intel as an analog design engineer. She gained experience in mixed-signal circuit design before joining Analog. In her current role, she works on consumer hearables such as earbuds and wearables including fitness trackers and health monitors.
Her main focus is designing ESD pad rings, the borders of specialized circuits built around a microchip’s outermost edge to protect it from the discharge, which can damage circuit paths or introduce latent defects that lead to failures later in the chip’s life cycle.
“On a chip with multiple voltage domains, you have to plan how the protection structures are placed and connected across the whole pad ring—and get it right,” Ashwath says. “A mistake there could cause a chip to fail in the field in ways that are very hard to debug afterward.
“It’s detailed work that requires understanding both the device physics and how the whole chip fits together.”
Part of the job is designing and creating an integrated circuit’s building blocks, including ESD protection structures and other mixed-signal blocks. Ashwath conducts rigorous checks to verify they work as intended before being integrated into a chip.
She collaborates with ESD advisors, layout designers, and the digital team that designs the chip’s digital logic.
“I work with them to make sure my analog circuits and their digital blocks work together correctly,” she says. “No two days look exactly the same.”
In 2024 she was recognized with the company’s Impact Award for her “exceptional work on a critical project with significant cross-functional business impact.”
Presenting the final product
Ashwath was selected to represent Analog at events after a senior leader encouraged her to ask for high-visibility opportunities, she says.
“Most of my time is spent on designing circuits and simulations,” she says. “At CES, I stood in front of customers, engineers, and members of the press, explaining our technology and answering questions on the spot.”
The earbuds she demonstrated monitor minute vibrations from a user’s heart and lungs, according to the Analog website. The vibrations can detect arrhythmia, a leaky heart valve, or fluid in the lungs.
“Hearables are evolving from playing back audio to becoming health-monitoring platforms,” she says. “The ear turns out to be a good location for picking up physiological signals, so these devices can capture vital signs while someone is simply wearing them normally.
“The hard part is achieving high signal quality. The signals you’re trying to detect are very small and buried in the noise from the person’s movements and the surrounding environment.
“That’s where analog front-end design becomes critical. Extracting a meaningful signal from a noisy real-world environment is fundamentally an analog problem.”
Being face-to-face with customers at the conference was new to her.
“What struck me most was seeing how people react to the technology,” she says. “When you’re designing a block, you’re focused on specifications and margins. At CES, after explaining what the product does, I had a better understanding of why it matters to them.
“That connection between the circuit work and the final product is something you don’t always see from the design bench.”
Since the CES, Ashwath has presented other technologies she’s worked on. At the annual National Association of Music Merchants show in Anaheim, Calif., she demonstrated the A2B Automotive Audio Bus to the audio industry. The bus uses a low-cost unshielded twisted-pair cable to carry multichannel digital audio, control data, synchronized clock signals, and power in fewer than 50 microseconds, according to Analog.
“IEEE connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”
At the company’s Global Technology Conference—an internal event held in Boston that draws engineers from the company’s more than 50 sites around the world—Ashwath led a demonstration of its solutions for augmented reality smart glasses.
“Each of these events has a different audience,” she says. “Learning to explain my technical work to different people has become a skill I’ve acquired.”
The most rewarding part of her job, she says, is seeing the end result of her work.
“You spend months on a design, and there’s a long wait between finishing it and finding out whether your instincts were right,” she says. “When the measurements match what you simulated, that’s the most satisfying moment in this job.
“The other part is knowing my work ends up in a real product. The circuits I design go into devices people actually use every day.”
Giving back to the community
Like many engineers, Ashwath joined IEEE to access research published in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. It keeps her current in a field that keeps moving, she says.
During her first year of membership, in 2021, she discovered other perks including networking and educational opportunities.
“IEEE connects you to a community outside your own company,” she says. “Attending lectures and technical talks exposes you to approaches and problems you wouldn’t encounter in your own work.”
She eventually began seeking out volunteer opportunities, specifically with IEEE conferences and journals, because they are “how you stay current with what’s happening in circuits and systems beyond your own day-to-day work,” she says.
“As an analog designer,” she says, “being connected to that broader community matters. The field moves, and you need a way to keep learning from it.”
She serves as a peer reviewer of papers for several IEEE conferences including the IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and the IEEE International Midwest Symposium on Circuits and Systems. ISCAS is the flagship conference of the IEEE Circuits and Systems Society. MWSCAS is the oldest U.S. conference on the technologies.
“Someone has to assess whether submitted work is technically sound and worth presenting,” she says, “and that only happens if practicing engineers are willing to put in the time.”
The combination of learning from the community and contributing to it is what makes her membership worthwhile, she says.
“Analog design is a field where you’re always learning. Just when you feel you understand one architecture, there’s another one to learn,” she says. “Being an active learner isn’t optional in this field; it’s the requirement, and being part of the IEEE community helps with that.
“IEEE also connects you with academia, which you don’t get much exposure to once you’re in industry.
“Reviewing papers means reading what researchers are working on, which is often quite different from how the same problems get approached in a product environment. That connection between industry and academic work is valuable in both directions.”

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

articles.title: Paso a paso para invertir en criptomonedas y cuál es su valor este viernes 23 de octubre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 81.652,76 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de 0,419% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de 0,658% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.401,9 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0,06%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 743,82 dólares, con un cambio de -0,27%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 59.419 dólares, tras una variación de -3.311961.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de -2,44% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: Canva lanzó Craft, su primer modelo propio de generación de imágenes con inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
Canva presentó Craft, su primer modelo de inteligencia artificial para generar imágenes entrenado íntegramente por su propio equipo de investigación, con el que la plataforma de diseño busca competir con los sistemas de Google, OpenAI, ByteDance y Meta.
El modelo ya está disponible para todos los usuarios de Canva a nivel mundial desde la pestaña Dream Lab del menú de la aplicación, según informó la empresa en un comunicado publicado en su sala de prensa.
También puede usarse a través de la API pública de Canva, pensada para que desarrolladores integren la herramienta en plataformas de marketing, comercio electrónico o sitios de impresión.
Craft genera imágenes de hasta 2.000 píxeles de resolución en más de 30 proporciones de aspecto distintas. Canva explicó que el sistema funciona en dos etapas: primero interpreta el pedido del usuario y arma un plan de composición que define qué elementos aparecen, su escala, su jerarquía visual y el texto que debe incluirse; después, un segundo modelo traduce ese plan en la imagen final.
Esa arquitectura en dos pasos busca resolver un problema habitual de los generadores de imágenes: el texto ilegible o mal ubicado dentro de la composición. Según la empresa, separar la planificación del renderizado permite un control más preciso sobre cada elemento, de modo que se puede editar una parte de la imagen sin alterar el resto.
Entrenado con plantillas de diseño, no con fotografías
A diferencia de la mayoría de los modelos de imágenes, que aprenden principalmente de fotografías, Craft fue entrenado con millones de plantillas hechas por personas de la biblioteca de Canva: pósters, publicaciones para redes sociales, presentaciones, infografías, menús y piezas con mucho texto.
La empresa sostiene que ese enfoque le da al modelo una comprensión más profunda de los principios de diseño, como la jerarquía visual y el espaciado, en lugar de limitarse a imitar el aspecto de imágenes terminadas.
Canva afirmó que, tras el entrenamiento inicial, ajustó el modelo con aprendizaje por refuerzo y con retroalimentación de sus diseñadores profesionales, que evaluaron más de 25 mil comparaciones entre pares de imágenes frente a modelos de la competencia. Según la empresa, cuando las evaluaciones automáticas y el juicio humano no coincidían, prevaleció el criterio de los diseñadores.
La compañía afirmó que Craft debutó en el cuarto puesto entre los modelos de generación de imágenes más avanzados según DesignArena, una plataforma de evaluación colaborativa del sector, y que eso convierte a su laboratorio de investigación en el segundo más avanzado del mundo en esta categoría. TechCrunch, que citó el mismo ranking, no pudo verificarlo de forma independiente más allá de lo informado por Canva.
Una base de más de 250 millones de usuarios
Canva aseguró que más de 250 millones de personas usan la plataforma y crean más de 400 diseños por segundo, una escala que, según la empresa, exigió optimizar la velocidad del modelo mediante una técnica de destilación que redujo la cantidad de pasos necesarios para generar cada imagen. Ese trabajo sienta las bases de Craft-fast y Craft-ultrafast, dos versiones más económicas que la empresa prometió lanzar próximamente.
TechCrunch recordó que Canva ya contaba con varios modelos de imágenes de terceros integrados en su plataforma, por lo que el nuevo sistema propio también le permitiría a la empresa reducir costos de licenciamiento con otros proveedores de inteligencia artificial. El medio agregó que investigadores de Leonardo.ai, la plataforma de generación de imágenes que Canva compró en 2024, participaron en el desarrollo de Craft.
Las imágenes generadas con Craft pueden convertirse en diseños editables por capas a través de Magic Layers, otra herramienta de Canva que separa los elementos de una imagen para que puedan modificarse por separado. La empresa planea además sumar Craft a Canva MCP, un conector que permitirá a asistentes de inteligencia artificial externos, como ChatGPT y Gemini, generar imágenes listas para usar dentro de un flujo de trabajo más amplio.
Según TechCrunch, Canva proyectaba 4.000 millones de dólares en ingresos el año anterior, aunque recortó su pronóstico de crecimiento para este año. El lanzamiento de Craft se da en ese contexto, mientras la empresa intenta diferenciarse de otras plataformas que también integran generación de imágenes con inteligencia artificial.
La compañía indicó que el acceso a través de Canva MCP estará disponible próximamente, sin precisar una fecha exacta, y que las versiones Craft-fast y Craft-ultrafast se lanzarán en los próximos meses.
